item.description:
**被忽略的事实：我们早就活在"看不懂的黑盒"里**
Tao 把"AI 给出我们理解不了的证明"当作一个未来时态的担忧，但有一个更尖锐、被几乎所有人回避的事实——当代数学家从未亲手验证过他们所引用的绝大多数定理。整个现代数学运行在一张巨大的"社会信任网络"上：每个人都在相信别人相信过的东西。从这个角度看，LLM 的黑盒证明并不是一个新的认识论威胁，它只是把这条本就存在的信任链上的某一个节点，由人换成了机器。真正发生变化的，不是"能不能理解"，而是"能不能追问"——同行可以被追问 *"你为什么走这一步"*，而当前的 AI 回答不了 *"你怎么想到的"*。所以未来数学的分水岭不在证明长度，而在**可被盘问性**（interrogability）。
**教学倒置里藏着一条认知科学的隐藏法则**
Tao 把实分析课"倒着上"——先用实数，再构造实数——这不仅是教学技巧，它触及了一条被哲学家长期忽视的规律：**人类对数学对象的直觉理解，几乎总是先于它的形式定义的发明**。牛顿-莱布尼茨用了微积分 200 年，epsilon-delta 才被写下来。这个结构与儿童语言习得完全同构：先流利说话

item.title: [Business of Sport] How do you Save West Indies Cricket | Carlos Brathwaite
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、这不是板球问题，是价值捕获问题

Carlos反复描述西印度球员如何在IPL、BPL、CPL被买走、被变现，但变现的收益"not for the benefit of West Indies cricket"。这其实是体育版的上游供应商困境——西印度群岛生产"原材料"（球员），下游平台（BCCI、特许联赛、广播商）完成加工并捕获溢价。Shea Hope、Russell、Pollard在这个结构里像可可豆、咖啡豆、油棕——未经加工的作物运往孟买、迪拜、伦敦，加工后以数倍价格卖回。整个发展中世界的贸易困境，被西印度板球以最纯粹的形式演绎了一遍。

更隐秘的时间线是：Chris Dering提到的 1997年巡回赛经济结构变化（客队自费、主队全得），其实是体育界版的"注意力经济协议"——比YouTube出现早10年，比Spotify早11年，西印度板球就已经在体验今天OnlyFans作者、Substack写手、TikTok创作者的集体命运：你是内容本体，但不是价值归属。

二、那根球棒就是整部纪录片的全息投影

注意Errol的球棒故事的叙事结构： - 本地工匠起步 - 帝国中心（英国Newbury）短期培训两周 - 深夜1:30哭着完成作品 - 球棒随球员飞到印度（世界最大板球市场） - 通过全球广播成为"Remember the Name"

这正是西印度板球模式的微缩版——本地根基 + 帝国回响 + 全球不朽。但请停下来注意一个细节：球棒成了传奇，Errol没有。他接到了邻居按喇叭、朋友上门的注目，但没有一个全球可规模化的品牌。这就是整个CWA问题的核心——传奇被不断生产，但传奇的制造者无法规模化变现。打动人心的手工性，正是无法规模化的致命原因。

三、Globetrotters类比可以推得比Carlos更远——而且更可怕

Carlos把西印度板球比作被NBA挤出主流的哈林环球旅行者，这个类比精准得令人屏息。但他没说出的是：今天的环球旅行者，归一家叫Herschend的主题公园公司所有，作为怀旧产品运营。

这就是遗产品牌的致命陷阱：如果西印度板球不作为还活着的竞争者存活下来，终局不是消失，而是比消失更残忍——被某个娱乐集团收购，永远演绎自己的历史，穿着栗红色球衣，在中立场地给思乡的印度裔、斯里兰卡裔侨民表演"曾经的西印度板球"。保住了logo，失去了灵魂。这才是Carlos在节目里真正害怕的东西，虽然他说得很含蓄。

四、跨领域连接：真正该模仿的是HYBE，不是Cricket Australia

西印度板球面对的是15个主权国家 + 约8种货币 + 共享一支国家队——这是欧元区的不对称冲击问题在体育里的化身。巴巴多斯救不了多米尼克，但球队是唯一的泛加勒比资产。经济学家叫这"集体行动难题"。

这时候管理模板不应该从板球内部找。Cricket Australia在管理一个主权国家，CWA在管理一个松散文化邦联。真正可借鉴的模板是： - 诺莱坞 vs. 好莱坞：产量冠军、价值末端——因为缺乏发行基础设施 - K-pop前十年：日本厂牌捕获价值，直到HYBE学会端到端垂直整合（练习生→IP→巡演→周边→粉丝经济） - 牙买加雷鬼音乐：征服世界，牙买加没有拿到录制音乐产值

Carlos模糊地指向了"遗产品牌"方案，但更锋利的说法是：CWA需要抄的不是板球管理模式，而是HYBE模式——放弃比赛日门票为主的旧模式，拥抱从球员培养、品牌IP、内容分发、商品化、海外中立场比赛的闭环控制权。所谓"heritage brand"要活下去，必须变成一个内容公司，而不是一个板球协会。

五、意外观察：Carlos本人就是方案的一部分，但他可能还没意识到为什么

他说自己从评论员跨到董事会，是"愿意把名字和尊严押上"。但真正让他稀缺的不是球员身份，而是一个极罕见的技能组合：打过职业板球 + 做podcast + 写newsletter + 研究私募股权 + 懂足球底层俱乐部的所有权结构。整个加勒比大概不超过5个人同时具备这组技能。CWA面对的信息断层——球员无法跟商业脑袋对话、商业脑袋不懂更衣室——需要的恰恰是翻译器，而不是另一个董事。

如果西印度板球真的在未来10年翻身，回头看，节点不会是找到一个阿拉伯金主，而是球员—管理者—故事讲述者这个新角色类型的出现。Carlos正在无意识地定义这个角色，但他谈这件事时还把它说成"我也想拥有一支低级别足球俱乐部"——他低估了自己在西印度板球语境里的结构性稀缺性。这是整期节目最意外的点：救世主已经在场，但他还把自己当球迷。

📝 转录文本

Cold Open: Four Balls, One Bat

For me it meant a lot more than just the 24 runs. I wasn't even in the initial squad for the World Cup, so those four balls felt monumental and they probably lived long in cricket folklore. One of the more special things about it as well is the bat that I used was actually made from scratch by my best friend, and then in the finals walked out with it from ball one and ten balls later it hit four sixes.

"Carlos Braithwaite, remember the name!" Ian Bishop immortalised the performance with "Remember The Name" — and we were World Cup winners.

I think culturally cricket is probably the biggest connector in the Caribbean. You talk to most cricket fans around the world — who they like to watch, West Indies is already the second team. You're dealing with 15 plus sovereign nations. So every single thing in West Indies cricket is fractured, and the only thing that brings it together is a winning West Indies team.

If you look back to 2014, it was a 70% pay cut. West Indies would have made nothing from that tour. Cricket Australia would have made everything. As a collective, something needs to be done to ensure that West Indies cricket survives. But I like to look at it more as: how do we get West Indies cricket to thrive?

Welcome to the Studio

Host: Carlos, welcome to the Business of Sport, and to have you in the studio as well. This is special.

Carlos: No, special for me. When you reached out, I pinched myself a little bit and was like, is it real? I have been a big fan of the show. We spoke off air about my love of football, and I did try to dabble a little bit in understanding what lower league football ownership may look like. And one day I probably would love to own a team.

It really started from that — just listening to the vast range of guests you've had on, from the top of the top to the ones at the bottom of the pyramid, understanding the journey, understanding the business of what they go through. Obviously you've had some cricketers on as well. So hopefully you can do justice to someone listening, like many of your guests have done for me.

Host: I love that, because I think it's fair to say when we started the show, if you'd had that kind of list of ideal guests, everything on the football ownership side would have been the big clubs. You would have thought, "yeah, I want the Chelsea in or I want the Man U."

Carlos: You probably don't want mine.

Host: Well, it depends on what they come and say. But some of the best conversations that we've had have been with the lower league clubs — because those are the ones that you don't hear about every single day. They're not huge companies at all; you're talking 10 to 20 million turnover businesses. And everything that they do is about serving that fan base. So to hear that that resonated with you is great.

Dark Days in Fandom

Host: To say that you pinched yourself when I reached out makes me feel very embarrassed, because I'm going to get something off my chest early days. I've had some dark days in fandom and sport. I was just writing a few of them out here:

  • Chelsea losing the 2008 Champions League final to Manchester United.
  • England rugby getting hammered in a home World Cup where we didn't make it past the groups.
  • England football losing back-to-back Euros finals recently.
  • Carlos Brathwaite winning the T20 World Cup for West Indies in 2016.

Those are like — lit. That really, that hurt, that one. So it's nice to look you in the eye.

Carlos: I mean, it was incredible.

Host: I've never seen any violence on the little sports — I think I'm safe from across the table.

Carlos: Exactly.

The 24 Runs: A Flow State in India

Host: What an innings. The 24 runs — I made the guys watch it before, in the studio. I said, "This is how you strike a cricket ball." Do you get asked about that more than anything else?

Carlos: Yeah. I'm sure people are probably tired of me telling the story now, but it was just one of them times — as a professional sportsman, you talk about the flow state, and that day was just a day that for me, it meant a lot more than just the 24 runs.

It was 0–4, England. It was in India, the biggest cricket market in the world. A lot of hard work went into it. I wasn't even in the initial squad for the World Cup. I only got drafted in after Pollard missed out through injury. And I look back at all the practice and preparation — from playing first class cricket, to getting the call to go into the pre-season or pre-tournament trip to Dubai, and everything that we did in the lead up to that.

So those four balls felt monumental, and they probably lived long in cricket folklore. But for me, the narratives before that lead up to it.

Errol's Bat: A Friend's Craft

What was most special — or one of the more special things about it as well — is the bat that I used was actually made from scratch by my best friend. I had my own bat company, Trident Sports, back then, and I tasked him with making a cricket bat. Anyone in our village — if something needs doing, he'd be the one to come and do it. Very good with his hands.

I just challenged him: "Can you make a bat?" And he was like, "Never done it, but maybe." The first couple of times he tried it, it was horrendous — I think he'd accept me saying that. But then I flew him to England to work with the guys at Newbury at the time, the Keelys. And they sent him back with the first bat that he properly made under their guidance, and two clefs, and they told him: "Make a bat for Carlos."

He only spent anything like two weeks, two and a half weeks with them. Goes back home at 1:30am at night, woke his wife up shouting, screaming — he's in the garage, and he'd finished this bat for Carlos. I took it, felt okay — I just felt alright. I took it from him.

I got the call, let's say a few days later: "You're going to need to meet up with the team." I was like — actually, I was going to use the bat maybe in the net, maybe not use it at all, but now I may actually have to use the bat. "So can you just shave it down here, shave it down there?"

Took it with me to the World Cup. I remember playing against South Africa, and the bat I was using was a little too light. I think it was Vissa — David Vissot was bowling, and he was bowling a lot of cutters into the wicket, and he was swinging through the line of the ball and missing. He called for the heavier willow, which is the one that Errol made, and I used it, hit a six off Rabada, we went on to win the game against South Africa. And then I kept using it in training in the lead up, and then in the finals walked up with it from the jump — from ball one, and ten balls later it hit four sixes.

Ian Bishop immortalised the performance with "Remember the Name," and we were World Cup winners.

Host: I've recovered now. Now I know there's a story. You've made that work.

Host: What an amazing story behind that. He must have been inundated — do people know that? Were people calling him up going, "Can you make me a bat please"?

Carlos: Yes. There's a photo of my family — people started to honk the horns when they passed my house. People came over to watch the last delivery with my dad, and my dad is my biggest critic. So he was crying, and I video-called him when we were actually celebrating. They kind of saw all these celebrations. They couldn't be in India. My girlfriend, now wife, was there. So everyone got a little piece of it. But yeah, there were like 15 people in my living room back home celebrating the moment. So yeah, it was good.

First Coach, Toughest Critic: My Father

Host: Has your dad always been your toughest critic?

Carlos: Yeah. A hundred percent. First coach. He says that at three years old, he'd get home late. He worked for Banks Beer — the biggest beer in Barbados — but he'd be a driver. So when it's Christmas time, you know the amount of orders that they push off. He'd leave home at like 5am sometimes, get back home at like 11pm, and I'd be up with a bat in hand, and he has to throw balls for me until I get tired and then go to sleep. And he says I could drive a cricket ball at three years old better than I could when I was playing to national cricket.

But yeah, he was the biggest critic. But a top, top man. People would leave their home to come watch cricket with my dad. Sometimes I'd get home from a tour and there'd be my friends lying down on the floor, just chilling, chatting with my dad, and I'm like, "Y'all didn't know I was coming home. Why are you here?" But yeah, my dad is a big draw card.

Cricket as Caribbean Connector

Host: Talk to us about cricket in the Caribbean, the importance of it.

Carlos: Yeah — I think culturally, cricket is probably the biggest connector in the Caribbean. The only thing that would come close, probably, is music. And there are things that individual countries do really well that the Caribbean kind of gets behind them for — so you think the Jamaican athletics, Trinidad and athletics, Bahamas, etc. But when you talk about what, as a Caribbean group of islands, connects you, there are probably two things: the University of the West Indies, and West Indies cricket.

And I think any person that grows up in the Caribbean, you interact with cricket in some way — whether that is playing in the street like I've done many a time, or being forced to play at lunch, being forced to play at physical education, being exposed to it, being played at schools, at your club, in a park somewhere. Yeah, it's definitely a part and parcel of Caribbean culture.

The Pathway: Street to International

Host: And as a kid, what's the route to the top? What's the route to international cricket?

Carlos: The funny thing is, if you go beyond cricket, it's probably the only sport that you can see a route to the top. Maybe athletics — but even in athletics, if you're not in Jamaica, you're probably thinking you have to go overseas for your scholarship. But cricket — you walk outside, it's being played in the street. So that's your initiation; or your dad, your older brother, whatever, going and play.

For me, I can remember my dad taking me to cricket on Saturdays, and every single one at the club would have to throw balls at me. If he's batting around the field, the opposition would be throwing balls at me. You go to school, you play school cricket. If you're good enough, you play under 13, under 15, under 19. There has been off and on under 17s as well.

But I think the biggest challenge for West Indies cricket is what happens after under 19. There are six territories that play first class cricket. Four are actual islands — Barbados, Guyana, Jamaica, Trinidad. The other two territories are Windward and Leeward Islands. So the islands at the top of the Caribbean chain — the Antiguas, Anguillas, St Kitts and Nevis, etc. — they'll be Leewards. And then St Vincent, St Lucia, Grenada, Dominica are Windwards.

So for them, it's an even more fractured path, because now they need to play for their island first. Let's say you're Dominica and you play for Dominica. Then if you do well in the Windwards Tournament, you then move on to be selected for Windward Islands. And then you play against Barbados, Guyana, whoever, to then be selected for the West Indies. So that is your path.

If you can do it under 13, under 15, under 19, straight into first class cricket by 21, it feels quite seamless. I think the challenge is when you get guys 20 to 25 who haven't quite made it yet — it's very difficult for them to then get back into that pathway and to be successful. So that is a challenge systemically that we have to work on and we have to find a way to find a solution for. But the general pathway is schools cricket, underage cricket, first class cricket, international.

Big Challenges Facing West Indies Cricket

Host: I mean, we should probably just talk about big challenges facing West Indies cricket, as we're on it — because you have to have two weeks.

Carlos: Oh yeah, we can do really long-form content here, right?

Host: Let's try. Let's try and bring it back. No no, I want to — we'll be serious about it. Because what you've just described is something that is so intrinsically linked to the region. It's woven into the fabric of culture. It is a huge source of community. And it's under threat right now.

We've had lots of conversations on this show about the dangers that cricket faces. West Indies cricket is in a situation at the moment financially where it seems to be — well, it can't almost self-sustain. It's just had a loan from the ICC. That has meant that they've had to restructure some of their cost bases, which means that domestic competitions are cut, which means pathways are challenged. Cash in the bank is less than two million dollars. It's a real moment of concern.

But it's also one of those ones where it's surely like — we have to be sitting here and going, right, okay, what needs to happen to save this? Because this is too important.

Survive vs. Thrive

Carlos: It's interesting, because when you talk about culture, the first thing we talk about with West Indies is culture. But when you look at international cricket — I don't want to be arrogant by saying this — but I think West Indies not being in international cricket, you miss part and parcel of the fabric of what West Indies bring. You talk to most cricket fans around the world: they love the country, obviously they want their country to win. But if you ask them who they like to watch, or who they'd root for, West Indies is always the second team.

I feel as though, as a collective, something needs to be done to ensure that West Indies cricket survives. That's the first part of it. But I like to look at it more as: how do we get West Indies cricket to thrive? Because we can sit here two years from now and say, "We'll just get another $16 million loan, and we'll keep West Indies cricket flowing. They'd have the odd win here. They'd have the odd win there. There'll be celebrations." But is that West Indies cricket surviving? Or is it actually thriving — and then trying to challenge to be number one Test team, trying to win a World Cup again? That is where I would like to look at it.

Host: My big concern with that loan, and looking into all of this, was exactly that. It's like life support. It's not investment allowing growth. You're having to cut systems that are in place to build growth, the talent. It's the pathways now that are suffering. You're getting money to keep the lights on — but what's the point of keeping the lights on if the sport can't grow and develop?

Carlos: Yeah, and that's where it is challenging — because you think about it, and do you want West Indies cricket to be here? Yes. But do I want it to be here in any iteration where it's just guys playing in my room? No. I want West Indies, as an entity, to thrive — provide that pride that West Indies cricket and fans felt in the 80s and the 90s and the noughties.

I can still remember Brian Lara's 1-5-3 against Australia, winning the game. Courtney Walsh hardly made a run, but he left the lonely ball and then put the bat behind. Those are the sort of things that West Indies cricket bring. We don't only win or lose — but we entertain. But at some point in time, someone has to fund the entertainment.

Pioneers Without Profits

So I think I break it down into what's happened before, and then what we can do moving forward.

When you look in the past — I keep saying West Indies have always been pioneers. We cracked Test cricket. And in talking with Sir Clive Lloyd, actually Australia was a big part of why we cracked Test cricket. He took a lot of learnings from what they were doing well — four fast bowlers, etc.

But then you look at 50-over cricket: pioneers, first three finals, won two of them, lost the third. T20 cricket: first team to two T20 championships. And then even T10 — which is not international format, but you look at Abu Dhabi T10, and the West Indies players were always top of the leaderboards, were always captains or senior players of teams that won.

So it feels like every single time there's a new development in cricket, West Indies are at the forefront. However, we're seldom ever able to monetize it for the good of the organization. So we keep producing talent, talent, talent. That talent gets picked apart, taken away, they get monetised. Your talent is monetised, but not for the benefit of West Indies cricket.

It's probably above my pay grade. I don't know how to stop the rot. But you look in the past and that's definitely what happened. If you think back to Kerry Packer — he found a way to get the most entertaining players to come to Australia, play in pink, and then make money for his television station to bring entertainment to the shores of Australia.

We don't have a market in the Caribbean where we can fly any and everyone in. Because even if you do, they may only go to Barbados — and then the Guyanese feel left out, the Trinis feel left out, the Jamaicans feel left out, or vice versa. And then if you only service four of those, well — there's Anguilla, there's Antigua, there's St Vincent.

So it's a very difficult proposition for whoever is at the head, because you're now not trying to service the interest of one nation. If you're CEO or President of England and Wales Cricket Board, or Cricket Australia, as much as you obviously have different boards to deal with — it's still one country. You're dealing with 15 plus sovereign nations.

So even if we were to get enough money to fly people in to play cricket against us, you still then need to have it in different places, different markets. Those different markets are very small markets. So every single thing in West Indies cricket is fractured. And the only thing that brings it together is a winning West Indies team. You have the winning West Indies team here. You have everything else below it fractured. And if you don't find a way to solidify it, then you can't enhance and fund a winning West Indies team to keep everything below it unified. That's the issue — a vicious circle.

Host: So you can't have the talent if you don't have the leagues and the structures to allow the talent to make it up to the top of international cricket. You look at the 25% pay cuts that have been put into contracts of players now — this cost cutting measure to try and make the business financially sustainable against the loans — the big challenge is, from you know, it's been losing players, and it's West Indies, but also obviously a more broader kind of global cricket challenge of players focusing on T20 franchise type contracts and being freelancers, if we want to call it, rather than centrally contracted cricketers. And if that's a problem for the West Indies, something like this where you reduce the pay that they would get from a central contract — just instead of trying to correct that issue, it will encourage more players, quite rightly in many cases, to do that.

The 1997 Shift and the 70% Pay Cut

Carlos: I look at a 25% pay cut, and I look back to 2014 — it was a 70% pay cut. And that was when you had the debacle in India and whatever went on. I was captain of West Indies A at the time, and we were on tour in Sri Lanka. Conversations were happening: should they just get rid of the team that doesn't want to play because of the pay cut, and bring the A team?

I called a few meetings, and I was just like, well, there's a reason these guys are doing it. I had read the contract — my wife had read the contract — and I was just like, point out anything for me that is untoward. They're not going to change one contract for Carlos Brathwaite. It's a contract for 15 men. But if there's anything that looks a little way that I should know, tell me. And she was like, "Hmm, you sure the pay was this before?" And when I looked at it, it showed the pay of Tests, ODIs, and then first class and List A. And it's an A-team tour, so it'd be first class and List A fees. And I was like, "Hmm — this is going to be a problem."

They said that before they left Barbados, got to Sri Lanka — the team got to India just after we got to Sri Lanka — and apparently that was the first time they saw their contracts. And then it was like, "nah, we're not playing for this."

So you're talking about an era that saw 70% pay cut. I then went on to play Test cricket against a Steve Smith, who was as he is now, all-conquering, and you're thinking: I've got to run in for five days and bowl at this man, and I'm making maybe 25% of what he's making. And then if you look at it and you zoom out: West Indies would have made nothing from that tour. Australia would have made everything.

So you look at the economics of the sport beyond the 25% pay cut in 2026 — the writing was on the wall since 2014. And I listened to CWI CEO Chris Dering talk about 1997, where the whole economics changed — where instead of getting a fee for touring, away teams now basically funded theirself and then got nothing back. So you think the West Indies that were all-conquering back then — you imagine having them for free. Just tell them, "oh yeah, Future Tours Programs say you have to rock up and play, but you get nothing back and you pay your own way" — for a team that has to sustain 15 plus islands, that may be the income that allows you to not only survive but thrive.

Who Hosts, Who Earns

Host: This came up because of the recent tour that West Indies is doing to India at the moment, right? That was where I was properly seeing it and understanding it. And I must admit, you know, just from a business perspective, I couldn't believe it — because it's sport and sport does crazy things, but you know, you think how does that work? I get how it works when you're the big countries who host tournaments and host more series than others, and therefore keeping the money generated from that series through the broadcast rights etc. — for them is a great thing. But if West Indies is touring more than it's hosting, if you're going into these places like India where there's a huge cricket market and they're making let's say 20 to 30 million over a series, as Dering, I think, said in this one, and West Indies aren't getting money for it — how is West Indies ever meant to support itself to generate enough money if you're not getting access to the cash that you're playing a role in generating in the first place?

Carlos: Obviously I'm West Indian, like proud West Indian, I love to talk about West Indies, I love to find a way to get West Indies out of the mire. I couldn't as a player.

Host: Oh yeah, you gave them one hell of a moment though, didn't you?

Carlos: But if you look beyond West Indies, I think when you're talking culturally, Sri Lanka is massive as well. You're talking about Kumar Sangakkara, Mahela Jayawardene — I was thinking back to the '96 World Cup, the blue Sri Lanka with the yellow stripes, Aravinda the silver with the helmet. Sri Lanka has given us so much as well. But then when you look at what they get — South Africa, World Test Championship holders, winners at the moment, and they don't still get a big piece of the pie.

I see a lot of people challenge the economics of the game and blame the BCCI. And I actually salute and celebrate the BCCI, because they have proven that cricket as a game is worthy of private investment. Without that shift, we won't be talking about the economics of cricket. We'll just be talking about a moment here, a moment there — a game, innings, a Test, looking back at 2007, 2005 Ashes, how great a series it was. But actually, they've proven that if you do it the right way — and granted, I love 1.8 billion people in the Caribbean…

I love 1.8 billion people in Barbados, for all it's a Caribbean — and I don't think across the 15 territories you've got 1.8 billion. So they definitely have a lot more to work with than we do, and that's fine. But they have proven that cricket, if run properly, is investable.

I think the challenge for boards like West Indies and South Africa and Sri Lanka is getting a little bit more of the pie initially, to then be able to sustain it — so that if they do run it properly, at least you wouldn't have to penny-pinch here and there. For a country like South Africa, you wouldn't have to choose between a Test team to New Zealand or your SA20. Small decisions like those — I feel the economics of the sport need to change.

And we were inundated with franchise cricket — it came from absolutely nowhere. Like one day it was country pride, the next day West Indians were being called mercenaries, then it's now casual contracts. Like in a decade, everything has turned on its head, and we haven't kept pace with the money that's coming into the sport and finding ways to ensure that the foundations of the sport — which is still the territories — are looked after, and then building upon those for franchise cricket. Everyone is still scrambling to realize what has happened, and then how to maneuver around it.

The IPL Auction

Host: How was it playing in the IPL? You've played for — was it three? I think Delhi, Sunrisers and Kolkata, right?

Carlos: No, it's surreal. I think the first thing about IPL is the auction. There's nothing like it. I can't think of anything else in sport where the way teams are selected is almost as interesting as the actual tournament itself.

Like we love football, and we love the transfer window and deadline day way back when you had the reporters outside —

Host: Jim White.

Carlos: The reporters outside the ground, yeah.

Host: He was hanging around for Peter Odemwingie.

Carlos: That was generational. That is probably the closest thing to the IPL auction. Imagine when it cuts from one report to the next — you're just hanging off the edge of your seat. Who was bought? Who was sold? What news did you get? That's the auction. And that in itself is massive.

I remember it used to be up watching the auction. I was one of the first people that messaged Sunil Narine to tell him he was selected — and he was a big CSK fan. I hope he doesn't mind me saying that. He got bought for KKR, and I messaged him. I think he only saw the message when he woke up. It was a big price as well, wasn't it? I think it was a decent — I can't remember how much he was bought for initially, but yeah, it was a decent amount. And I was happy for him, because we played great together in Trinidad. I played for Queen's Park, and we were good. We shared a house for a season — about four or five of us, like big brother house. We'd play FIFA, beat people, win games, and just be like so good. So we always had that rapport.

And then I remember my auction time. I was up, and I was like, okay cool. My agent messaged me and told me, you know, these teams are interested, I actually do have a good feeling about you getting picked up this time. I was like, yeah, it's fine, I mean, I've never been picked up before, I ain't so open to change now. I'd played Test cricket, so at least people knew — "he went to Australia, he handled himself well, whatever." And then I got the first bid, and I was like, yeah, cool, I could be in the IPL — rub my hands together. And then I realized it was still bidding.

I was like, huh? And I was like, alright cool. And then it kept going up, and going up, and I was just like, wow. So I got out of bed and I watched it. Agent called me — "You're watching, da da da da da." So we were like on the phone together as it was going up. And then I woke my wife up — she was my girlfriend then. We were on a staycation, and I was just like, "I got a bid in the IPL." She said, "Oh cool, congrats." She hates when I wake her up from sleeping. And then I told her the price, and she was like, "Alright, alright, whatever." Back to sleep. And I was like, "I'm serious!" And she was like, "Alright, alright, whatever." So then my agent had to call her, wake her up, and he was like, "Yes, Carlos is just telling you the truth. He's not messing about. He was bought in the IPL by Delhi Daredevils." I can't remember how much it was at the time. And she was like, "I genuinely thought he was messing me about."

So my first IPL — or my first brush with the IPL — was actually convincing my girlfriend that I got bought in the IPL, and for the amount that I got bought for.

Host: But that money, that's super important, right?

Carlos: Yeah, 100%. I think for me at the time it was about the opportunity as well — to get to the IPL, to be able to interact with international players. Because I played CPL, and coming out of CPL I'd been injured and missed the full season just before. And I'm a pessimist at times, but this was probably height of my pessimism. I wrote out a list of all the players in the Caribbean that could potentially be bought before I was in CPL. And then eventually got picked up for Tridents. And I remember being able to talk to Shoaib Malik, to Shakib Al Hasan. Guys that, you know, I played against Shakib in my debut, but I never knew him. Never talked. I thought I'd be in the dressing room with a Shoaib Malik — and then the next year I was playing, I can't remember, it was Antigua. And I remember interacting with a Martin Guptill, someone who I loved from afar, just the way he plays, he tall, he elegant, but powerful. And I'm just like, yeah — like if IPL is this on steroids, I want a piece of that.

Delhi's Young Team

Host: Who was in the Delhi team when you joined them that year?

Carlos: It was a young team. So Rishabh Pant.

Host: Oh.

Carlos: Yeah — and when I saw Pant, I was like, bro, you're 18 at that time, maybe 19, and you're wearing seven seven seven on your back. Like the cojones you must have — like, what are you wearing? Triple seven? Yeah. So having had him sit there — I fully get it wrong, he's lived up to it. But in the moment I was just like, wow bro, good — I mean, he must have got a pair on him to be wearing seven seven seven. But he backed it up, and yeah, he was top. Like, you could see — because straight away he was going to be a legend. So Pant was in that team. Sam Billings, Karun Nair.

That's the beauty of the IPL and franchise cricket. One of my favorite videos is looking back at a video about 2am in the morning: myself, Karun Nair, and Sam Billings playing FIFA. There's the biggest bogey in my nose — Sam Billings is about to score on Karun Nair again, and Karun pauses it and Sam accuses him of being a cheat. And I just got the phone like this, so I'm like, my face is like half of it, but in the background you can see Karun and Sam just having it out. And it just — like this is so good. An Indian, Englishman, and a Barbadian in the same room playing FIFA and just having a blast.

That is them, and that's the magic, right?

Marketable Personas and West Indies Aura

Host: 100%. And for West Indies players, when you have platforms like this — when you have West Indies players, you said in short form cricket they are box office. Whether it's in the past watching your Pollards, or your Russells, and all of that kind — they are the players when they come on that pitch, and the people that they're excited for, right?

Carlos: Yeah. But I mean, even just came back from the Legends League or Masters tournament in Dubai, where we won. And one of the guys there was saying that, you know, this is the first time that he's played with Bravo, he's played with Gayle. Like he's played against them, but actually playing with them — like there's still that aura about them. And it's that aura that West Indians have that make us marketable.

So again, the challenge for Cricket West Indies is: how can you coexist with franchise cricket? How can we, one, continue to create not only marketable personas — because you have to be good at your job. You can't just sing and dance without getting people out or scoring runs. So continue to make quality cricketers who are also marketable, but then try to get some of the finances and monetization from their success, regardless of how far they go.

The Conversation at Home

Host: Taking away outside eyes looking in — what's the conversation like at home? How do people assess it? What ideas come up with, say, right, this is what we need to do? Is there a strategy, or are people in this kind of doom situation?

Carlos: It is a little bit of a doom spiral — but I think not a lot of people know what goes on. So, taking back to 2014, when I came back from that tour, I met someone who I think was picking the laundry at the hotel at the time. They were like, "Man, Carlos, don't be like these men. Don't go and chase money and don't want to play for West Indies." I was like, "Well, do you know why they wanted to strike?" He was like, "They always want more money, they always want money, don't beat nobody."

So I said: "Well, if you had to leave work on Friday, making X a month, you come into work on Monday and your boss slaps a contract on your table, and so you're doing exactly the same work, but now you'd be paid 70% less — what would you do?"

"Brathwaite, I would leave, I would leave."

I said, "Exactly." But for a cricketer, the international team is the West Indies, so you can't leave. Now, what franchise cricket has offered is the route to be able to top up your finances along with playing international cricket. But international cricket is still the gold standard, and everyone still understands that.

So whether it's in the dressing room or around the traps, everyone knows international cricket is a gold standard. And, you know, I tell people that I'd love to salute publicly Shai Hope and Jason Holder. I think they did it the right way. They played Test cricket for as long as they were wanted, let's put it that way. They gave their all for West Indies cricket. And I think Jason Holder is in the part of his career now where he's playing a lot more franchise cricket and a lot less international cricket, and Shai Hope will eventually get there. But a look to what Shai Hope has recently done in India — and there's a content creator in the Caribbean who said, "You know, there are no Trinis in the XI." And everybody under the comments were just saying, "Forget that, scrap that. We don't care who plays. We just want West Indies to do well. The boys are doing well."

I think it was just before the 4th or before the 5th T20, and they were just like: "Put your energy in supporting the team. The team is doing well."

So again, it's that cycle — which can be negative, but it can also be positive. Because the team did so well, everyone underneath them rallied around them. But it's hard to get the team doing well consistently if the stuff underneath it isn't sustainable, isn't solid. You think back to the Gabba — Shamar Joseph with his 7-for. I remember I was in Dubai, and I woke up and looked at the score, and I think 5 were done. They had a little bit of a partnership somewhere, but when I saw the score, I then went and started watching the game, and then no wickets fell for like 5, 6, 7 hours. I was like, nah. And then like turn it off, it fell straight away. And then all of a sudden it was the miracle at the Gabba.

So I think when the team does well, every single person in the West Indies, the diaspora — they come together, they unite, as we call it, they rally. But the challenge is to find a way to get the systems underneath the international team to be so robust that you're able to produce cricketer after cricketer, team after team, year after year — and then you almost make the ecosystem a lot more connected, a lot more united, more often.

Pinnacle: Playing for the West Indies

Host: If you're a kid growing up in the Caribbean, and cricket is your ambition — do you think the pinnacle still is playing for the West Indies?

Carlos: I still think that, yeah. 100%. So a couple of things. In my era, it definitely was only West Indies, because franchise cricket probably came about after you started to play professionally, and you realise there's another opportunity there. Whereas now I think the game will probably go in the next five to 10 years where franchises own players — like the football model — and you get released to play international cricket, eventually get there.

But the other thing is: you don't get big contracts unless you're doing well in international cricket. So there's a guy called Kevon Cooper who, in the times when Bravo was dominating with his slow ball, he was probably the next best at it in the Caribbean. He had a little bit of a dodgy action and he was called a couple of times, but that action meant that his slow ball was undetectable. When Bangladesh Premier League started, he was leading wicket taker for the first three out of four years, and by the end of season four he had the most wickets along with Shakib Al Hasan — but he would always be bought for the same price. Whereas you'd have had players who wouldn't have done what he's done but they were playing international cricket, and they were able to go for the six-figure sums when he would have been 60, 70% of that.

So there is always value on doing well internationally. If you do well internationally, that's when you make your name, that's when people understand who you are. So look at Shai Hope now — he probably needs to have a couple of accountants hired to be able to deal with the amount of cash that he'll get in this coming IPL. But what did that come from? He's had amazing CPLs. I think three CPLs now, he's been top three run scorers, and he didn't get that big IPL deal because of that. He got that big IPL deal because he played for West Indies, dominated for West Indies, and on the international stage, he's put a catalogue together, a set of stats, a set of performances, and a real set of impact for a prolonged period of time — that franchises go, "you know what? Here's somebody that we can invest in. Here's somebody that would add value."

So you can be picked up, don't get me wrong. You can be a bottom feeder of sorts and play a little gig here and a little gig there, play the odd game, sub for most of it. But once you're playing international cricket and performing at international level, you'll always get opportunities.

Advice to Young Players

So I think moving forward — and I interact with a few young guys in Barbados and I tell it straight like it is. I didn't think that this era would like that, but they actually do still come to me for advice.

Host: Lovely. It probably doesn't happen for them very often, does it? Like straight talking.

Carlos: I would call out on the scene — this is BS. This is not on. If you want to be a professional cricketer, you can't do X, you can't do Y. I give them it straight, and they'd come back, they'd hold their hands up.

And I tell a lot of them: you can go and you can make 10 grand playing in a tournament for two weeks, and that's fine. As a young man, I would never be able to tell, and I would never want to tell someone to not take an opportunity to get finances. Because the other challenge in the Caribbean — cricket is a poor man's sport. So a lot of the persons that come into cricket come from very humble beginnings. So when a player gets the opportunity at a young age to be able to get sums of money that they would have never seen before, who am I to say that is not a good opportunity?

What I would say is: the opportunity to get $10,000 now for two weeks — appetizing? Yes. However, if you sacrifice that $10,000 and you score two first class hundreds this season, and you make the West Indies team in two years' time, that same contract could be $100,000. What do you want to do? Do you want the easy way out, which is quick gratification? Or do you want to put in the hard yards, ride the highs and lows of performance, failure, maybe getting dropped when you shouldn't have been — but then to come out on the other side with a body of work that now makes you a hundred grand plus player? Are you happy to get ten grand a tournament?

And when you put it like that, and you're asking the question, all of a sudden you start to see the gears turning. Some will still go off and play franchise cricket, because bills need to be paid, and I appreciate that, and I've done the same. I've sacrificed, and sometimes I've chased the money. But what is the end goal?

I think a lot of players — more players than we think — really love, respect and value West Indies cricket, and they want to play for West Indies. What we need to do, now we've stepped into the administrative side of things, is continue to make that appealing for them, continue to show the importance of it, and then continue to give them loyalty and support whilst they are playing. So that when the next opportunity comes, they can say, "You know what, I'll be paid less for West Indies, or I'll be paid less for Barbados, but the way they've treated me, the way they've supported me, the advice that I've been given, the way they've stuck to their word — I prefer to give them this month and tell franchise cricket to wait."

Host: And when you say you applaud Hope and Holder — is that the way they approached it with that type of mentality?

Carlos: It looked so. Now, I don't know the intention — maybe it was for them to look good, and they did a good job of that. But that was the type of thing they did. They gave West Indies cricket, Barbados cricket, a full go. Not just one game here, not one game there. They committed to series after series after series. They put in top, top performances when their performances were in spite of, not because of, the systems that they had to endure. And now they've shown the world how good players they are. They're two good blokes as well. But they've shown the world how good they are at cricket. And now the cricket world invests in the talent that they've shown at the highest level.

Giving Back: Administration and Mentorship

Host: When you say you're in the administrative side now, what are you doing?

Carlos: So I'm on the BCA as a director on the board. From the administrative side of things, that is one part of it. But I also feel that you should give back to the game. So if a young player messages me to ask me about a particular league or tournament, about a contract, about a decision — I wouldn't charge them a commission or whatever. That's my giving back.

I feel like the more that my era, and the era before, can build rapport with this current era and eras to come — you almost become a sounding board. Something that we didn't have back then, because we didn't understand franchise cricket. I don't think many people still understand it. So being someone who's played a disgusting amount of leagues and for them, a disgusting amount of teams —

Host: You're pretty promiscuous.

Carlos: — how can I help a young man navigating the tricky world of franchise cricket? So yes, from admin standpoint I am part of the BCA board of directors, but I still see my role as more than that — formally and informally just trying to help the next generation.

Host: You guys have had some absolutely amazing athletes, players, people — right, as West Indies cricketers. Do you think players are used enough to help combat some of these challenges, to help overcome some of these challenges? Could more former players be brought into the West Indies cricket setup? Or is it too simple to just say names can help fix some of this?

Carlos: I would say it's too simple. Because before I was on the board, everything looked simple. I just thought: just do this, just do that. And don't get me wrong, we still make mistakes as a BCA board, but there's so many hidden challenges — that when you get around the table and you want to do X, you also have to look at the impact on A, B and C, and the historical context with Y and Z, and "guys, we're just talking about X, but X is never done in isolation."

So as ex-players, one challenge that you'd have to get over is your brushes with the board, with the institution — because a lot of players have been burnt. So a lot of players that have made the name and don't need West Indies cricket — so when I say don't need West Indies cricket, they don't have to go into coaching. They don't have to go into admin. They've made their money. They've made their bed. They're happy to go into business in another realm or maybe just take over doing something else away from the game. Sometimes those are the brightest minds — but because they are so burnt by what's happened to them in their career, maybe why their career ended, they don't want to come back into the same institution.

So for a lot of players, it probably is on the player to make peace with what happened in the past, and then try to be, I guess, a shining light for the future.

And I don't think all past players know it, but I think the best combination is probably a few businessmen, a few bright minds in business, and a few bright minds that have played the game — understand business so they can relate to certain things, but they also have the knowledge of playing the game, being in the heat of battle, understanding what goes on in your dressing room.

Because in my short time of being a director, there's certain things that were put forward and I was like, "I'm telling you from being close enough to players and having played recently — that won't fly."

Hidden Operational Challenges: $80 Million in Airlines

Host: There was one operational thing, a stat I saw — I was like wow, that highlights some of the challenges you face. Maybe this is right, maybe this is wrong, how do you — over 80 million US dollars has been spent by West Indies Cricket with domestic airlines over the last 15 years. 80 million dollars.

Now that is not — probably that's not the fault of West Indies cricket. Well, what that is is a reality of existing in this type of ecosystem where you're moving in between so many different locations. There is an administrative and operational challenge which a lot of people wouldn't even consider. I think about travel and accommodation costs and all of that, but when you actually see it then written down and put in that kind of number — it's a massive challenge to balance this all out against the other business challenges that you will have, more closely linked to the cricket.

Carlos: 100%. And I think it takes something like a million dollars in charter fees to get between islands. So when you see decisions made, like all the white ball series — we played in one island now. So, for example, we hosted Sri Lanka earlier this year, and all the T20s and all the ODIs were played in Jamaica, because logistically it makes sense. If you had to say we'll play two in Jamaica, two T20s, then we'll fly to Antigua and play one T20 and one ODI, then we'll fly to St Kitts and play the last two ODIs — there's three million US in just freight and air travel costs. That's before you pay players, that's before you put on a game of cricket.

There was a number, and I think it's like close to a million dollars again, a day to put on a game. And that is production, that is catering, that is the rates that you'd pay for security, and all that.

Economics of Test vs. White-Ball

So then other decisions that were made — like we're going to play less Test cricket and more 50-over cricket, more T20s. The per-day rate of putting on a game is the same regardless if it's a T20, a 50-over, or one day of Test cricket. So essentially you could sacrifice a Test match and play three ODIs, two T20s, and that would be the same as one day of a one Test match. But if you had to look across those five days of a Test match, and across those five days of white ball cricket — where would you generate more income? You'd probably get more TV rights for the white ball series. You'd get more bums on seats for the white ball series.

So then when you're asking about how can you move the game forward, those are decisions come into play. Do we play Test? And everyone loves Test cricket, I love Test cricket. But economically, can we afford to put on a Test match? Or does it make more sense to put on a three-match ODI, three-match T20, and then host it all in one place?

Where I think we can get better is — I've seen in football how you have like naming rights. There's no naming rights of any stadiums in the Caribbean. There's no regional airline. So you can't — like the Qantas in Australia, they could subsidize the travel and just put Qantas at the front of the shirt. There's no regional airline that touches every single Caribbean destination. And then you can approach them — probably Caribbean Airlines is probably closest. Can you have them on the front of your shirt? But then what, do they give you a better rate than the independent charter?

So all these are economic decisions that aren't now subsidizing the sport. They're actually critical decisions, and impacting whether you play Test cricket or ODI cricket, where you play it. I love to play England in Guyana — rags a little bit — but you have to play England in Barbados, Antigua, St Lucia, Grenada, the tourist destinations, because then all the tourists from England come, they have a blast like you did in Barbados.

Host: Oh yeah.

Carlos: And then we're able to get some money in the coffers. So all the decisions around the cricket are actually not cricket. They're just trying to drive revenue, and that's a scary place to be.

Host: It was one of the best sporting things I've ever been to. Being in the Oval — well, the Kensington Oval — and the atmosphere in that stadium. We were in there for an hour after play stopped — when you said Banks Beer, I was like, okay, that brings back the memories, the rum punches that were in the jerry cans going around there. To see that for Test cricket — that was what was amazing.

Now, on the flip side, I have it burnt into my memory — I think it was against Pakistan recently — like, it was white seats everywhere, and you're just going like — and this is not West Indies alone. I mean, if you look at South Africa, Australia in the first Test a couple of weeks ago — what, last week even — it was very similar.

We sit here arguing for Test match cricket a lot, but I also sit here, and we critique sports for not — you say, "Look, if you don't make money, it's very hard to justify your ability to exist." So there has to be — as you said — if you're not maximizing something commercially, if you've got inventory that's being left on the side, if you're not — let's talk about media, you know — if you're not doing the right media kind of content stuff, if you're not leveraging your talent and your athletes — because people follow talent and athletes now just as much as they follow teams. And what an amazing way, when you have these characters, why are we not trying to take them to a global audience who then buy into these guys, so that they'll see "oh yeah, I want to go and watch that West Indies game, because I've seen them go and do whatever right in a different walk of life."

These are the types of things, and it's easy to say, right, this is the thing. I'm very conscious it's always easy to say packaging it together and making it valuable is good. But I think my point is — when I saw that stadium, it's like cracking. Like if this is going to maintain, you can't rely on attendances and match day income. You've got to make sure that there's something around this.

Carlos: When you look at CPL, I think CPL does it really well. But the challenges that CWI have are quite different to CPL. So CPL is able to have ultra-focused marketing for, let's say, a month to six weeks. And that marketing goes from island to island. But brands and businesses also know this is like peak. They'll get people out, people will see it, it's absolute hype.

But then, if you ask CPL to do what they do for a West Indies-Pakistan Test series — how many Pakistan nationals are in the Caribbean? How many nationals of Pakistani descent? How many people are going to travel from Pakistan? Like there will never be the same amount of eyeballs on a Test match versus Pakistan than it will be against England. Yeah. Or — probably Australia doesn't even come into that realm. I think we only make money when England or India tour. India by virtue of TV rights, and England because of TV rights and traveling fans.

Host: And the Dots, yeah.

Carlos: That is where economics lie. So for two years out of a four year cycle, India will come to town, England will come to town, you'd make money. For the other two years, you have to adhere to the Future Tours Program. So your Pakistans, your Sri Lankans, your Bangladeshis — New Zealand did a white ball tour this year. So they come to town, and then West Indies are truly just hoping that the players do well so that the national pride or regional pride is intact. But commercially, absolutely nothing happens.

Host: And of course, if you get to host an ICC tournament, right, those are other big opportunities. Can you host a T20, one-day World Cup or similar? Because that was — like some of the numbers in there — I mean, if you just looked at the swing, it reminds me a lot of sports habit, you know, where they work in four-year cycles. If you've got like Test series at all, World Cups, et cetera. But you know, it goes from, I think it was $88.4 million in 2024, which was World Cup hosting year — then suddenly that drops to 40.9 million. And the operating result of that is a $23 million profit turns into a $28 million loss. That's the kind of stuff we're talking about here — when you're saying your financial model that you've got to create has to be durable enough to sustain these ups and downs. Because you know your down years are coming. But when they do come, have you done enough in those years where you can make hay?

Carlos: The other thing with that 23 million profit is you don't know how much of that would have been needed to pay off the losses from before. So you may have had debt before that, so some of that 23 million profit is absorbed. And then how much of that can you actually use, because you've got to put down and save for a rainy day for another two years, or to the four year cycle.

Private Investment: A Heritage Brand

Host: Are there any private investment opportunities? We're talking about culture, we're talking about the fabric of Caribbean islands and kids and passion and identity, which cricket is so woven into. Private investment opportunities to support this, to build, to give some capital injections to be able to allow a bit of growth and investment — and that could be long-term loan systems. I'm not saying give money away, I'm saying in any — in a business capacity, are there opportunities to do that?

Carlos: So I love the way you think this way — love the podcast — because I do a newsletter, and one of the things that I looked at a few months ago was: Can private equity save West Indies cricket? And again, the challenge comes back to 15 sovereign territories. You can't say you're giving money to the Netherlands. Who is the Netherlands? The Netherlands actually made up of St. Vincent, St. Lucia, Dominica, Grenada. So you then have to look at them independently and individually.

But I tried to decipher a way where fans can still own some of West Indies cricket. There are no season tickets in cricket. Why not? Why can't a fan pay monthly or annually to ensure that they get first dibs at tickets whenever the tour comes to town? It allows the diaspora to then have season tickets as well. Then you create a whole media machine around it, and you ask your players to do a little bit more — so they get content that Instagram doesn't see, or that Twitter doesn't see, or whatever. So you feed into that, and they pay for it. So that's one angle.

You then have a percentage of the institution to continually be held by the boards — because you can't lose the culture. You can't have West Indies all of a sudden playing in lime green and purple. That is not West Indies. So you need to —

Host: Yeah, there's a limit, right?

Carlos: There is a limit. I'm pleased.

Host: Corporate capitalist mentality right here — I'm not saying we want to play in lime —

Carlos: You want to play in lime green?

Host: Correct.

Carlos: So there needs to be a part of it that goes back to the boards. So for cultural decisions, the boards still control that. But then I would love to open up a portion of it for private investment. And you pump money in, you basically give running capital to the smaller nations — well, all the nations, that's 15. Because I think Chris Dering said it takes like 20 to 25 million a year to run.

The Globetrotters Parallel

Using West Indies as a legacy brand. So this is where I take West Indies out of being a cricket brand and turn it into a legacy institution. So you think, the next newsletter piece is comparing the Globetrotters to West Indies cricket. The Harlem Globetrotters once upon a time, people would pay them to tour. Once the NBA came in, then the NBA had the same amount of entertainment value as the Globetrotters. Now franchise cricket is similar to what the NBA — or similar to West Indies cricket, what the NBA done to the Globetrotters.

Because if you look at it historically, Globetrotters and West Indies cricket were cultural symbols. That's when, you know, Blacks couldn't play in the NBA. That's when, you know, you talk about colonization and the diaspora in England and the Windrush generation were well behind the West. And you think back to the whitewash flag and all that. So these institutions meant more than the sport that they played, and the entertainment that they served. But behind it were businesses.

I don't think Cricket West Indies, and West Indies cricket as an institution, realize that we are a heritage brand. So I personally would be looking to someone who has revamped Ralph Lauren, someone who revamped Harlem Globetrotters. Is there a car company out there that is a legacy brand, fell off for five years to a decade, and then a CEO or a group of people came in and saved it and brought it back to the top?

That is how we need to package West Indies cricket. Not "won two World Cups in 2012 and 2016, won the first two 50-over World Cups in 75 and 79." But actually: this is a legacy brand, a heritage brand. They need investment to be saved — because you first got to survive before you can thrive. You think of Test cricket, you got to learn to draw Test matches before you can learn to win them. How can we get West Indies cricket to a point where it's sustainable first, and then you can push on and make it institution that actually thrives?

So I'd love for private investment and private equity to come in and save West Indies cricket. But a part of it would be ensuring that we still play maroon and not lime green and purple.

Host: This guy — he's got it. That's the best case that I've heard for doing this. When you're going out and having a conversation around this, everyone will go to the cricket, right? They just, they will — because it's the easy, obvious thing. But what you're talking about here is kind of the theme throughout this whole chat: it's more than cricket. If I got the opportunity, and I was interested, and I had these big coffers like some of the funds do — even if I'm a passionate, wealthy individual investor — an opportunity, a properly structured opportunity to invest in a heritage brand like West Indies — if you're calling it a heritage brand, if you're telling me you're going to bring in, you know, a former CEO or leadership team from industry that has done this type of thing — like, I'm in, right? Knowing that everything in this space is a risk anyway. So we're taking a risk regardless. But I would love a piece of that. I would love to be on that journey to try and make that work, rather than just pumping cash into another new IP system or whatever. That's compelling.

Carlos: That's a part of the excitement as well. You'd be so surprised. I do a podcast with Nikhil Uttamchandani called Super Over. And we've interviewed so many West Indies players that were at the CPL, or haven't been released yet but we have them banked. And even being a player and sharing dressing room with some of these players — to hear almost everyone, if not everyone, talk about the love for West Indies cricket, you'd be so surprised. And so many people have said they want to be a part of taking West Indies back to the glory days.

The challenges off the field make it that it disillusions some players, having to get the opportunity to go elsewhere for easier life and more money, because they've done all they could do on international level. Or you know, they got so many gripes with the board and with the institution that they just feel like away is better. Fine, that happens. But at the core, I think so many people want to save West Indies cricket — but not only throw something at it and save it, they want to be a part of it.

If I had to call Shai Hope now, or if I had to be a fly on the wall — you know how seismic an opportunity his performances in India were, because of how bad West Indies have been. It means so much more to him, to West Indies cricket, for him to be taking the team on his shoulder, on his back, and putting in those performances. Because I know he does — because we've had private conversations. You want to be the catalyst that brings that institution back.

Neutral Venues and the Middle East

So if you can find someone with deep enough pockets — and the other thing is, if you do find someone, I mean, the Middle East has proven that it wants to invest in sport. So let's say ex-Middle Eastern sheikh or private investor wants a bit of cricket and they look at West Indies as that heritage brand, they want to pump some money in it. Playing cricket in the West Indies is a challenge. We're in Bangladesh tour, in Sri Lanka tour, we make no money. Why can't we play Sri Lanka in Qatar? Why can't we play against Bangladesh in Saudi Arabia? No reason.

But Saudi Arabia might be able — or Qatar or Kuwait — might be able to fund it to the point where their local television station can have the rights and absorb the costs. They can actually get people from Sri Lanka, from Bangladesh, from India, from Pakistan — who are expats, who are immigrants, who want to come and watch. And you can actually have Test cricket, ODI cricket, T20 cricket being played at a full house, in one of these different places in that neutral — yeah — but actually bringing some revenue.

Host: And you think it could be a full house? You think if you moved it, you wouldn't lose?

Carlos: Well, I don't know those markets. I don't know them that intrinsically. So I can't come and say, if you move it to Kuwait, you'll definitely get 50,000 people. I can't say that without knowing the market itself.

Host: But you think there would be enough potential?

Carlos: There will be interest. Definitely, definitely there'll be interest. As I said, West Indies are the second team of almost everyone in world cricket. And if you can play on that emotion, play on the heritage — and to use the Globetrotter example, have a travelling band of cricketers playing the trade here, there and everywhere. Playing good cricket is obviously most important. But the entertainment value — there's so many good teams that aren't entertaining. And when West Indies are good, they're also entertaining. So imagine taking that now to different markets — whether it be new, whether it be old — and just saying: ensure that we don't lose money, and that we can make money whilst putting out a good entertainment product.

Content Strategy and Storytelling

Host: We talked before we came on about the media opportunity. The biggest danger now for anyone — well, not the biggest danger, but I think what people get bored of now is just another sports documentary series without any real purpose, story, reason, narrative. Everyone wants to be a Drive to Survive type thing, as we were saying. But that doesn't mean that there aren't amazing stories to be told, and if you get them right, they are the most powerful tools that sporting organizations can use to build some of that interest.

Like, to me, West Indies fits in that. There is an amazing story to tell here. If you've ever watched Welcome to Wrexham type thing, one of the reasons that's been successful in my eyes at least, and one of the reasons I loved it, is because it was only partly about football. So immediately it kind of stood out as something different. And from the West Indies story perspective — whether you play, you could play partly on the history and the heritage. You can go around and look at what it means to each of the islands and how it varies in those places, where the money flows go at the moment and where the challenges lie.

You can do a job of almost using a piece of content like this as a bit of a pitch deck. If I got an opportunity to look inside West Indies cricket with a major distributor — whether it's a Netflix or a Disney Plus or an Amazon or whatever — I would, as a fan, be absolutely fascinated. Because I think there's a story in there. I think it has everything. I think it has the people. I think it has the broader value, like a cultural angle. And I think it has the sport.

Fire in Babylon and Beyond

Carlos: And to add on to that, I think it was in my year in High Performance Centre when Fire in Babylon came out. And that was well before Drive to Survive. But it just gave you context. It just showed you why these teams were all conquering. It showed you the magnitude of what they played for before they even went on the field. They had interviews in there either from fans or from players talking about how people from the Caribbean diaspora living in the UK would walk into work with the chest up because West Indies have won. So it meant more than just winning a game.

And even though I talk about it, it got goosebumps. I remember watching that documentary and just feeling immense pride to be a West Indian, to watch the forefathers lay the ground that I walk on.

And I think past Fire in Babylon, you've had the era with Brian Lara, Carl Hooper, Courtney Walsh, Curtly Ambrose — those stories haven't really been told. And then you can lead into the 2012, the 2016 World Cup wins. There was Courtney Browne and Ian Bradshaw 2004 here in the UK Champions Trophy. Those sorts of things, if we can produce them often enough, consistently enough, it then raises the pores of a younger player who's at academy level or primary school level, and it just continues the pride.

So we've got a situation where we're begging for people to appreciate the history of West Indies cricket, but we're not telling them the stories of why we are proud of West Indies cricket.

Host: And if you're going to build a heritage brand value around this, telling the stories of why it matters in the first place is everything, right? Combining a modern-day content strategy with a look at the establishment of the value — well, it seems like it would be really cool.

Carlos: Yeah. We had Clive Lloyd on the podcast, and I think Nikhil and I, we sat back and we just like — did we ask enough questions? Like it was two of us here and there — Clive Lloyd was there, and we were just like, you know —

Host: I had those moments. Petr Čech sat there, and I just — I said, I just grinned at him for like an hour and 45 minutes.

Carlos: You know, you got granddad sitting by the fireplace, and everybody just there sat just listening to these stories. But then yeah, like we are privileged to be able to sit — have him sit across from us and tell it. If you watch the episode, you're privileged enough to hear it. But you don't get to go into the mind any further.

Because yeah, they did what they did on the field — that's one. The second thing is, what was the reason for it — two. But then, how did you every single day wake up and push toward this passion with this purpose and why? So if you can encapsulate all of that into a series — be powerful.

Host: Yeah. Okay — that's our challenge. Any producers out there? I know there are. I know there are a few. Come on. And there's more than enough drama, I can imagine.

From Critic to Participant

But you know, I think, as you said, if you're looking at — rather than always just being the people that sit here and go "oh isn't this bad" — eventually to change fortunes, you have to be the one that, you have to try and be a part of a solution.

Carlos: Yeah. And I think for me, that is why I did put my name in to try to be a director of the board. Because it's so easy — like I've stepped into commentary, I absolutely enjoy it, but we do have a privilege where we just sit, we watch the game. And I don't want to devalue the preparation we do before — but we sit, we watch the game, we call it as we see it. And then there are certain things that we are made aware of, and we can just say "this is wrong, this is wrong, this is wrong," or "this is good, this is good, this is good." But we don't always offer solutions.

I just felt, looking from the outside, it's quite easy to say "this should happen, that should happen." But isn't it more powerful to put your face, put your identity, put your — sometimes respect — on the line to try to get something done? And I think you mentioned earlier about players coming on board. That is one of the reasons that players, I think, can be good administrators — because we've heard no so often in our careers. "No, you're not going to bowl." "No, you're not going to bat right now, we're going to send somebody before you." "No, you're not being selected." "No, you're not going on the tour." "No, you're not getting a contract." That we are okay working hard and then being told no — but it's working hard to win hopefully a decision, or a group of decisions, that potentially save something that's given us all that we've ever dreamed of, and sometimes more.

So maybe it is for a few past players to come in and put their neck on the line, and say "I'm going to try this and try that," and everything won't work. I think you're naive to think that in a small market, multiple different islands, that there's just a silver bullet that says West Indies cricket. But at least you can try things, and you can hold yourself to a certain standard that you did whilst you were playing as a professional — all the whilst appreciating that there are a lot more no's than yes, because you're accustomed to it as a player anyway.

Closing

Host: I mean, that's a brilliant way to round it out. Because I would never want it to seem or sound like it's easy. Whenever we sit here and chat about these discussions, you do always have to find a balance between "why is something like this or why something like that?" But recognizing that there isn't one quick fix for it, but also recognizing that you can pull it apart piece by piece and try and solve those things individually, rather than trying to fix one collective thing that seems impossible to do — then that's a good way to do it. And I think you summed that up brilliantly there.

But honestly, from the cricket chats we have, it's amazing to hear about it. Because it is a heritage, it's a massive part of this sport. And as a cricket fan growing up and all of that, West Indies is a major part of my love for cricket. So hearing about it is brilliant. And I hope it turns around. But I'm so grateful for you coming in and talking us through it — because it's pretty cool to hear it. And I'm delighted that there was a nice story behind your cricket bat to cheer me up, anyway, and all other England fans out there still harboring a grudge. Where are you?

But no, seriously — I love it. It was really cool to have you in, and I'm so pleased you enjoyed the show. So thank you for coming and actually sitting in the chair with me. I appreciate it. And hopefully — hopefully there are some investors out there, there are some producers that they will —

Carlos: Yeah, exactly, yeah. No, hopefully guys get in touch, right? Come on. Let's go and raise a bit of money, and let's go and produce some really cool content.

Host: That's a call out to do it, if you're not. But yeah, anyway — appreciate it, man.

Carlos: Pleasure. Loved it.

item.description:
## 一、这不是板球问题，是**价值捕获**问题
Carlos反复描述西印度球员如何在IPL、BPL、CPL被买走、被变现，但变现的收益"not for the benefit of West Indies cricket"。这其实是体育版的**上游供应商困境**——西印度群岛生产"原材料"（球员），下游平台（BCCI、特许联赛、广播商）完成加工并捕获溢价。Shea Hope、Russell、Pollard在这个结构里像可可豆、咖啡豆、油棕——未经加工的作物运往孟买、迪拜、伦敦，加工后以数倍价格卖回。整个发展中世界的贸易困境，被西印度板球以最纯粹的形式演绎了一遍。
更隐秘的时间线是：Chris Dering提到的 **1997年巡回赛经济结构变化**（客队自费、主队全得），其实是体育界版的"注意力经济协议"——比YouTube出现早10年，比Spotify早11年，西印度板球就已经在体验今天OnlyFans作者、Substack写手、TikTok创作者的集体命运：**你是内容本体，但不是价值归属**。
## 二、那根球棒就是整部纪录片的全息投影
注意Errol的球棒故事的叙事结

item.title: [a16z] The AI School Kids Love More Than Vacation | Alpha School's Joe Liemandt
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

从「教不会」到「不想教」：教育系统的根本性误诊

Alpha School 最震撼的发现不是「2小时学会6小时的内容」，而是一个被所有教育改革者系统性忽视的事实：传统学校的瓶颈从来不是认知带宽，而是动机架构。

过去一百年，我们把教育问题诊断为"信息传递效率不足"——于是不断加课时、加作业、加教师、加评估。但 Joe 揭示的真相是：信息传递只占学习问题的 10%，剩下 90% 是动机问题。而工业化教育系统恰恰是一个反动机设计——它让孩子在"永远失败 1/3 以上"的区间里挣扎（时间制课程的必然副产品），然后用考试告诉他们失败是他们自己的问题。

这里有个让人意外的推论：AI 替代教师的真正威胁不是便宜，而是情绪稳定。LLM 可以无止境地提供 80-85% 正确率的个性化挑战——这是任何面对 30 个学生的人类教师在生理上都做不到的。教师不是输在知识上，是输在"心流工程"上。

跨领域连接：游戏设计师比教育学家更懂学习

Joe 顺口提到的"视频游戏开发者都知道失败率超过 2/3 用户就脱离"——这句话值得整个教育学界停下来思考 50 年。

游戏行业用 40 年时间，在没有任何学术委员会监督的情况下，解决了学习科学界 100 年没解决的参与度问题。暴雪、任天堂、Supercell 的难度曲线设计师，掌握着比任何教育部长都更精确的"认知心流算法"。为什么？因为游戏行业面对的是无强制力的注意力市场——用户随时可以离开。而学校有强制出勤权，所以从不需要真正解决吸引力问题。

更深层的洞察：Alpha 本质上是把"义务教育"重构为"订阅制产品"。当 Joe 说"magnet marketing（吸引对的人，排斥错的人）"时，他不是在说营销策略，他是在说整个教育哲学的根本转变——从"我们必须教所有人"（公共事业心态）变成"我们必须让想学的人上瘾"（产品心态）。这就是为什么 edtech 过去都失败了：它们把产品塞进一个反产品的分发系统里。

真正颠覆性的洞察：焦虑的替代品不是乐观，是「做难事的权利」

最反直觉的一点：Alpha 的孩子不是因为"轻松"而爱上学，是因为他们被允许做真正困难的事情。50% 的孩子选择上学而非度假——度假意味着无所事事，上学意味着解谜、挑战、团队协作完成四年级 MBA 测试。

这里藏着一个关于当代儿童心理健康危机的根本性诊断：我们这一代父母以为孩子不开心是因为压力太大，所以给他们更多舒适；而真相可能相反——孩子抑郁是因为被剥夺了"做有意义困难事情"的机会。所有被动化的童年（刷手机、看视频、被精心安排的"活动"）本质上都在传递同一个信息：你的能动性无关紧要。

跨领域连接到心理学：Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi 的"心流"理论说得很清楚——幸福来自技能略低于挑战的区间。现代教育系统把孩子要么放在挑战过高（跟不上进度就是永久失败），要么挑战过低（学得快的被迫等）的区间。两种情况都是心流杀手，而两种情况都制造心理问题。

一个预测性的大胆判断：五年内，"学校是否按学习曲线个性化"会成为儿童心理健康干预的一级指标，比屏幕时间、睡眠质量更能预测青少年抑郁率。因为心流剥夺是比我们想象中更严重的发育伤害——而这个伤害在工业化教育里是系统性的、每天 6 小时的、持续 12 年的。

一个被低估的时间炸弹：Alpha 毕业生进入大学市场

Joe 一句话轻描淡写："我需要地方让 Alpha 的孩子去读大学"。这句话里埋着一个将在 2030-2035 年引爆的高等教育危机。

想象一个场景：第一批真正在 Alpha 式环境长大的孩子，18 岁时已经做过真实的创业、拿过 MBA 级别的团队考核、建过 LLM、在非洲做过一年服务——他们走进常春藤大学的 100 人大课堂，看到的是什么？是他们在 10 岁就已经超越的学习方式。

这不是渐进竞争，这是消费者革命。就像当年习惯了 iPhone 的用户不可能再接受 Nokia 的功能机——这些孩子不会"适应"传统大学，他们会公开嘲笑它（Alpha 第一届大学生已经在校报写专栏骂了）。常春藤的真正护城河从来不是教学质量，是身份信号和校友网络——而 AI 原生一代可能是第一代不需要这两样东西来证明自己的学生。

提问： What would you say to the parent who's saying, "I'm sending my kid to Ivy League school. I know it's not perfect, but this is a new institution. Why should I take a risk?"
