item.description:
## 从「教不会」到「不想教」：教育系统的根本性误诊
Alpha School 最震撼的发现不是「2小时学会6小时的内容」，而是一个被所有教育改革者系统性忽视的事实：**传统学校的瓶颈从来不是认知带宽，而是动机架构**。
过去一百年，我们把教育问题诊断为"信息传递效率不足"——于是不断加课时、加作业、加教师、加评估。但 Joe 揭示的真相是：**信息传递只占学习问题的 10%，剩下 90% 是动机问题**。而工业化教育系统恰恰是一个**反动机设计**——它让孩子在"永远失败 1/3 以上"的区间里挣扎（时间制课程的必然副产品），然后用考试告诉他们失败是他们自己的问题。
这里有个让人意外的推论：**AI 替代教师的真正威胁不是便宜，而是情绪稳定**。LLM 可以无止境地提供 80-85% 正确率的个性化挑战——这是任何面对 30 个学生的人类教师在生理上都做不到的。教师不是输在知识上，是输在"心流工程"上。
## 跨领域连接：游戏设计师比教育学家更懂学习
Joe 顺口提到的"视频游戏开发者都知道失败率超过 2/3 用户就脱离"——这句话值得整个教育学界停下来思考 50 年。

item.title: [YC Root Access] Fixing the $300 Billion Medical Billing Problem
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、意外观察：Candid 的真正商业模式是"做市场萎缩的赢家"

大多数创业者都想"扩大市场"，但 Nick 说了一句极反直觉的话："如果 Candid 赢了，我们会让这个市场缩小。" 这是一种罕见的"反增长式护城河"——他们定价远低于 5% 的 cost-to-collect 行业均值，故意让竞争对手在这个价位上"做不出利润"。

这与 Costco、Amazon AWS 的"价格压制策略"同构：用自动化换取对手无法承受的价格带。但更深层的意外在于——医疗账单市场之所以是 2000-3000 亿美元，恰恰是因为它的低效。Candid 的终极野心不是分蛋糕，而是让蛋糕消失，然后在剩下的更小但更干净的蛋糕里拿走大份额。这是一个"效率吞噬市场"的典型案例，和 Stripe 让"商户整合支付接口"这个赛道消失的路径完全一致。

二、跨领域连接：医疗账单 = 国际货币结算 = 法律合同协商

RCM 看起来是医疗问题，本质上却是"一千个主权国家之间的货币清算"：每个保险公司就是一个有自己货币、关税、法律的独立国。而且，这些"国家"的规则很多不公开——Nick 特别指出："法律文件是公开的，所以 Harvey 能起飞；医疗规则大部分不公开，所以 RCM 领域出不了 Harvey。"

这是一个被严重低估的洞见：AI 能否在一个行业产生颠覆性公司，关键不在于数据量，而在于"规则是公开还是私有"。

  • 法律 → 公开判例 → Harvey、Legora 快速崛起
  • 客服 → 半公开 FAQ → Sierra 快速崛起
  • 医疗账单 → 规则私有、需七年逆向工程 → 没有一夜爆款，只有 Candid 这种"长期考古型"公司

这意味着，未来 AI 创业的真正金矿不是"文档密集型行业"，而是"规则黑箱型行业"——保险、海关、税务、特种制造验收、专利审查。这些领域谁先用七年把黑箱变成结构化规则引擎，谁就垄断了下一波 agent 浪潮的"地基权"。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：Candid 的护城河不是软件，是"认知债务"

你以为 Candid 的壁垒是代码、是 AI、是客户关系。都不是。

他们真正的壁垒是：Nick 本人亲自做了一年半的 biller。

这是一个被创业圈严重误解的现象。大家都知道"创始人要 do things that don't scale"，但 Nick 展示了一种更深的玩法——他把自己变成了"行业语义的最后一公里压缩器"。他亲手处理每一笔赔付、打每一个电话、处理每一个 edge case，这些不是在"维持运营"，而是在把隐性知识（tacit knowledge）压缩成结构化规则，这正是 LLM 时代最稀缺的资产。

更惊人的是，这解释了为什么"预 AI 时代苦熬的公司，在 AI 时代反而赢得更漂亮"：

  • 他们已经把混乱变成了结构化规则引擎（Candid 的 "rules engine"）
  • LLM 对他们是乘数而非基座——因为基座已经建好
  • 而纯 AI-native 的新秀没有这一层"文明化地基"，agent 会在混乱数据上疯狂幻觉

这跟围棋 AlphaGo 之前几十年的人类棋谱沉淀是一个道理——AI 的真正跃迁不是取代经验，而是对已有结构化经验的放大。Nick 的"一年半苦工"相当于给未来十年的 agent 军团提前铺好了棋盘。

顺带一个 "aha"：Nick 最后那段关于"保险公司和医疗机构的系统应该合二为一"的愿景，本质上是在呼唤一个"医疗版的 SWIFT 升级到 Blockchain"的转变——从异步双边清算走向同步共享账本。真正的终局，可能不是更强的 AI，而是让 AI 无用武之地的架构重构。这才是 Candid 真正的北极星，但他自己都没明说。

📝 转录文本

开场

[music] Today I'm here with Nick Perry. He's the co-founder and CEO of Candid Health. Um Nick, welcome to YC.

Thanks for having me.

Candid Health 做什么？

What does Candid Health do?

We automate RCM for healthcare providers. So we've rebuilt the entire medical billing stack that healthcare providers use to bill insurance from the ground up to be automation and AI first.

What's the problem that Candid is trying to solve?

It is extremely difficult if you're a healthcare provider to get paid for providing the services that you provide — whether that's from patients or insurance. And the core challenge is: if you're one provider, you may be seeing patients from hundreds or up to a thousand insurance companies. And all of those insurance companies have different rules for how to submit claims.

So you as a provider need to constantly be on top of the latest rules for how to submit claims to each payer. So if you are a therapist and you're seeing — just doing the same therapy visit throughout the day — if all those patients have different insurance, the actual literal claim you submit for that same service to each payer will look different because it has to comply with all of their rules. And staying on top of that in an automated way is extremely difficult to do.

账单到底是怎么产生和支付的？

When I go to the doctor and I get a bill, what's on that bill? Who actually pays?

Like, I know this sounds simple, but it's actually a lot behind that. There are a bunch of ways that that might get paid for, but the simplest way is: you as the patient are going to owe some amount of that. So that's the patient's responsibility.

If you literally go into the doctor, they are probably going to collect a copay from you up front. That's part of what you might owe. Then you're going to go do the visit, you're going to leave, all the visit will get typed up into a claim. The claim will be submitted to the insurance company, and then the insurance company applies your benefits against that claim and then they decide you need to pay more.

Maybe you have co-insurance or maybe you have a deductible. Those are kind of the other two main ways. Deductible is some amount you will pay before your benefits kick in. And then co-insurance is — you as a patient may just owe some percentage of a visit. So if it's a $100 visit and you have 20% co-insurance, insurance will pay 80, you'll pay 20.

That would all happen after the fact and the insurance will pay whatever they're going to pay. So you'll go in, you'll pay your copay, and you'll find out two weeks to six months later if you owe some other component.

技术上如何运作：Claim Form 与编码

And technically how does that work? There's something called billing codes. Like we as patients aren't familiar with this, but the doctors are. What was that?

Yeah. So it's probably easiest to think about it on a piece of paper. There is a physical claim form that most insurance companies will still accept today. The vast majority of claims — 95% — are submitted electronically, but you can kind of think of it as this form.

There's a bunch of stuff that goes on that claim. A lot of it has to do with the patient, the provider, where the service was, and the insurance information — kind of metadata about the visit, unrelated to what actually happened in the visit.

And then there are some bits about what actually happened in that visit: - What diseases / ICD-10 codes did the patient present with - What services (CPT codes in the United States) were provided against those diseases

So you will come in, at the front desk they'll collect your insurance card. They're capturing your name, who's your insurance, who's the patient, date of birth — all that stuff that needs to go on the claim. And then when you go into the visit, what comes out of there are the ICD-10 codes and CPT codes. Those go on the claim, and then that whole claim gets shipped off to insurance.

保险公司如何处理 Claim

Got it. And then the insurance company matches that towards the specific plan that a patient has?

So step one is: insurance decides if this is even their patient. If the insurance at that point doesn't want to adjudicate, they'll look at that — that's called a rejection. They'll be like "this isn't our patient" is effectively what they're saying.

Assuming you got past that, then insurance says — they don't say this but what they mean is — "okay, this is our patient. We're going to apply the benefit, and if there are benefits, we'll apply those and pay it out accordingly."

The next step is they decide if this is in or out of network. If you have a comma in the wrong place in the address, or have other typos, the claim will get adjudicated out of network — and that has big consequences for the patient. The benefit structure for in and out of network is very different. Out of network, we're in an era of high deductible out-of-network plans. So the patient ends up paying a lot more cash out of pocket.

If it's in network, they will pay it out according to those benefits. They may decide this service has no benefit — we don't pay for this thing. And it gets really complicated because every insurance company has different rules and different plans. There's no standardization of what they're required to cover. There is some, but it's not universal, not comprehensive.

Self-funded vs. Fully-funded Plans

On the employer side, aside from Medicare and Medicaid and a couple others, you get your insurance through your employer. There's a thing called a self-funded versus a fully-funded plan. Most big companies have self-funded, meaning they decide their insurance benefits. It's their insurance dollars.

But that means they decide what gets covered in the benefits, too. So now the insurance company has this complicated job of deciding — is it Aetna's insurance plan, and they decide what it is, or is it this employer's one, and what does that employer have for their benefit? They're trying to adjudicate it across all of these different benefits.

And then that all spits out from this giant granulator — what is your copay, co-insurance, and deductible? And what does the insurance company pay the doctor?

速度与积压

How fast does this happen? How fast after the patient visit does the provider or patient know?

It can really depend. If you are super speedy, the fastest payers will do it in a week and a half, which is actually pretty good. But that's not most everyone's experience.

What ends up happening is the billing department of the provider is backed up and it's very manual clicky stuff. If it doesn't get coded immediately, it gets put in some queue for a couple more days. All of a sudden it's been three weeks before that claim's even been submitted. Then the insurance company adjudicates it, then it goes into a queue for a person to process back at the provider — takes a few more days. And that is how we end up with cases that can take six months.

If you do everything as fast as you can — for some of our customers who are very speedy — on the fast end it's about a week and a half, on the slow end it's five or six weeks. And that's if you're doing all the stuff right on the provider side.

拒付之后的"侦探工作"

And if the insurance has rejected, what does the provider have to do?

There is an entire detective-like process — and this is why RCM is such an expensive and time-consuming process — of figuring out why it was rejected or denied, because the payer does not tell you very clearly. They'll send back these CARC/RARC work codes. They're very vague high-level things you can look up online, but they are so high-level they don't tell you exactly why.

So what often happens is you have to call the payer, and now we're in a very long set of wait times. Once you figure out why it's been rejected or denied, you go do whatever it is to fix it.

  • If the patient doesn't have active insurance → call the patient for new updated insurance
  • If the claim is denied → decide if you want to appeal
  • An appeal would be: "your medical necessity policy says you don't cover this, but you should cover it for X, Y, Z reasons"

You can appeal that, but you might also just take the denial.

市场规模与切入策略

The US healthcare system is a huge portion of GDP, and admin is a really big piece of it. How does Candid Health attack this?

The market's somewhere between $200 and $300 billion for medical billing. About 50% of it is inpatient — health systems, hospitals. The other 50% is outpatient / ambulatory — primary care, mental health, etc.

  • The health system side is dominated by two or three players: Epic, Cerner, Meditech.
  • The outpatient side has hundreds of EMRs and billing companies — way more fragmented, largely because there are so many different medical specialties.

Eventually we want to work with everyone, but we had a padding problem. The incumbents all have these crazy moats in feature breadth. This is way before agents when we started the company. Software features were a moat — if you had to support enough check-the-box things, it's hard to go replace an incumbent. Which is why there hasn't really been a big new billing company in 30 years.

乘上数字健康浪潮

The vector we used — which I think was the only one you could have used in the last 25 years — was the digital health wave. We started in the last batch right before COVID. All of a sudden there were laws around you have to cover telemedicine. So we had this birth of a very fast-growing digital health wave that we basically rode.

Those digital health companies were looking for a "Stripe for medical billing." It wasn't a huge market at the time — we kind of joked about it being paid R&D — but they're awesome customers doing amazing work. We were going to start here, build the core of what we need, and then expand.

Then digital health just exploded. That let us really focus on the core of billing: how do you submit claims correctly the first time? How do you reverse-engineer the rules of all these payers, pull them into the platform, so you know how to submit claims correctly the first time?

We didn't need to build scheduling. We didn't need to build patient billing — people were using Stripe already. We could plug into a lot of other things and focus on the part we really wanted to focus on.

第一个客户与初创信任

Why did the first customer trust you?

I think I had a lot of credibility coming out of Palantir. Two, this is such a good example of the "hair on fire problem." I didn't realize the rest of it was — they will take a brick to put the fire out.

Our first customer, I was meeting one of the founders in a cafe, telling her about: "Hey, I want to work on RCM. I think it's really hard for these reasons. How's it going for you?" The line I remember vividly — this happened eight years ago — was she said:

"I will let you work on any part of RCM because I hate this so much and it is so hard."

保险公司是不是故意为难？

Is it fair to say there's a misalignment between insurance companies and providers?

I do think that is true. I would not — it has not been my experience where insurance is actively trying to do deceptive things. I heard all these anecdotes when we first got started: "Tuesday afternoon the boss would be like, deny all the claims." I've never actually seen that having done this for seven years.

But what I do think is going on is: they do have very different incentives. - Insurance is incentivized to be careful about what they're paying out, and how much. - Providers are incentivized to get paid for what they are doing.

The hard part is it's not reverse-engineering how to do it once. It's not a set-it-and-forget-it problem. It's how do you keep up with all of this change and evolution of these rules — the feedback loop.

从 API 到自动化平台

Let's go back to that first customer. What was the first product like?

Our very first product that we shipped was literally just an API. They would submit the data we needed to submit claims — and then honestly, at that point it stopped. We would manually submit the claims because we were building out the rest of it. We would actually literally look at every electronic claim before we submit it.

I literally did this for days. We didn't have reporting built, so I would build out all the reporting in Google Sheets for our weekly meeting. Over time we were building up more and more features. On day one it was literally just an API for data capture.

Did it get out of control?

I think we got crafty with our internal tooling. I was Candid's biller for a year and a half, figuring out how to do this. Some friends tease me — maybe we did it too long that way. But I learned a lot and it helped inform our product on all these different edge cases.

RCM is not a power law where a small number of things drive most of the pain. It is an extremely long tail — a death by a thousand paper cuts problem. You have to get this exposure and call the insurance companies to figure out what's actually going on.

产品演化：三块"睡莲叶"

Our evolution has been:

  1. Sold the outcome only — we called it medical billing, send the claims and we take care of everything. You couldn't buy just the software because there was no software to buy.
  2. Co-built our actual software platform with another customer — mostly constrained to just the billing set.
  3. Extended on both sides — built patient registration, copay collection up front around an in/out visit.

Those three major evolutions all happened before agents and LLMs got big. The last one has been the introduction of AI and LLMs — more of an addition to the platform, as opposed to a fundamentally different platform, because the platform was already automated.

AI、Agents 与成本

Can the models handle this stuff?

Our vision is to automate RCM. We're not dogmatic about what we want — the best tool for the job.

  • Agents are really good at some things. If I have denied claims and I'm going to appeal by calling payers or going to paper, several companies have agents solving that.
  • We have a different philosophy: go upstream and submit the claim correctly the first time. Avoid that denial altogether.

Tokens are still very expensive. We could have an agent do it, but that is not a very cost-effective way. We can just use software — cheap, deterministic, no hallucinations.

On a single claims journey, you might have: - Deterministic software applying rules (cheap, deterministic, happens every time) - Machine learning models to predict denials - Agents when we didn't hear back or want to appeal - A person on the most extreme cases

创始人的背景

Tell me about your background.

I was at Palantir for five years. The team I joined was the same team my co-founder was on and where we met. It was stood up by Shyam, the COO at the time, to solve whatever the most pressing growth problem was.

Palantir has a great reputation for amazing people to learn from. Several of us went on to work in external stuff with customers. I went into the commercial side and did mostly healthcare — pharmaceutical work, then some work with payers. That was my first exposure to claim adjudication and RCM. I saw it from their side.

When we were leaving Palantir, I wanted: 1. A big problem — a big market 2. An important problem — something I really cared about

RCM checked both boxes.

发现 PMF 的时刻

Can you describe the journey after the first year and second year?

We always had really strong traction. But you never really know. There was a moment where we ran an RFP with a really big private-equity-backed MSO where we beat one of the legacy incumbent competitors that had been there for 25 years.

That was my moment of: "Oh wow — we're a four-year-old company that just beat a 25-year-old company in a really competitive process." They were pumped about automated RCM — which was our north star — and we weren't even feature-complete.

团队与文化

Tell me about the team.

We've hired a pretty similar profile the entire time. The most important thing about the company is your culture. If you get the culture right, a lot of the rest will figure itself out.

My co-founder and I are deeply involved in hiring basically everyone at Candid still. Everyone gets interviewed at some point by me, Doug, or a couple other amazing interviewers.

We actually don't do functional interviews generally. We look at much more fundamental stuff: - Do you have high horsepower? - Are you gritty? - Are you introspective?

We have one "life story interview" at the end — not a trick question, just asking about their life, what went really well and what didn't. That scorecard hasn't changed since the first day we started the company.

未来两三年的议程

What's on your agenda for the next two or three years?

We are big and fast-growing, but we are only scratching the surface of this market. We could have 1/280th of it and still have a billion in revenue.

Rate-limiting factors: - Size of our sales / distribution channels — can we work with EMRs and be their white-label billing partner? - At the limit — the people and culture. It is impossible for a 100-person company to absorb a 10,000-person company and maintain its culture.

获客路径

How did the first 10 customers happen?

I just went through my network and LinkedIn. I came up with lists of companies, found their founders, looked for connections, and emailed my network for intros. It grew from there.

Because we cared about creating delight and doing a really good job, the investors of our customers started hearing about us at board meetings and started putting us in touch with other portfolio companies. That still happens today.

医疗支出中的占比

What percent roughly of healthcare spend is this?

About 5% more or less. In the most extreme cases, 15 to 20%. There's a concept in medical billing called "cost to collect" — the amount of money you're spending to collect your money.

Most people are in the 5–10% range. A lot of that is people involved — because everyone's software was built 25 years ago, it's very clicky and manual.

But you don't need to charge 5% with your software.

No, we charge much lower than that. If Candid wins, I think we shrink the size of the market. We want to operate at a level that our competitors literally cannot operate at — because we're so good at automation internally.

买方关心的两个数字

The two numbers people care most about: - Net collection rate — the percentage of the dollars you expect to collect - Cost to collect — how much it costs to collect them

For every $100 a provider might charge, they might only get $85, and they'll spend $10 to get it — netting out at $75. Because our ethos is "submit claims correctly the first time," net collection rate goes up and cost to collect goes down.

为什么 RCM 没有 Harvey？

Where will AI have the biggest impact in RCM?

There hasn't been a Harvey, Legora, or Sierra in RCM. The scribes grew very quickly. In RCM on claim adjudication — not one of those. The main reason goes to the data they all need to thrive.

  • In law, stuff changes but documents are broadly public. If something changes, it's public, you can ingest it.
  • In RCM, the rules for how to submit claims — a thousand insurance companies, changing every quarter — most are not published. Some are published in a PDF, but most are not.

The only way you can learn is you're actually submitting claims and calling payers — a person or an agent — and reverse-engineering. You're building these rules. We've been building that data set for seven years, and that is a really important part of why we're so good.

Agents help us more quickly and expansively cover all the data exhaust around what we're doing. We have customers with hundreds of billers. Agents can look at the data and suggest: "these users are doing this thing 100 times a day — this is automatable."

The curation of rules is probably the most important application of LLMs right now — because they can look at a bunch of data and data exhaust more quickly than people doing it.

The challenge with RCM is it's not document-based, it's logic-based. Imagine if you were trying to keep track of all the ifs and thens in a prompt. You can't manage that. You need the versioning, you need to test rules. Managing these rules in context, trying to submit claims at scale, becomes very challenging — that's our rules engine.

Series D

You just raised a Series D.

$120 million from Sixth Street. They're awesome partners — they know healthcare extremely well. They work with a lot of private equity groups, private equity roll-ups, big medical groups. Getting our name out there as we move into this more traditional market is a really important part.

使命：让医疗变好

How does healthcare become better as a result of all this?

Basically everyone you and I know has paid for a medical bill they probably didn't need to pay for. It's not that there's some bad guy — it is so easy to make mistakes.

There's one insurance company I know that if you put a comma in the wrong place, they will adjudicate your claim out of network. So what might have been a $25 copay is now a $1,000 charge.

Patients may not even notice it. Explanations of benefits are hard to parse — says "this is not a bill" but looks a lot like one. Even if you know something's wrong, so many people don't have the time to go fight insurance. Doctors take the oath "do no harm" — we should include financial stuff into that too.

Agent 战争的隐忧

Do you foresee a world where we all have personal AI making us better patients?

I don't see why not. I bet you could train an agent to do that. I do worry about what happens when payers are investing in agents too. Agents calling agents — we'd just have agent warfare.

What I would like to see — ideally — is a world where the provider billing system and the payer adjudication system are the same system. The claim adjudication systems used by payers are even older than the billing systems used by providers — mostly built in the 80s. The core of the problem is that these are different systems with their own logic. Ideally, policies log on the payer's side, claims hit that, and it instantly adjudicates. No clearinghouse batches. No arguing.

加入 Candid 的理由

What are the most exciting things to work on?

We've been building that automation layer, the context layer — how to submit claims — for seven years. That's a really interesting asset to build on top of.

解耦自动化层

Our go-to-market historically has been a rip-and-replace motion — like what Stripe used to be. Reality is not everyone can do that. Multi-year contracts with billing partners are common.

Before, we couldn't work with them. Now we've started to detach the automation layer — agents, rules engine, data modeling, orchestration — from our platform. So we can sit it on top of another billing system and orchestrate it. We're abstracting away that billing system into what is effectively a clearinghouse in healthcare. That opens up tons of TAM.

Instant Payments

Something we're spending a lot of time on right now is instant payments. People have had this pipe dream for a long time: submit a claim, know it's going to get paid, instantly pay the provider.

The hard part: payer rules change. What happens when something that was getting paid no longer gets paid? How quickly can you identify it and turn off the instant payment? No other billing system has that granular control — we do.

Most healthcare providers are large but not super high-margin. Cash flow matters so much. Being able to pay sooner and provide that reliability is really valuable. It goes back to that core asset — the context, knowledge, and rules for how to submit claims and what's going to get paid.

对创始人的建议

Any specific lesson you wish you knew when you started?

A lot of people at seed stage talk about product-market fit and iterating on product. I wish somebody had pushed me to build a financial model sooner.

At the end of the day, if you squint at each company, it's a spreadsheet. Investors invest in spreadsheets. They're comparing spreadsheets of which they wanted to invest in. Having clarity around what you want to do by when — it forces you to back into the planning: "to be competitive with other spreadsheets, I need this in place by this point."

For whatever reason, none of my friends starting companies were like "we need to talk about our spreadsheets." It was almost looked down on. I found it to be the most clarifying planning tool.

结束

Nick, thanks for coming back to YC.

Thanks for having me.

Yeah, this is a very interesting conversation.

This is great. Yeah, thanks. Thank you. [music]

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、意外观察：Candid 的真正商业模式是"做市场萎缩的赢家"
大多数创业者都想"扩大市场"，但 Nick 说了一句极反直觉的话：**"如果 Candid 赢了，我们会让这个市场缩小。"** 这是一种罕见的"反增长式护城河"——他们定价远低于 5% 的 cost-to-collect 行业均值，故意让竞争对手在这个价位上"做不出利润"。
这与 Costco、Amazon AWS 的"价格压制策略"同构：**用自动化换取对手无法承受的价格带**。但更深层的意外在于——医疗账单市场之所以是 2000-3000 亿美元，恰恰是因为它的低效。Candid 的终极野心不是分蛋糕，而是**让蛋糕消失**，然后在剩下的更小但更干净的蛋糕里拿走大份额。这是一个"效率吞噬市场"的典型案例，和 Stripe 让"商户整合支付接口"这个赛道消失的路径完全一致。
## 二、跨领域连接：医疗账单 = 国际货币结算 = 法律合同协商
RCM 看起来是医疗问题，本质上却是**"一千个主权国家之间的货币清算"**：每个保险公司就是一个有自己货币、关税、法律的独立国。而且，这些"国家"的规则很多**不公

item.title: [Invest Like The Best] Why Free Intelligence Won’t Change Everything
item.dc:creator: Invest Like The Best
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

关于"仅仅是智能"的几个意外视角

1. 他的投资组合本身就是他的论点——而他可能没意识到

Cliff 用了整场谈话论证"要拥有智能的互补品"（complements to intelligence），然后在最后半推半就地承认自己 80% 仓位压在 Carvana 上。这不是巧合，而是他的仓位结构即他的理论自证：Carvana 的护城河是物理基础设施——翻新中心、物流网络、二手车估值的本地密度——这些恰恰是智能永远无法蒸馏（distill）的东西。

更有趣的意外观察：他说"我超配 Carvana"的那一刻，其实是在说"我做空了纯智能"。一个坚信智能会被商品化到接近免费的人，必然会把净多头暴露在反智能资产上。这是对冲基金文化里罕见的"你的头寸即你的世界观"的纯粹案例。

2. 智能真正的敌人不是复杂性，而是时间——这连接到奥地利学派

他用混沌理论（蝴蝶效应）解释智能的边界时，几乎踩在了 Hayek 的"知识问题" 门槛上但没推开门。Hayek 1945 年论证：中央计划者无法获得分散在数百万交易中的"时间与地点的具体知识"（knowledge of time and place），因为价格本身才是压缩这些知识的介质。

Cliff 在后半段说"价格是包裹在激励里的信号"——他其实在不自觉地复述 Hayek。真正的意外联系在这里：如果智能需要"触碰现实"（touch reality）才能前进，而现实的信息已经被价格高效压缩了，那么 AI 的终极瓶颈不是算力，是实验周期——小鼠要长大，细胞要分裂，混凝土要凝固。这意味着生物时间常数（biological time constants）会取代摩尔定律成为下一轮技术进步的隐性约束。能把实验周期砍一半的公司，比能把推理成本砍 100 倍的公司价值更大。

3. 一个没人在定价的巨型财富转移：粘性价格的液化

他举的"垃圾收集 agent"例子，表面是个小玩笑，底下藏着一个万亿美元级的洞察。整个消费经济依赖于行为经济学意义上的"粘性价格"——消费者懒得切换、懒得谈判、懒得比较。银行存款、保险续保、订阅服务、公用事业，全部靠这个护城河活着。

跨领域连接：这其实是 Daniel Kahneman 的"System 1 税" 的宏观化——我们每人每年给惰性付的隐形税。一旦 agent 普及，这笔税会被瞬间清零。这意味着： - 整个零售银行业的 NIM（净息差）结构会崩塌； - 保险行业的"客户保留率溢价"会消失； - SaaS 的"自动续约=永续债"模型会破产； - 但这笔钱不会凭空消失，它会以消费者剩余的形式再分配——而消费者剩余不进 GDP，不进企业利润，也不进税收。

最意外的推论：我们可能正在构建一个比历史上任何技术都更"通缩"的系统，但这个通缩根本不显示在传统宏观指标里。央行会被困在一个"数据上通胀温和、实际购买力飞涨"的测量黑洞中——这是 CPI 篮子从未遇到过的情形。

4. 教育观里的一个隐藏悖论

他对孩子教育的建议"要让孩子不用模型也能做基础运算"——听起来保守，其实是最激进的 AI 乐观主义。因为他的真实论点是：人类保留智能的目的不再是执行，而是指挥。这把教育从"培养工匠"重构为"培养指挥家"。

但这里有个没说破的黑暗推论：指挥能力的分布比执行能力更不均等。一个二流小提琴手仍可糊口；一个二流交响乐指挥却毫无价值。如果所有工作都变成"指挥 AI"，收入分布会从他说的"钟形"或"钻石形"变成赢家通吃的幂律——这与他前面说的"商品化会压平不平等"结论恰恰相反。他的两只手这次互相打了起来，而他可能没察觉。

📝 转录文本

Why Free Intelligence Won't Change Everything

Invest Like The Best — with Cliff

Opening: The Two Stories

"I can see all these incredible ways to use AI and I use a gajillion tokens and I can see how I could use a gajillion more. Everyone uses as many tokens as me. We are so short — it's going to be this huge thing that's going on forever, and everyone who's in the buildout is going to make a fortune, right? On the other hand, the cost per token is going to collapse. And so maybe actually we're totally overbuilt, right? And I can tell both stories with equal certainty."

Intelligence Is a Ratio, Not a Height

Host: You called me saying "it's just intelligence" was sort of the theme of our conversation. Describe that simple idea.

Cliff: There's this idea that if intelligence starts at like an amoeba and it gets better and better — then it's like a monkey, then it's like a person, then it's like Einstein, and then it goes zoom and becomes God. I think that's something of an intellectual mistake. What people have wrong there is they're missing what are sort of the real limits of what intelligence can do.

Another way to put it: if you think about intelligence as an unbounded scalar — like the height of a tree — that isn't correct. What you should really think about intelligence as is more like a ratio, like the roundness of a ball.

What the ratio is calculating: intelligence is a gadget, and we use it to make predictions about the universe. We start with a thin scattering of facts about the universe — relatively few of them — and the universe is complex, and we use intelligence to interpolate between them. So as your intelligence goes up, your ability to color in the spaces gets better.

Some domains are really amenable to that — mathematics, you can solve it. In those areas you kind of get to perfect. But for most of the interesting stuff — most of the questions in the world — the mathematical term is: they're complex dynamic systems.

That basically means they're kind of like weather, in the sense that you can't just guess your way. You can't make a closed-form answer. You can try to simulate it, but your simulation will have some degree of error — in your initial conditions or in each step going forward, because at a minimum your steps are going to be truncated. Your error will build, and invariably after the simulation runs for some period of time you'll be off by some amount.

So for mixing cream into your coffee, or predicting the weather, or thinking about how groups of people are going to interact with each other — intelligence just isn't that powerful.

My sense is that what you get is this increasing intelligence to the point where you're making all the predictions something super smart could make, which turns out is a relatively small set of all the interesting things you'd want to know about the world. To get past that, you then need to go out and get more information about the world. And that just takes time. You have to do experiments. You have to touch reality.

But one interesting corollary: one of the things you can turn your intelligence to is reducing the cost of intelligence — which we're seeing. So what you end up getting is: everyone gets unlimited, really great, very "round ball" intelligence, essentially for free. It won't actually be free, but really good-enough intelligence is rapidly falling in price. And it turns out really good-enough intelligence will solve the vast majority of questions where people need to use intelligence.

Chaos Theory and the Butterfly Effect

Host: Can you say more about why this notion of a complex adaptive or dynamic system means that even perfect intelligence — or whatever intelligence we have in a bottle 10 years from now — will still be limited in its applications?

Cliff: Nonlinear dynamic systems. The famous story — how these were discovered, this came into the branch of mathematics that became chaos theory — is: back in the day there was a guy building a weather forecasting model on big computers that took up rooms. He runs the model and it makes predictions of pressure and temperature over some forecasting period. He's like "cool." Then just to make sure it's still working, they reset it and run it again. It starts out basically the same, but then the results start to diverge, and by the third, fourth, fifth day of the forecast, the results were entirely different.

The guy thought: "Darn, I must have a bug." He begins the process of trying to figure out why the computer isn't producing the same results in repeated runs. It turned out the technician who had loaded the data into the computer in the second run had rounded off one decimal less on all the initial conditions for pressure and temperature. You'd have thought that would produce a small, consistent error over the whole forecast. But that small error, through all the repeated steps — you take your current conditions, calculate your next set, they compound — produced an entirely different forecast. Unrecognizable weather. One model said it was 70° and sunny, the other said 20° and pouring.

People called it the butterfly effect — in principle, a butterfly could flap its wings in Africa and lead to a hurricane in North America. Many systems we're interested in have this characteristic. You can know everything about pressure and temperature, but you can't write down an equation that would easily tell you there's going to be a hurricane. You have to model it. And the model is going to be grained at some level — unless you actually go to the step of having the whole universe.

Ultimately, in the limit, if you want to simulate the whole universe, what you actually need is the whole universe. You can't do that. There are many circumstances where simulation is super useful for approximations, and in those circumstances you can use intelligence to solve them, but there are many more where it doesn't work. Intelligence is limited by the sort of fundamental unknowability of the universe.

What "It's Just Intelligence" Means for Business

Host: Back to this notion of "it's just intelligence" — what does that mean about where you think we're going from a more practical standpoint?

Cliff: We're all going to have a team of 200-IQ people working full-time in our pocket. And that team itself will have a team it can deploy — many more. They're going to be trying to figure out all the little optimizations we're too lazy to do. Every company will make similar teams available to their employees.

There's a lot of businesses where that's not good for them.

Consumers are boundedly rational. They only have so much cognitive space. So you go to a consumer and say, "Look, we'll take your money, we won't steal it, we'll pay you a decent interest rate — you don't have to think about it, you can go about your life." The consumer doesn't say, "If I think about this every day, I could save $400." The consumer says, "Ah, sounds good enough, I'm going to move on." But with an agent, the agent will continuously optimize for them.

There are also companies where what they produce fundamentally is some sort of artifact that is just crystallized intelligence. I'm by far not the first person to realize AI could be bad for certain software companies. An AI model is kind of a general-purpose intelligence tool, and many software tools are kind of crystallized, hardened pieces — projections of intelligence.

So as I've been thinking about companies, I've found it helpful to assume everyone has really great intelligence and ask: what's left?

The line I've been using when people push back is: "You don't understand how hard this is, how complicated this is, how many smart people have had to think so long about this." My handwavy and approximately-right response is: okay, sure — but that's all just intelligence.

To follow this logic all the way through: if intelligence becomes cheap and ubiquitous, what you want to own are the complements to intelligence. The complements to intelligence are:

  • Data
  • Attention — love, affection, emotional attachment
  • Physical proximity
  • Scale
  • Regulatory capture (a little cynical, but yes)

For some businesses, their finite ability to deploy intelligence — be it economic (cost of it, only a certain size company, no access to 10,000 of Google's best engineers for 10 years), or just organizational lag — the ability to deploy way more intelligence to your business, and your competitors to deploy more, and your customers to use lots of intelligence, can work out to be better for you. Or, if intelligence is a barrier to serving your customers, the lack of it is. Or it can be bad for you if your customers' lethargy is a fundamental element of your economic value.

Meta from Space: A Case Study

Host: Maybe pick like Meta as the perfect example of a company that owns perfect complements to ubiquitous cheap intelligence.

Cliff: The core business at Meta is personalized TV. It used to be social media, but now it's personalized TV. People really like watching Instagram — it's discovered I love dark British humor, and it's great.

Look at Meta from space, the highest view. They have $250 billion of revenue and they spend $250 billion a year. Some gets accounted as cost, some as capex. It doesn't really matter — they spend it all. What do they spend it on?

A reductionist view: they spend it all on intelligence.

  • They're buying data centers → intelligence-producing tools.
  • They're buying inference → literally intelligence.
  • They're paying really smart people to write algorithms → intelligence.
  • They're writing code → intelligence.
  • They're surveying videos → intelligence adjacent.

In some highly reductionist sense — and you shouldn't take this literally — all they buy is intelligence. And if the price of intelligence is falling by a factor of 100 over the next 5 years, first principles, their costs kind of go away.

On the revenue side: all the creators. How much more quality creative can every creator make with access to intelligence that's 1/100th the cost and 10,000 times more effective? The point is: probably better. Meta in turn may not take their costs to zero — maybe they spend more than zero and do a far better job of picking the videos to show people next, making the content more enjoyable. On the ad side, advertisers could make far better designed, better targeted, personalized ads, which Meta can target much better, and advertisers can build much more slippery funnels.

All of this is downstream of what Meta possesses — which is not destroyed by ubiquitous intelligence — which is data and attention. They have enormous amounts of data about how people view videos, and enormous amounts of attention. These things compound each other.

I don't think the availability of cheap and ubiquitous intelligence is going to cause people not to be interested in watching funny 20-second videos. If anything, Meta can win some time on the margin from other things people do with their time.

Aside: Grindr

A company that benefits in theory from a lot more intelligence is Grindr. Grindr has been constrained over its life by the fact that it's just not that big a company. They've got lots of attention and lots of data, but their ability to build all the things you could imagine building on a finite-sized team and budget has meant Grindr can't be all the things you could imagine it could be. Mental model: what if you had 10,000 of Google's best engineers to go work on your problem for 5 years? What could you do? Grindr is one where maybe they could do more.

The Frontier Labs as Businesses

Host: Historically the conversation has been about the gap in intelligence between closed source and open source. Increasingly it's about the gap between what's publicly available from the labs and what's privately used by them inside their own businesses. Riff on the labs as companies through the mind of an investor.

Cliff: As I've watched models get deployed: you start with very inadequate models able to do a very small subset of jobs. The models get better and work their way up the stack. With each successive step up, the frontier model has unlocked a larger addressable market. But behind it, once models get saturated — once evals get saturated — you'd never use a frontier model for a chatbot in a customer service application. You'd be an idiot.

Those areas clearly commoditize. There's this wave of hard tasks where you really need a frontier model, and behind that you don't. Friends who are big Frontier Labs bulls say, "Don't worry, we can also along the whole efficient frontier produce cheaper tokens." Maybe they can, maybe they can't. The trend has been rapid commoditization — see the rise of Chinese models. At a minimum the cost has been collapsing.

Even if they have a position where the tokens necessary to do tasks well behind the frontier — it might not be a very big market. It doesn't cost that much in the scheme of things to deliver, and it's competitive even if they're a cost leader. A cost leader in a commodity, in a shrinking commodity market.

Programming was this huge use of models. As you push forward, the question becomes: for the next layers of intelligence, do you still have bigger and bigger places to go after? The bull story: "People will pay anything for a model that can figure out how to cure cancer." Maybe. But figuring out how to cure cancer requires touching reality, and I'm not sure more IQ gets you that.

If you don't believe there are super-incredible use cases where you can charge an enormous amount for more intelligence, you get to a diamond-shaped demand frontier: initially wider and wider uses, then more and more rarefied. How often do you really need a 300 IQ?

Reasonable outcome: very few use cases for super-elite intelligence; lots of use cases for very good intelligence; that very good intelligence is highly competitive and commoditized. If frontier labs can become cost leaders, there's a margin to make — but then there's also rampant deflation. How big is the market if good-enough intelligence is very very cheap?

Devil's Advocate: Jevons and Intelligence-Creates-Demand

Host: Jevons paradox, right? As it gets cheaper, we'll just want to use more of it. And historically, new uses of intelligence have been discovered by highly intelligent people. My friend says "intelligence creates its own demand."

Cliff: Jevons paradox is a narrow example of price elasticity of demand. All markets are U-shaped. Initially, when the product is terrible, no demand. Product gets better, people pay a lot but don't buy much. Price goes down, market rises — Jevons paradox. Eventually further price decreases don't drive enough demand; market shrinks; price to zero → market goes to zero.

Example: fiber optic communications. The cost of moving information used to be super high; people moved very little. Through innovations, cost went down a lot, amount of info moved went up a ton, market grew for a long time. Then the market stopped growing, cost kept falling, market kept shrinking. Nowadays Cogent Communications routes 30–40% of all IP traffic across the internet through one of its divisions, and Cogent is a few-billion-dollar market cap company. Not a very big industry.

Jevons paradox is a statement about a particular spot on a curve — doesn't have to be true everywhere.

Can more intelligence create more desire for intelligence? Maybe. But to answer questions you need to touch reality. If you had a model thinking about physics, it could think lots of interesting thoughts, but eventually it needs to do experiments. There'll be an incredible time of cool discoveries — papers already written where if someone had read all three they'd have realized this, but nobody had. Models will read all the papers and figure it out. All kinds of great stuff will fall out of that. At some point we're kind of finished with that, and then it's about hypotheses outside what we know, where even a super-smart model won't be meaningfully better at guessing than the smartest person — and the smartest person's odds are super low anyway.

My own use of AI: I've totally commoditized my model usage. I'm lazy — I'll tell a Grok-bot to build things, and because I don't want to use up my Grok-bot weekly tokens, I subscribe to everything and have it build on a server using all those subscriptions. I actually don't know what model I'm using anymore. I used to know which was better or worse. All of this is being optimized on the back end for me.

Automated Experimentation Companies

Closing the loop in the physical world is going to be great and accelerate learning. But there are speed limits. Being smart has limits. If you're going to build an automatic biology testing lab, connect it to a computer, the computer comes up with an idea, runs an experiment, iterates — awesome. But if the experiment requires breeding mice and mice need a year to grow up and die, that experiment is going to take time. You might have 5,000 great ideas, pick 20, your odds might be 1% — turns out 10 times better than the average researcher, amazing — still 1%.

Not pessimistic. Discovering things already in our corpus that we forgot — awesome. Better directing research — awesome. Automating research to move faster — awesome. We will push the frontier. But not: "Suddenly the model looks around and says, 'You guys missed it — here's a new world you can't comprehend.'" I don't think that's where we're headed.

Supply vs. Demand Investing

Host: The market, especially in private markets, has been very focused on investing in supply-related stuff — how we're going to build and serve all the intelligence — versus demand-related stuff. What do you think about that first batch of companies?

Cliff: Super hard. I've willfully been ignorant about them, and probably I'm worse off for it. There's this big buildout, and you're trying to forecast inference demand. I can't forecast supply or demand within several orders of magnitude. How much more inference will people use as intelligence gets better and cheaper? Really hard. How much better and cheaper inference is going to get? Equally hard. Even if you guess at those, then there's the whole value chain, and you need to be at the bottleneck to capture rents. Then your actual competition with competitors in that piece of the value chain.

My own use of AI as a consumer: increasingly I'm having AI make a 3Blue1Brown-style video explainer so my daughter can see a nice 5–10 minute video on powers or circumference or something. Super cool. I don't think I'd do that if it was going to be $5. There's real price elasticity. I'll film myself working out and have my Muse app give me tips on form — I'll do that for very little money, but not if the price point is real. I'm probably much less sensitive to price than most people. AI demand is going to be really sensitive to price, which intrinsically limits in some sense the amount in total consumers will be willing to spend.

Capital Cycles and American Dynamism

Host: Many of the best entrepreneurs are personally invested in this supply buildout. If you watch SpaceX's investor day, this is basically the theme. Arguably the greatest entrepreneur of all time is dedicated to building out data center supply. Why are so many of the best entrepreneurs dedicating their lives to the buildout?

Cliff: This is a huge infrastructure buildout of a huge and important technology. It'd be impossible for that to happen without a strong price signal and a ton of talent. You may have the causality backwards. Could you imagine a telling of the story where nobody interesting who'd made no money was building out the AI?

That's probably the best answer. This is a huge and important project, only happening because super smart and talented people are focusing their lives on it. They will have and deserve to make lots of money. It's just very hard — from where I sit — to figure out where one would invest along this and whether you'll make any money doing it.

I've decided to focus on the longer-term equilibrium results. Instead of betting on which railroad tycoon makes money and how many railroads we need, I'm trying to think: once you have railroads, what comes next? I'd love the foresight to figure out that CPG brands come next.

What History Teaches Us

Think of American society right now as a household saving for a house. We're building a house, all feeling pinched because resources are dedicated to this big AI infrastructure. Electricians, plumbers — doing these tasks, raising costs elsewhere. Undoubtedly we're going to get a lot of value. We'll keep pushing until we overdo it. People have to make tons of money along the way, otherwise they won't keep pushing. Because of lead times and the winner's curse, invariably the last person to stop will regret it.

Combine that with the dynamism in the technology — much more true than for historic infrastructure buildouts. Even going down to the chip level, the potential for AI to commoditize things like Nvidia — a lot of what Nvidia does ends up being intelligence. They literally make flat files sent to Taiwan. Flat files are very hard to make, but what they have is a lot of people who think really hard. In theory you could make them. If you step back a little from the frontier, the cost of making something comes way down.

TSMC

I don't want to carry myself around as a TSMC expert. What they do has better attributes. They did a super hard thing requiring process power built over years, hard to replicate, less amenable to AI because it's so physical — many little things not even legible to an AI, like some guy in the system who kind of knows you have to do this. Because of so much demand, and because they haven't been able to meet it, they've caused everyone in the world to seek to copy their moat. Not a great fact.

More generally: businesses with physical proximity or physical scale might benefit if they can use intelligence to serve customers better or have lower costs.

Complements to Intelligence: A Deeper Look

Host: Walk through the natural complements to intelligence. Physical proximity — how would you think about DoorDash, Uber, businesses with local density effects?

Cliff: If you're the low-cost producer of something — stylized example. If everyone has an AI agent, many decisions get offloaded to the agent, because the agent helps optimize all the pennies, dollars, nickels you were leaving on the ground.

Consumer choices as a spectrum. One end: maximizing bank deposits — I can almost entirely defer to the agent's judgment, as long as it's FDIC-insured, I just want the highest rate. Other end: picking my favorite sweater — all my judgment. AI can source things, but I need to decide.

Say garbage collection is something I can defer. Right now, if I'm in the waste collection business, I might be great, but it's really hard to get people to switch. You don't know what you pay for garbage collection off the top of your head. You have to do all this work to get people to pay attention to switch — even if you're offering a better service at a lower price.

You could imagine my agent and their agent talking: "Hey, I'll save you 50 cents a month." Agent: "Will the garbage go away?" Yes. No problem, I'll change. First-order effect: you move to the low-cost provider.

Second-order effect: It'd be more efficient for society if all of us on my street had the same waste collector — one truck drives the street. But coordination is hard. Now the guy with two customers on the street can go to everyone and say, "I'll offer you 50 cents lower." Everyone switches. Local effects: everyone moves to the low-cost producer, who in turn becomes a lower-cost producer. Better business where the low-cost guy wins more volume at much lower margins.

Many companies have mixed effects pointing in different directions.

Agents and the Future of Investing

Host: What do you think the impact of agents is going to be on your world?

Cliff: Hopefully better in terms of what I do. In the long term we'll probably get competed out.

When computer-aided chess came along, there was a long span where freestyle chess was better — the human working with a computer program outcompeted either human or computer alone. Humans and computers thought about things differently and were synergistic. In investing we're in that era now. There are things I understand about the world the model just doesn't, by virtue of being a person. There's information I have about the world that isn't in models — as much info as is on the internet, not everything is on the internet. While that's true (which will be a while), my ability to use models to assist me and make judgments will make better judgments working together.

You could imagine the gap diminishing. I don't think models will be able to predict the future — the future is intrinsically unpredictable — but the model's distribution of outcomes may be the best you can do, and adding a human might be like adding my judgment to whether it's going to rain in seven days. "Cliff, I don't really care what you think. I'm using the forecast — however you fudge it, you'll make it worse."

There's a lot to investing — judging management, for example. Maybe models will judge management. Interview them. Figure it out. Then it gets really interesting: how do you raise capital? "I'd like to run an amusement park." Model: "Sure, here are six locations with a 51% chance of working, and as long as you're really committed, I've assessed you have a 51.2% chance of succeeding — you're actually slightly below average." "Okay, what can I do better than average?" "Have you thought about running a go-karting park?"

Fortunately, I don't think it'll affect my career that much — it'll take a while.

Price as Miracle

Host: What about replacing price as the organizing principle and signal that coordinates economic activity?

Cliff: Price is a miracle, because it's a signal wrapped in an incentive. Price is an incentive — it causes you to want to buy more or less of something as it goes up or down. It's also a signal — it says something about the relative value of something, the scarcity, the cost to produce. A miracle of a mechanism to coordinate things. You'd be really hard-pressed to find a better system, even with unlimited intelligence.

Host: Three levels of intelligence use: (1) prompt and get something back; (2) a watchtower that runs scheduled tasks in the background; (3) always-on, proactive, figuring out its own way to use its own intelligence. If level three applies to everything — pricing, efficiencies, optimization?

Cliff: Price sharpens markets. There's a lot of stickiness to prices — a well-known macroeconomic phenomenon, price stickiness. There's a lot of lazily priced stuff — think about deposits. It's a competitive world, but not as competitive as it could be in theory.

If everyone has agents working on their behalf, constantly optimizing, the price of garbage collection will move around a lot more as all input costs evolve. Every garbage-collecting company constantly rerunning its financials, trying to figure out its true marginal cost, bidding every customer. Every agent switching to the lowest-cost provider. You won't just pay $60 a month for 12 months and then have the guy come back and say it's a 5% increase to $63 next year and you don't notice. Garbage collection will vary by day. Much more accurate, much more rapidly moving prices.

Capital Markets and American Innovation

Host: Anything interesting percolating in capital markets, in ways of financing things?

Cliff: It's fun to pause and congratulate ourselves as capital markets for what we're doing with AI. People were worried about a decline in American dynamism. We just redeployed what is it — 3% of GDP? — into this highly speculative venture, basically on the turn of a dime. A remarkable thing. Maybe it should be 2%, maybe 6% — but it's amazing we can redeploy resources at this scale this quickly. No one else in the world has been able to do it. The inability to move investment in productive resources can be a binding constraint on productivity growth, especially with rapid technological progress.

Americans are doing different things today — every day people are waking up and going to Pennsylvania and building a data center. That wouldn't happen without this infrastructure that's somehow been able to move this enormous amount of capital.

Deep innovation? The fundamental idea that people are taking risk on speculative ventures and slicing up the pie in different ways is sort of irreducible. People have come up with lots of different names for what are essentially the same things over time. I don't think that's deeply different.

I'm sure we'll discover all kinds of fraud and bad behavior eventually, when the water goes out. But given the magnitude of this, I suspect it's pretty clean. If you read about the railroad buildout, the amount of waste and fraud — there's always some, but this is a lot of people trying to do the right thing. The governance parts we take for granted — America's capital markets are incredibly underappreciated. Any person can buy $100,000 of stock, get a portfolio of well-run teams building companies doing mostly the right things, do it instantly at basically no cost, and sell as soon as they're done. The whole system is just very underrated.

Why America

My pet theory: an interplay between genetics, cultural evolution, and institutional evolution. People who came to the United States were the subset most interested in taking risk — coming to the US was very risky. Risk-taking has a meaningful genetic component, so that tendency is more common amongst Americans. When risk-taking is more the norm, you get buildups of cultural and institutional reinforcements. It's understood people can take risk and fail → bankruptcy laws that make sense → labor laws that support it → venture capital. All reinforce each other. Then success stories. A whole soup.

Host: So if there's a moon base, you'd be bullish on that community?

Cliff: Yeah — great way to put it. The US has been persistently innovative. If there's a moon base, I wouldn't be shocked if it's ours. Even though the Chinese are brilliant and numerous and the Europeans exist.

On Rates

Host: Comment on that chart of the 10-year rate — looks flat for forever basically our whole lives.

Cliff: I'm no macro expert, but one observation: when society is building, making a giant investment in the future, you consume less today. All resources going into the AI buildout are about the future. The plumber building a data center isn't making today's consumption — he's making future consumption. One piece of a complex puzzle: rates are higher because we're inducing people to save for the future. And the way you do that is you pay them.

Portfolio and Advising Companies

Host: Your portfolio is roughly 80% Carvana, 5% Meta, basically five things. What's the speech look like when you advise them on using AI?

Cliff: It starts by making sure everyone is vibe coding — starting at the board and CEO. Everybody needs to start building. They need hackathons. I brought this to Carvana and they said, "Yeah, we call them pizza parties." Not so much that you'll build hugely useful software, but you teach everybody what can be done. That changes expectations.

The second thing: the CEO needs to turn to the head of IT and say, "I want my Grok-bot / Meta Muse / agent / whatever to access every system in the company on a read-only basis — everything I could look up by asking somebody, I want in a prompt." The guy will say, "That's really hard, we have teen trillion problems with that." Yes — that's my point. I want that. It's a big process, system by system. If you get there, that gets you to the starting line — read-only access.

Next: the CEO uses this everywhere; everyone gets jealous and wants it; "You can have it too, but we need to work out permissions." Then: "I'd like to put data into the system." "Fantastic — we need to work out write permissions." Then: "I'd love to change a system — we did this vibe coding thing, I'm confident we could do it." "Fantastic — we need a process to manage changes."

Four bullet points → years of work. Impossibly hard. The question: are you in a business where you have time for that to happen before someone who starts from go meets you?

Best Time Ever to Start Companies?

Yeah — until tomorrow. People are such a pain in the butt when you're running a company. The idea that you have all these agents makes it so you can do so much more with so many fewer people. But if you can easily do something, so can everyone else. There has to be some wedge where the thing you build produces enduring value. Does it have a path to lock-in or proprietary data in this world where agents are happily changing providers every day?

Then the further thing: if there's an obvious path to enduring economics, everyone's trying to do that — very competitive. The really great outcomes are the ones that make no sense. You shouldn't do it at all. But then it turns out there is a path, or the world turns.

Underrated Sources of Edge

Attention, data, physical proximity — super or more valuable in the future than today. Most of these are appropriately weighted.

Interesting question: does this make aggregate corporate margins go up or down? Everything we're talking about argues down — many businesses make margin because of lazy consumers → more consumer surplus everywhere.

But reading research reports from the '90s when the internet was coming, they said the same thing. So maybe the base rate here isn't great — but the main reason they were often wrong was aggregation economics (Ben Thompson). A lot of aggregation theory breaks down when consumers only look at the first thing on Google — but if your agent looks at everything, being ranked first doesn't matter, and core things like quality and price and service become more salient.

Another downstream effect: you'll be able to build more complicated businesses. A lot of industries are horizontal because complexity is high — hard to do what's above and below without undue complexity. With AI agents and cheap, ubiquitous code and intelligence, you could build the whole vertical stack. A full-stack pet care business doing everything from pet food through pet insurance, pet hospitals, pet vets — historically multiple layers. Because you can solve coordination and reduce principal-agent problems, those businesses are possible. Maybe they're higher margin — more efficient, more consumer surplus. Carvana is an example built before this was easy. Maybe people can do it in other verticals.

Wealth and Income Distribution

Two stories.

Concentrating: All the people who made money on labs, Nvidia, data — increasing returns to small groups.

Flattening: With cheap, ubiquitous intelligence, all the rent-takers in the economy get smoked — the software company charging bowling alleys, whatever. Sucks for them, but lowers the cost of bowling, which raises living standards for everyone who bowls. People who make less money spend more proportion of their income on bowling — flattening effect. All the money the average American gives to Bank of America goes away from Bank of America — capitalists lose, average consumer wins. Leveling.

Plus: a whole professional class whose role is intelligence — take big corpuses, apply them to circumstances. If those get commoditized: everyone gets the best, particularly good for those who can't afford the best. Those individuals earned extra rents because they were smarter — they drop to their next-best alternative. In theory flattens the curve.

Counterargument: Returns to initiative, ambition, intelligence could go up — models are a bicycle for the mind on steroids. Smart people with initiative accomplish so much more. Increasing returns to that subset — steepens the curve.

"Truman asked for a one-handed economist. I seem to very distinctly have two hands on everything."

Lots of Crosscurrents

The AI buildout — on the one hand I can see all these incredible ways to use AI; I use a gajillion tokens and could use a gajillion more. Everyone uses as many tokens as me. We are so short — huge thing going on forever, everyone in the buildout makes a fortune. On the other hand, the amount I get per token is going to the moon, I'm a pretty unusual guy, people are going to adapt more slowly, cost per token is going to collapse — maybe we're totally overbuilt. I can tell both stories with equal certainty.

Picking vs. Sizing: A Portfolio Experiment

Host: A friend has been running an experiment. Break investing into (1) picking what to own and (2) how much. He runs his own portfolio construction in one lane; the second lane completely hands construction off to an AI harness. What he's found is the AI lane is drastically outperforming — AIs are really good at optimization, they've read every paper on portfolio construction, bet sizing, Kelly criterion. Thoughts on this future where the investor's job is just picking?

Cliff: Time scales are interesting. AI will encroach on this business starting at shorter time scales and working up to longer. The verification loop matters — your friend's claim is based on results over not-even-20-year results.

The march of AI into markets has already started — I don't know how Renaissance Technologies did it, but it wouldn't shock me if people investing over shorter time scales — seconds, minutes, hours, weeks, months — find themselves delegating more and more to models. Makes perfect sense. You could bifurcate: a fully quantitative strategy, enriched with human-designed qualitative analysis, then a quantitative strategy to incorporate the qualitative. Many multistrats do these sorts of things. There are so many ways to be successful — models have added more dimensions of freedom.

Why 80% in One Position

Say more about how you feel comfortable having a position that big in the face of research suggesting it's a crazy way to build a portfolio.

A lot of that research looks at price changes in securities prices, less focused on thinking about it the way someone who owns a company might. We're talking about Carvana — were it not for my sense that Carvana's infrastructure and brand and everything else is so differentiated that there are few scenarios where it works out really badly, I wouldn't feel so comfortable owning so much. It might just be as simple as that.

That portfolio approach would have worked absolutely — but if you discovered Walmart or Home Depot or Fastenal back in the day, you wouldn't have taken full advantage of it. All the people who did really great tended to be very concentrated — but of course the history is biased, you don't read the history of those who didn't.

A lot of that literature is what most people looking for average or slightly-better-than-average results should do, totally the right thing. But that's not what I'm looking for. I like Carvana a lot. It wouldn't upset me if the stock went up a bunch and I felt compelled to diversify — that'd also be okay. More of a trade-off between expected returns and knowingly taking an unusual risk.

Education in the Age of Free Intelligence

Host: Comment on how you're thinking about your kids' education.

Cliff: Step way back. What is the benefit of personal intelligence in a world where there's infinite intelligence from models?

You might say "useless — someone with a 50 IQ can navigate the world just as well as someone with a 150 IQ." I don't think that's quite right, and intuitively doesn't feel right. The more intelligence you have — and the more crystallized intelligence (education) — the better you are at communicating with a model and telling a model what you want.

I'd have a tough time having a deep conversation with the model to create leading quantum physics experiments, because I don't know anything about quantum physics. The model could try very hard to explain things to me, but in the end it'd be explaining in crayon and Nerf. Hard to get to the leading edge, hard to get the best out of what the model has to offer.

In an area where I have some expertise, the model and I can communicate effectively, I can direct the model to my will much better. To direct a model — an important skill in the future — you have to understand something about the world. Smarts and education help. You can't ask it to "assume a stochastic process" unless you know what one is. It could teach you, but that's a lot of friction instead of this figuring this all out. You don't have to work out the math, but you have to know what it is.

So: teach kids a bunch of foundational skills building on one another, where in the end they have to be able to do them kind of without models. Not because they'll do them without models in the future — but because if they don't know multiplication, matrix multiplication will be really hard. If they don't understand what matrix multiplication is at a high enough level, they don't have to do it really well, but they have to understand what the model is doing. So they can direct the model.

Increasingly my view: spend a bunch of time with kids basically separated from these models, teaching them basic skills we think are important. What those are is really hard.

On the flip side — some English teachers say, "I don't like models because kids just cheat on their Shakespeare essays." You're not being ambitious enough. If kids are cheating on a Shakespeare essay, give them something a hundred times harder and more ambitious and have them use models to their fullest extent. Have them bring the work product back, make sure they didn't just prompt the model, make sure they own it. Ask them why it's like this. Force them to justify it.

Kids need to be good at using them. And they need to be taught they can do anything.

Closing

Host: I learn so much every time we talk. This conversation is a valuable set of food for thought — a different perspective from the most common one of unlimited buildout forever, short everything forever, no cap on demand for intelligence. Thank you for your time.

Cliff: Thank you.

# 关于"仅仅是智能"的几个意外视角
## 1. 他的投资组合本身就是他的论点——而他可能没意识到
Cliff 用了整场谈话论证"要拥有智能的互补品"（complements to intelligence），然后在最后半推半就地承认自己 80% 仓位压在 Carvana 上。这不是巧合，而是**他的仓位结构即他的理论自证**：Carvana 的护城河是**物理基础设施**——翻新中心、物流网络、二手车估值的本地密度——这些恰恰是智能永远无法蒸馏（distill）的东西。
更有趣的意外观察：他说"我超配 Carvana"的那一刻，其实是在说"我做空了纯智能"。一个坚信智能会被商品化到接近免费的人，必然会把净多头暴露在**反智能资产**上。这是对冲基金文化里罕见的"你的头寸即你的世界观"的纯粹案例。

item.title: [Lex Clips] Why Grigori Perelman's proof of the Poincare conjecture took years to verify | Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个令人意外的观察：佩雷尔曼的"三小时讲座"不是知识传递，而是免疫系统反应

表面上看，佩雷尔曼在 Stony Brook、NYU、Princeton 的巡回讲座是在"解释"他的证明——但仔细想想，这个解读是错的。他的论文已经在 arXiv 上公开，技术细节早已可被阅读。 那三小时里，一小时佩雷尔曼讲，两小时听众抛出"第 247 页引理 412 怎么推"——这其实不是在传递信息，而是一场对抗性压力测试：数学共同体在实时检验这颗大脑能否承受随机扰动。证明的"真"不在纸上，而在于那颗大脑能否在被任意敲击的位置发出一致的回声。换句话说，Lex 对话中那句"the entire thing lives in his mind"不是修辞，而是认识论的核心事实——数学真理的最终载体是一个能被对抗性探测的人类神经网络，纸只是入口。

跨领域连接：数学卡在"前 Git 时代"，而它处理的对象恰恰最不该有所有者

对话里有一句看似平淡但极具穿透力的话："the draft belongs to you"——草稿属于你。这是数学出版的默认模型：你写、你更新、社区只能在外部评论。可是请注意一个巨大的反讽：数学处理的是宇宙中最非个人化的对象（素数、流形、不变量不属于任何人），却采用了所有知识领域中最个人化的作者权模型。 软件工程早在二十年前就用 Git 和 Pull Request 解构了"作者拥有源文件"的观念，维基解构了百科，开源解构了产品——而数学的 arXiv 本质上还停留在 PDF 作者制。这背后有一个更深的张力：数学家在气质上是极端独立的（Lex 的客人也承认这一点），但他们的真理生成机制却是所有学科中最依赖社群验证的——比物理更依赖，因为物理还有仪器可以独立复核，数学只有彼此的大脑。个性最独立的职业，承担着验证最依赖协作的任务——这是一个尚未爆发的结构性矛盾，而 AI 生成证明正是把它推向临界点的那根撬棍。

隐藏的系统性真相：AI 不是在冲击数学的"产出"，而是在冲击"产出即过程文档"的独特结构

对话者担心的是 AI 论文的审稿负担，但真正的危机更深。数学是地球上唯一一个"最终产品"和"过程文档"是同一样东西的学科——证明既是结论，也是推理的全部记录。在制药、芯片设计、建筑工程里，产品（药物、芯片、大楼）和文档（临床试验报告、仿真日志、施工图）是分离的，所以 AI 可以帮忙写文档而不动摇信任链。但在数学中，当 AI 产出一个"证明"时，它同时冒充了产品和过程。于是我们突然发现：佩雷尔曼范式之所以 work，是因为纸背后那颗能被审问的大脑；而 AI 证明背后没有能被审问的"page 247 lemma 412"持有者（至少现在还不能像那样抗压回答）。因此，Lex 的客人提到的"Lean 形式化 + 众包评注 + 研究报告式讲解"这三件事，表面上是三条零散的改良建议，深处却是同一个结构重建：把"信任"从"作者的大脑"迁移到"机器可验证的核与社区可协作的壳"的双层体系。这不是数学的工具升级，而是数学认识论自佩雷尔曼以来的第一次范式转移——而且几乎没有人用这个尺度在谈它。

📝 转录文本

1. The verification ritual: how Perelman's proof became community truth

The only thing worse than that system, I think, is not having that system. Because the way that, like, our mathematical epistemology, the way that we arrive at truth, is deliberately slow and careful and precise.

Go back to Perelman's solution of the Poincaré conjecture. He puts these papers on the archive, and then people around the world are, you know, shocked by this, and so they invite him to come give lectures. He gives — he comes to Stony Brook, he comes to NYU, he comes to Princeton. He's going all around the country and the world, and he's giving three-hour long impromptu explanations of, you know, maybe an hour is him explaining what he's doing, and the next two hours are people saying, "On page two hundred and forty-seven, Lemma four hundred and twelve, I don't understand how you do this." And then he goes to the board and gives them a half-hour lecture on how he does that.

So the entire thing lives in his mind. He's done the best he can to communicate it on paper, and then it's up to us, the community, to go back through it very carefully, very — in a detailed and precise way — and agree, yes, this is a real proof of the Poincaré conjecture. And that took years to do and a whole lot of human effort.

So coming up with a solution is only the first step in the process, and that process has to be deliberate, and it has to be community-driven. And so that's what the journal system is trying to accomplish.

2. The lone-genius myth vs. the collaborative turn in other fields

— So you make a really interesting point and it kinda highlights this traditional view of a pure mathematician as this, like, lone genius who, you know, solves this singular problem and then goes explaining it to the world.

In many other fields, we have moved past the point where we can't individually advance, you know, circuit design or aircraft design or protein folding or any, you know, astronomy, and we have to work together in these billion-dollar collaborative projects. And again, I'm an engineer, so I'm thinking leadership is obviously the thing that a community needs when it's having this kind of crisis of organization and individuality moving towards a more collective model.

And that's interesting because I know so many mathematicians, and, like, by kind of organization, this is a very independent group of people who don't like being told what to do, who don't like being told what to study, who are very independent by their very nature. You know, we like solitude and working alone. That's why we, you know, spend so much time doing it.

3. A contrarian view: don't waste the crisis

— I think that's a really good point. I mean, it's interesting just to see the differences in working styles, even between math and physics, you know, with things like the Large Hadron Collider.

So I mean, let me take a contrarian view for these things, which is — you know, you should never let a good crisis go to waste. I agree the journals were overloaded, the conferences were overloaded. It always strikes me that we're doing so much work, you know, to review these things, to handle all these things, and now we're faced with the task that someone's gotta review all these AI-generated papers. And some of them are important, but, you know, it's really hard to get your community on board with doing that.

You know, I don't know what's gonna happen, but I would really be in favor for finding new models — not to replace the old ones, but to relieve some of the pressures that have come about.

4. New models: crowdsourced verification of AI-generated proofs

So, you know, I'd love to see models where, you know, maybe we take a more collaborative effort to verifying some of these AI proofs, right? So some of the OpenAI results that have dropped, you know, improvements on Fast Fourier Transform — you know, there's been tweet streams with people improving the constant. I don't really know what to make of that. You know, I'm not even on Twitter.

You know, and it seems to me that we need to figure out other modes of working, you know, for organizing what are the state of all the improvements, but also how do we organize and tame these ideas?

So it's kind of striking that, you know, the way that we think about publications is — you work hard on your draft, you post it on arXiv, and that's your draft. You know, you might update and create a new version at some point or a third version, but the draft belongs to you. It's not really up to the community to add notes. "Hey, I think you can do this argument differently. Hey, I think this is simplified this way." But maybe there are some kinds of things that we need other models for, you know, allowing crowdsourcing for our understanding to evolve. I'd be all for that.

5. Research talks, Lean, and rethinking what a paper is for

You know, the other thing is — I love giving research talks. You know, one of my favorite parts about giving research talks is you can take all of the messy complexities of the paper, the things where you just knew you had to dot the I's and cross the T's, but that wasn't really what excited you. There was some key idea, and there was some special case that really illustrated why that idea was powerful. And that's the part you really want to explain to people, because when asked, someone asks me about Lemma 57, I don't even remember it, right?

And maybe, you know, this idea that a paper is just this monolithic thing designed to be, you know, written down and completely formalized — well, now we can trust Lean formalizations to some extent for some of the technical building blocks, and that can allow us to rework the way that we do the writing in the first place, so we can put more of the emphasis on the work on, you know, the promulgation of those ideas.
