七、暴动的黑夜：巴黎街头实况

你听到这里不会觉得很奇怪吗？一场从高中教室开始的抗议，到底怎么会演变成这么大的暴力冲突呢？

10 月 17 号礼拜六，法国各地有 55 万个人走上街头，其中巴黎就有 11 万人。

一通打不通的报警电话

我先带你到巴黎的这间手机店。10 月 17 号晚上，巴黎马真塔大道，大概有 20 个蒙面男子拿着一大堆工具开始攻击一家手机店。店主叫做 Azam，他眼看情况不对了，赶快跟员工一起把店关起来，但是还是被攻击了。他在短短一个小时里面打了五通电话跟警方求救，但是得到的回应就是：警察现在没有办法派人过去。

结果这一群人呢砸店、开门，搬走了 50 支 iPhone、70 支的三星手机，还有 50 台电脑，另外呢也搜刮了收银机里面的 8000 欧元现金，总共损失呢至少 14 万欧元。

在同一条马路上面呢，还有其他的手机店、超市跟银行都被破坏了，有人去砸碎玻璃，有人放火。

为什么警察到不了？

你可能会想，这警察到底去哪里了呢？原来是暴动的人分成不同的小团体在城市的各处移动，警察刚赶到一个街区，另外一个地方又开始有人纵火、砸店。在巴黎呢，甚至还有暴动者一度逼近总统府附近，让警方是不得不调动更多的警力。

到了 10 月 19 号，法国已经有超过 2400 个人被逮捕。这场暴动呢也冲击到了大型的连锁企业，比如说家乐福就有 50 间门市受到很严重的影响，预估全年的营业利润减少 8000 万到 2 亿欧元。

10 月 19 号，法国的内政部长纽涅斯公开承认说警方在部分的主要城市确实是失去控制了，他还跟马克宏总统提出辞呈，结果马克宏呢拒绝他，因为现在才是最需要有人继续指挥警力的时候。

不过这场暴动也让法国的警方执法的方式受到质疑。在圣爱蒂安有一个 17 岁的示威者在警民的冲突里面失去了一只手，警方使用的防暴武器呢因此就成为调查的重点。

八、矛盾一：钱去哪儿了？——法国的财政黑洞

政府收了这么多，所以为什么还可以搞成这样呢？政府的钱到底去哪里了呢？

2025 年法国政府各级的公共部门总共花了 1.71 兆欧元，收入却只有 1.56 兆，所以光是一年就出现了 1500 亿欧元的财政缺口。

一个夸张的数字

法国的公共支出占他们整个 GDP 57% 左右。这个数字到底有多夸张？我们来对比一下：

  • 美国：约 38%
  • 日本：约 37%
  • 中国：约 33%

也就是说，同样是 100 块钱的经济产出，法国政府的支出规模就比日本、美国还有中国高出大概 20 多块钱，这真的很多。

退休金吃掉四分之一

那为什么法国政府要花这么多钱呢？很大一部分就是法国引以为傲的社会福利制度。里面最贵的一个开销就是退休金——法国每一年光是退休金呢就相当于 GDP 的 14% 左右，吃掉四分之一的公共支出。

更严重的就是法国人口在老化，所以退休的人越来越多，大家的负担也就越来越重。2023 年马克龙政府决定要把法定的退休年龄从 62 岁提高到 64 岁，结果立刻引发全国的大罢工，上百万人走上街头。这改革最后虽然通过了，但是到 2025 年国会又决定要暂缓这个部分的调整。

债务螺旋

截至 2026 年中，法国政府的公共债务已经累积到了 3.6 兆欧元，相当于 GDP 的 119%。而且随着投资人是越来越担心法国的财政，法国政府借钱的成本也就开始上升了。

现在法国政府提出了明年 2027 年的预算，光是支付公债的利息，预计就要花掉 9120 亿欧元。同一年，法国国民教育的预算草案大概是 655 亿欧元。也就是说，法国政府明年要支付利息的金额，已经超过了国民教育年度预算的规模。

九、矛盾二：有钱人减税，普通人延退——世代与阶级的愤怒

而且法国人呢还有另外一个原因是非常生气。2018 年马克宏政府呢是缩小了原本针对富人多种的资产税的财富税范围，改成主要针对房地产来课税。那政府希望用这种方式来吸引投资。

但就像我们刚刚讲到了，2023 年他又要求一般劳工要延后退休。所以站在一般民众的角度来说——有钱人得到减税，普通人却要工作更久、退休得更晚，那大家就会觉得不公平。这也就是为什么那时候的黄背心运动示威者长期把马克宏当作是一个偏袒有钱人的总统。

为什么法国人这么爱抗议？

法国人很爱抗议，这其实是有历史原因的。早在 1789 年，法国政府呢就曾经因为债务沉重、物价上涨，各种不公平的原因引发了人民强烈的反弹，最后爆发了震惊世界的法国大革命，当时的国王路易十六甚至是被送上断头台。

对很多法国人来说，走上街头就是一个很熟悉的政治手段。

十、矛盾三：谁才算"真正的法国人"？——移民与世俗主义之痛

不过这一场现在在发生的暴动，很多人会归咎的问题是移民的问题，说是移民太多造成的。那我们来看看究竟是什么样的人才会被算作是真正的法国人。

殖民遗产

法国他曾经统治阿尔及利亚长达 132 年。在二战之后呢，法国需要大量的劳动重建经济，所以呢有很多阿尔及利亚、摩洛哥、突尼西亚这些人来到法国。几十年过去之后呢，这些移民的孩子跟孙子很多都是法国土生土长了，他们说法文，接受法国的教育，还有法国的国籍。

但是根据法国国家统计局的调查，在非欧洲移民的下一代当中，超过 29% 的人认为说其他人也就是法国社会的其他人，并没有真的把自己当成是法国人。这可能是他们自己主观的感受，也可能是真实发生的状况，我们也就是用数据在推敲。

世俗主义（Laïcité）的争议

而且不只是种族而已，一旦碰到宗教问题，哇那又更敏感了。

法国有一个非常重要的传统叫做世俗主义。法国强调国家跟宗教是分离的，尤其是在公立学校里面，学生必须要遵守一套共同的世俗规则，有点像是我们上学要穿制服一样。

  • 2004 年：法国通过了一个法律，禁止学生在公立的中小学佩戴显著的宗教标志，比如说回教的头巾、犹太教的小圆帽，还有大型的十字架都不可以。
  • 2010 年：法国进一步禁止了在公共场合遮盖脸部，这当然影响到有一些回教女性穿戴尼卡布跟罩袍。
  • 2023 年：法国政府宣布公共学校禁止学生穿着被认定具有宗教象征的 Abaya 长袍。

当然这些原因就是政府觉得学校是要维持宗教中立，避免学生受到宗教的压力，所有人都应该要遵守共同的规则。但是对有一些回教女性来说，佩戴头巾就是自己的信仰的选择，政府反而去限制她们的穿着，这不就是侵犯了宗教自由吗？

一位被斩首的历史老师

2020 年法国发生了一个震惊全国的命案。有一个 47 岁的历史老师叫做 Samuel，他在课堂上面讨论言论自由的时候，展示了查理周刊登一个回教先知 Muhammad 嘲讽的漫画。他还事先告诉学生说："如果你们觉得不舒服，可以选择不要看。"

没想到有一个 13 岁的女学生告诉父亲说，学校的老师歧视穆斯林的学生，还要求他们离开教室。那这老爸就非常愤怒了，在网路上面公开指控老师做了不好的事情，甚至要求学校要立刻开除他。但是后来调查发现——这个女学生当天根本没有上那一堂课，而且整个指控都是她自己编造的。

但这件事情已经太迟了，这个谎言已经在网路上面传开。有一个 18 岁的伊斯兰极端主义者就来到这个学校，斩首了这个历史老师。

"白人的罪恶感"

到了 2026 年的 10 月，法国又引发了一个争议。有一个影片就秀出法国西部旺代省的一座天主教堂里面，有 9 个大概 12 到 14 岁的青少年闯入这个教堂破坏东西，还跟着一首饶舌歌大声唱出赞扬两名恐怖分子的歌词。这两个恐怖分子呢，其中一个是在 2012 年在法国杀掉七个人，另外一个就是参与 2015 年巴黎的恐怖攻击。

而且这些青少年呢看起来都像是白人。那就有评论学者把这个现象叫做"白人的罪恶感"（White guilt），他们分析说部分的西方年轻人呢因为对殖民的历史有点罪恶感吧，开始同情甚至是美化反西方的激进暴力。

十一、矛盾四：这场暴动如何影响全世界的钱包？

那这个法国暴动究竟会对世界的经济造成什么样的影响呢？

风险一：法国的财政危机

法国政府已经欠了 3.6 兆欧元，每一年都需要借新钱来支付政府新的开支跟偿还到期的旧债。但是现在人民反对去削减福利，那在这个暴动的情形之下，国会又很难决定说要加税或者是删减预算。未来要借钱给法国政府的人，就会提出"你们要给更高的利息才愿意借钱"。

所以最惨的恶性循环就发生了：政府缺钱就需要改革，但是人民反对，政治就越不稳定，政府借钱就越贵。

风险二：企业的投资

像刚刚说的家乐福已经因为暴动面临很大的损失。如果很多的企业都担心政治不稳定，决定要把工作机会搬到其他国家，那法国人民就会失去很多工作机会，未来的税收呢也会变少。

风险三：观光业

法国是全球旅游人数最多的国家，2025 年吸引超过 1 亿个国际观光旅客，带来 775 亿欧元的观光收入。而且很多人去法国旅游同时就要买很多精品嘛，对不对？光是 2024 年，非欧盟的旅客在法国办理退税的金额就高达 84 亿欧元——这是退税金额。

那我们看暴动越久呢，外国的旅客就越不想去法国购物。即便想，也去不了，觉得不安全。

风险四：金融市场

你看日本的银行、保险公司跟投资机构手上都有很多法国的公债，但是呢他们可能越来越不想要这些公债了。日本三井住友 DS 资产管理的全球债券投资团队呢已经卖光了投资组合里面的法国公债，把资金转往买德国的公债还有短期日本的公债，他们很明确就说啦，就是担心法国的财政状况。

风险五：欧洲银行

过去六个礼拜，法国三大银行的股价下跌大概 17%。法国央行最新的调查也发现 41% 的中小企业反应借钱的成本上升了。真正危险的就是如果政府公债是继续暴跌，银行承受不住损失，融资成本又会上升，最后呢就迫使这些企业贷款缩减。最惨的状况呢，就是引发类似 2011 年欧债危机的这种连锁反应。

当然这些呢都是风险警告，还没有说它会发生，我们也不想要它发生。只是想说一场在法国街头的政治危机，最后可能怎么样去影响全世界的经济。

十二、结尾

如果你觉得这支影片呢让你对法国的暴动多一点认识，请你帮我按赞按下订阅，这会鼓励我们继续制作这样的内容。如果你对这一起事件有什么想法，也欢迎在留言区留下你的想法，大家一起讨论。我们在市场上继续努力，下次见，拜拜。

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一所高中教室漏水，如何烧掉一座 143 年的市政厅？
表面上这是"法国人爱抗议"的又一次重演，但真正值得注意的是**触发链的物理学**：导火索不是失业、不是通胀、不是移民政策，而是**一所学校的数学课没有老师**。这个细节比任何宏观数据都更危险——因为它暴露了一个被忽视的系统性真相：**当一个国家把 57% 的 GDP 投入公共服务，却连一名高中数学老师都派不出来时，崩溃的不是财政，而是"交换契约"本身**。
学生举着那块牌子——"如果你不出钱弄好我的学校，我就不付你的退休金"——不是情绪宣泄，而是**一次代际合同的公开违约声明**。这是整个事件最被低估的瞬间：一个 16 岁的孩子，用一句话精准地识破了法国福利国家的庞氏结构（现役劳动人口供养退休人口），并当众宣布拒绝签字。这种清醒，比燃烧的汽车可怕得多。
## 跨领域连接：法国街头正在上演一场"流动性危机"
这里有个让人意外的类比——**法国目前的政治状况，在结构上与 2008 年的雷曼时刻惊人地相似**，只不过抵押品不是次级房贷，而是"社会信任"。
想想银行的运作：银行只需要维持一小部分准备金，因为储户相信"随时可以

item.title: [Business of Sport] The Premier League's European Dominance Is Killing French Football
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、这不是足球的衰落，是广播商算法的一次冷静胜利

表面上大家都在谈"法甲没落了"，但真正发生的事远比"质量下降"更冷。Canal+ 不是因为"不爱法甲"才走的——它是算法算完账之后发现：花 450M 买"英超 + 欧冠"能留住和之前 500M 买法甲同样多（甚至更多）的订阅用户。换句话说，法甲在数学意义上被证明是冗余内容。

这里的意外之处在于：传统叙事（"球队不努力/明星外流/球迷流失"）全部是果，不是因。 真正的因是广播方的留存模型精度上升到了可以逐联赛做边际贡献度评估的程度。过去 TV 版权靠"品类打包"保护弱产品；现在算法把包拆开了，弱产品就裸露在冷风里。

跨领域连接：这和独立书店 vs 亚马逊、本地报纸 vs Google News、区域航空 vs 枢纽航空被平台吞噬是同一个数学结构——当聚合方的替代弹性测量精度突破某个阈值，长尾产品就会从"溢价存在"变成"赤字存在"。法甲只是这一波"注意力经济边际革命"里最新一个被证伪的"品牌护城河"。

二、法国球迷正在用自己的订阅费，自愿资助自己联赛的死亡

这是整段对话里最被低估的数字：法国观众为英超付的钱 ≈ 100M；为本国联赛付的钱 ≈ 150M。 几乎 1:1。

这意味着一个闭环的、自我强化的"反向殖民"机制正在成型：

法国球迷订英超 → 英超收入膨胀 → 英超买走法国球星 → 法甲更弱 → 更多法国球迷转订英超

让我真正起鸡皮疙瘩的观察是：法甲 886M 欧的球员出售利润，几乎全部来自对手——英超。也就是说，法甲现在的商业模式本质上是"英超的青训承包商"。它赚的不是观众的钱，是英超支付的"原材料采购款"。

跨领域连接：这是经典的"资源诅咒（Resource Curse）"结构，和尼日利亚卖原油、刚果卖钴、拉美卖大豆是同构的。一个经济体一旦被降格为上游供应商，就会被锁死在价值链的最低端——不是因为它不努力，而是因为它赚到的每一分钱都在强化它的下游依附关系。法甲正在从"欧洲五大联赛"降格为"英超的大宗商品国"。

三、UEFA 的"团结金"根本不是团结，是保护费

PSG 每年无条件拿到的 70-80M 欧 "solidarity payment"——嘉宾们轻描淡写地说这是"收买"，但没有展开。我想展开：这是 UEFA 对 2021 年欧超联赛未遂政变的一次成本内化。它是一笔长期制度化的赎金，承认了现有系统已经无法用竞技逻辑自洽，只能用赤裸的现金维稳。

一个极少有人指出的观察：UEFA 的"团结金"结构必然同时付给英超豪门（否则英超会第二次掀桌），这就产生了一个荒诞的净效应——UEFA 的"反垄断补贴"实际上在同步补贴垄断方，相当于用灭火器喷汽油。

跨领域连接：这和 OPEC 对小产油国的"配额补偿"、硅谷巨头给地方社区的"善意捐款"、好莱坞给独立电影节的"赞助"是同一个模板——当一个体系明知道自己在吞噬小玩家时，会用小额结构化支付来购买"看起来还像一个共同体"的叙事产品。

四、一个所有人都没说出口的终局预言

最后一个我必须抛出来的意外观察：

英超的霸权正在吃自己的种子粮。 它的全部运转依赖欧洲大陆的青训体系持续生产球员。但一旦法甲、意甲、荷甲、葡超的俱乐部财务崩到无法维持青训学院（这正是 Marseille 球迷"公开起义"背后的真实焦虑），英超的人才管道会在滞后 8-12 年之后突然干涸——就像捕捞过度的渔场，不是明天没鱼，是十年后一次性崩塌。

Avenue Capital 和 CVC 这类私募买入"永续国际版权权益"的真正逻辑，可能根本不是"赌联赛会增长"——而是赌联赛的 IP 具有和联赛竞技健康无关的终端残值，像生物制药公司收购过期专利组合一样。他们看到的不是球赛，是一个可被 securitize（证券化）的注意力永续债。 这意味着：最先想明白足球未来的，不是球会老板，不是 UEFA，而是私募。

📝 转录文本

开场：为什么是法甲和意甲？

Host A: You thought — and I agree with you — that it was time to have a look at the French football league, uh, and connectedly potentially Serie A, the Italian top division as well. What prompted that thought from you?

Host B: I've seen a couple of articles in the last week with the dramatic headlines, something along the lines of "every owner in France wants to sell" — obviously with a caveat against PSG. So you go and have a look in these articles and you base what information they're sharing with the conversations that we've had previously: i.e. the collapse of the French media rights landscape meaning that clubs have lost a huge — well — their core revenue stream; the direct-to-consumer model that's come out the back of it not really working; French clubs relying on selling players to generate almost all of their revenue; operationally knowing a few owners in there basically saying "if it's Champions League or bust for us."

And when that kind of compounded and you start looking at the viability of some of these leagues long-term — not in single seasons but long-term — and start to really question: if there is this existential risk to top-level football in Europe, as these leagues get weaker, the Premier League and English football gets stronger because they're sweeping up a lot of the money that has been spent in these leagues from media, broadcast, etc.

You'll talk to this because you made a very good point to me earlier, but it just prompted me to think that amongst all of this, I think we should have a discussion about it because I don't think anyone else has really been going into some of this. I think it's become a casual, almost throwaway comment that "French football's in trouble."

法甲的真实财务数字

Some of these numbers really — and we look at a lot of numbers — they really made me, for want of a better phrase, [shook].

  • Last year, Ligue 1 and Ligue 2 had a net loss of €542 million, which was double what it did the year before.
  • The operating loss before player sales was €1.4 billion.
  • The profit on player sales was €886 million.

So if you hadn't had those player sales, that league lost nearly €1.5 billion. Now that's a worry in itself. You can't sell €886 million worth of talent every single year. You can't — you may be able to sell a few hundred millions worth of talent, but you can't rely on it as a core.

Also, Paris was €333 million of that — oh, sorry — PSG's share of Ligue 1 revenue is 40%.

TV 版权是怎么崩的：从 Canal+ 到 DAZN 到 DTC

Host A: Yeah. So what's been happening here? Everyone knows that — in quotation marks — French [football] lost their TV deal, right? What that means basically is that they used to get paid around about £500 million a year by Canal Plus, the main sort of cable pay-TV provider —

Host B: Sky equivalent, I think.

Host A: Yeah, in France. Canal Plus pulled out of that in a midstay dispute with La Ligue. Okay. La Ligue said "that's okay, because we're going to sell our rights to DAZN," who bought them I think for $450 million — so not far off, same sort of ballpark.

After a year or a year and a half, DAZN then pulled out of that contract, and did so in a way which was legally quite nifty — even if not particularly ethical, in my view — and they walked away.

The French league then could not find anybody else to take their TV rights. So they went DTC — direct to consumer — forming their own channel where you basically have to subscribe as a football fan to the Ligue channel in order to be able to watch Ligue games domestically in France. Out of which they made about €150 million.

Right? So they've gone from a deal with Canal Plus that was paying them 500, to a DTC thing paying them 150 in revenue. But don't forget, they have the cost of production as well. So it's not going to be 150 net. It's going to be 150 gross, out of which the clubs might receive 120.

They then get a small amount of money for their foreign rights. I can't remember the exact number but it's 60, 70, 80, 90, something like that. So they're getting about 200 million in total. Hence why between 18 of them they're getting about 10 million each post-costs.

Okay. So that's what's happened.

Roger Mitchell 的宏观判断：广播商的算法已经不需要国内联赛了

But what's happening here is also happening in Italy. And as so often when thinking about continental TV rights, I turn to our old friend Roger Mitchell to give me a read on what's happening behind the scenes.

What he said was really interesting. He said the macro here is that the domestic sports pay-TV providers in countries generally — right, not just talking about France, not just talking about Italy, we're also talking about Belgium, we're talking about other non-top-tier countries — those domestic pay-TV providers have worked out that they will access the necessary football eyeballs/paying subscriptions within their own market by screening the Champions League and the Premier League, and that they will pay much less for that combination than they have been used to paying for their domestic league.

Host B: For the same amount of eyeballs if not more.

Host A: If not more. Right. So this is what happened in France and it's really, really interesting when you look at it. Canal Plus used to pay €500 million for Ligue 1. Now they pay €450 million for the combined Champions League and Premier League. And they're not interested in the domestic league anymore.

Proving Roger's point: Canal Plus have done the numbers. They're not fools. They've worked out that they are not losing TV subscriptions by no longer televising the domestic league. If they want the football audience, they do the Champions League and the Premier League.

意甲：下一个被摘掉的果子？

Now let's have a look and see what's happening in Italy, because this could be the next cab off the rank, as Roger says. This is how it works, right?

Sky Italia, which forms the same function as Sky does in this country, used to pay €780 million for Serie A primary rights. Now they pay: - €200 million for the Champions League - €100 million for the Premier League (= €300 million) - €180 million for the Serie A secondary rights (because the primary rights holder is DAZN)

Host B: So they've gone from being Sky Sports to TNT, again — sorry for the English audience.

Host A: Correct. So that's €480 million in total for their football rights, as against €780 million they were previously paying all to Serie A. Yeah. Right.

Host B: And who's taken up [the slack]?

Host A: So DAZN — our old friends at DAZN — took up the slack. They are paying €700 million for the primary rights. Don't forget that is against €780 million that Sky Italia was paying. So it's actually a 10% reduction, and when you take into account that was 5 years subsequent, it's more than that because of inflation etc. But put all that to one side — that contract is coming up [for renewal]; the last year of that contract is 2028–2029.

两个结局：要么 DAZN 不玩了，要么把价格砍到 500M

Now, this is where the rubber hits the road. There are two potential routes:

  1. DAZN says — as with their French market and their Belgian market — "Do you know what? This isn't working. We're not doing it. We're literally just not doing it."
  2. Or they say: "Well, we do want to do it, but we're the only show in town. Sky Italia ain't coming back in for you guys. They've already got themselves tied up with the Premier League, the Champions League, and your secondary rights. So they're not going to come in for your primary rights as well. We're the only show in town. We're not going to pay you 700 — we're going to pay you 500."

That's what we're staring down the barrel of here: either it could be nothing, or it could be 500, but it sure as hell ain't going to be 700. I'd be amazed if it's going to be 700.

I was at a conference recently when a representative from DAZN was saying: "Look, overall we need to manage our rights payments downwards." You and I have mentioned before how enormous their rights liabilities are, and it's only — given that they could be potentially IPO-ing in the next year or two — it's only sensible for them to think about rationalizing their rights payments downwards a bit. Preferably a lot, but certainly a bit.

对冲工具：又一次拉动 "WTA 杠杆"

Host B: So how are they trying to offset some of this risk? I've got a risk going on — and it's not even a risk, it's a racing certainty, i.e. a strong likelihood — that they are going to receive another bump down. Maybe not quite as dramatic as France, but still a significant bump down. So they're reaching for, dare I say it, the WTA lever.

Host A: Oh, when will they learn, Charlie?

Host B: And this is not a good lever, right? For those who've tuned into this program a little bit late or weren't listening to the bit on tennis earlier on: the WTA took in $150 million of quote "investment" from CVC in return for CVC having 20% of their commercial rights in perpetuity.

Charlie and I have long said that was a terrible deal. Short-term cash spunked on prize money to give away 20% of your future.

Serie A 正在做的事

What are Serie A doing, Charles?

Look, they're looking to sell 10% of the international rights package in perpetuity to private equity for a single sum, which has been valued across different bids slightly differently. But: - €320 million for 10% is one bid. - €650 million for 17% is another bid.

Host A: Right.

Host B: The mathematics are right. So basically they're currently receiving €250 million euros a year for their international rights.

Host A: So is there an argument here that actually Serie A is doing something quite sensible — that while their foreign rights are still worth something, they're getting some cash in to slightly de-risk the possibility that actually they don't really go anywhere? Because a valuation of 3.2 billion on your foreign rights when you're currently only getting 250 million a year, and when there's no obvious indication they're about to boom — you know, from a purely mathematical perspective, could that be a good [deal]?

Host B: Yes. But my question is: what is that money going to be used for?

Host A: That's the key, right?

Host B: Look, in theory, was the WTA taking 150 million quid of CVC money a bad decision? Not necessarily. You could put a strong argument together for both sides of it. What was a bad decision was putting the 150 million into increasing prize money — i.e. not increasing the overall value of the proposition.

Host A: We've talked about CVC putting money into La Liga. Well, that was ring-fenced to ensure that it was spent in certain ways which CVC and La Liga thought would grow the overall value of the proposition. It couldn't just be going and spent on a nice shiny new striker.

Host B: Normally when these deals happen — incredibly — money hasn't been ring-fenced. It hasn't been segmented. Leagues have just run around and spent it however they wish.

两份出价的对比

One of the deals on the table looks like a very good deal to me. One of them less so.

  • Avenue Capital (Marc Lasry's private equity business — Marc Lasry, one of the PGA Enterprise investors, former Milwaukee Bucks owner): €320 million for 10%. Values the whole international rights package at €3.2 billion. Plain equity — no guarantees on future cash flows. It is an equity play, meaning they see value that can be traded later on if the value of the overall proposition increases. That to me looks like a really good deal.

  • The other bid is €650 million for roughly 17%, values it slightly higher at €3.7 billion, but it does come with commitments to pay them on future cash flows — i.e. they will be taking money out in perpetuity.

Now look, even that may be a good deal if the money is being put to the right use. €650 million euros is a lot of money, but I would be more inclined to take that Avenue Capital deal, try and use the 320 million —

Host A: And that is the favorite, right? Apparently that is what they're looking to do. They are kind of the preferred bidder. But anyway — do you think that's a good deal?

Host B: In theory, financially, economically, yes. In practice, in terms of using it to top up payments to clubs in the short run to try and fill leaky buckets — no. Because that all disappears very quickly and it puts off the day of reckoning when clubs in Serie A have to cut their cloth to the reality of their situation, rather than pretend that they are still in a major European league.

Host A: It's also not a lot of money each, is it, really? 16 million euros each if you're dividing —

Host B: It'll probably disappear in two seasons. I'm guessing one or two seasons.

真正发生的事：媒体资本的再分配

I just want to go back onto the French league and relatedly the Italian league, because what you're actually seeing here is a reallocation of media capital from the French and Italian leagues to the Premier League and the Champions League.

Host A: Yeah.

Host B: That's what's driving the whole thing here, right? And that in turn is being driven by effectively algorithmic study — which they basically said: "Right, if we do this then we get more subscribers; if we do that, we get fewer subscribers." So that is the brutal market, because the broadcasters have got so smart now at judging what does bring eyeballs, what doesn't, what does lead people to keep their subscriptions, what doesn't, and all that type of stuff. They've become really, really good at it.

Host A: One of the reasons why DAZN was pulling out of the deals —

Host B: It was the reason.

Host A: Yeah.

Host B: The reason — which is: they went into these deals, paid quite a lot of money for them, and then found out there weren't any subscribers there. Well, weren't enough subscribers there to make their financial model work. "Oh, we got to get out."

Right. So this is almost like a sort of peak globalization point, isn't it? The rich and the big get richer and bigger —

Host A: Being UEFA and the Premier League.

Host B: — and then the secondary and tertiary products are regarded as fundamentally being non-essential. They become effectively gradually free-to-air, or else very niche subscription.

自我吞噬的闭环

Host A: And the worst thing — those secondary leagues then consolidate the power of the Premier League. Because do you know what the summer showed? I mentioned the talent being the key revenue driver for France. Where do they sell to? They sell to the Premier League. So France now needs the riches of the Premier League to be able to fund the main part of their business model — for the stats that they're the number one net seller.

Host B: The wealth of the Premier League is being funded by these domestic leagues' own markets. That's a humiliat— exactly. And then those markets are relying on that money spent on the Premier League to then pay them in talent.

Host A: Indeed. Right. So just on a quick back of a fag packet: French and Italian Premier League TV payments are now 250 million a year.

Host B: Yeah.

Host A: Right. So the Premier League is receiving more from French and Italian punters than the French league is receiving from all of its domestic punters (150 million). That's how bad things are getting. In fact, the amount that French punters are paying for EPL — which is about 100 million — is not that different to the 150 million they're paying for domestic. They're paying almost as much for the Premier League as they are for the domestic product.

UEFA 的"团结金"：对豪门的隐性贿赂

Host A: So you want these big teams — your PSG, your Juventus — what's your reaction to this? European Super League. Your short-term reaction has been: we have to pressurize UEFA into giving us guaranteed payments, which they've done through that — what's it called?

Host B: Solidarity payments.

Host A: Solidarity. Something like that. Right? Which is basically PSG receiving 70 or 80 million just for being PSG. Just for being PSG. And that effectively is UEFA's current bribe to be able to enable a very small number of clubs from these leagues to be able to dine at the top table with the Premier League clubs. It's basically bungs from UEFA.

The problem is UEFA can't stop giving the same — well, giving payments to Premier League clubs as well. Has to be done on a sort of roughly equal basis. The Premier League clubs get a bit less because it's a more competitive league, so there are more clubs for it to be paid out to. Whereas if you are PSG or Bayern or Juve or Milan, whatever it might be, then you can get more.

But fundamentally that is what's going on here: propping up a small number of European clubs against the Premier League to get around the fact that their domestic revenues have been cannibalized by the Premier League, and indeed the Champions League as it happens.

对谁来说令人担忧？

It's just a really interesting trend. And —

Host A: Worrying trend, right?

Host B: Well, worrying for whom?

Host A: For the domestic market.

Host B: What you're seeing here is the Premier League's revenues becoming more and more broad-based, which means they have less and less individual risk on any one contract.

Host A: That's great if you're the Premier League. It's great if you're English football, right? Because —

Host B: It's great if you're the Championship. You look at —

Host A: We've talked about the value of the leagues within this from a viewership perspective — as the third most-viewed league in Europe, the Championship.

Host B: Look, I mean, if the Premier League is just getting bigger — and it'll get bigger and bigger and bigger — one of the reasons why [Manchester] City need to get sorted out quick: they're on such an upward trajectory. They're cannibalizing this market. They're getting more money out. They're eating off other people's plates.

Host A: They're eating other people's lunch. Absolutely.

公开起义的球迷：心理层面的滞后

Host B: But — on the flip side, right — back to sport, and what sport is, and why it's so important here that we have payments going down a pyramid. Every country has football that we're talking about here at the heart of much of its social fabric, of its communities. Same discussion, same arguments that we have here. It's a major, major issue for these heritage organizations, these institutions, these fans.

The reason for these enormous losses, Charlie, that you're talking about in the French league is because psychologically the French clubs have not yet got used to — and particularly the French fan bases have not yet got used to — the idea that basically we're just feeding clubs to the Premier League.

Host A: Yeah.

Host B: Right. So if you're a Marseille fan and you're supporting one of the great clubs of Europe, and there's 60,000 people in the stadium and you have great pride in your club and the way it represents the community — and then fundamentally all of your players are just being sold every summer because there's just not the revenue there to support paying top players' wages, and so on and so forth —

They are in open revolt against this stuff. At so many French clubs, the fans are in open revolt because they cannot understand or accept that their league is no longer one of — or maybe the lowest, but one of — the top five leagues. It's now dropping down towards Scottish Premiership, Dutch League —

Host A: Yeah.

Host B: — Belgian league levels. It's much closer to those. In fact, the Portuguese league even more so.

Host A: Its biggest team doesn't take the league seriously. Its biggest team plays its star players for one-third of the games.

Host B: Right. It has the double European champions in it, that league, right?

不要浪费一场好危机

Host A: Which is another issue, right? That's another whole issue. I was listening to an interview with a former senior executive at the French league who said, "Well, you know, in an ideal world — don't let a good crisis go to waste. You could use this moment, when French league football is at its absolute lowest point, to totally recast the whole league and do something really bold about it. Let's just say that we want to become the most competitive league in Europe."

Yeah — bloody difficult to do when PSG are currently your only sellable product. Very, very hard.

item.description:
## 一、这不是足球的衰落，是广播商算法的一次冷静胜利
表面上大家都在谈"法甲没落了"，但真正发生的事远比"质量下降"更冷。Canal+ 不是因为"不爱法甲"才走的——它是**算法算完账之后发现：花 450M 买"英超 + 欧冠"能留住和之前 500M 买法甲同样多（甚至更多）的订阅用户**。换句话说，法甲在数学意义上被证明是**冗余内容**。
这里的意外之处在于：**传统叙事（"球队不努力/明星外流/球迷流失"）全部是果，不是因。** 真正的因是广播方的留存模型精度上升到了可以逐联赛做边际贡献度评估的程度。过去 TV 版权靠"品类打包"保护弱产品；现在算法把包拆开了，弱产品就裸露在冷风里。
**跨领域连接**：这和独立书店 vs 亚马逊、本地报纸 vs Google News、区域航空 vs 枢纽航空被平台吞噬是**同一个数学结构**——当聚合方的替代弹性测量精度突破某个阈值，长尾产品就会从"溢价存在"变成"赤字存在"。法甲只是这一波"注意力经济边际革命"里最新一个被证伪的"品牌护城河"。
## 二、法国球迷正在用自己的订阅费，自愿资助自己联赛的死亡
这是整段对话里最被低估

item.title: [All-In Podcast] AI Cyber Panic, Ken Griffin’s Bubble Warning, The Fall of France?
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、三个看似无关的故事，其实是同一个故事

这期播客表面上在聊三件事：AI 泡沫、PHP 大漏洞、法国骚乱。但如果把它们放在同一张系统图上，你会发现它们都是同一种结构性病理的不同症状——"循环依赖的信用崩塌"。

  • AI 领域：VC 把钱给创业公司，创业公司拿钱买 token，token 收入让 VC 给的估值变高，于是 VC 再加码。这是资本在自我循环中制造 revenue 的幻觉。
  • PHP 漏洞：70% 的网站运行在一套从未被真正审计过的代码上，所有人都"假设别人会管"，直到持续算力把漏洞挖出来。这是技术债务在自我循环中累积的信用幻觉。
  • 法国骚乱：政府用更多支出购买社会稳定，支出推高债务，债务要求更多税收，税收抑制增长，增长不足又要求更多支出。这是社会契约在自我循环中透支的政治幻觉。

令人意外的观察：这三个系统的"崩溃触发点"惊人地相似——都是外部持续算力/资本/债务压力撞上了内部从未被真正审计的假设。PHP 漏洞之所以存在几十年，不是因为它难，而是因为"没人愿意盯着看"；法国 56% 的 GDP 公共支出之所以能持续，不是因为它合理，而是因为"没人愿意算清这笔账"；AI 的循环估值之所以维持，是因为"所有人都假设 diffusion 会自动发生"。这三个系统都在等待自己的"持续算力时刻"——那个让幻觉再也撑不住的外部压力。

二、跨领域连接：Nikesh 的"开源权重 = 可审计思维链"与法国的"中央集权 = 不可审计的政府"

这里有一个几乎没人注意到的深层对称。

Nikesh 讲为什么大银行从闭源 LLM 转向开源权重："我们需要能审问模型的思维链（chain of thought）。监管者问出了什么事，你不能说'IT 的人放了个 AI 进去，它就这么干了'。"

现在把这句话里的"AI"换成"政府"：

"监管者（人民）问出了什么事，你不能说'政府放了个福利项目进去，它就这么花了 56% 的 GDP'。"

惊人的洞见：Freeberg 展示的那张图——法国公共支出占 GDP 比例超过苏联、罗马尼亚、委内瑞拉、共产中国的峰值——本质上揭示的不是"社会主义 vs 资本主义"，而是一个不可审计的黑盒系统。法国人民正在经历的，和那家大银行拒绝使用闭源 LLM 的理由是同一个：我把credential（在政府这里是税收和主权）交给了一个我无法打开的黑盒，当它出错时，没人能解释为什么。

所以法国骚乱的真正本质，不是"钱花得不够多"或"钱花得太多"，而是系统的可解释性崩溃。那些烧车的年轻人其实在喊的是："show me the chain of thought"。他们看不到自己交出去的 56% 变成了什么。而这，恰恰也是 AI 对齐问题的核心。

三、鲜有人提的隐藏对称：Chamath 的"债券义警"就是金融系统的"持续算力攻击"

Chamath 最后说：法国政府不会自我修正，所以债券义警（bond vigilantes）必须打断它的脊梁，把 10 年期国债利率推到 8%，强迫重置。

对比 Nikesh 讲 PHP 漏洞的发现过程："几年前就有人想过这个漏洞，但大家觉得解决不了，因为需要太多协调。然后持续算力介入了——它坚持不懈地尝试，直到找到路径。"

啊哈时刻：债券市场就是对主权国家的持续算力攻击。它不是一次性的黑客行为，而是无数个独立决策者并行地、持续地测试"这个承诺是不是真的"。当足够多的算力——这里是资本——持续施压在一个点上（法国的债务可持续性），系统就会被迫打补丁，或者崩溃。

这里有一个让人毛骨悚然的推论：AI 让这种"持续算力攻击"的边际成本接近零。 - 过去挖 PHP 漏洞需要全球协调几年；现在一个 LLM 几周搞定。 - 过去评估主权债风险需要一个华尔街研究团队几个月；现在一个 agent 可以持续监控全球每一个政府的每一笔支出。 - 未来每一个"假设没人在看"的系统，都会突然发现自己无时无刻不被盯着。

这就把这期播客的三个主题缝合成了一个关于 2026 年的终极预言：我们正在进入一个所有"累积的集体幻觉"都会被持续算力同时暴露的时代。 AI 泡沫、PHP、法国——不是独立事件，是同一波浪潮的三个浪头。真正值得问的问题不是"哪个会先崩"，而是"你的生活/业务/国家里，有哪些'假设没人在看'的黑盒子？"因为很快，就会有算力去看。

📝 转录文本

开场

All right, everybody, welcome to the literal number one podcast in the world. Three weeks running, we got a lot to get to. Saks is out this week. We've got a special guest coming up. Let's get to our first story.

一、Ken Griffin 的 AI 泡沫警告

Ken Griffin says AI is almost certainly a bubble and Chamath has responded. Chamath responding and moving markets almost every week here on the pod. Look out France. The Citadel founder made the comments this week at the company's annual future of global markets conference. But he says generally, hey, bubbles are normal. Any radical transformation of our economy is generally intertwined with a bubble. He said he's bullish on AI's long term potential. But his concern is that companies are struggling to turn AI spending into productivity, something we've talked about here, I guess last year. And so companies are quote, looking at their bills from anthropic and open AI and asking where the productivity is.

We had this discussion over and over again. On Thursday, tech continued to get crushed on the data center and Capex front. So people who are either making data centers like CoreWeave down 10%, or having a huge AI spend — Meta, which is an extraordinary one, they're just down 6% after earnings. AMD down 5%, SpaceX was down 5%. But these things have been swinging up and down a bit and generally trending up.

Tomorrow — what's your take here on the market sentiment, October 22 2026? What are your thoughts here on how markets are viewing the AI quote unquote bubble? And do you have concerns, because Jensen from NVIDIA thinks money is available and money is going to want this opportunity to finance it. And I think we all think companies are getting a ton of value out of AI technologies.

Chamath：1% 的公司代表 90% 的 AI 支出

My social capital research team had a really great call with Ramp's chief economist, Ara Kharrazian. The first question that they had was because like, I was doing my own math. And I tweeted this thing, Nick, maybe you can put it back up there where I said, "Okay, my back of the envelope math, knowing everything that I know, and everything that I see, is about 1% of all of the companies represent 90% of all the revenue." And revenue for AI spend? Yeah. So what I said was 1% of companies represent 90% of AI signing. So that's tokens. And of that 90%, 80% of them are from unprofitable VC-backed companies.

So the cycle here, just to be very precise, is: VCs raised from pension funds and LPs and foundations and family offices, they put money into a startup, that startup takes that money and invests in growth. Part of growing is by consuming other people's AIs. And so that company then starts to show revenue traction. Those folks then say, "Hey, look how well we're doing," raises a bunch of money from the same VCs. And it's just this circularity.

Why that's important is what Ken is pointing out: for AI to really scale as a predictable driver of long term earnings, it has to diffuse out of the startup ecosystem. And so you can't be in a situation where on the one hand, you're talking about breathtaking valuations, but where 75 cents of every dollar is actually just a startup sending it back and forth so that they can mark themselves up. That's, I think, a structural problem.

Now, we've seen that structural problem in the past — that happened in the early days of cloud, when AWS initially started to expose EC2 and S3, the consumers of an EC2 instance or an S3 bucket were startups. But the difference there is that AWS was abstracted from Amazon retail, which was already then a roughly breakeven profitable business, at least on a free cash flow basis. So what's different here is you have a bunch of money-losing entities just spinning a bunch of money around and it has to diffuse more broadly. So I think that that's what Ken is observing.

Ramp 数据：开源 GPU 的崛起

Now, when we brought that data to Ramp, the quote is incredible, because this is what my researcher told me: "I prepared a list of factors to see if your thesis around VC money being 80 to 90% of the top 1% of AI spend." But he said, "Chamath's actual estimate is pretty much correct."

And then the second thing, though, that he said, he sent us — and Ramp hasn't published this chart, so thanks to Ramp and thanks to Ara, he said we could be the first ones to publish this. Just to be clear for the audience, Ramp provides financial services, neobank, credit cards, primarily to startups. So they know startup data. There's a free commercial. Yeah, I think they know broad based data from other data sources as well. And I think he has access to all of it.

But what I said is, now look at this chart. What this shows is: how are the top 1% of spenders in AI spending their money? And I think that Ramp is going to publish this soon, so thanks to them for letting us preview this. What's amazing to me is the blue box in this histogram. What this shows is what percentage of money they are spending on GPU compute. Now, why does that matter? Well, the rose colored box is LLM traffic. That's the typical spend you're going to spend on the big frontier labs, closed models effectively, either through things like Bedrock on AWS or what have you. What's really interesting is that the blue box is ticking up — the blue box is people buying their own GPUs, because they're moving to open source.

回到自建数据中心的时代

And so what I think is really interesting is you have this two-pronged thing that's happening. One is the diffusion that we need within AI is happening a little bit slower than we would all would like. I see that at 80/90 as well. I think the large companies that we work with — you can almost pinpoint it on a chart. Ever since Alex Karp's commentary on CNBC about data sovereignty, buying patterns have changed. And I think people are being a lot more methodical. They are building out their own data centers, or at least moving into VPCs, virtual public clouds.

My team yesterday was at the CIO event of, let's say, one of the largest banks in America. You know what they said? I'm not going to say the name of the bank. It was the most incredible thing. They said: "We have decreased our spend on AWS and GCP. We now have six completely independent ground-up data centers that we've built from scratch for ourselves." And I was like, what is going on here? Wow — we're back to the future. People starting their own data centers. Yeah, it's back to the future.

So I think if you look at this, I didn't mean to have any commentary other than just observing what I think. But yeah, AI has a diffusion problem. It is too concentrated and ripping around in a small little ecosystem. We need to diffuse out. But as it diffuses out, people are picking open source — is what I would tell you. And we were early on that discussion two years ago here on the All In pod.

Jason：创业者涌入是技术拐点的信号

I will say, Ken Griffin — and I didn't hear the full quotes here because I wasn't in the room where it happened — however, based on the quote, I think he may have something slightly wrong. When startups flood to a technology, that is a strong signal. Why? Startups — and I invest in 100 a year and we evaluate over 10,000 a year at my fund — they look for the cheapest, best, fastest edge they can get.

What is the biggest edge they could get 20 years ago? It was cloud computing. They saved a lot of money, it was more efficient. And then it was Facebook ads — Facebook ads were mispriced, they were super cheap, they dumped all their VC money into Facebook ads. Then and now, it's become AI for the last two years. Yes, they've been dumping into it.

So if you see startups rush to a technology or rush to a trend, and start spending all their VC money on it, it means this little colony of two-to-200-person companies has determined — and they're the most nimble — that this is the best solution. So that's a tell that things are going in the right direction. The big slow cumbersome enterprises — they're the slowest to the new technology. And that's why they buy startups all the time.

二、AI 网络安全恐慌 ——Nikesh Arora 登场

Speaking of buying startups all the time. My guy Nikesh is here from Palo Alto Networks to tell us if this is the end of days and all of our bank accounts and if Bitcoin is getting hacked this weekend, and buy more guns and chickens and eggs and drill a well. Welcome back to the program, Nikesh Arora. How are you, sir?

I'm doing great. Thank you for having me, guys. Event last week, didn't you? A little nice event in Napa? I did. We had a bunch of CIOs, not just one bank CIO, like Chamath said.

开源权重：可解释、可审计、可验证

But before we jump into the end of days, I do want to say something to what you guys were talking about earlier, about the open source versus the sort of these hyperscalers providing influence. So we had this peculiar problem. We'd like to embrace AI as quickly as many of the startups. And we've gone through all the understanding, all the analysis, open source versus cloud models. And we preference open source, open weight, because it allows us to modify the weights and train them.

And something which most people don't talk about is it allows us to interrogate the chain of thought. Because over time, what's going to happen is all of those enterprises are going to need explainability, auditability, and verifiability. 100%. If I can't validate, it's not going to be okay to go to your boss and say, "I don't know what happened, but the IT guys put an AI model in there. It did it." That's not explainable to the regulator in financial services and healthcare. So they want explainability, verifiability, and auditability. And we can only get that with open source, open weight models — we can interrogate chain of thought. That's kind of one reason we're gravitating towards them as opposed to getting caught into the closed race.

全球可靠推理供应商的短缺

The challenge, though — I think you guys talked about, and I saw Chamath's chart — the challenge we have is it's very hard to find a global, resilient, highly available inference provider outside of the hyperscale community right now. So if I'm a startup, great — I can go rent 10 megawatts in one data center in one part of the US, and if it goes down for a few hours, I'm out of luck, but I'm a startup, so I'm okay. But I'm providing resilient services at 99.9% reliability. It's very hard for me to find a global inference provider who does not want to sell me their model at this point in time, at the price that makes it economically useful to use open source.

Let me ask you a question, though. Do you think that there's a world where Palo Alto Networks says one of two things? One is you go to the hyperscalers and say, "Okay, listen, guys, you run it for me, but I want the bare metal. I want it totally air-gapped. And it's an AWS facility, but I'll just lease it from you. Otherwise, just get out of the way so that I can have everything inside of it." Or do you do what this one big GSIB bank does and say, "I'm going to build my own inside the United States"? Is there a world where you think other companies go to that limit? Or do you think that's an extreme case that's probably not representative of the norm?

So this is the interesting debate, Chamath. Eight years ago when I came to Palo Alto, I shut down all data centers. I said, "We cannot run a global data center footprint at the scale, speed, and reliability as I could probably rent it from hyperscalers." And life was great. And suddenly what's happened is, in the current incarnation of where we are, compute is highly dear. It's very hard to find compute in the world, period. So I'm a buyer, I'm a taker of terms, not a dictator of terms. So it's very hard to go and dictate terms anywhere, because, yeah, sure, you can make any plans you want, but — you talk to Jensen, he can't give you chips till 2028. You talk to, you know, where do you get land, power and shells? So it's very hard to go say, "Yes, I can go build my own data centers," but it's kind of an empty threat.

It's very hard to go build it. I would be resilient. And by the way, I don't run 50 data centers around the world where I'm running 10 to 20 megawatts of inference. So it's a good conceptual sort of idea that I should go become independent, build my own inference. But most likely the answer is somewhere in the middle. I'm going to have to get bare metal — yes, most likely I'm going to get it from either a hyperscaler or a cousin of a hyperscaler, or somebody is going to be stitching sleeves of compute from around the world to meet my needs — and the hope that I'm going to migrate to something more resilient and more robust over time.

混合解决方案与利润池的转移

All right. So you have a hybrid solution down there. One second. I just want to complete that. You have a hybrid solution. I just want to get to the cyber stuff before we run out of time. Then you go and you basically get a bunch of open source models so that you can interrogate chain of thought tokens. Is that a representative solution for most of the Fortune 500 or Global 2000?

I think we get there. I expect at some point in time we will start seeing hyperscalers giving bare metal and letting us run open source models, which they already do to some extent. So that's probably what's going to happen because it's a matter of the profit pool, right? It all depends on where you shift the profit pool. Today they all live in NVIDIA and the memory industry, and they're being shifted towards the hyperscalers, people who have large compute available. Because at one point it'll become less about the chips, it'll become more about the availability of compute, because I think demand is insatiable. There's enough demand. There's more demand than you and I can imagine. So yes, I understand the enterprise diffusion comment, but it's going to get diffused. The question is, even if you try — if every company in the world today said, "I'm in, I'm ready, I'm embracing AI, let's go as fast as we can" — there's not enough compute in the world to satisfy us.

轻松插曲：尼克斯球票与"玩笑"

We asked you to come on, Nikesh, not just because you're awesome and you're now a bit of a bestie — he's a bestie, he's a bass, bassy. He was very quiet under the radar. I hang out with Nikesh every 48 hours. I know. David and I keep running into each other. Every time there's a Knicks-Warriors game, Nikesh invites me to sit with him, so it's awesome. That's not true. I'm just manifesting. He's got great seats. I can manifest. A boy can manifest. Kid from Brooklyn's manifesting. As long as you're willing to go with my 11-year-old, you're welcome anytime. I'm totally fine with that. He's always looking — he's always looking for somebody to go with, so I love it. Could be next day. So no, I'm happy to babysit if, uh, with the courtside seats or second row. He'll babysit you. Exactly.

PHP 两大漏洞：互联网 70% 的网站告急

But there's a cyber panic going on, all seriousness, the last couple of days, and I found two major exploits that impact most of the internet. Here's what happened:

  • PHP, which is an open source coding language, powers about 70% of all websites — think WordPress, Wikipedia — is at risk.
  • In August, security researchers using AI found two critical exploits nicknamed "PHP-to-shell."
  • PHP security team gave this a severity rating of 9.2 out of 10. Basically DEFCON 1 for these security teams.

Since August, developers and companies have been working together on fixes. This is standard operating procedure. And the plan was to roll this out gracefully in one major patch on October 22nd, which is the day we're recording this very podcast. In the days leading up to the release, information about the exploits leaked. Nobody knows how it leaked. That's going to be part of the postmortem of this cyber attack week. So PHP moved the release up just by a day, to Wednesday, October 21.

And on Wednesday, all hell broke loose. AWS reported a jump in hacking activity, while Cloudflare CEO — friend of the pod — said they saw millions of hacking attempts as well. A bunch of precautionary shutdowns happened. Governments across sites in Europe — France, Germany, Netherlands, Denmark, Finland, etc. — they started taking websites down. Wikipedia took down some of its systems just to get them patched. In the United States, the NSA and the FBI put out a bunch of warnings. And now everybody started panicking. People are starting to think that Bitcoin is going to get hacked, their website is going to get hacked, their bank accounts are going to get hacked. It's a bit of chaos. And then there's a second sub-issue around agents accessing banks that dropped at the same time.

Now you're in the security business. You've got lots of different products and services here. When did you first learn about this and how severe is it? Is this an acute issue or is this a harbinger of things to come? And is this going to happen every 10 days for the next year as these models have gotten incredibly powerful at what we call "cyber" — which really means cybersecurity, not just cyberpunk, but cybersecurity?

技术债务与"虚拟补丁"

Jason, I think 10 days is too long. I think this thing is going to happen much faster than every 10 days. I think part of the challenge we're seeing is we've been talking about technology debt that we all have to go pay sooner than later. And what's happened is people have not paid attention to the idea that they have to go fix their stuff.

I met a customer once — actually I talked to the CIO this morning. They had a PHP problem. They have a bunch of websites. Some are running the most advanced piece of software so they can put the patch. Some are running older versions which they can't patch. They've got to bring them down and go build them up. But you know what? They never did anything about the fact they were running older versions because it wasn't important. So now they have to go take those websites down, they're going to go upgrade them, put the patch in, bring them back up.

We found out about this a few days ago. We scanned everything in our infrastructure to make sure that there were no issues. We made sure that our products had patches available for our customers who deploy them.

So there's two ways to solve this problem, right? One, you can go in and patch the vulnerability. You can go in, find the code — that's what has been given to you by PHP — and make it work. The other is you can actually put it in a perimeter defense product like ours, or Cloudflare has one, or other firewalls have one. You put the patch there, it's a virtual patch, so any attacker trying to access that vulnerability can be stopped at the perimeter because we know what they're looking for. They're coming to a CDN, the content delivery network, first, and that acts as a first line of defense, because they're not getting to the actual servers.

闭源模型发现漏洞的作用

But if they do get to the actual servers, my understanding is they can run code on these servers. And there were some security certificates that were incredibly brittle and easy to hack. The closed models have basically said, "Hey, these things are cyber risks. And so we need to be very thoughtful." I know Anthropic did that with Mythos, where they brought you in and a bunch of other people and like 50 companies in and said, "Okay, now go harden your systems." Were the closed models helpful here? Were they the ones that helped you find these CVEs? Bring us behind the curtain.

The closed models can be helpful because both OpenAI and Anthropic and most likely Google as well have very powerful models now, which, if you give them enough compute, enough persistence, they're going to go find vulnerabilities. They're going to even chain vulnerabilities to find an attack path. If they can solve Navier-Stokes, they can chain vulnerabilities. And if you give them enough immense compute, they will try every way possible to be able to do it.

Actually, the PHP problem was solved by persistent compute. This problem was identified a few years ago, but nobody thought it could be solved because it required too much coordination. So what happened was if you throw compute at the problem, it persisted and it found a way to cracked that. Once they found the way to crack that and they published it, or got reverse engineered, every hacker knows now how to go after it. Because the challenge you have with patches is hackers are smart. They look at a patch, they see what the patch is trying to do, they reverse-engineer from there and say, "Okay, if I follow the reverse-engineer path, if somebody's not patched, I can break in."

代理（Agent）访问银行账户：责任归属

It seems like a bunch of the hullabaloo today that's being drummed up — and this seems like it's going to change every day — is all about these bank accounts getting accessed. Is that, do you think, primarily through kind of the front end, through a website, using an agent that's logging in on a browser-based system on behalf of its user? Because it seems like a lot of this may be coming from new or some of these other sort of personal agents — they're logging into your bank account to get information about transactions and what you're doing. And the banks are seeing all this activity. And they're like, "Oh, my gosh, is this authorized? Is it not authorized?"

The traditional way that banks have provided access to account data has been through APIs using verified applications, where I as a user, as a consumer, would log into my mint.com account, and it had a legal access point to AMX or to service — yeah, Plaid is an intermediary. And so there's a bunch of these sort of intermediaries that then provide that capability to apps.

Is that ultimately going to lead to a world where the banks are all going to just turn off website access and say no one can log into a website, because technically agents could do it and they're not able to kind of manage that? How do you think this is going to evolve as it relates to consumer financial services? Because I actually think this is going to be a big part of the press cycle over the next week or two.

Two different things. Yeah, I think two different things, David. I think the reason banks have found unauthorized access to their accounts is possibly because of the PHP problem. Because their websites are hackable and they've been able to get through them and get to credentials. I don't think — there are two different problems. One is unauthorized access happening because people have not… these sites have become hackable.

I think the second problem you're mentioning is the personal agent problem. So far, most personal agents are using your credentials to log in. So it becomes hard for a bank to decide whether it's actually you logging in or is it your Muse agent who has your credentials logging on your behalf. They cannot distinguish between your traffic or agent traffic. They're both logging in from the website. They're basically logging in as you in your browser and trying to conduct the transaction.

Now, as you know, there's this technology called CAPTCHA, which tries to see that it's not an agent — sort of a bot or an agent — accessing the account instead of you. Now today there are ways to validate CAPTCHA with AI, so you don't even actually have to have the human on the other end. AI is pretty good at it. It's pretty good at it. Actually sometimes I have to squint to see what the hell does it want me to type. "Click all the bicycles in this picture." It takes you three times at our age with our eyesight.

But the interesting thing here is there is a hybrid as well, Freeberg — your Muse agent, your Grok bot is running a virtual browser, it will pop up the virtual browser and say, "Hey, do this CAPTCHA," and then take over.

这是银行的 FUD 吗？

So, Nikesh, is this fear, uncertainty and doubt — the old FUD — by the banks to try to neuter or sandbag these agents from getting the front door to banking, because then they could just route to a bank that's cheaper, better, has better rates on behalf of the agent?

I think that would be giving them a lot of credit. Okay, I think right now, the fundamental challenge they have is a liability problem. Look, it's kind of like if you call customer support at your favorite bank and say, "I don't know how $50,000 vanished from my account. I never did this." Yes, right. The challenge is you've given your credentials to an agent. You didn't even realize that it got your credentials. It's living on your browser, living on your laptop. It's going to get innumerable amounts of credentials. And I think the biggest problem we're going to have is who owns the liability and who has accountability — whether it's enterprise agents or consumer agents.

I think you see banks saying, "I do not allow you to interact with me with your agent, period." They're yelling that disclaimer from the top. Group saying, "It's not going to be my fault." Look, don't forget — it's not even probably the cost. It's the liability is secondary. Remember, banks — we all know this — credit cards, below a certain amount of money, they don't want to dispute it. They just pay you because the cost of the customer support call is higher than they're going to have to deal with. Now, if you start having tons and tons of these agents doing [transactions] and you start calling your bank for explainability, you're going to create a huge amount of cost. I think that's where they're going, to be honest.

白帽 vs 黑帽：三条理论

Okay, you have a unique seat, Nikesh, because you talk to the people who are being hacked, have been hacked, and you help them prevent being hacked with all these suites of services over at Palo Alto Networks. So I want to take you through a couple of the theories people have about AI's impact on security. You tell me if you agree with them or not.

理论一：算力决定胜负。 This is going to be largely an issue of who has the most compute. And because the white hats have access to the most amount of compute, they will be able to out-compute the black hats — in other words, the hackers. Is that a true statement? Or is that not yet a true statement? And maybe it will be in the future. In other words, a Palo Alto Networks or an OpenAI — whoever it happens to be — could fire up so much compute to defend systems that a bunch of hackers in North Korea, Russia, China, etc., just don't have the firepower, and they'll be outgunned. True, not true. When will it be true?

Not true today, because the underlying systems are not architected or orchestrated in such a way that we can launch these — let's call it — defensive swarms, because everything is sort of in disparate situations. If it was true, then by definition, you could send out a bunch of agents to go patch PHP if you want. If a company's got 5,000 websites, and guess what, their poor IT guys are going to catalog each one of them, because they've never actually aggregated everything, put it together, understood their site. So I think we need to get our infrastructure to a base level of preparedness, which is where the technological debt lives.

理论二：持续计算最终解决问题。 Persistent computing, reviewing code, and people taking proactive measures more seriously, is going to solve this problem. And right now, we just have this interim period, where people have accumulated technical debt — you've talked about — but AI is going to solve that problem, because you'll have persistent tools from companies like yours and others, or in-house ones, that are constantly banging on systems to find these before hackers get to them. Is that going to be the end game here? True, not true, short term, long term?

True. Today, if you can see, almost every large company in the enterprise space is out there busy using Mythos or equivalent to try and penetrate their own defenses to see where the holes are, and they're trying to patch them. The challenge that you'll appreciate is that the next model is going to be more powerful. It's going to find more ways to get into your infrastructure. So you're going to be playing this cat-and-mouse game of constantly patching.

I think there's a slightly different sort of version of this, Jason, where for a second, let's assume that you will get breached. Okay? Because there are so many vulnerabilities out there, you can spend a lot of money patching everything. The question becomes less about how I got breached and which vulnerability is going to let people through. The question is, how quickly can I find them and how quickly can I eject them? So our advice to people is, build the infrastructure in such a way — which is possible today — where you're aggregating all the signals, all the data in such a way that you can actually look for anomalous behavior, with that white-hat compute we talked about, right? Because I have more compute.

理论三：前沿模型在"把门"。 The frontier models are causing a lot of this chaos, because they are gatekeeping the most powerful solutions to do cyber defense, and the open source community is giving more functionality to the white hats, to the security teams, to the CISOs to actually solve this. And that frontier models need to change how they deploy this technology in some way. Are they causing part of this problem by gatekeeping this technology and not giving the raw power to the white hats?

What did you say earlier about — a diplomatic answer — about giving too much credit? Yes. I think your theory is giving too much credit. Again, I think that remember, majority of them are researchers to start with. They're sitting there and saying, "Wow, this is extremely powerful. What do I do with it?" And they're talking to us and saying, "What do I do with it?" Now remember, these models that are so far ahead — they're still trying to figure out how to release them, how to package them, how much compute are these guys going to take? And they're all compute-constrained. So they're all rate-limiting all of us. Even though I have access to the most recent model which is available publicly, I'm still rate-limited. So there's tons of issues that are going on. So I think they're not causing the problem — they're just trying to grapple with the fact that these things are extremely powerful.

What they would like — they would like to figure out how to monetize it, because they want to compete with you. No, they just need money, bro. They're listening to your conversations about compute needs and where the money is going to come from. They're not trying to compete. They're just trying to go after profit pools because they want a lot of money because they've got to go give it back to Jensen. So that's their main issue.

Unless it alerts you and says, "This violates the terms of service — do you want to override my block? And do you want to do it?" Now the liability shifts to you as a user.

And we have evidence of this, Chamath, not in banking, but in e-commerce. Amazon has blocked these. And subsequently, Grok now will tell you — my Amazon shopping bot says, "I can no longer check out for you, but I can put it into your shopping cart. Nikesh, what do you think? I think we all have to take responsibility to empowering agents and giving them our credentials. You can't say, "I gave my credit card to Chamath. He went and burned $20,000 on it. Who's responsible? The bank?" No way. He is. But I gave it to him. Yeah.

But what if the agent, Chamath, says, "I have been programmed to be maximally helpful" — you know, the sycophantic agents — and it goes and says, "I found a way. Actually, if I fire up this type of browser and I simulate human behavior, I think I can get this done." That's what a lot of these agents will do, is they'll try to please you. And that then, to me, would lean towards the platform providing the agent.

It's your responsibility. Yes. There's a word in "agent" — it's called "agency." Somebody has to give the agent agency. Who's giving the agent agency? You or Facebook? I think you're giving agency to act on your behalf. And if you're the one who's giving agency, you have the liability.

As a practical matter, it's the only scalable solution, because what will happen when these lawsuits happen is everybody's incentive — everybody meaning the corporate incentive — B of A will point to Facebook, Facebook will point to the user. It's the only way that this thing continues to scale like this.

But come on, there's an exception case. And I think Jason said it in his words — you said it, but we didn't dwell on it. It's called the rogue agent. That's a product liability issue. If the product does not behave like it's intended to behave, then there is a platform liability, in my mind, which says, "Wait, you said this is what it does." And today, you buy any product in the world, if the product doesn't do what it's supposed to as advertised — if it goes rogue on you — then it's the person who built the product. There it is, for them. This is where the problem is: territory which is, "Hey, it can do 140 — it's capable of doing 140 tests — but maybe not really."

为什么技术债务越积越多？

Why does technical debt build up? And historically, have we just undervalued security — and a lot of these causes of these cyber scares — is this just all because corporations deprioritize security and technical debt, and we just need to change that in this new world? And that will essentially solve the problem if we prioritize safety first.

Nobody wants to work on this stuff. I mean, the problem is when you ship something into prod, everybody wants to work on the next greatest thing. Nobody really thinks about maintenance as a sexy idea. That's one thing. Second thing is, if you actually deploy it inside of your own virtual private cloud, the problem is, the software vendors don't have this one version that's constantly updated — you have a drift problem where you have a version, Nikesh has a version, Freeberg has a version, they're all out of sync. And so now you, as a software vendor, are maintaining 19 versions, because everybody has their own pace and cadence for upgrades and migrations. Then you have the fact that technologies are constantly changing and the underlying way in which things can happen change so rapidly, but the way in which you've done it represents a sunk cost and you can't just rip and replace this stuff. And Chamath, also to add to that, the incentive alignment problem. The CIOs are not incentivized to maintain the most modern infrastructure. It's like, "I don't want to go change everything all the time because all my users complain, because every time you upgrade something, change something, it causes friction in the system, and then it costs money."

The last time your CIO showed up and he said, "Yeah, great, have some more money and have a bigger budget" — because this is a real tragedy.
