### 1. 这不是三次独立战略，是同一个剧本演了三遍
Jassy 这场访谈里最被忽略的事实是：他正在用**同一套剧本**跑第三轮，而几乎没有人识别出这个模式。
- **2001–2003**：内部基础设施痛点 → 诞生 AWS - **2022**：履约网络过度建设 → 区域化重构 → 速度与成本双降 - **2024–2026**：AI 算力稀缺 → 垂直整合 + 2200 亿美元 CapEx
而最微妙的证据藏在 Annapurna 这桩收购里。Jassy 亲口承认：**他们当年不是为了 AI 芯片而买的 Annapurna**，最初只是想做一张虚拟化网卡（NIC），把服务器"几乎 100% 让给计算"。但同一个团队后来做出了 Graviton，又做出了 Tranium。换句话说，Annapurna 是一个被买下的"**芯片期权**"——Jassy 当年并不知道未来需要什么芯片，但他知道自己需要**一个可被反复召唤的芯片团队**。十年后这个期权兑现为对抗 Nvidia 的筹码。这是教科书级别的"可选性资产（optionality asset）"投资，但以收购形态呈现，让大多数

item.title: [Business of Sport] The Premier League Is Eating Europe, Rahm Walks Away From $100m, & Infantino Rises Again
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、所有故事其实是同一个故事：体育"中产阶级"的塌陷与"金融提取层"的降临

表面看，本期节目在讨论四件不相关的事——WTA 的财务困境、LIV Golf 2.0、因凡蒂诺的政治求生、法甲的媒体权崩塌。但把它们放在同一张桌子上，你会看到同一个系统性现象的四副面孔：一层"金融提取层"正在体育产业的中间层上方悄悄凝固。真正的游戏已经不在球场上，而是在税法条款、永续权利金、NOL（净营业亏损）结转和 DTC 替代曲线里。

  • CVC 用 1.5 亿美元换 WTA 20% 永续商业权益；
  • BC Partners 用 3 亿美元债务工具，试图锁定 LIV 高达 50 亿美元的 NOL 税盾——相当于以折扣价购买未来 10 亿美元的企业所得税抵免；
  • Avenue Capital 用 3.2 亿欧元买意甲国际版权 10%（永续）；
  • UEFA 的"团结付款"则是用联赛收入内横向转移，把 PSG、拜仁、尤文强行留在"顶级俱乐部"的角色里。

让人意外的观察：所有被"救助"的组织都以为自己拿到了资金——但本质上，它们正在把自己转化成一种税务工具、永续现金流资产或政治工具。资本方的真正回报根本不在这项运动是否兴旺上。这就是为什么 BC Partners 派出的是债券基金经理（Ted Goldthorpe），而不是股权投资合伙人。

二、BC Partners × LIV 的真正本质：制药业的"税务倒置"被搬进了高尔夫球场

Pat 对 BC 结构的拆解是本期最重要的技术性洞见，但他没有把这个模式和一个更宽的图景连起来。

跨领域连接：BC Partners 对 LIV 的操作，本质是一种"损失收割（loss harvesting）"。这种玩法在以下几个产业早就是标准动作： - 大型制药公司的"税务倒置"：以收购爱尔兰壳公司的方式降低有效税率； - 美国地方报业的私募股权收购（Alden Global Capital、Gannett）：接盘亏损报纸，不是为了做新闻，是为了抽离房地产与压低劳动力； - 加密货币寒冬里的"NOL 猎人"：2022–2024 年专门以极低对价收购破产加密公司，为的是把它们的净营业亏损用在其他赛道的利润上。

Dean Burmeister 那段关于"kids and rhinos"的采访之所以令人毛骨悚然，是因为他正在无意识地扮演制药公司代言人：讲一个关于使命的温情故事，让观众忽略背后其实是精密的财务工程。Pat 感到"slightly distasteful" 的那一刻，其实隐约闻到了ESG 式话术首次大规模入侵职业高尔夫的味道——道德叙事成了税务结构的糖衣。

三、FIFA 的真正统治者不是因凡蒂诺，是迈克尔·里基茨

Sephrin 失败的表层原因是"没趁热打铁"。但真正的深层原因是：他误读了 FIFA 的权力地理学。

当牙买加足协主席 Michael Ricketts 坦白"this is about the cash"——4000 万美元比道德立场重要——他不是在腐败，而是在精准表达一个被欧洲长期低估的政治集团的理性偏好：加勒比 + 非洲 + 亚洲小国。这个集团手握不成比例的 FIFA 投票权。Montigulani 之所以退出竞选，是因为他发现连 Concacaf 内部的小岛国都不买他的账——而这些小岛国名义上在他治下。

跨领域连接：这个结构与联合国大会的投票政治几乎同构。欧洲永远以为自己掌握着"道德话语权"，但联大上的小国集团早已学会用投票换基础设施——这正是中国"一带一路"外交的核心机制之一。因凡蒂诺本质上在 FIFA 内部运行着一个微缩版的"全球南方外交体系"：他发给小国的世界杯分成，就是他的 BRI。

Sephrin 以为自己在对抗一个腐败对手；他真正面对的，是一套替代性的全球治理体系。他输，是因为他从未真正理解自己在和什么对抗。而 UEFA 现在转向"法律途径"，是典型的欧洲式回退——当政治牌打不开时，去诉诸规则。但他们将再次发现：规则本身也是政治的产物。

四、把四段故事缝合在一起的那条隐线：在关键时刻的集体精神退缩

节目开场，Pat 嘲弄 Charlie 的"reverse Kirsty"——需要被打一巴掌才能上场。如果你带着这只耳朵听完整期，会发现每一个失败案例的本质都是同一种精神退缩：

  • Sephrin 本来攻势正盛，却在关键一拳收了半力；
  • WTA 主席明知财务模型不可持续，却不敢对球员说真话；
  • LIV 的律师在法庭上大声宣称"球员自由是我们的基石"——所有人都知道这是弥天大谎，但没人敢当面戳穿；
  • 法甲俱乐部明知自己已经不是顶级联赛，却集体拒绝完成心理哀悼；
  • John Rahm 为什么能走？因为他敢于把 1 亿美元无担保债权一次性清掉——他是整期节目里唯一一个真正做出"硬选择"的人物。

最让人意外的转折：Charlie 和 Pat 自己也在同一个模式里。他们自嘲"没人比我们更喝 LIV 的 Kool-Aid"，"别人都不聊 LIV 了只有我们还在聊"——这段自嘲其实无意中暴露了体育商业评论的最大结构性偏差：评论者与被评论对象共享同一种"再给一次机会"的乐观偏见；他们用"下周我们再看看"的节奏，推迟一个早就该做出的终局判断。

这就是本期播客真正的"啊哈时刻"：在体育资本主义的末端游戏里，真正敢说"结束了"的声音，永远来自圈外。圈内权威——无论是球员、主席、投资人，还是评论员——都因为生计、情感或叙事惯性，被困在"再等一下"的集体幻觉里。John Rahm 之所以显得突兀，是因为他做了一件圈内人几乎不会做的事：他不等了。

WTA 的财务迷局：Valerie Camo 的"同酬使命"

Should we crack on with the podcast that I sent you — out of interest, from the WTA?

Yes, from the chairwoman, I think, of the WTA — Valerie Camo. She went on the Andy Roddick podcast Served. It was just interesting for us because we had speculated a couple of weeks ago about the WTA's finances — because it had become apparent during the US Open tennis, during presentations that were made to players and their agents at that time, that the cash balance of the WTA at the end of this year was likely to fall as low as $15 million, and that during the course of 2026 it looked like they were going to have lost on an operational basis $25 to $30 million — having taken in $150 million of third-party investment from CVC four years ago, which is being paid out annually in tranches of $30 million. The last tranche of $30 million is next year, 2027.

So we were speculating about what does this actually look like? Basically what's happened is that all of this extra money that's been taken in has been sprayed around on increasing pay levels. We were not very optimistic about the idea of using capital investment to boost prize money before revenues are able to afford it. We weren't absolutely sure that's what had happened, or indeed that the equal prize money was necessarily the one driving force, but we speculated that that looked as if it were the case.

And Valerie Camo came on this podcast of Andy Roddick and said: 100% our main target, our main focus, is equal prize money. That's the entire point of the WTA — was founded to achieve equal prize money.

Which I think is just so odd. Right? Now, everyone knows the foundation story of the WTA — Billie Jean King in the 1960s, turning up for a tournament, I think it was in Italy, and the men were being paid five times as much as she was being paid to be there, and she resented that and thought: "We need to get together, we need to form a women's tour."

So yeah, it's true that in the foundation story there is a recognition of the fact that men were being paid in a different universe to what women were being paid at the time. But I don't think it's the case really that the entire foundation of the WTA is simply to achieve equal prize money.

Prize money is an outcome. Prize money is a sort of end goal, and it may even be a very laudatory part of your objectives — your stretch objectives over a protracted period of time. But to basically say "my job as chairman, my main job as chairman is to achieve equal pay" is odd — unless you understand the job as fundamentally answering to the players.

And what became clear during this interview — she referred in several places to the fact that fundamentally her bosses are her players. Now, this is a strange situation because effectively the players are the players of today. They're not the players of yesterday and they're not the players of tomorrow. So on a normal circumstance, you'd assume that whoever's running the WTA would think: "Okay, I had to balance the priorities here. I have to think about the players of today and do the best I possibly can. But at the same time, I also have to think about the players of tomorrow as well, because what we can't do is mortgage the future to make the current players happy."

And yet that is exactly what has happened. They have taken in $150 million worth of investment from CVC in return for 20% of their ongoing commercial rights. So effectively they're promising away the future in order to pile up cash today — and all in the pursuit of equal pay today. Not equal pay on a gradual basis as revenues support it. No, equal pay today, even though revenues do not support it.

— Cash for the five years from the start of when CVC invested, but it's equity dividends in perpetuity. — Exactly. — Right. So in other words, those who play now, you get benefits from the cash. Those of you that are going to play in 10 years, you'll actually have money taken away unless we can find another way to generate the money to put into the prize pool. — Right. And that was what was interesting.

WTA Finals = 女子体育的"超级碗"？

Did you listen to the podcast twice? Yeah. The conversations we've had have been off various bits of media looking at the finances. It did paint a very stark financial picture. The media in the last few weeks, when it was talking about the loss this year, a lot of that was attributed to the change in location of the WTA Finals, losing them a year early from Riyadh — which actually she said was quite interesting, referred to as a kind of "end of the cycle" type thing rather than a break in the contract.

Was there anything else in there that would stand out this year? No, I don't think there was. It was basically that: the WTA Finals.

And this whole conversation was about the importance of the WTA Finals to the WTA. Basically, she's putting all of her eggs in the idea that the new WTA Tour Finals that are going to be held in Charlotte, North Carolina from next year, 2027 onwards, that she's going to be able to make that into such a big deal commercially that it will be able to pay the bills. She's talking about turning it into the Super Bowl of women's sport.

Right? And look, I think I've got to grant some latitude when people use these types of shorthands. I don't want to hold them to every single — you know, be arsey about it and saying, "Well, it's not exactly like the Super Bowl." But let's reflect on the fact: it really is not like the Super Bowl.

Here's a key difference. What is the pinnacle of NFL? The Super Bowl. What is the pinnacle of tennis? Grand slams. This is a core, core difference. It cannot be the Super Bowl because it's not the thing which the whole year leads up to.

— But for the WTA, well, no, it is a thing — it's the whole thing in the calendar year. — For the public, the only bit that counts here is what the public think about it. There's no good the players thinking "this is our Super Bowl." The whole point about Super Bowls is what the fans think. That's why they all want to watch it — because they know it is the pinnacle of their sport. And this is not going to be the pinnacle of tennis. And therefore, if you think that you are going to turn this into something which is more successful commercially than the grand slams, or as successful or even close to it being successful, I think you're deluding yourself.

Yeah. But look, it's an idea. It's a concept and it's a breadth of proposition to try and make more money. And if we're being hypercritical of them, it's that they're not making enough money, which is why they're having to dip into the investments into the organization.

I'm all for the Tour Finals being made more commercially successful than they currently are. If she wants to market it as the Super Bowl, if she wants to get partners in who want to pay for that — which she suggested in the conversation that she had, or they were doing deals with partners who had that…

She said that they already had a title sponsor. So if they have done that — we're calling for them to make more money so that if they're going to pay players equal to the men, they can afford to do so.

He did ask — he did say, "When's the prize money going to start paying for itself?" He did push.

I don't think you can do that interview without asking about the CVC investment.

— I completely agree. But therefore, I just — from what I know and from what I know doing — I would imagine that interview was done with CVC investment being taken off the table. — It sounded that way. Because you can't have that chat without talking about CVC's $150 million injection. Even in passing — there was no reference to it at all.

If I had done that interview, if I was her, I would have been doing it the same. She was right in lots of ways about where she was positioning tennis, but it kind of just emphasizes the challenge, and really the question marks over it.

她的叙述 vs. 她的数学

I just want to read out — because it shows you the position that women's tennis actually is in — when she was describing the strength of it, she says:

"We have more opportunity than any other women's sport and some of the men's. We are the only women's sport that is truly global. One-name superstar athletes known all over the world. We aren't a startup. We're the legacy. We have the most powerful deep fan base — balance between men and women. Take all of this together and layer the integration with the men's game. You put all of that together and who has it better than us? Why shouldn't we be ambitious?"

Now, no one would argue against that. Where it starts to lose its weight is when she says "fiscal discipline is our ambition." When she says that — "my background is financial and strategic" — and then on the flip side you come out and make a statement which really surprised me. It was kind of quite loose, but it was: "other sports have had to prove and then get" — and she was referring to prize money, i.e. as if saying "you said to me the cart comes before the horse here; most people have to prove it."

Yeah, but I mean that's what business is. You don't go and get a big shiny office before you can afford the rent. You don't hire a market-leading CEO before you can pay the salary. In these situations, there just seems to be that disconnect of: your business doesn't justify the means of your spend.

You're starting off — all serious sports industry commentators are starting off — from a different position from her. We are making the assumption that the number one priority of sports business is to create something which is sustainable, growing, pays prize money out of its revenues, blah blah blah. But she's not. She's starting from the position of saying, "Oh, that's all great. That's all fine. I get that. But my number one priority is paying the women as much as the men get, even though we've got half the revenues."

Now if you start off from that position, effectively what she then has to do is retrofit a strategy to achieve something which is non-negotiable. And that is how it came across in this thing — which is that in taking the job, she has had it made clear to her by the players: it is non-negotiable that you achieve equal prize money. It is your job to achieve equal prize money.

对 WTA 主席，是否该抱有同情？

Do you have any sympathy? Can I just quickly ask that — because she then went on to talk about the lack of inventory really that they have to work with. We discussed this last week and we said look, at some stage, if the players want that equal prize money, the players are going to have to maybe take a bit of a commercial hit, because they are going to need to package some form of rights up to allow the tour to sell them, so that they can make more money commercially as a tour.

Six out of 10 of the top paid players, men and women — Forbes said — are women. In that stat, men are making most of their money on the court; women are making most of their money off the court. So women are getting fantastic pay from brands and commercial partners. And then they want on-the-court to match it. Whereas the men on the court are making a lot of money because the tour is generating more money, but they may not be as commercially viable across the board as a lot of the women are.

Charlie, you asked me a question. Do I feel some sympathy for her? And the answer is no.

First of all, she's agreed to take the job. Secondly, she has decided not to do the thing that real leaders do, which is tell some uncomfortable truths. And the uncomfortable truth to tell here is: "Look, if you're asking me to achieve equal prize money, I can do that with your support" — this is talking to the players — "okay? If what you're saying is that you want to max out yourself on your own personal commercial income, and that on top of that you want me to achieve equal prize money with the men based off an inventory which is basically tiny — which is the Tour Finals plus some brand sponsorship for the tour as a whole, but where those brands aren't getting access to the players because the players already signed their rights away to other sponsors themselves personally — I'm sorry, that's not achievable."

So if you really believe in what Billie Jean believed in — start pooling your own. Put your own money where your mouth is. But they don't want to do that. They want to have their cake and eat it. They want to be able to be much better paid in sponsorship terms than the men and then also equally paid in terms of the prize money. And there isn't the money there to pay for it.

Which brings us back to the Tour Finals and the "Super Bowl of women's sport." When she was asked what do you mean by that, she's like, "Well, obviously the tournament itself, but then we're also going to have a fanfest." So it's a sort of copycat of what Craig Tiley did in Australia with the Australian Open. "And we're going to have a women's sport conference." Right? Well, the women's sport conference won't butter much toast commercially. That will be at best a break-even type thing. Worthy, no doubt, but a break-even type thing. And the FanFest — well, let's see. Let's see what that looks like commercially. But I somewhat doubt that that is going to be the thing which turns this into effectively being able to replace the money that CVC's been pumping in.

Because that's what's going to have to happen here — the $30 million a year that CVC's been putting in is going to have to be replaced. And effectively from listening to that podcast, it is going to have to be replaced by revenue generated mostly from the Tour Finals. Which — if she pulls it off, and if that Tour Finals event ends up making $30 million bucks profit a year and that's able to replace the CVC money, notwithstanding the fact that 20% of the future's been promised away but leave that to one side — then I think I'd have to stand back and say: wow, what a job she would have done.

So I'm not saying that it can't be done. I'm saying that I think it would be better for sports leaders to front up to the reality of the challenge to their stakeholders. Doesn't mean say so you don't go on and try and achieve it. You can still have stretch targets, you can still have ambitions, as she puts it, but taking it as read that that's definitely going to happen when effectively your bank balance is currently at zero strikes me as a massive risk.

And I do think the WTA Tour Finals can be — let me be quite clear — can be better, bigger, bolder than it currently is. Yes. Do I think it will be? Yes, I do. Having it in a big serious sports city like Charlotte as opposed to in Riyadh — do I think that's infinitely better? Yes. Do I think they'll get much bigger crowds? Yes. Do I think they'll get bigger TV audiences? Yes. Do I think they'll get more mainline sponsors? Definitely yes. So that's not the question. The question is: there's a $30 to $40 million a year hole here which needs filling. Do I think that that's the sole answer to that? Bit more skeptical.

Player freedom. Do I think that player freedom is the cornerstone of LIV Golf? BC Partners 真正在做什么：债 vs. 股，与 NOL 税盾

I just want to ask you one other question, Charlie. Since you have a sort of financial fund management side to your life — Ted Goldthorpe, this guy from BC Partners, is a debt partner there, which is to say that he invests money as debt. This feels to me like under normal circumstances this would be an equity investment. And yet the fact that it's Ted Goldthorpe from BC Partners suggests that it's a debt investment. How does that work? How can you — because equity value is not non-existent, right?

Okay. Well, do you remember we were kind of laughing about this? We were joking. Do you remember when the news first came out? We said this cannot be an equity play. There has to be another financial motive — with very intelligent people running various types of financial institutions recognizing an opportunity to gain some value off the misfortune of LIV Golf and/or the people that have been left on the shelf.

So what do you think Ted's doing?

The point is that they have recognized that off the losses that LIV Golf made — $5 billion — that presents a significant opportunity for them to gain some tax exemptions in the future. So they're $5 billion in net operating losses, as they call it. And this is where it gets technical. So trying to keep it simple for myself and everyone else:

You can offset those net operating losses — the taxes associated with future profits that you make in your portfolio — against net operating losses in other ventures that you're involved in. So governments traditionally did this to try and remove some of the distress on struggling businesses, to give them an opportunity to recover. Private equity has been taking advantage of this because they know they can front cash to get companies out of situations, and what they want to do is look at their broader portfolio and say: right, so in this case, if BC and its sports portfolio — it kind of wants to run a CVC-type model — let's say they made $5 billion in profits over the next few years. They could offset the corporate tax — corporate income tax, which is about 20% — they could offset $1 billion of that against the $5 billion losses that would be associated with LIV's debt currently. I.e., they pay no tax.

Right? So effectively the deal here — and this answers really well a question that's been lurking ever since I saw Ted's face, thinking "what the hell is a debt guy doing in this?" — I'm looking at it, thinking, okay, so what you're basically saying is that BC Partners is potentially buying $5 billion of tax credits — which nets out at $1 billion, cuz it's 20% — effectively $1 billion of tax credits in return for $300 million of debt.

It looks like that, right? Drip-feeding this money in as well most likely. So, you know, I think it's $50 million. They put $4 million up at the beginning to cover some of the bankruptcy. I think that could extend to $50 million.

I then think — and I'm not sure, but I think — these challenges they've got now around when they can pull out: if certain players aren't signed, or if they don't get to the stage they need to to continue, they can pull that money. No more than $50 million would be committed. If they do get to the stage, then the $300 million is still on the table. But absolutely, from what it looks like, the real value to BC Partners is for the money that they can save in the future on a broader sports portfolio by offsetting the taxes of any future profits on their other businesses.

Now, if you look at it like that, then it's a good deal for them. What's not to like?

And that explains a lot. But then what we don't want to see — and I think where you have the challenge, and where we know golfers have the challenge — is: don't sit on a panel and spin it to us as a "$100 million equity investment and an opportunity for players" who are sitting there facing massive losses because they've had to convert their cash into equity if they want anything to do with this. This is why I find it a bit distasteful.

Because some players, particularly golfers, actually are quite smart. But some are not, and some can be easily taken in — and these are years of their life which are the critical earning years. And these people in some cases should be going off and making their career back again on the main tours, qualifying for majors, cementing legacies and all this type of stuff. And you've got slightly slimy, slick-suited Americans sitting on panels at sports conferences talking about how this is going to be this amazing new equity play and the players are so lucky to be involved — when in actual fact is ultimately potentially — and I must say potentially because we don't know — but it's potentially a piece of financial structuring really, where if it does come off great, but if it doesn't come off then BC Partners win anyway.

"It's not just about golf. I think golf is just a part of life. All of this is way bigger than life. It's probably above my pay grade. Long may it continue."

We do think it's got a chance, but I want to be really clear about how this is happening and why this is happening — and you guys need to know that you are taking a risk."

It's like when people advertise financial offerings in this country, or even gambling — actually have to say "by the way, this is a risk. You do know that you are taking a risk, right? You do understand that this is not a slam dunk." It seems to me that this has been sold to the players — in fact, not even "it seems to me," I know from speaking to players who have had it sold to them, who said no, who perhaps are a little bit more worldly than Dean Burmester — who have said it's basically just sold to you as being: "you'd be fools not to. This is an amazing opportunity."

And if you're in the journeyman bucket, that may be true. If this pretty much guarantees a few hundred thousand of cash and prize money each year or participation fees or whatever, if it comes with equity ownership whatever that is, that could be better than the alternatives for you on other tours.

So the question is: does that deal make sense to BC/LIV 2.0 and what they want this product to be? But I think, as you said, the point is you should just come out and explain it. You say, "Look, if we want to give you this opportunity, this is how it needs to be done. There are lots of different incentives at stake here for all of the people involved. If it works well and we do our job, you are going to benefit from it." But being pitched as "you'll be a fool not to be a part of it" is where we fall from reasonable justification to kind of fanciful.

And I don't think it's over-egging it to say that is how it's being pitched — because that is also how it was pitched at Sportsco the conference two weeks ago. It was not pitched as "this is going to be very challenging, but we could pull it off." This was pitched as "this is the greatest thing ever."

Yeah, I know. Which was the problem. It made you feel stupid for thinking that this couldn't hit $100 million team valuations very quickly, which was why we had a problem with it a couple of weeks ago.

FIFA 政治：Infantino、Čeferin、Montagliani 与消失的挑战者

So moving on to another favorite topic of ours — which is the FIFA President, Gianni Infantino. Johnny.

Charlie, do you want to summarize the last two months — effectively since the FIFA Forward Enterprises story came out?

Well, obviously FIFA Forward Enterprise happened, the whole world lost the plot. It seemed like Gianni had to go — whatever that meant, however they did it. It seemed like the position was pretty much untenable, coming out of a World Cup where there'd been a lot of heat on him.

Anyway, there was Čeferin coming out, the president of UEFA, making some pretty strong statements saying UEFA would boycott FIFA competitions. They did for a little bit and then they redacted that. But I remember we did say in the last update we did probably a month or so ago — I think we think if you were going to do this, you had to strike while the iron's hot. As Michael Ricketts, the Jamaican head of Jamaican football said, great statesman — '$40 million if they're getting that on revenues of, you know, seven figures a year — that money is going to become far more important than the moral standing that you have to take in a general assembly meeting.'"

When it first came out, there was a much stronger argument to say that you could have turned those nations purely based on: it was no longer right for that man to hold that position for a multitude of different reasons. Čeferin wanted to do this democratically, as you said, but the reality is that I don't think there was a democratic opportunity here based on the time between what happened and that next vote. Brilliant. Thanks a lot for that. I agree with all of that. So I'm not going to rehash it. I remember speculating at the time — and speculating from a position of some strength, having spent some time in the Caribbean professionally — that I thought it was slightly surprising that Montagliani felt that he was in a strong enough position to state Concacaf's position as being anti-Infantino, when Infantino's one of his main power bases is the small Caribbean countries. And I was like, "Okay. Wow. If Montagliani's really managed to get the likes of Jamaica onside, and indeed the smaller islands than Jamaica — wow. Okay. Infantino is in real trouble if that's happened."

That was then exploded a few weeks later by Michael Ricketts, who you mentioned, who's the head of Jamaican Football Federation. I was like, "That's my boy. That's the Michael Ricketts I know and love. That's the guy." But at the same time thinking: I wonder what that means for Victor Montagliani's position — not his own position within Concacaf, but his position as being Čeferin's wingman in getting rid of Infantino. If you've got people like Ricketts coming out and saying "it's all about the cash," does Concacaf — does the head of Concacaf supporting Čeferin — really mean that he has the support of all of the countries in Concacaf? Evidently not.

And it now emerges that Montagliani's backed away from being the person who himself will challenge Infantino. And part of that's because he sort of feels that the re-election for Concacaf is coming up at the same time more or less. Montagliani would be regarded as a shoo-in for that job. But he feels that he couldn't stand for two at once. If he was the existing head of Concacaf, he could then apply to be the head of FIFA, and if he failed, he'd go back to Concacaf. But with both elections being at the same time, he feels he can't stand for both at the same time and say "I'm going to give my full attention to whichever one it is," because it becomes clear — well, actually if we elect you head of Concacaf, you might then just jump ship and go and do FIFA anyway.

If he thought he was going to win — but the risk-reward is tilted against it, and he's walked away. That's the bottom line.

But I think that indicates — yeah, sure — the confidence that he has in his ability to beat Infantino. Yes, indeed. So effectively him walking away has left the cupboard bare in terms of: if Montagliani can't win, no one can win. He was the guy who definitely could potentially win.

法甲的实际数字

So last year, Ligue 1 and Ligue Deux had a net loss of €542 million, which was double what it did the year before. The operating loss before player sales was €1.4 billion. The profit on player sales was €886 million.

So if you hadn't had those player sales, that league lost nearly €1.5 billion. Now that's a worry in itself. You can't sell €886 million worth of talent every single year. You may be able to sell a few hundred million's worth of talent, but you can't rely on it as a core. Also, Paris was €333 million of that. Oh, sorry — PSG share of Ligue 1 revenue is 40%.

Yeah. So what has been happening here?

Everyone knows that, in quotation marks, French Ligue lost their TV deal. And what that means basically is that they used to get paid around about £500 million a year by Canal Plus, the main cable pay TV provider — Sky Sports equivalent I think — in France. Canal Plus pulled out of that in a midstay dispute with Ligue. Ligue said, "That's okay because we're going to sell our rights to DAZN," who bought them I think for $450 million. So not far off, same sort of ballpark. After a year or a year and a half, DAZN then pulled out of that contract — and did so in a way which was legally quite nifty, even if not particularly ethical in my view — and they walked away.

The French Ligue then could not find anybody else to take their TV rights. So they went DTC, which is direct-to-consumer, which is forming their own channel where you basically have to subscribe as a football fan to the Ligue channel in order to be able to watch Ligue 1 games domestically in France — out of which they made about €150 million.

So they've gone from a deal with Canal Plus that was paying them 500, to a DTC thing paying — well, getting 150 in revenue. But don't forget they have the cost of production as well. So it's not going to be 150 net; it's going to be 150 gross, out of which the clubs might receive 120. They then get a small amount of money for their foreign rights — I can't remember the exact number but it's 60, 70, 80, 90 something like that. So they're getting about 200 million in total. Hence why between 18 of them they're getting about 10 million each post-costs.

Okay, so that's what's happened.

Roger Mitchell 的宏观判断：欧洲 Pay TV 的"剧目重排"

But what's happening — because what's happening here is also happening in Italy. And as so often when thinking about continental TV rights, I turn to our old friend Roger Mitchell to give me a read on what's happening behind the scenes, because he often understands what's happening with the TV rights negotiations and the movement of different contracts very well.

And what he said was really interesting. He said the macro here is that the domestic sports pay TV providers in countries generally — not just talking about France, not just talking about Italy, we're also talking about Belgium, we're talking about other countries which are non-top-tier countries — those domestic pay TV providers have worked out that they will access the necessary football eyeballs paying subscriptions within their own market by screening the Champions League and the Premier League, and that they will pay much less for the combined Champions League and Premier League than they have been used to paying for their domestic league — for the same amount of eyeballs, if not more.

So this is what happened in France, and it's really interesting when you look at it. Canal Plus used to pay €500 million for Ligue 1. Now they pay €450 million for the combined Champions League and Premier League. And they're not interested in the domestic league anymore. Proving Roger's point — saying that Canal Plus have done the numbers, they're not fools. They've worked out that they are not losing TV subscriptions by no longer televising the domestic league. If they want the football audience, they do the Champions League and the Premier League.

意甲：下一个倒下的多米诺骨牌？

Now let's have a look and see what's happening in Italy — because this could be the next cab off the rank, as Roger says. But this is how it works.

Sky Italia, which forms the same function as Sky does in this country, used to pay €780 million for Serie A primary rights. Now they pay €200 million for the Champions League, €100 million for the Premier League — so that's €300 million — and €180 million for the Serie A secondary rights. That's a certain number of Serie A matches, because the primary rights holder is DAZN.

— Yeah. So they've gone from being Sky Sports to TNT again. Sorry, for the English audience. — Correct. So that's €480 million in total for their football rights, as against €780 million they were previously paying — all to Serie A.

Right. And who's taken up… so DAZN, our old friends at DAZN, took up the slack. And they are paying €700 million for the primary rights. Don't forget, that is against €780 million that Sky Italia were previously paying. So actually it's a 10% reduction, and when you take into account that was five years subsequent, it's more than that because of inflation etc. But put all that to one side, and that contract is coming up in 2028–2029 — that is the last year of that contract.

Now this is where the rubber hits the road. Because there are two potential routes that happen here. One of which is that DAZN says — as with their French market and their Belgian market — they say, "Do you know what? This isn't working. We're not doing it. We're literally just not doing it." Or the second route is they say, "Well, we do want to do it, but we're the only show in town. Sky Italia ain't coming back in for you guys. They've already got themselves tied up with the Premier League, the Champions League, and your secondary rights. So they're not going to come in for your primary rights as well. We're the only show in town. We're not going to pay you 700. We're going to pay you 500."

That's what we're staring down the barrel of here: it could be nothing, or it could be 500, but it sure as hell ain't going to be 700. I'd be amazed if it's going to be 700. I was at a conference recently when a representative of DAZN was saying, "Look, overall we need to manage our rights payments downwards." You and I have mentioned before how enormous their rights liabilities are, and given that they could be potentially IPOing in the next year or two, it's only sensible for them to think about rationalizing their rights payments downwards a bit — preferably a lot, but certainly a bit.

意甲的回应：拉"WTA 把手"

So how are they trying to offset some of this risk? I've got a risk going on — and it's not even a risk, it's like, I would say, a racing certainty. Having already seen a bump down in their rights, they're going to see another bump down. Maybe not quite as dramatic as France, but still a significant bump down.

So they're reaching for, dare I say it, the WTA lever.

— Oh, when will they learn, Charlie? — And this is not a good lever.

For those who have tuned in a little bit late or weren't listening to the bit on tennis earlier on because you're not interested in tennis: the WTA took in $150 million of "quote investment" from CVC in return for CVC having 20% of their commercial rights in perpetuity. And Charlie and I have long said that was a terrible deal. Short-term cash spunked on prize money to give away 20% of your future.

What are Serie A doing, Charles? Look, they're looking to sell 10% of the international rights package in perpetuity to private equity for a single sum which has been valued across different bids slightly differently. But €320 million for 10% is one bid. €650 million for 17% is another bid.

The mathematics are right. So basically they're currently receiving €250 million a year for their international rights.

So is there an argument here that actually Serie A is doing something quite sensible — which is that whilst their foreign rights are still worth something, they're getting some cash in for them to slightly derisk the possibility that actually they don't really go anywhere? Because a valuation of 3.2 billion on your foreign rights when you're currently only getting 250 million a year, and when there's no obvious indication they're about to boom — you know, from a purely mathematical perspective, could that be a good — ?

Yes, but my question is: what is that money going to be used for? That's the key.

Look, in theory, was the WTA taking $150 million of CVC money a bad decision? Not necessarily. You could put a strong argument together for both sides of it. What was a bad decision was putting the $150 million into increasing prize money — i.e. not increasing the overall value of the proposition.

We've talked about CVC putting money into La Liga. That was ring-fenced to ensure that it was spent in certain ways which CVC and La Liga thought would grow the overall value of the proposition. It couldn't just be going and spent on a nice shiny new striker.

Normally when these deals happen, incredibly, money hasn't been ring-fenced. It hasn't been segmented. So leagues and whatever have just run around and spent it however they wish.

One of the deals on the table looks like a very good deal to me. One of them less so. Avenue Capital, which is Marc Lasry's private equity business (Marc Lasry — one of the PGA Enterprises investors, one of the great lads, come back on that — and former Milwaukee Bucks owner), they have a deal reportedly on the table: €320 million for 10%. So values the whole international rights package at €3.2 billion. Is plain equity. So there's no guarantees on future cash flows. It is an equity play, meaning they see value that can be traded later on if the value of the overall proposition increases. That to me looks like a really good deal.

The other deal — for Serie A, yeah. Not so for Avenue. The other bid, which is €650 million, so more money up front, for roughly 17% — values it slightly higher at €3.7 billion but it does come with commitments to pay them on future cash flows. I.e., they will be taking money out in perpetuity. Now look, even that may be a good deal if the money is being put to the right use. €650 million is a lot of money, but I would be more inclined to take that Avenue Capital deal — try and use the €320 million.

And that is the favorite, right? Apparently that is what they're looking to do. They are kind of the preferred bidder, whatever.

Do you think that's a good deal? In theory, financially, economically, yes. In practice, in terms of using it to top up payments to clubs in the short run to try and fill leaky buckets — no. Because that all disappears very quickly, and it puts off the day of reckoning when clubs in Serie A have to cut their cloth to the reality of their situation rather than pretend that they are still in a major European league.

It's also not a lot of money each, is it? Really — €16 million euros each dividing. It'll probably disappear in two seasons. I'm guessing one or two seasons.

大图景：媒体资本从法甲、意甲向英超与欧冠的大迁移

I just want to go back onto the French league and relatedly the Italian league — because what you're actually seeing here is a reallocation of media capital from the French and Italian leagues to the Premier League and the Champions League. That's what's driving the whole thing here.

And that in turn is being driven by effectively algorithmic study — which basically said, right, "If we do this then we get more subscribers; if we do that, we get fewer subscribers." So that is the brutal market, because the broadcasters have got so smart now at judging what does bring eyeballs, what doesn't bring eyeballs, what does lead people to keep their subscriptions, what doesn't — all that type of stuff. They've become really, really good at it.

— One of the reasons why DAZN was pulling out of the deals. It was — — The reason. Yeah. Which is they went into these deals, paid quite a lot of money for them, and then found out there weren't any subscribers there. Well, weren't enough subscribers there to make their financial model work. "Oh, we've got to get out." Right.

So this is almost like a sort of peak globalization point, isn't it? Which is: the rich and the big get richer and bigger — being UEFA and the Premier League — and then the secondary and tertiary products are regarded as fundamentally being non-essential. And become effectively, gradually free-to-air, or else very niche subscription.

And the worst thing — those secondary leagues then consolidate the power of the Premier League. Because you know what the summer showed — I mentioned the talent being the key revenue driver for France. Where do they sell to? They sell to the Premier League. So France now needs the richness, the riches of the Premier League to be able to fund the main part of their business model — for the stats that they're the number one net seller.

The wealth of the Premier League is being funded by these domestic leagues' own markets. That's a humiliating thing. Exactly. And then those markets are relying on that money spent on the Premier League to then pay them in talent.

Indeed. Right. So just on a quick back of a fag packet: French and Italian Premier League TV payments are now €250 million a year. Right. So the Premier League is receiving more from French and Italian punters than the French league is receiving from all of its domestic punters — €150 million. That's how bad things are getting. In fact, the amount that French punters are paying for EPL, which is about €100 million, is not that different to the €150 million they're paying for domestic. They're paying almost as much for the Premier League as they are for the domestic product.

豪门的反应、UEFA 的"团结付款贿赂"

So you want these big teams — your PSG or Juventus — you know, what's your reaction to this? European Super League?

So your short-term reaction, which is what it has been: "We have to pressurize UEFA into giving us guaranteed payments" — which they've done through — what's it called? Solidarity payments. Solidarity. Something like that. Which is basically PSG receiving €70 or €80 million just for being PSG. Just for being PSG. And that effectively is UEFA's current bribe to be able to enable a very small number of clubs from these leagues to be able to dine at the top table with the Premier League clubs is basically bungs from UEFA.

The problem is UEFA can't stop giving the same — well, giving payments to Premier League clubs as well. Has to be done on a sort of roughly equal basis. The Premier League clubs get a bit less because it's a more competitive league, so there are more clubs for it to be paid out to. Whereas if you are PSG or Bayern or Juve or Milan, whatever it might be, then you can get more.

But fundamentally that is what's going on here. UEFA are propping up a small number of European clubs against the Premier League, to get around the fact that their domestic revenues have been cannibalized by the Premier League and indeed the Champions League, as it happens.

It's just a really interesting trend. And a worrying trend, right?

— Well, worrying for whom? The domestic market. — What you're seeing here is you're seeing the Premier League's revenues becoming more and more broad-based, which means they have less and less individual risk on any one contract. So it's great if you're the Premier League. It's great if you're English football. Because if you're — it's great if you're the Championship. You know, we've talked about the value of the leagues within this from a viewership perspective — as the third most viewed league in Europe, the Championship.

Look, I mean, if the Premier League is just getting bigger — and it will get bigger and bigger and bigger. One of the reasons why City need to get sorted out quick, you know. They're on such an upward trajectory. They're cannibalizing this market. They're getting more money. They're eating off other people's plates. They're eating other people's lunch. Absolutely.

But on the flip side — back to sport and what sport is and why it's so important here that we have payments going down a pyramid. Every country has football that we're talking about here at the heart of much of its social fabric, of its communities. Same discussion, same arguments that we have here. It's a major, major issue for these heritage organizations, these institutions, these fans.

The reason for these enormous losses, Charlie, that you're talking about in the French league is because psychologically the French clubs have not yet got used to — and particularly the French fan bases have not yet got used to — the idea that basically we're just feeding clubs the Premier League. Right. So if you're a Marseille fan and you're supporting one of the great clubs of Europe and there's 60,000 people in the stadium and you have great pride in your club and the way it represents the community and all this type of stuff — and then fundamentally all of your players are just being sold every summer because the revenue is just not there to support playing top players' wages and so on and so forth — they are in open revolt against this stuff.

At so many French clubs, the fans are in open revolt because they cannot understand or accept that their league is no longer one — or maybe the lowest — but one of the top five leagues, is now dropped out of that. It's now dropping down towards Scottish Premiership, Dutch League, Belgian League levels. It's heading in that — in fact, it's much closer to those. In fact, the Portuguese league, even more so.

Its biggest team doesn't take the league seriously. Its biggest team plays its star players for one-third of the games. Right. It has the double European champions in that league, right? Which is another issue — that's another whole issue.

I was listening to an interview with a former senior executive at the French league who said, "Well, you know, in an ideal world, don't let a good crisis go to waste. You could use this moment when French league football is at its absolute lowest point to totally recast the whole league and do something really bold about it." Right? "Let's just say that we want to become the most competitive league in Europe." Yeah — bloody difficult to do when PSG are currently your only sellable product. Right. Very, very hard.

Anyhow, one to keep an eye on, Charles. But thanks for raising it.

结语

— No, not at all. Great discussions. Hey, look, that was a mixed bag today. — It certainly was. — Really plenty to go through. Um, guys, hope you enjoyed it as always. Keep the comments flowing. I'm sure there was plenty in there for you guys to get stuck into. Thank you, Charlie, and we will see you all next week. — Thanks, Charlie.
