item.description:
## 一、藏在"外行星"隐喻背后的组织熵减
a16z 把 Chris Dixon 的新基金命名为 "Frontier"，表面是扩张加密基金，实则是一次**组织人类学的自我修正**。他们借用《萤火虫》里"外行星"的意象，承认了一个尴尬事实：当垂直化策略（vertical strategy）走向成熟，组织会不自觉地**用分类系统压缩现实**——而最有趣的创业者偏偏诞生在类目之间的裂缝里。
这里有个让人意外的观察：**a16z 实际上在用生物学里的"生态位空缺"原理来对抗自己的科层化**。他们并不是在"投资一个新领域"，而是在给组织留下一块**故意不被定义**的保留地，让那些不符合现有抽屉的创业者有归处。这与禅宗的"留白"、与博物学里的"杂草地带（weedy edge）"——生物多样性最高的那条过渡带——是同一个结构。
更深的隐喻在这里：**crypto 并不是被"吸收"进主流，而是被"稀释"后留下了一个认知空缺**。当 Stripe、华尔街都开始用稳定币，"crypto 投资人"这个身份反而失去了锐度，于是必须退回到更原始的"异类"立场。所谓 Frontier，本质上是**对"已被命

item.title: [Latent Space] Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的洞察：Modal本质上不是云服务，而是"时间形状的套利商"

全球GPU市场有个隐藏的几何学问题——所有算力都以矩形出售：横轴是"3年固定周期"，纵轴是"N张GPU常驻"。但真实的AI需求形状是锯齿状山脉：白天爆发、夜间空闲、新模型发布时陡升、旧模型淘汰时暴跌。Erik说"the median sandbox in Modal today is like 8 seconds long"——8秒的需求 vs 3年的供给。

这就是Modal的真正生意：它买入矩形，卖出波浪。这跟你想的"卖GPU"完全不同——它在做时间形状的套利。

跨领域对照：这跟电力行业的"基荷电厂 vs 调峰电厂"同构，跟保险公司"聚合不相关风险"同构，甚至跟航空公司"把365×24的固定座位切成浮动票价"同构。Modal本质上是算力界的高盛——它赚的不是硬件差价，而是"时间粒度转换"的中间价。Erik在采访里一次次强调"we aggregate many thousands of customers and demand gets very smooth"——这就是保险精算师的语言，不是云厂商的语言。

二、意外的发现：他们差点杀掉自己最大的产品，而救活它的是"用户的用户不是人类"

Sandboxes在2023年发布后几乎没人用。2025年夏天团队还在讨论"要不要把它关掉"。然后它突然爆炸——现在占收入三分之一。

真正的拐点是：客户变成了AI本身。Lovable、Ramp的后台agent、neolabs的强化学习——这些不是人类用户在"选产品"，这是agent在被训练去调用API。这意味着SaaS史上第一次出现了一个诡异的产品发现路径：你的PMF信号来自训练数据。

更诡异的是Erik观察到的"折旧抵抗"（Deprecation Resistance）：Modal的旧版API语法已经被永久铸造在LLM的训练集里，agent会固执地写出两年前的语法。这是全新的技术债形式——类似核废料的半衰期或宇宙微波背景辐射：一旦你的代码进入训练集，就像光锥上发射出去的信号，再也收不回来。你被你自己过去的API形状困住了。

这指向一个被低估的战略判断：在agent时代，API设计的第一次机会就是最后一次机会，因为"重构友好度"这个开发者美德在训练数据永冻层面前几乎失效。

三、跨领域连接：Neocloud的真正身份不是云公司，是"算力期货投行"

Erik轻描淡写说了一句令人震惊的话："these are very very sophisticated financial engineering companies"。他描述的neocloud运作方式其实是： 1. 找Anthropic/OpenAI预售5年算力合同 2. 把合同拿去华尔街抵押融资 3. 用融资的钱向Nvidia下单 4. 交付给预售方

这完全不是云计算。这是航空公司的收益管理 + 美国国债的预售机制 + 油田开发的"产量支付融资"（Volumetric Production Payments）的混合体。Erik甚至提到"GPU as collateral for loans"——GPU正在被证券化。

而Modal刻意不走这条路——因为PLG模式让他们没法锁定长期合同。这揭示了一个被忽视的张力：基础设施市场正在分裂成两个物种——金融结构驱动的neocloud（本质是对冲基金），和产品体验驱动的平台（Modal）。两者的核心能力栈完全不重叠：前者需要CFO和华尔街关系，后者需要分布式系统工程师和社交媒体。

四、一个被埋没的创业启示：Erik承认Modal早期增长主要靠他"compulsive tweeting"

一个做底层基础设施、技术极度深度的B2B公司，第一桶金来源是创始人在推特上发癫——这打破了几乎所有"B2B销售团队驱动"的教条。他说"founder-led marketing"——"what I'm good at is just posting and being terminally online"。

把这个和Taylor Swift类比（Erik自己用的类比来反驳"模型是商品"的说法）连起来看，你会发现一个隐藏规律：在信息过载的市场里，赢家是能持续制造"注意力脉冲"的实体——不管那是艺人的新专辑、OpenAI的新模型、还是基础设施创始人的推文。Modal、Anthropic、OpenAI、Taylor Swift在这个维度上是同一种生物。

📝 转录文本

开场：Modal 的业务与起源

— Thanks for coming on. Eric Bernhardsson from Modal. Could you explain the business a little bit and maybe how you got here?

Yeah, so we — the easiest way to put it is we build AI infrastructure. So we offer a compute platform and a storage platform that enables a lot of customers like Decagon and Suno and Runway and Cognition and many others to essentially build AI applications. So what that means in practice is a lot of inference, a lot of sandboxes, sometimes training and fine-tuning, sometimes batch jobs and other things. So we have basically built a software SDK that enables customers to move really fast and build this — we manage all the capacity underneath, make it easy to deploy and scale and run these things in production.

— So you were on Latent Space like 2 years ago. A lot has happened since then. How big were you back then, and how big are you now?

I actually don't remember where we were, but it's probably at least 50x in terms of revenue and users and usage and stuff like that.

— I use it actually for a side project that I have — turning 2D images into 3D models. Just hosting models there.

What do you think? Any feedback?

— I love it. That's why I use it over any competitors.

Good.

从 Spotify 到 Better.com 再到 Modal

— Before you started Modal, you were at Spotify and also at better.com, right? What were you doing at Spotify?

I actually did a lot of different things at Spotify, but my main contribution was I built a music recommendation system. The first version — I joined after school in 2008, 2009 maybe — and spent seven years at Spotify, and most of that time was building basically from scratch a music recommendation system and built up a small team and we launched a bunch of features like Related Artists and Discover Weekly and a bunch of other stuff. So a lot of matrix factorization, a lot of compute-intensive stuff. And arguably a lot of what later became the genesis of Modal was just building AI applications and realizing the infrastructure sucks — like, there's got to be a better way to do that. So a lot of the rationale for Modal was kind of building a tool I always wanted to have throughout my years at Spotify.

— So Modal was more of an offshoot of the stuff you learned at Spotify, not much from better.com?

Better.com was a little bit of a side tour. It was kind of a roller coaster. Long story about the company, talk about it separately, but I was CTO for 5 years of Better and grew the tech team from two to three/four hundred. So I learned a lot about management and building teams and hiring, and also learned a lot about developer productivity. Thought a lot about tools and things like that. Did a lot more full-stack stuff, but yeah, kind of came back to what's close to my heart — infrastructure and AI and machine learning — after that.

— What was better.com doing again?

Mortgages.

— How did you get into that?

This guy Zach Frankel, who I didn't know at that time, ended up recruiting me to Better as the CTO. The company was 10 people, and for whatever reason, the founder Vishal — very interesting guy, very very smart, a little crazy in mostly positive ways — we got along very well. So we started building it in 2015, and I spent 5 years growing that company. Eventually it turned out that doing mortgages is pretty hard, and interest rates went up very quickly after the pandemic, and that caused a lot of issues at the company. But by then I had already left.

— That was like 2020, 2021 when you left. So you left before you had the idea for Modal?

It's hard to say. I had a lot of random ideas when I left Better, and I actually wasn't sure if I wanted to start a company. During the pandemic I sort of almost took like a sabbatical. I had two kids — I mean, I still have two kids, but at that time they were two and four — so I decided to hang out and took some time off and was working part-time, hacking on certain things, wasn't sure maybe I should do some consulting. I started building stuff and I just got super pumped about this idea that eventually became Modal. But Modal was like the third thing I built. There were a few attempts before then that went nowhere, but Modal was the first idea where I thought, "This is kind of cool, I should do this. This could be a really cool platform."

— Were the other ideas also in a similar vein, like developer tools?

The first thing was like some sort of web scraping thing which went nowhere, but actually in hindsight maybe could have gotten somewhere.

— Was this before the ChatGPT launch?

Yeah. 2021. ChatGPT was late 2022.

Luigi、工作流调度与 Modal 的雏形

To rewind a little bit for context: when I worked at Spotify, I released an open-source framework called Luigi, which is workflow orchestration. It's the same category as Airflow and Prefect and Dagster — sort of a dated category to some extent, people don't talk about it as much, but for a while it got a lot of attention. I never turned it into a business.

A couple years later, in 2021, when I was thinking about business ideas or things to work on, I came back to workflow orchestration and started hacking on a bunch of ideas of orchestrating code running in the cloud. And what I realized was that the core puzzle piece is not just orchestrating the compute — it's executing the compute. I realized that's actually a bigger problem to solve. So in a way I left it on the shelf and said, "Actually, I'm going to go to this other thing over here and I'll get back to the workflow scheduling in a little bit" — but I never got back to it.

Long story short, I ended up building Modal, where the focus was more: let's figure out a way to make it easy to run code in the cloud. The focus was initially fairly general-purpose. In a way, we've come full circle more recently. We focused on so many different applications — the idea was let's just make it super easy to run code in the cloud: could be GPU code, AI, machine learning, could also be data stuff. Focused a lot on how do we scale it, how do we make the developer experience awesome. Realized super early that in order to do that we'd have to go very deep in the stack — build on file system, built on container runtime — and did a lot of hard engineering challenges.

You mentioned ChatGPT. That was actually not quite the killer app, but if you remember, that fall another thing came out around the same time, which was Stable Diffusion. And Stable Diffusion turned out to be a killer app for what we were building. At that time we were only four or five people. We started seeing a lot of people coming to us who wanted to run a Stable Diffusion model, and then we realized maybe GenAI inference is actually a really good use case for us.

— How were they finding you?

I'm this compulsive tweeter. I was even more [compulsive] than now — I'm too distracted by building a company now — but I always tweeted a lot, I always blogged a lot. I think I had a little bit of a following. So in the early days a lot of what drove the growth was just me compulsively tweeting about Modal and what I was building and getting people excited and writing long blog posts about where the cloud is going. I call it founder-led marketing. I always feel like you kind of have to lean into what you're good at, and what I'm good at is just posting and being terminally online. So it still works — I think a lot of our growth is: we're just kind of good at social media and being online a lot.

第一个客户、首次融资与早期增长

— How long until you had your first customer? Also, did you raise early on?

We didn't raise for a while. I actually self-funded it for a while, even with up until the first few employees — which in a way was kind of nice because it made me really frugal about money and wanting to see ROI. I wasn't taking out a salary for a while, for a long time actually. At some point it became a problem because I needed the money. But we didn't raise for a while, and until early 2022 raised a seed round.

So at that point I'd already been working on it for about a year. Akshat joined as the CTO and co-founder about five years ago now — August 2021 maybe. But then it took until basically late 2022 for us to see any meaningful revenue.

— I guess that's when ChatGPT came out.

Yeah, and Stable Diffusion, in our case, was the main thing. We went from $100 a month in November 2022, and the next month we did $2,000 a month, and then January 2023 we did $30,000 all of a sudden. Finally I felt this massive anxiety thing off my chest — I'm like, maybe we're actually onto something. It feels like we're onto something. And then 2023 we grew very fast, and we've been growing very fast since then.

— That $30k-a-month moment — was that just a couple big customers or very diverse?

It's just one, and I don't know if I ever talked about who that was, and if they even know it, but I think they suspect — it was a company in New York called Mage. They were doing Stable Diffusion in a company. At some point, in the first quarter of 2023, they were 80–90% of our revenue. But after that it started diversifying a little bit. Late 2023 we got Suno as a big customer. They were a big chunk of our revenue for a while too. Over time we actually have really good revenue diversification now.

— For the Stable Diffusion stuff, I remember using it for ComfyUI. I'm assuming a lot of people were using ComfyUI, like running ComfyUI workflows on it.

Some people were, but the people that were using Modal tended to be more low-level stuff — they did complicated stuff. What they liked with Modal is that it's always been pretty hackable. So they deployed their own custom workflows with adapters and custom inference and a lot of optimizations. And all the stuff we had done in order to get the developer experience to be really good turned out to be really good for also running production workloads. Because autoscaling turns out to be actually a very similar problem — you want to scale up containers up and down very fast. So we just happened to be very well positioned to capture a lot of those workloads in the early days.

为什么要自己重建工具栈

— Did tools for autoscaling not exist? Like why did you have to build those yourself?

In general my thesis is: every new era of technology kind of runs up against limitations of tools — whether that's the web, the cloud, mobile, PCs, or AI. It's often the case that tools exist, but they're often not particularly good, and you kind of need to rethink a lot of those tools in order to reap the benefits of this new world and really turbocharge and start building for it.

You saw this with cloud — we had to invent things like Kubernetes and Docker. In a similar way, with GenAI, you could build these things on the prior generation of tools — you can build these things on top of Kubernetes and Docker — but those technologies are built for a very different type of workload. They're built for very steady backend workloads: an even steady number of requests running at pretty low utilization, because CPUs are normally pretty cheap, so people don't really worry so much about cost.

But now you're entering this new world and you have very expensive GPUs, you want to manage capacity and utilization, you have very large models that you need to load over network into CPU into GPU — and it turns out a lot of these tools were just not built for that. So we felt we had to rebuild a lot of that. I mentioned the file system, but we also spent a lot of time over the last few years building some really cool stuff around CPU snapshotting, GPU snapshotting, we built our own autoscaler and scheduler and all kinds of capacity management tools. We kind of feel like you have to do that because you can't build for this new generation of software on top of — you can't build a wrapper on top of the old stuff in order to do the new stuff. You kind of need to start over a little bit from scratch.

— Did you see any weird behaviors on the platform? Was there anything that broke while you guys were scaling?

Capacity is always from time to time been a challenge — how do you get hundreds and thousands and tens of thousands of GPUs. That's always challenging. We had to go multi-region very early. I think that was kind of a fateful decision in hindsight — doing that and just biting the bullet. We always thought of our capacity management as one big pool — over the entire world. We don't think of it as separate clusters running in each region. That was one of the very consequential decisions we made early.

I mean, we've obviously had bugs and outages, and I hate — as much as I would love for Modal to be 100% uptime, and I think recently we've basically hit four or five nines — but throughout the history of Modal, of course we've had scaling issues and things like that.

云容量市场的演变：从 Spot 到 25 家云、再到三年期合约

— Do you guys use AWS, GCP, all these cloud providers underneath? Do you also buy any infrastructure?

Let's talk a bit about cloud capacity, because I think it's actually changed a lot. In the first few years, we got almost all the capacity from the hyperscalers — spot and on-demand capacity, mostly spot capacity running in all the different regions, initially AWS but also GCP, and over time Azure. We started renting some capacity from Oracle pretty early because we wanted A10s and A100s and we got really good rates on those. Over time we added a couple more clouds doing reservations. But still, up until basically end of last year, most of our capacity was either spot or one-year reservations.

— "Spot" means you're just renting it right there and then?

Exactly. And it's also preemptable, which we had to deal with. But it sort of works in aggregate because you can aggregate capacity from many hundreds of regions basically.

That model worked really well until we started running up against — I mean first of all, Modal started growing very fast and we needed more capacity, but fundamentally also the cloud market started changing a lot. So in the last year, in order to get the capacity we need, we had to work with a much larger set of clouds. We actually work with almost 25 clouds at this point. And in many cases, in order to get the capacity we want, we have to go and do three-plus-year deals, and you have to pay a meaningful amount of money up front. And you're locking in pricing on a three-year term.

So we had to spend the entire last 6 to 9 months rethinking how we get capacity. We had to build a whole procurement desk — we have four guys working full-time basically all they're doing is procuring capacity, calling neoclouds, doing deals, vetting the capacity. We've had to build a whole engineering team, basically 10 people, just managing bare-metal capacity from all over the world and dealing with network issues and bad drives and GPUs falling off the bus and all these things.

We don't own capacity. We rent all the capacity so far, typically on three-year deals. And that's a big decision — like, should we buy, should we keep renting? I'm actually not mega dogmatic about it. I think renting is nice because there's a certain amount of capital efficiency to it. If you're buying — first of all, there's an obvious operational complexity: you have to deal with vendors and suppliers and power and cables. But there's also financial complexity: how do you fund it? Should you raise equity? Then you can raise a billion dollars and go buy hardware for it — that's a very dilutive way to do it. You can raise debt, but if you raise debt, you typically want to have locked-in long-term revenue to pay the interest rates — so that's also not trivial.

We look at the economics, we look at the operational complexity, we look at the risks. It's a complex trade-off, and we're open to buying. There's other constructs too — to get the capacity we need for 2027, it's going to take a lot of work on going a lot of different avenues to lock it up.

— Do you have to hire a lot of finance people to do all this stuff?

You know, I've had to spend a lot of time on this. These are very expensive assets. It's kind of staggering — you're starting to see AI investments becoming several percentage points of GDP of the US, you're starting to see interest rates in America shooting up in the last few weeks. And at this stage, you go and look at the neoclouds — these are very very sophisticated financial engineering companies. So yeah, we look at that, and it's possible we might have to do similar things ourselves. I would rather focus on being a very lean software company doing the things we're good at. I don't think it's good in general for software companies to own hard assets — in the same way as, should you own your office? I don't think that's necessarily the right solution for most companies. But of course, in order to get the capacity you want, everything's on the table.

供给紧张会持续多久？

— And I guess the supply is going to be constrained for a while, so you kind of have to do that. Do you agree with that, or do you think this is just a moment in time?

I don't necessarily agree with that. Nvidia is delivering several hundred thousand Blackwells a month, right? And I don't want to say the market is 100% efficient, but in general, if you're willing to pay a high price, you can get GPU capacity. If you're willing to pay more than everyone else — and of course Anthropic and OpenAI are buying up as much as they can — but fundamentally there's constantly supply coming on the market. So I don't necessarily think it's a fully cornered resource.

Prices are going up, and it's worth kind of reflecting on that — the normal state of hardware is kind of like gravity: eventually hardware prices always go down. So we're a little bit in a weird period of time where hardware prices are going up. It's hard to say how long this is going to last — could be another 6 months, could be another 36 months, really hard to know. But I fundamentally don't think it's true to say you need to buy capacity. To me that's a little bit almost like the great toilet paper shortage of the pandemic — like, a run-on-the-bank type situation.

That being said, capacity is going to be tight for a while, and prices are going up. Luckily I think it's not even necessarily bad for us if prices go up, because scarcity also means we can charge more from our customers. And the fact that we have a lot of reservations locked in at a rate means to some extent we're effectively long GPU prices already. So I don't necessarily worry too much about prices going up. I do worry more about actually prices collapsing. I don't think that's going to happen anytime soon, but that would be a quite bad thing for a lot of the players in the market.

— Why would that be bad?

It would be bad for anyone who's locked in a lot of supply. They paid too much. There's a risk of buying at the top. And again, I don't worry about that much — I don't think it's going to happen anytime soon — but like I said, hardware prices in the very long run tend to go down. So it's worth reflecting on that. Right now, your capacity is constrained, and that leads to, in economic terms, a scarcity rent. Who captures the scarcity rent? I think that primarily goes to two places — mostly Nvidia, but also to some extent neoclouds. Anyone owning capacity has better economics — that's undeniably true today with capacity being constrained.

Long term, in the very long run, I don't think that's necessarily entirely true. There's always going to be a little bit of a premium you can get from owning GPUs, but is it worth the risk of holding this very expensive asset on your balance sheet? I'm not so sure. We're going to see — it's going to take a few years to get through this. In the long run we might own some, we might rent some, maybe a combination, maybe do some other crazy stuff — joint ventures, who knows, maybe some complex SPVs or whatever. Everything is on the table.

与 OpenAI、Anthropic 争夺 GPU

— How do you compete with OpenAI and Anthropic in buying GPU capacity? I'm assuming they'd want to buy up literally everything that's available.

They are. And a lot of the prices going up is a reflection of that. That being said, Nvidia is shipping a lot of stuff. I think also, to some extent, Nvidia prefers a little bit of diversification — they don't want a small number of large buyers, much in the same way as you see hyperscalers getting a little bit of a constrained allocation. Nvidia prefers to see a lot of neoclouds and alternative clouds getting more allocation.

A little bit of what we see in the market — this is more speculation — is we see smaller clouds that are a little bit more risky to work with being more of an opportunity for us. Where maybe Anthropic and OpenAI prefer to buy from the tried and true. Part of it is also because they had to do a lot of training runs, so they need to have very large blocks. But there's plenty of capacity out there. You can get 32 nodes in Armenia, you can get 128 nodes in Indonesia. We love that kind of — we can go out there and get a lot of smaller capacity all over the world. Pretty good prices.

— Is it pretty much just: if someone offers you a certain number of GPUs, that's all you care about? You don't care how reliable it is, or if it's some janky warehouse?

I mean, sometimes it's kind of a janky warehouse, it feels like. But we do have a spec sheet. When we talk to vendors, the first thing we do is we send them a spec sheet. We say: we need this number of IOPS, the CPU needs to have this many — whatever the PassMark scores are — we need to see minimum north-south bandwidth, egress and ingress. So we do have a list of requirements.

Often we try to do an acceptance testing period where we get one node and run some tests. Over time, to some extent, it also involves a little bit of a leap of faith. Sometimes we sign very big commitments — tens or hundreds of millions of dollars — and we start working with the vendor that we still don't fully know. And a little bit — just like SemiAnalysis has a ClusterMAX, I kind of feel like we almost have our own "Modal MAX score" internally. I know which vendors I like more than others, and we prefer to do additional deals with the vendors that we've seen have very good reliability. Not just reliability — it's also, are they very responsive when we have support issues? Do they fix the issues we ask for? The turnaround time — if things go down, how quickly do they fix it?

需求是不是无限的？要不要"囤货"？

— Do you agree that the demand for intelligence is basically infinite? And if so, why wouldn't you just buy up as much capacity as possible, and if you over-buy, you can just sell it to somebody else?

I think it's very easy to say when there's a scarce resource, "let's just buy as much as you can." But first of all, if we bought it today we couldn't utilize all of it — we could utilize a lot of it.

— But you can sell it off to somebody else who wants to use it, right?

The challenge is if there was something in the market that happens, there are a lot of correlations that happen at the same time: prices going down and utilization going down and the market for reselling capacity vanishes at kind of the same time. I'm sitting here and I'm extremely aggressive — buying capacity every day, raising money to buy. Overall I'm very bullish. But I do want to point out there are tail risks here, and when those tail risks happen, it could get very bad.

Part of it is: maybe I'm just old and I've seen this in the past. I actually had my first job in 1999, so I saw the dotcom crisis and the great financial crisis. I want to build a company that is around for 20 to 30, 50 more years. So we can certainly go out and buy an insane amount of capacity right now and try to just corner the market — but do you know about the Hunt brothers? It's a legendary story in trading. They tried to corner the silver market. It failed spectacularly. So cornering the market in general can be not a good idea.

We are in general very very aggressive, but we're ramping up at an aggressive plan that basically matches our demand growth and matches where we want to try to get to at the end of next year in terms of run rate.

非 Nvidia 加速器与"硬件瓶颈再下游还有瓶颈"

— Are you only buying up Nvidia stuff, or also capacity from other types of companies?

We're looking at it. I think the alternative accelerators are starting to get very interesting. Ironically, every year in the last 5 — maybe even 10 — years, I've been saying, "next year it's going to be the year of non-Nvidia accelerators," and then I'm always wrong. But I do think 2027 might be the year of non-Nvidia accelerators finally. We'll see if I'm wrong this year too.

AMDs are starting to get really good scores on certain things. TPUs are obviously used very widely internally at Google, seem to work really well. I don't know much about Trainium — I don't feel like I see quite as [much], but the team is very good, I know they're working on a lot of the software stuff. Hardware is hard in a certain way — software is easier — and that makes me feel like, if we fix the software layer for these accelerators, there's going to be a lot of demand for them. Fundamentally, with Nvidia being such a bottleneck, we'll probably see more alternative accelerators.

That being said, there's bottlenecks further down the pipe. There's TSMC and ASML — maybe a deeper bottleneck to all of this anyway. But long-term, monopolies don't always last. I think it'd be healthy for the market to have more alternatives. As much as I love Nvidia — to make that clear, they're obviously an amazing company with an amazing product — I do expect to see a little bit more diversity in the market. Also things like Cerebras and Groq.

— What are your thoughts on some of those providers?

I think they're pretty exciting. You see them doing really well on certain workloads. And there's some interesting people doing hybrid, disaggregated inference where they run Nvidia for the prefill and Cerebras for the decode and things like that.

— I've never heard of that actually.

Yeah. And Groq too, because a lot of these things — certain things are compute-bound, certain things are memory-bound — you can mix and match. I think that's quite exciting. It starts to get very complex when you're deploying these things in practice, but I do think there's a lot of opportunity in these more complex hardware setups.

Neocloud 的金融炼金术

— Are there any learnings you get from some of these neoclouds — Nebius and others — in the way they're doing things vs. what you're doing?

One of the things that's very interesting with neoclouds is how can they expand so quickly. The most crazy example is like Nscale, which went from nowhere to having hundreds of billions of dollars in their pipeline despite barely having any capacity. How can neoclouds grow so fast?

The answer — this might be obvious — is: they go out to Anthropic or OpenAI or some big buyer and say, "Hey, do you want to buy 5 years of chips? Sign this contract, we'll give you a good rate." Then they take that contract and go to Wall Street and say, "Look, we got this big buyer, they committed to $10 billion worth of chips, we just need the money right now." And they raise the money, go to Supermicro and Dell and Nvidia and get the hardware, install it, and now they deliver it to the customer.

So you have this very nice financial construct where you can basically pre-sell things that you haven't even bought. And that means you can scale up extremely fast. That's what we've seen with these neoclouds — they can scale very very well. Modal, because we've always had more of a PLG focus and not the ability to lock in long-term contracts in the same way, it's a little bit more challenging from a financial perspective to scale that fast. Even though I think in the long run we'll get to the same point. But that's been kind of a fascinating thing to see with these neoclouds — especially CoreWeave and the big ones — being very savvy with how they raise money, and thinking about GPU as collateral for loans and all these things.

— What's the relevance of — I forget who it was, but some financial company said "we're going to turn GPUs into an asset class." Is that just because they need to raise money? What's the relevance of that?

There's a bunch of startups — there's Silicon Data and Compute Exchange and a few other ones that are trying to create price indices and indexes and trading derivatives. I think it's interesting. There are a number of challenges with compute as an asset class — it's definitely not as homogeneous as other asset classes. You have different network, different locations, different disks, CPUs, reliability.

That being said, you can say the same thing about oil, and we kind of created relatively commoditized tradable assets out of oil. It remains to be seen. At this scale where we are with the AI data center GPU deployment, we do need to be a little bit smarter with risk hedging and how we share risks and more insurance and things like that. I'm very happy that people are thinking a lot about this. That being said, I'm not entirely sure if we're going to see GPUs becoming the Henry Hub, Brent crude type super-commoditized tradable asset.

Modal 的两大产品：Functions 和 Sandboxes

— I want to shift the conversation to Modal Sandboxes. Before that — what are the different products Modal has?

The two big products that we have: number one is Modal Functions, and number two is Modal Sandboxes.

Modal Functions — we launched that back in 2021. The idea of serverless functions that are very easy to deploy and very easy to scale, and we manage all the capacity. That turned out to be really good for inference and for managing GPUs. We actually never had a dedicated inference product or a GPU product per se — we never thought of Modal as a neocloud. There's a risk of getting sucked in that direction, becoming a neocloud, selling what I think was like rectangular — here's a three-year, you get this many GPUs. We've always been very good at: you deploy something, you can scale it up, you have very cyclical or bursty stuff, we manage all the capacity. The beautiful thing is because we have many many thousands of customers, we can aggregate that capacity and smooth workloads — very smooth aggregate demand which we can manage very efficiently.

Modal Functions was the core. We launched it in 2021, started seeing product-market fit in 2023, and now it's about two-thirds of our revenue, empowering a lot of — in practice it's mostly inference, but you can use it for all kinds of other stuff.

Modal Sandboxes — we launched that in 2023 and it actually took a while to see product-market fit. Why did we launch it? We realized a lot of people we talked to were using LLMs to output code. This was me and Akshat talking over lunch one day — maybe they need a place to run that code. And we realized we kind of have a lot of the infrastructure already to just take code and run it, because we already built the primitives for managing containers and isolation, we already had gVisor as an isolation primitive. So we got excited about that idea. Nokia wrote a prototype and launched it in basically one day or two days.

Zero — I don't want to trivialize it, we did see some growth, like some people picked it up, we had some early users who enjoyed it for certain things. But overall it was a pretty insignificant source of revenue going into the summer of 2023 — two years later. We even discussed, "Do we even need this product? Should we shut it down?" Then it just started exploding.

What really happened: LLMs got really good at generating code. I feel like that was when they went from being able to refactor functions and write snippets to generating full apps. We started seeing a lot of growth coming from vibe coding, companies like Lovable and other ones. Then companies like Ramp started using Modal for background agents, and we started seeing tremendous growth coming from a number of neolabs doing reinforcement learning on Modal sandboxes.

Sandboxes is now about a third of our revenue. We consider it basically our second product. To me it's really exciting because even back in the early days of Modal, I always knew Modal is about creating a whole toolkit of products. We always wanted to be almost like a cloud — you have the storage and the compute and a bunch of different ways to work with it. We always wanted to be a multi-product vendor. But that wasn't necessarily true in practice until now, where I think it's clear we have Functions, we have Sandboxes, we're working on a bunch of other stuff too — training, batch. That evolution into becoming a multi-product company has been amazing because that was always so core to the vision even in the very early decks. I had a bunch of slides on this, but it wasn't necessarily true to the external world until recently.

下一个大赌注：训练、Batch、低延迟语音、Agent

— Do you have anything in the works that you think is going to be like that next product? Any predictions about the market?

I'm very bullish on training. I think training is kind of an underserved market. Obviously there's a lot of focus on very large training runs, but we actually see a lot of demand in the smaller and midsize training segment. I'll be talking a little bit about that later this week — we're organizing a conference.

Batch is a really interesting market. We see a lot of demand for customers that need — we had a customer the other day that needed to transcribe 5,000 years of audio. They had millions and millions of audio files, we had a lot of capacity, so we let them do that — took a few days. I think there's some really interesting use cases there.

Very bullish on low-latency stuff. Once we get the audio — the speech-to-speech models, the voice models — working, I expect that to be a very interesting market.

Then of course all this agentic stuff. In a way I have mixed feelings about the word "agentic" because in certain ways I think all software will become agentic. So it's almost like, to me, what does it mean to be agentic? I think all software in a certain way will become AI-powered over time. But clearly there's a set of building blocks of doing more LLM-powered software that seems to be common across all the different use cases. The way I think about Modal is: we're in the business of building building blocks. We want to give you amazing generalizable, battle-tested, general-purpose, composable building blocks. There's some really interesting stuff with the agent use cases.

— That's interesting you bring up training, because in another podcast maybe a year or two ago, you said you were not focused on training specifically. What changed?

We've been building a training product for multiple years on and off. I wouldn't say we never been focused on it, but a year or two ago we were a much smaller number of engineers, and by virtue of being smaller we had to focus. Inference became our sole focus for many years. But we're bigger now — we're 150 engineers — we have opportunities to also place bets in other markets.

I'm also really interested in continuing the list of things: post-training, reinforcement learning. There's some really exciting stuff. Many other things around storage and building data warehousing and feature stores and real-time streaming pipelines. The long-term view of Modal is: you want to build some cool AI — we got you covered. We got all the building blocks, come to us and we'll help you take all these building blocks and compose them. That's the beauty of software — you can build almost anything if you have the right building blocks. That's very much the company and product we want to build.

— When you say training, are you focused on bigger enterprises doing huge training runs?

No. They're going to go and do big hyperscaler or neocloud mega-deals and get 100,000 GPUs or whatever. But there's a little bit of an underserved market of researchers iterating, or people training smaller models. Text-to-speech and speech-to-text models. Computational biotech is actually a market where we see a lot of demand — we have a lot of customers in that space, training relatively modest models you can train on 64 GPUs. Recommendation systems. A lot of traditional machine learning. There's a lot of things where you don't need 100,000 GPUs. We're not going to focus on that for a while, but there's a lot of stuff in the slightly smaller markets that are relatively underserved. It's very hard to set up training clusters.

— Have you noticed since GLM 5.2 or Kimi K3 or maybe Kimi 2.5 — that a lot of people are using those and fine-tuning them?

If anything, I've actually seen the other direction. The value prop of fine-tuning a couple years ago was: open-source models, they're not quite as good, but if you take a small model and fine-tune it on your specific domain, you can actually reach the frontier in terms of quality and cost. Today I would say the open-source models are so good that you can basically just swap them out and run — instead of the frontier ones — Kimi K3 or DeepSeek 4.1 or GLM 5.3, and they're basically almost as good as the frontier model at a much lower cost. So we still see a lot of demand for post-training. I do think it's a really interesting space and we're working on some products in that space — both SFT and reinforcement learning. I would also say fine-tuning is no longer the thing that you kind of have to do — it's very optional. Open-source models work really well just off the shelf too.

Sandboxes 的技术护城河与未来

— Back to sandboxes. What did you have to update about the sandboxes that existing sandboxes did not allow for?

Not a whole lot. The thing we've always been very very good at — we're infra geeks — we're very good at scaling and reliability. That explains to a large extent why we have, in my opinion (I don't have numbers), by far the largest market share in the space. We're just very good at running hundreds of thousands or even millions of sandboxes. I'll say we've had to rewrite our systems a bunch of times in order to handle that scale.

The sandbox space in general is not the most differentiated space, but we're working on some really cool stuff. Over time we've had to add support for VMs — virtual machines — we previously built our sandbox product on gVisor, but now we offer fully virtualized machines as well. Turns out for certain use cases you kind of need full Linux compatibility. We've had to build better primitives for more interactive — piping data back and forth between sandboxes, working with file systems. We've had to spend a lot of time on snapshotting.

A lot of the things that in the long run will differentiate will be really cool things like forking sandboxes, snapshotting, resuming snapshots, live migrations in general. The novelty of sandboxes was always this sort of ephemerality — you can spin off sandboxes for a few seconds — and that's something I want to pull more in. There's a lot of really cool stuff you can do: decoupling the agent and the harness, decoupling it from sandboxes, having agents control many sandboxes, forking sandboxes, snapshotting things, running basically very short-lived — maybe one per command. I think there's a lot of cool stuff there. We've already spent a lot of time on snapshots, but there's a lot of cool stuff to be built there as well.

— You brought up snapshotting a couple times. What's the use case?

The big thing for me: today a lot of sandbox workloads are kind of lift-and-shift. People think a lot about sandboxes almost like, "I have my dev box, now I'm going to shove it in the cloud, I'm going to have an agent control it, maybe I'll run the harness inside the sandbox." I don't know if long-term that's the right way to think about compute for agents.

A much better model would be: you're going to have these very long-running agents, which to me are kind of durable execution workflows. They're going to run 24/7, and every once in a while they're going to run commands. Having the ability to spin up a sandbox in 100 milliseconds, run a few commands, shut it down and snapshot it — the faster you can get that wake-up-go-to-sleep cycle, the more you can create sandboxes that only run for a very brief period. And that will make compute much more efficient. It will also enable you to do some really cool things — forking, moving things around. Imagine Claude Code: instead of having a very linear, sequential flow, kind of branching and running hundreds of agents at the same time.

I think a lot about CI as another illustrative example. For most of the history of CI — GitHub Actions and things like that — you had a very sequential flow: you slowly install a bunch of stuff, then you run the test suite, then generate some reports. You can break it up into shards, but it's kind of annoying. What I would love to do is take your entire test suite and just run every single test in its own sandbox, and just parallelize the hell out of that. Run a thousand sandboxes.

— Why can't that be done?

The problem is there's too much overhead around starting and stopping sandboxes. So the more you create frictionless starting and stopping, the more you can enter a world where you can do this extremely bursty, large-scale, run as much as you want in parallel. I'm an infra geek, like I said, I get very excited about these things. Once we figure out all these primitives and the right building blocks, I think it's going to unlock a lot of really cool stuff that we previously could not do with software.

— Why hasn't that already been built? Previously people would want to parallelize as much CI as possible.

You can, but the overhead — it's like Amdahl's law. The overhead of parallelization right now is very high. In GitHub Actions, we parallelize in the Modal test suite. But what that basically means is: if you take your test suite and split it in two, now each of those shards both need to do all the installs and the test setup, and that takes a long time — minutes. But let's say you can do the test setup once and then snapshot the container, and now you clone it and run the test suites independently. A lot of the benefits — you can't materialize those benefits until you get the friction and the overhead down.

— The transaction cost.

与 Anthropic 的合作与 Hugging Face 事件

— I think you guys have a partnership with Anthropic and they're using sandboxes for something like Modal sandboxes.

Yeah, the managed agents with Anthropic — there's a sort of bring-your-own sandbox integration. So you can use Modal for those.

— How did that come about?

I think Anthropic is trying to create a thriving ecosystem and community. They make money from inference, so I think it's very much in their interest to promote — for everything else — as much of an ecosystem as possible. They want to have the largest possible surface area, as long as you use Anthropic for inference. So it makes very rational sense for them to partner with us as a sandbox provider.

— Also, I feel like we have to bring up the Hugging Face incident. Are you okay talking about that?

Yeah, it's all there.

— Could you just briefly describe what happened? They were using the Modal sandbox, but it wasn't your fault.

I forget all the details of the exploit. What you're referring to is the fact that Modal was involved. Basically the agents running inside — that exploited Hugging Face — they discovered a vulnerability in an app that was deployed on Modal, and they used that as almost a springboard for getting full internet access, is my understanding.

To be clear, this is an app running on Modal that was hacked — it was not Modal that was hacked. It's like AWS: a lot of people run stuff on AWS, occasionally those apps get hacked — does that mean AWS got hacked? No, of course not. There are a lot of people running apps on Modal, and one of those apps got hacked.

But there are some lessons we can learn. One of the things we've been reflecting on: could we have more sensible security restrictions by default? To use the AWS analogy — S3 used to be very easy to accidentally make an S3 bucket public, and AWS realized this doesn't necessarily pose a security problem for AWS per se, but a lot of their customers accidentally leak data. So S3 made it much harder now to make S3 buckets public. In a similar way, we're exploring — can we make security a little bit more restrictive by default, without necessarily destroying the magic?

As a separate sidetrack: agents are getting really good at cybersecurity. As a separate learning from this incident, we started using agents internally quite a lot to try to find vulnerabilities. So far hasn't found anything, but they're very good at probing into very deep parts of the system, trying to exploit things, trying to escalate and get out of sandboxes. It's something we're exploring very actively right now.

— How exactly do you get the agents to run through the codebase? You're just like, "Hey, find security vulnerabilities"?

No, you just put them in a sandbox and tell them, "Can you try to escape?" Just try to escape from the sandbox. It's like escape-the-room but for agents.

— When did you start doing that?

A few months ago.

— Like when Fable came out?

Yeah, roughly around the same time.

My view on cybersecurity: I actually think [agents] are very good at finding vulnerabilities, but you can also use them defensively very well. Companies like Modal and many other companies — I'm sure every CISO is thinking about the same thing: how do we use agents defensively to fix all our vulnerabilities. Over time, actually, I'm not that nervous. I think agents and cybersecurity — all the breakthroughs in cybersecurity will make the world safer, if anything.

— Do you think all the big cybersecurity companies are just cooked?

I don't know if that's true. When I think about cybersecurity, a lot of what you're selling is effectively fear, and that's almost like a branding and marketing strategy as much as the core products. Brand and things like that are arguably more valuable in the era of AI. I wouldn't necessarily jump to the conclusion that they're cooked. They have deep relationships with the enterprise customers, big sales teams who are very good at telling spooky stories. I think they're going to continue to be very good at that.

— I just ask because, yeah, you're doing it yourself. You're not going to one of the Palo Alto Networks. But I guess it's only giant enterprises that care about that — also they can blame somebody if something goes wrong.

That is true. Yeah, you kind of want to hire in many cases just an established vendor in order to blame them. It does reduce a little bit the need for us to bring in pentesters — human pentesters — which most startups do on a regular cycle. Maybe previously we would do it — I actually don't know what the cycle was, but I think we used to do it once every six months roughly. Maybe now we only need to do it once every year, I don't know.

With all of these things, humans can also use them to get more efficient. I'm kind of a believer that humans with AI are even more powerful now. Maybe we can bring in pentesters who are really good at using agents and find vulnerabilities even faster. I'm an optimist. I started a company — I'm generally optimistic about everything. But I certainly don't think humans are cooked or companies are cooked. In the era of AI, a lot of companies are going to figure out how to use AI to be even more efficient.

开发者体验在 Agent 时代是否还重要？

— I want to transition to developer experience, because you guys focus a lot on that. Does developer experience even matter anymore?

I think it still matters. The context — the thing you're talking about — is: now with agents, right? The docs are already there, the agents are going to look at the docs.

To that point, almost all the things that make developer experience good also make the agent experience good — that's what we've seen in practice. Things like having good docs, having descriptive error messages, having fast feedback loops. Certain things have changed. The other day I was setting something up with Cloudflare, and I find Cloudflare notoriously annoying to work with sometimes. I threw an agent at it and it was able to configure a bunch of things in Pulumi for me. Agents do make it a little bit easier to work with things that are harder to work with in the past — the human toll of dealing with YAML has arguably gone down a little bit because you can tell your agent to deal with it. But for the most part, the things that make developer experience good also make agent experience good.

To some extent, infrastructure over time anyway becomes more programmatic. That's always been the thesis about sandboxes — things that you previously had to configure using YAML should just be an SDK, more imperative: launch a sandbox, do stuff with it, tear the sandbox down, rather than declarative using some sort of DSL. It also pushes a different interface that maybe previously didn't exist. In either way, SDKs are as relevant as they always were, if not more.

— Is there anything you changed in your product just because most people are running agents on it?

We also run a lot of internal tests where we tell agents to build a mobile app and run it. A very concrete thing that is kind of funny: we've actually seen that because of agent training data, it's very hard to deprecate things now. Agents often love using old versions of Modal syntax, and it's kind of hard to nudge them away from that. So we've had to be a little bit more conservative going forward with how we deprecate and remove features. We have to be very careful to update every single example that's out there online. There's also an insane amount of Modal code that's now online that goes into the training data.

Another thing: similar to search engine optimization, there's agent engine optimization. We often run internal benchmarks where we ask an agent, "Hey, can you deploy Stable Diffusion for us? Use whatever tool you want," and we see if it recommends Modal or not. Those things are very useful for us to track over time. Or, "Hey, spin up some sandboxes," or, "Hey, rank all the sandbox vendors." So we spend a lot of time doing those things.

— What do you do about that? You say, "Hey, build this Stable Diffusion thing," does it recommend Modal or not? What do you do about that?

I think that's harder. It's like search engine optimization — primarily through content. You just have to put out a lot of content. You can also, to some extent, see the perception a little bit more — you can ask an agent, "Rank all the sandbox vendors by reliability" or "rank all the sandbox vendors by price," and see. Agents are a little bit more prone to misunderstanding pricing and things like that. So we spend a lot of time making content more clear and more understandable for agents, because we know all the indexing — everything that's out there and talking about Modal.

— Have you thought about just making a bunch of GitHub repos and having the agents write a bunch of Modal code in there? Slop cannon.

I think the truth is that is probably something you can do. My guess is LLM training data today is probably quite insensitive to what's AI output in the first place, and you can probably create a lot of slop. We thought about it — I don't love that idea. But in theory, much like SEO in the early days and still to some extent, auto-generated content is a very effective strategy. I think it's possible you could do those things today.

FDE（Forward Deployed Engineers）与 PM 的角色

— I want to switch to FDEs. Apparently you guys hire forward-deployed engineers. What do they do?

We're in a new era of building applications that we couldn't build just a few years ago, and we see a lot of companies that need a little bit of help. We started investing in FDEs a couple years ago, but it's really been this year we've scaled it up a lot. We started this year having four FDEs, now I think we have 24 or something like that. So we've grown a lot.

It's not exactly the Counter model, but they do a lot of heavy customer engagement. They work with a lot of customers on performance tuning, especially with LLMs — we see there's so much benefit from sitting down with customers and training draft models and tweaking parameters in vLLM and SGLang. When customers run into issues, FDEs often work with customers trying to figure out how to work around that.

Another thing we've used FDEs a lot for: proactively, if we see certain customers over-provisioning with Modal — customers requesting too much CPU or too much memory, for instance — that's kind of expensive. We try to catch those things and sit down with those customers: "Yo, you're spending a lot of money on Modal right now, we can actually help you save money."

Of course, with active deals, we help them migrate code from other platforms.

We never have the intention of becoming a service-heavy business. The goal for FDEs is: A, to be part of the sales process and closing deals; B, to serve customers and do customer support; but C — the most important thing — bridging gaps in the product that we later want to turn into real features. Anything an FDE does, my question is always: long-term, how do we turn this into product, so we don't need an FDE for this?

— Do you guys hire PMs — product managers?

No.

— Would you say these FDEs are kind of pseudo-ish PMs?

It's a little bit of a different function. Certainly on the more customer-facing side they are. But there's a separate part of product management which is more inward: what are the next building blocks Modal should invest in? Looking at 10, 20 different customers all asking for slightly different things — what are the patterns, how do we turn this into product? We do have people doing product with us, and it evolved — we've had people become product managers after previously being either devrel or engineers, just showing strong aptitude on thinking very strategically about what we have to build.

I'm not anti-product management. I do think a lot of companies in the past hired product managers too eagerly. I can see it in a lot of products — you can tell there's just eager product managers that thought of widgety things and just shipped them. Doing product management at an infra company really well is very very hard, because it takes a very deep level of strategic thinking, thinking about what are the foundational building blocks, where do we want to be in one to two years. The truth is, building infrastructure is very hard, and how do we make sure we don't end up with 35 features that are kind of similar looking but all do slightly different things. That level of thinking is something that is very rare to find, and for that reason we haven't aggressively tried to build up a product management team yet.

团队结构在 GenAI 时代的变化

— How would you say your teams have been evolving since GenAI?

In a funny way: yes, I do think team structures have changed a lot, but I'm actually not convinced it was GenAI driving that. One thing I've seen a lot: there's been a swing back towards being an IC, that I think is very very positive for the space. If you look back at the space 10 or 20 years ago, everyone wanted to be in management because that was a way you would get more money, more recognition, more prestige. That shift actually started even before GenAI, but I do think it's heavily accelerated with AI.

We make it very clear to everyone at Modal that manager vs. IC — there's no difference in prestige. Everyone is just a member of technical staff. It's about ultimately your contributions. We see a lot of ex-managers becoming ICs because they want to go back and build code. There's been a shift away from non-technical managers. Everyone, pretty much, including me — I still write a lot of code at Modal, and Akshat too, and pretty much everyone in the tech team, and a lot of people who are not in the tech team still write code. That to me is a recent phenomenon. I actually don't know if it's necessarily caused by GenAI, but GenAI has greatly accelerated it because it lowered the cost of writing code — it's even easier.

— If you have non-technical people committing code, how do you do code reviews?

We do code reviews, but we think of it as optional. My view is: code reviews in large part are people trying to escape the accountability of merging things into production. If you have that culture, then to me that's a sign that you need to invest way more in CI and CD — CI in particular but also CD, continuous deployment.

We do code reviews — when I write code, occasionally I'm asking authors, "Is this in line with how you think about things? I hope I'm not changing the architecture fundamentally." But we also make it clear internally that code reviews are quite optional. If you're just changing docs, if you're just doing some basic stuff, don't wait for a human to look at it — especially in the era of AI. Why do you need a human to look at every piece of code?

That does require you to have very good controls internally around testing. For an infra company — we need one more nine than the average startup — in terms of uptime. These are investments you just have to make. You have to build systems that are very resilient. You have to have rate limits everywhere. You have to decouple systems. You have to make sure nothing is a single point of failure. You have to have extremely good test coverage. Agents are actually really good at writing tests these days, which, a few years ago, I thought was one of the major things missing in agents. Now they're actually quite good — because it takes a little bit of kind of needing to step out of what you're trying to do for a second and be a little bit like devil's advocate to write good tests. But now they're quite good at writing tests too.

— Do you guys use frontier models for coding, or have you experimented with the open-source ones?

We experiment with everything. Initially was a lot of Cursor, then of course Claude and Codex, and now a lot of people are using Nightshift and all these open-source stuff or other stacks. I don't have a strong point of view. I want people to experiment and try different things. We use frontier models, use open-source models. We're trying to do a little bit more dogfooding internally now that we're actually running inference for a lot of the open-source models at a very large scale. It's also helpful to use our internal endpoints for a lot of agentic development, so we try to promote that a little bit.

关于 on-prem、BYOC 与多租户哲学

— Something I read maybe a year or two ago — you were saying you didn't think there was going to be a big on-prem business for you guys. Have you changed your opinion on that?

No, I have not changed my opinion. I'm a cloud maximalist. To take a step back: when the cloud came in 2008, 2009, my first reaction was, "That's crazy — why would I want to take my code and run it on someone else's computer? That's insane." And then 6 months later I was doing it. It took me 6 months to change my mind. It took probably enterprises another 15 to 20 years.

But you look at vendors like Snowflake, AWS — I think there's many examples, Datadog etc. The cloud is clearly winning. Multi-tenant systems are clearly winning. On-prem looks increasingly like a legacy business model. I actually think BYOC (bring your own cloud) and VPC peering — all of these things reflect sort of an outdated security model of "we need to protect everything inside our own network" — using the network as a moat. That I don't think is true anymore. We've moved on to more robust security paradigms like zero trust.

From our perspective also: the fact that we have full control over our entire infrastructure stack — we rent all the hardware, we deploy and manage all the infrastructure, we deploy and manage health and observe all the metrics on all the hosts — it means we can iterate very fast and build a greater product. That's very very valuable versus customers in the past who had enterprise editions that they had to deploy on customers' environment — they have to think very carefully about release management and dependencies. We don't care. If we want to introduce a new database, we can introduce a new database because we have control over it. We don't need to think about what customers have access to.

Multi-tenancy has so many different benefits. That being said, if we were to work with some very large Fortune 500 customer in the future and they ask for BYOC, we've done this in the past — we'll give them a number. That number is very high, and no one said yes to it so far. But who knows — at the right price I would still build it.

Separately, another thing which is interesting: in theory BYOC might also be a way to work with and get capacity in certain ways. We sometimes work with neolabs, and those neolabs already have very large capacity reservations, and the question is how do we get them to run Modal when they already have capacity. BYOC might be a solution — we can still keep the control plane in our environment. And the flip side of that: we could maybe even run other people's stuff on that capacity. So there's some fun stuff you could do in theory where you can aggregate all that capacity into one big pool. We're excited about some of those ideas. In general on-prem I don't know if we're ever going to do, but BYOC maybe — bring your own cloud. I keep saying "BYC" — I should explain acronyms.

融资的用途与业务的三大焦点

— Let's say hypothetically you are going to raise — I should send more money, like, soon — what would you use that money for?

Like I mentioned, in this capacity situation, a lot of the cash flow that's required is capacity prepayments. So that represents the best use of cash today. We're ramping up capacity very aggressively. Maybe we move into other types of deployment models in the future — ownership or whatever — but there's always going to be a cash component of that, some sort of down payment or prepayment. That is the greatest use of cash right now. There's of course other things — salaries, office spaces — but in the grand scheme of our financials, it's basically a rounding error right now.

— Do you think that's going to change?

No. The operating leverage that we have in this business is kind of insane. We have 200 employees — they cost a lot of money, but the GPUs cost a lot more money.

— If you had to say, what are the top three things that are your biggest focus right now?

  1. Capacity and the financial complexity. In general, how do we think about that space, how do we think about pricing and packaging, how do we think about the tension between ownership and renting? Should we go in a more neocloud direction, or should we go in the opposite — the sort of Counter precision? That's probably the biggest thing I think a lot about.

  2. Product strategy. I think a lot about what are the next building blocks. If we do more agentic stuff, what are the things we need? Are there certain storage primitives or compute primitives? In general, what is the thing that the world is going to wake up and realize they need over the next few years? Ideally we have that at that point. We've been pretty good in general at anticipating demand and building products in advance of it, with the serverless functions and the sandboxes. So what's the next thing?

  3. Culture and company building. We recently crossed 200 people. We're growing extremely fast — we'll probably hit 250 by the end of the year. When you're growing very fast, you have 250 people that are all trying to figure out how they can add the most value to Modal, and making sure that they have the right context, the right motivation, that they're excited to come into work every day because they get to build something incredibly cool and they know what makes Modal successful and what they can do. Aligning the incentives, making sure that people have a very positive culture where they have the implicit trust to do a lot of stuff but also the accountability to deliver the best things, and be held accountable if they're not doing it.

To me those are super critical things at this scale. When you're 10, 20, 30 people, you can all just sit in a room — it's all kind of implicit and you just feel it. People can read me, they can tell me when I get a little bit annoyed, they can tell when I'm happy. Now we're 250 people, and people don't necessarily see it. Of course there's a lot of new people — they're maybe a little bit nervous to talk to the CEO. So how do I remain approachable? There's the Dunbar number, which is more sort of faked than anything — at least the story behind it — but it is actually kind of real still, there's something around 150, 200. We're laying the foundation of the culture — it's very very important.

— How many people are you guys trying to hire over the next year?

We've grown about 4x on an annualized basis in the last 12 months. That's an unsustainable growth rate on a relative basis. You can double the team every year and that's not super hard to do. But 4x — what you start to see is cultural drift. You start to see islands of different working styles. You start to see people doing very speculative things. That's something I always watch out for in the engineering team. You go talk to an engineer: "What are you working on?" And it turns out they're building something fringe, like, "Is this really what you should spend time on?" So growing very fast has that cost — ramping people up. I don't know, I think by the end of the year maybe 250, by the end of next year — we're going to keep growing like 2.5x, 3x — so it's very likely we'll end up next year like 700 people or something like that.

— I'm going to assume most of those are engineers. What kinds of engineers?

Mostly engineers. We have sales a lot too.

Primarily systems engineers. We've always been very deep into Linux and file systems and scalable systems and networking and cloud. So people really good at those things. We're also looking a lot at — because we moved up in the stack a little bit, we're doing a lot of work in the LLM inference space, so now we're dealing with a separate set of concerns around CUDA and GPUs and MFU — maxing out the tokens you can get per GPU. Even though a lot of the work in that space, in my opinion, turns out is more systems-driven still — KV caching and routing is still very systems-heavy problems. But yeah, a little bit more GPU performance that kind of stuff.

We're starting to build up a research team. We're very excited about moving into stuff around post-training and distillation and better methods for quantization.

— For your customers or for internally?

Both. It's a little bit like with the FDEs — initially we'll do a lot of stuff with our customers to optimize their models, but over time figure out how do we turn those into products. We'll arguably fail in a certain way if every time a customer needs to optimize a model we have to go work with them. Long-term it has to be turned into products. So with the FDEs and with the research team, initially you're going to have to do a lot of work with the customers — and we are that — but over time we're also building a lot of internal tooling and over time internal products that are fully self-serve. So we're working on a lot of stuff right now in the post-training space but also in the GPU performance space. A lot of cool stuff.

下一代产品：更好的"积木"

— Back to the product strategy stuff — what are your thoughts? What do we need over the next year, 2 years?

It's incredibly hard to say. If I said I know exactly what we need to build, I think I would be delusional.

What we've seen so far, and what I believe on a more general level, is: we need better building blocks. This is a new era of software, and we're unlocking a whole new type of applications that could not be built a few years ago. Doing all the GenAI stuff, LLMs that output code that needs to run in an isolated way — there's so many new primitives that are needed to work with GPUs and work with LLMs. We built some building blocks so far, and that's unlocked a bunch of applications. Over the next few years, there's going to be so many more cool things.

I mentioned some stuff — I'm very bullish on training, I'm very bullish on batch jobs, I'm very bullish on certain things around agents and low latency. But in the end, we consider ourselves an infrastructure shop. We're not trying to build very narrow things. We try to build very general-purpose building blocks and put them in front of customers, and then those customers will combine those building blocks and build some incredible applications that we could have never anticipated.

推文闪电问答

— I want to go through some of your tweets. This will be the last part. Maybe you want to double-click on anything.

"A lot of long-running persistent sandbox stuff right now. Today feels lift-and-shift. I suspect sandboxes will evolve from devbox-in-the-cloud to something more ephemeral. One environment for every command, and snapshotting in between so you can pause, resume, clone."

We talked about this a lot. I'm fully — I think the median sandbox in Modal today is like 8 seconds long or something like that, which is kind of incredible when you think about it. Over time I think it might get even shorter. We want to support long-running sandboxes too — there are some very valid use cases around long-running sandboxes. But my vision is: the world needs to figure out how we can massively parallelize things and reduce the overhead of starting and stopping sandboxes.

"I don't know if I ran an IPO-ready startup engaged in a capex arms race with a competitor, it would be nice to coordinate and pace the arms race a bit."

No comment.

"The biggest downside of GPU scarcity is not that it's hard to get GPUs, but that almost all capacity is sold as a three-year rectangle starting 3 to 6 months in the future. That's not what demand looks like for most users."

Maybe just go a little bit deeper. One thing I think Modal has always been very good at is fully on-demand capacity. If a customer comes to us and needs 100 GPUs, we can typically give them that immediately. You don't even have to talk to a salesperson. A lot of workloads in real life don't look like these flat, rectangular workloads. They scale up and down throughout the 24-hour cycle. They maybe grow over time. They maybe have certain burst periods. To me that is a challenge with a lot of customers today — the primary way to get capacity is to buy these rectangular blocks. It's not great. The world needs to evolve, and that's fundamentally — I'm very biased, but — why I think Modal can play a very large role in that duration transformation of offering more flexible capacity. We can do that because we can aggregate many many thousands of customers, and the demand gets very smooth in aggregate. That's a lot of the value prop of Modal.

— Would you say that's a differentiator?

Massive differentiator, actually. If you want to very reductively break down Modal's value prop into two things: one is the developer experience — the ability to iterate and build things and not have to think about infrastructure. The other thing is the capacity stuff. The more and more I think about Modal and where we're going in the long run — we're aggregating the world's compute capacity, and we're very good at slicing it out very granularly. Because we built all this work around scaling up and down extremely fast, all the stuff around GPU snapshotting — we're working on some ways to make it much much faster. And that model works at very large scale really really well because you can aggregate lots of customers.

"Every month I keep saying our sandbox revenue might have plateaued, but it keeps going up 30% every month."

It's kind of nuts. Every month I'm like, "Well, sandboxes grew a lot, but clearly they kind of plateaued," and then they keep growing even more. A lot of VCs are like, "How did you know sandboxes was going to be big?" And the truth is I didn't. I thought it was going to be bigger than it was in 2023 for sure, but the fact that sandboxes is a third of our revenue today is insane. We're obviously very happy about it. We have a very large team investing in sandboxes. I don't want to trivialize it — we obviously do want to give ourselves a lot of credit for seeing sandboxes for what it is today a little bit back in even 2023. But I probably would never have taken a bet that revenue would be this large from sandboxes and the market demand would be so much.

"There's an interesting structural reason why inference providers should exist separately from model builders. The best model keeps changing a lot. Inference providers can easily reallocate resources between models since overall demand is quite smooth."

If you think about all the Chinese labs — and in the future hopefully more US labs too — every time a new lab releases the latest and greatest open-source model, you see big shifts in demand for these models. A challenge: if all these labs independently held capacity, they would see when they launch a new model, demand would go up a lot, and then another lab launches a better model and the demand goes down. In the background they're working on the next version. There's a structural reason why you're seeing demand shifting to the latest and greatest Chinese lab. It's not like everything just moves overnight, because a lot of models and prompts — there's a certain stickiness to it. But there's an argument that it's very easy for Modal: today we're running X number of thousand GPUs for one model, tomorrow we need to shift 50% of that to another model — sure, that's just what the system was built to handle. No one even needs to tell us to do that. It just magically does that.

模型是商品吗？智能会不会 plateau？

— So you agree that basically the LLMs are commodities. And if you agree, then where do you think the business for the big labs is going to be?

I'm not sure if that's necessarily true. Is Taylor Swift a commodity? She releases a big album and goes on a tour and makes a lot of money, and then there's a down year when she goes and records. I don't know if this is the best analogy — and then she releases a new album. She still has a lot of brand and there's a lot of power and makes a lot of margin. So as long as the labs can repeatedly launch new models, and as long as the margin they have on those models is such that they can pay off, amortize the cost of training those models — it could still be a decent business, I think.

— So you don't think that the intelligence is plateauing?

No, I don't think so. It remains to be seen. Models today are very good at doing things that can be trained very efficiently using reinforcement learning. We've seen that initially with coding and writing simple snippets — over time it's gotten really good at also writing production-level code. It's gotten really good at math. It's gotten really good at cybersecurity. These are all very verifiable things.

It remains to be seen — are models going to be really good at, whatever, cooking food? I don't know, things that have more diffused targets and maybe longer feedback loops. Humans probably — my feeling is — will be quite good and quite competitive with models for a long time in those domains. But certainly AI models are getting very very good, as I'm sure everyone can agree with.

— The models are already really good at coding. What other applications do you think, maybe that aren't as big right now, are going to become huge over the next few years?

I don't know, but I think anything that has kind of a verifiable —

— The computational bio, I think you mentioned.

Yeah. Computational bio — not exactly verifiable, but there's certain ways you can run simulations. You can use an LLM to output predictions, then you can do computational methods to simulate the molecular dynamics and get kind of feedback loops.

Material science is maybe another area where you have a little bit of that loop, where you can synthetically manufacture certain materials and measure the properties, and you just put an agent in the loop. I have a physics background, I'm pretty excited about that. So drugs, materials, what else — I'm drawing a blank, but I'm sure there's many other things.

— Cool. Those are all the questions that I had. Is there anything you wanted to talk about that I haven't?

I'm good. This is great. This is a lot of fun.

— Awesome. Thank you.
