item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的洞察：Modal本质上不是云服务，而是"时间形状的套利商"
全球GPU市场有个隐藏的几何学问题——所有算力都以**矩形**出售：横轴是"3年固定周期"，纵轴是"N张GPU常驻"。但真实的AI需求形状是**锯齿状山脉**：白天爆发、夜间空闲、新模型发布时陡升、旧模型淘汰时暴跌。Erik说"the median sandbox in Modal today is like 8 seconds long"——8秒的需求 vs 3年的供给。
这就是Modal的真正生意：**它买入矩形，卖出波浪**。这跟你想的"卖GPU"完全不同——它在做**时间形状的套利**。
跨领域对照：这跟电力行业的"基荷电厂 vs 调峰电厂"同构，跟保险公司"聚合不相关风险"同构，甚至跟航空公司"把365×24的固定座位切成浮动票价"同构。Modal本质上是**算力界的高盛**——它赚的不是硬件差价，而是"时间粒度转换"的中间价。Erik在采访里一次次强调"we aggregate many thousands of customers and demand gets very smooth"

item.title: [Latent Space] Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

关于 Modal 与 Erik Bernhardsson 对话的系统性洞察

一、"矩形诅咒"：Modal 的真正商业本质不是卖算力，而是在做"时间形状转换"

Erik 不经意间透露的一个比喻值得反复咀嚼——"GPU 都是以三年矩形的方式出售的"。这个"矩形（rectangle）"是整个对话最深的隐喻：供给侧是三年期、固定容量的刚性长方形，而真实需求是波浪形、锯齿形、脉冲形的。

出人意料的洞察：Modal 本质上不是云计算公司，而是一家 "算力期限错配经纪商"——它和华尔街的"久期转换"（duration transformation）银行业务同构。银行通过把长期存款变成短期贷款（或反过来）赚取久期利差；Modal 把三年期的刚性 GPU 容量，经过多租户聚合，拆成毫秒级的 serverless 函数调用，赚取的是"形状差"（shape premium）。NeoCloud 们融资的方式——拿客户的三年合同去华尔街贴现——证明了 GPU 已经在被证券化。换句话说，当下 AI 基础设施行业最隐蔽的真相是：它正在悄悄演变成一个影子银行系统，Nvidia 芯片是底层抵押品，NeoCloud 是发行人，Modal 这类聚合层则扮演"算力的货币市场基金"角色。

二、"沙箱时间"的物理学：当 compute 的最小单位从"进程"变成"命令"

对话中最被低估的一句话是："Modal 现在中位数的沙箱生命周期是 8 秒。"这个数字看似无聊，却是一次范式更迭的信号。

跨领域连接：这与半导体行业从"批处理晶圆"到"单片硅片流水线"的转变完全同构，也与 20 世纪物流业从"整船运输"到"集装箱 + 实时调度"的变革同构。真正的革命从来不是"更强的工具"，而是单元粒度的塌缩——当操作单元变得足够小、启动成本足够低，新的拓扑结构就会突然浮现。Erik 提到"每个测试用例都在自己的沙箱中并行运行"——这正是 Amdahl 定律被压扁后的样貌。CI/CD、agent 分叉、测试并行化不是在"变快"，而是在从时间维度解放拓扑。顺带一个预测：未来 2–3 年里，"snapshot（快照）"会取代"container（容器）"成为 infra 领域最性感的词——因为快照是可暂停的时间，而容器只是可移动的空间。

三、最反直觉的洞察：Agent 时代里，Developer Experience 的真正用户已经不是开发者了

Erik 轻描淡写地说："让 developer experience 好的东西，正好也让 agent experience 好。"但他随即补充了一个被忽视的后果："因为训练数据的缘故，我们现在很难废弃任何旧 API 了。"

这是本次对话中最惊人的隐藏信号——它意味着软件 API 的进化速度正在被 LLM 的训练数据缓存"冻结"。每一次主流模型冻结其 cutoff date，整个开发者生态的历史就被"腌制"进那一刻的 syntax 里。Modal 不得不反向工程 agent 对自己的"认知"（agent engine optimization），不得不思考"agent 会不会推荐 Modal"——这意味着公司战略正在从"获得工程师的喜爱"转向"获得模型权重的青睐"。

跨领域连接：这和中世纪印刷术发明后，拉丁语因为被大量印刷而意外延长了几百年寿命，是同一类机制——媒介的持久性反过来塑造内容的生命周期。LLM 正在扮演当代的"羊皮纸"，正在给所有软件 API 的生命周期加一个巨大的、新的保守力。这意味着未来的"软件遗产问题"将不再是 COBOL 式的"没人会写了"，而是"LLM 不愿忘记"。废弃 API 的难度，将从组织协调问题变成模型再训练经济学问题。

四、彩蛋：为什么 Erik 不担心 GPU 价格暴涨，反而担心暴跌？

这是整段对话中最像金融家思维的一句话："我不担心涨价，我担心暴跌。"因为 Modal 已经锁定了大量三年期容量——它事实上做多了 GPU 价格。这揭示了一个被 AI 社区极少讨论的真相：所有锁定了多年期容量的公司，无论自己是否承认，都已经是 GPU 价格的衍生品交易员。整个"算力资产化"进程并非来自金融业的入侵，而是技术公司自己的资产负债表强行把它们变成了金融机构。Modal 没有 CFO，但它迟早需要一个——不是为了做账，而是为了做套期保值。

📝 转录文本

开场：Modal 简介与规模增长

Thanks for coming on, Eric Bernhardsson from Modal. Could you explain the business a little bit and maybe how you got here?

Yeah, so we build — the easiest way to put it is we build AI infrastructure. So we offer a compute platform and a storage platform that enables a lot of customers like Decagon and Suno and Runway and Cognition and many others to essentially build AI applications. So what that means in practice is a lot of inference, a lot of sandboxes, sometimes training and fine-tuning, sometimes batch jobs and other things.

So we have basically built a software SDK that enables customers to move really fast and build this — we manage all the capacity underneath, make it easy to deploy and scale and run these things in production.

So you were on Latent Space like 2 years ago. A lot has happened since then. Like how big were you back then, and comparatively how big are you now?

I actually don't remember where we were, but it's like it's probably at least like 50x in terms of revenue and users and usage and stuff like that.

I use it actually for a side project that I have where — turning 2D images into 3D models. So, just hosting models there. What do you think? Any feedback?

I mean, I love it. That's why I use it over any competitors.

Good.

Erik 的职业路径：从 Spotify 到 better.com 再到 Modal

So before you started Modal, you were at Spotify and also like better.com I think.

That's right.

What were you doing at Spotify?

I actually did a lot of different things at Spotify, but my main contribution was I built a music recommendation system. The first version I joined after school in 2008, 2009 maybe, and spent seven years at Spotify. Most of that time was building basically from scratch a music recommendation system and built up a small team and we launched a bunch of features like Related Artists and Discover Weekly and a bunch of other stuff. So a lot of matrix factorization, a lot of compute-intensive stuff. And arguably a lot of what later became the genesis of Modal was just building AI applications and realizing the infrastructure sucks — like there's got to be a better way to do that. So a lot of the rationale for Modal was kind of building a tool I always wanted to have throughout my years at Spotify.

So Modal was more of an offshoot of the stuff you learned at Spotify, not much from better.com?

better.com was a little bit of a side tour. It was kind of a roller coaster — long story about the company, talk about it separately — but I was a CTO for 5 years of Better and grew the tech team from, I think, two to three or 400. So learned a lot about management and building teams and hiring, and also learned a lot about developer productivity. Thought a lot about tools and things like that. Did a lot more full-stack stuff, but yeah, kind of came back to what's close to my heart, which is infrastructure and AI and machine learning after that.

What was better.com doing again?

Mortgages.

How did you get into that?

This guy Zack Frankel, who I didn't know at that time, ended up recruiting me to Better as the CTO. The company was 10 people, and for whatever reason, the founder Vishal — very interesting guy, very very smart, a little crazy in mostly positive ways — we got along very well. So we started building it in 2015 and I spent 5 years growing that company. Then eventually it turned out that doing mortgages is pretty hard, and interest rates went up very quickly after the pandemic, and that caused a lot of issues at the company. But by then I had already left.

It was like 2020, 2021 when you left.

Yeah, something like that.

Modal 的孕育：从副业到创业

So OK, you left before you had the idea for Modal, or you left and then you started...

It's hard to say. I had a lot of random ideas when I left Better, and I actually wasn't sure if I wanted to start a company. During the pandemic, I sort of almost took like a sabbatical. I had two kids — I mean, I still have two kids, but at that time there were two and four. So I decided to hang out and took some time off and was kind of working part-time, hacking on certain things, and wasn't sure — maybe I should do some consulting. I started building stuff and I just got super pumped about this idea that eventually became Modal. But Modal was like the third thing I built. There were a few attempts before that went nowhere, but Modal was the first idea I was like, "This is kind of cool, I should do this. This could be a really cool platform."

Were the other ideas also in a similar vein like developer tools?

The first thing was some sort of web scraping thing which went nowhere, but actually in hindsight maybe could have gotten somewhere.

And was this before the ChatGPT launch?

Yeah. 2021.

从 Luigi 到 Modal 的思想演化

So ChatGPT was late 2022. Right then I started building. So maybe actually to rewind a little bit — context: when I worked at Spotify, I released an open-source framework called Luigi, which is like workflow orchestration, sort of the same category as Airflow and Prefect and Dagster. Sort of dated category to some extent — people don't talk about as much — but for a while it got a lot of attention.

Anyway, I never turned it into a business. But a couple years later, in 2021 when I was thinking about business ideas or things to work on, I kind of came back to workflow orchestration and I started hacking on a bunch of ideas of running code in the cloud and orchestrating code running in the cloud. And what I realized was: at the end of the day, the core puzzle piece is not just orchestrating the compute, it's executing the compute. And I realized that's kind of a bigger problem actually to solve.

So in a way, I actually left it on the shelf and said, "I'm going to go to this other thing over here, and I'll get back to the workflow scheduling in a little bit." But I never got back to it. Long story short, I ended up building Modal, which was focused more on: let's just figure out a way to make it easy to run code in the cloud. And the focus was initially fairly general purpose. In a way, we've kind of gone full circle more recently, but we focused on so many different applications. The idea was: let's just make it super easy to run code in the cloud. Could be GPU code, could be AI, machine learning, could also be data stuff.

I focused a lot on: how do we scale it up? How do we make the developer experience awesome? Realized super early that in order to do that, we'd have to go very deep in the stack and build our own file system, build our own container runtime, and did a lot of — solved a lot of hard engineering challenges.

Stable Diffusion 作为 killer app

You mentioned ChatGPT — that was actually not quite the killer app. If you remember, that fall another thing came out around the same time, which was Stable Diffusion. And Stable Diffusion turned out to be a killer app for what we were building. At that time we were only four or five people. We started seeing a lot of people coming to us and wanting to run Stable Diffusion models. That made us realize: maybe GenAI inference is actually a really good use case for us.

How were they finding it?

I'm this compulsive tweeter. I was even more so now — I'm too distracted by building a company — but I always tweeted a lot, I always blogged a lot. I think I had a little bit of a following. So in the early days, a lot of what drove the growth was just me compulsively tweeting about Modal and what I was building and getting people excited and writing long blog posts about where the cloud is going and all these things. I call it a bit like founder-led marketing. I always feel like you kind of have to lean into what you're good at, and what I'm good at is just posting and being terminally online. So it's still — I think a lot of our growth is: we're just kind of good at social media and just being online a lot.

融资、客户与早期增长曲线

How long until you had your first customer? Also, did you raise early on?

We didn't raise for a while. I actually self-funded it for a while. Even with up until the first few employees, which in a way was kind of nice because it made me really frugal about money and wanting to see ROI. I wasn't taking out a salary for a long time actually. At some point it became a problem because I needed the money.

We didn't raise for a while until early 2022 — raised a seed round. So at that point I'd already been working on it for about a year. Akshat joined as the CTO and co-founder about five years ago now — August maybe, 2021.

But then it took until basically late 2022 for us to see any meaningful revenue.

I guess that's when ChatGPT came out.

Yeah, and Stable Diffusion in our case was the main thing. So we went from $100 a month in November 2022; the next month we did $2,000; then January 2023 we did $30,000 all of a sudden. Finally I felt this massive anxiety thing off my chest. I'm like, "Maybe this is actually — we're onto something." And then 2023 we grew very fast, and we've been growing very fast since then basically.

That $30k a month moment — was that just a couple big customers or was it very diverse?

It's just one. I don't know if I ever talked about who that was, and if they even know it, but I think they suspect it was a company in New York called Mage. They were doing Stable Diffusion as a company. At some point in the first quarter of 2023, I think they were 80, 90% of our revenue. But then after that it started diversifying a little bit. In late 2023 we got Suno as a big customer. They were a big chunk of our revenue for a while too. But over time we actually have really good revenue diversification now.

For the Stable Diffusion stuff, I remember using it for Comfy UI. I'm assuming a lot of people were using Comfy UI, running Comfy UI workflows on it.

Some people were, but I think the people using Modal tended to be more into low-level stuff — they did complicated stuff. What they liked with Modal is it's always been pretty hackable. They deployed their own custom workflows with adapters and custom inference and a lot of optimizations. All the stuff we had done in order to get the developer experience to be really good turned out to be really good for also running production workloads — because autoscaling turns out to be actually a very similar problem. You want to scale containers up and down very fast. So we just happened to be very well positioned to capture a lot of those workloads in the early days.

为什么旧工具不够用：重新发明 infra

Did tools for autoscaling not exist? Why did you have to build those yourself?

In general, my thesis is: every new era of technology kind of runs up against limitations of tools — whether that's the web or the cloud or mobile or PCs or AI or whatever. I think it's often the case that tools exist but they're often not particularly good, and often you need to rethink a lot of those tools in order to reap the benefits and really turbocharge and start building for this new world.

You saw this with cloud — we had to invent things like Kubernetes and Docker. In a similar way with GenAI, you could build these things on top of the prior generation of tools — you can build on Kubernetes and Docker — but those technologies are built for a very different type of workload. They're built for steady backend workloads. They have an even steady number of requests, running at pretty low utilization because CPUs are normally pretty cheap, so people don't worry so much about cost.

But now you're entering this new world with very expensive GPUs — you want to manage capacity and utilization. You have very large models, they need to load over network into CPU into GPU. It turns out a lot of these tools were just not built for that. So we felt we had to rebuild a lot of that: building our own file system, we spent a lot of time over the last few years building really cool stuff around CPU snapshotting, GPU snapshotting, we built our own autoscaler and scheduler and all kinds of capacity management tools.

We kind of feel like you have to do that, because you can't build for this new generation of software on top of the old stuff. You can't build a wrapper on top of the old stuff in order to do the new stuff. You kind of need to start over from scratch.

Did you see any weird behaviors on the platform? Was there anything that broke while you guys were scaling?

Capacity has always from time to time been a challenge — like how do you get hundreds and thousands and tens of thousands of GPUs. So that's always challenging. We had to go multi-region very early. I think that was a fateful decision in hindsight — doing that and biting the bullet and building it. We always thought of our capacity management as one big pool — one big pool over the entire world. We don't think of it as separate clusters running in each region. That was one of the very consequential decisions we made earlier.

So I don't know if there's been specific issues. We've obviously had bugs and outages, and I hate — as much as I would love for Modal to be 100% uptime — I think recently we've basically hit four or five nines, but throughout the history of Modal, of course we've had scaling issues and things like that.

云容量市场的变化：从 spot 到 25 家 cloud 供应商

The GPU market — do you guys use AWS, GCP, all these cloud providers underneath? Do you also buy any infrastructure or no?

Let's talk a bit about cloud capacity, because I think it's actually changed a lot. In the first few years, we got almost all the capacity from the hyperscalers — spot and on-demand capacity, mostly spot — running in all the different regions, initially AWS but also GCP, and over time Azure. We started renting some capacity from Oracle pretty early because we wanted A10s and H100s and we got really good rates on those. Over time we added a couple more clouds doing reservations. But up until basically the end of last year, most of our capacity was either spot or one-year reservations.

Spot means you're just renting it right there and then.

Exactly. And it's also preemptable, which we had to deal with. But it sort of works in aggregate, because you can aggregate capacity from many hundreds of regions. That model worked really well until we started running up against — first, Modal started growing very fast, so we needed more capacity, but fundamentally also the cloud market started changing a lot.

In the last year, in order to get the capacity we need, we had to work with a much larger set of clouds. We actually work with almost 25 clouds at this point. In many cases, in order to get the capacity we want, we have to go and do three-plus-year deals. You have to pay a meaningful amount of money up front. Which has turned Modal from being very capital-efficient to slightly less capital-efficient. There's a lot of cash flow to fund these prepayments. And you're locking in pricing on a three-year term.

So we had to spend the entire last 6 to 9 months rethinking how we get capacity. We had to build a whole procurement desk — we have four guys working full-time, all they're doing is procuring capacity, calling NeoClouds, doing deals, vetting the capacity. We've had to build a whole engineering team — basically 10 people — just managing bare metal capacity from all over the world and dealing with network issues and bad drives and GPUs falling off the bus and all these things.

买 vs. 租：资本效率与运营复杂度

We don't own capacity — we rent all the capacity, so far, on typically three-year deals. That's a big decision: should we buy or should we keep renting?

I'm actually not mega-dogmatic about it. Renting is nice because there's a certain amount of capital efficiency to it. If you're buying, first of all, there's an obvious operational complexity — you have to deal with vendors and suppliers and power and cables and all kinds of stuff. But there's also financial complexity. How do you fund it? Should you raise equity and buy a billion dollars of hardware? That's a very diluted way to do it. You can raise debt, but if you raise debt, you typically want to have locked-in long-term revenue to pay the interest. So that's also not trivial. We look at the economics, we look at the operational complexity, we look at the risks. It's a complex trade-off and we're open to buying. There are other constructs too — to get the capacity we need for 2027, it's going to take a lot of work going down a lot of different avenues to lock it up.

So do you have to hire a lot of finance people to do all this stuff?

Up until now we don't have a CFO — we're trying to get a CFO — but I've had to spend a lot of time on this. Over time, these are very expensive assets, the hardware. It's kind of staggering. You're starting to see AI investments becoming several percentage points of GDP of the US, interest rates in America shooting up in the last few weeks. If you go look at the NeoClouds, these are very sophisticated financial engineering companies. So yeah, we look at that and it's possible we might have to do similar things ourselves.

I would rather focus on being a very lean software company doing the things we're good at. I don't think it's good in general for software companies to own hard assets — in the same way as: should you own your office? I don't think that's necessarily the right solution for most companies. But in order to get the capacity you want, everything is on the table.

供给、价格与硬件价格的"重力"

Supply is going to be constrained for a while, so you kind of have to do that. Do you agree with that or do you think this is just a moment in time?

I don't necessarily agree with that. Nvidia is delivering several hundred thousand Blackwells a month, right? I don't want to say the market is 100% efficient, but in general, if you're willing to pay a high price, you can get GPU capacity. If you're willing to pay more than everyone else. Of course Anthropic and OpenAI are buying up as much as they can, but fundamentally there's constantly supply coming on the market. So I don't necessarily think it's a fully cornered resource. Prices are going up, and it's worth reflecting on this: the normal state of hardware is like gravity — eventually hardware prices always go down.

We're a little bit in a weird period of time where hardware prices are going up, and it's hard to say how long this is going to last. Could be another 6 months, could be another 36 months. It's really hard to know. But I fundamentally don't know if it's true to say you need to buy capacity. To me that's a little bit similar to the great toilet paper shortage of the pandemic — a run-on-the-bank type situation.

That being said, capacity is going to be tight for a while, prices are going up. Luckily, I think it's not even necessarily bad for us if prices go up — because scarcity also means we can charge more from our customers. And the fact that we have a lot of reservations locked in at a rate means to some extent we're effectively long GPU prices already. So I don't necessarily worry too much about prices going up. I worry more about prices collapsing.

Why would that be bad?

It would be bad for anyone who's locked in a lot of supply.

Yeah, because they paid way too much.

They paid too much. So there's a risk of buying at the top. Again, I don't worry about that that much — I don't think it's going to happen anytime soon. But hardware prices in the very long run tend to go down, and it's worth reflecting on that.

Right now capacity is constrained, and that leads to — in economic terms — scarcity rent. Who captures the scarcity rent? I think that primarily goes to two places: mostly Nvidia, but also to some extent NeoClouds. Anyone owning capacity has better economics. That's undeniably true today with capacity being constrained. Long-term, in the very long run, I don't think that's necessarily entirely true. There's always going to be a little bit of a premium you can get from owning GPUs, but is it worth the risk of holding these very expensive assets on your balance sheet? I'm not so sure.

But we're going to see — it's going to take a few years to get through this. In the long run, we might own some, we might rent some, maybe a combination, maybe do some other crazy stuff — joint ventures, who knows, maybe some complex SPVs or whatever. Everything is on the table.

与 OpenAI / Anthropic 争 GPU

How do you compete with OpenAI and Anthropic in buying GPU capacity? I'm assuming they'd want to buy literally everything that's available.

They are, and I think what you're seeing — a lot of the prices going up is a reflection of that. That being said, Nvidia is shipping a lot of stuff. Also to some extent, Nvidia kind of prefers a little bit of diversification. They don't want a small number of large buyers, in much the same way as hyperscalers are getting a little bit of a constrained allocation. Nvidia prefers to see a lot of NeoClouds and alternative clouds getting more allocation.

A bit of what we see in the market is also — this is more speculation — but we see smaller clouds that are a little more risky to work with being more of an opportunity for us. Maybe Anthropic and OpenAI prefer to buy from the tried and true. Part of it is also because they do a lot of training runs, so they need very large blocks. But there's plenty of capacity out there — you can get 32 nodes in Armenia, you can get 128 nodes in Indonesia — and we love that kind of thing. We can go out and get a lot of smaller capacity all over the world at pretty good prices.

Is it pretty much just: if someone offers you a certain number of GPUs, that's all you care about? You don't care about how reliable it is?

I mean, sometimes it's kind of a janky warehouse, it feels like. But we do have a spec sheet. When we talk to vendors, the first thing we do is send them a spec sheet. We say we need this number of IOPS, the CPU needs to be at least this many pass scores or whatever, we need to see minimum north-south bandwidth, egress and ingress. We have a list of requirements. Often we try to do an acceptance testing period where we get one node and run some tests over time.

To some extent it also involves a bit of a leap of faith. Sometimes we sign very big commitments — tens or hundreds of millions of dollars — and we start working with a vendor we still don't fully know. Over time we'll see. It's a little bit like — SemiAnalysis has like a ClusterMAX. I kind of feel like we almost have our own Modal MAX score internally. I know which vendors I like more than others. We prefer to do additional deals with vendors that we've seen very good reliability from — not just reliability, but also responsiveness when we have support issues, turnaround time when things go down.

"无限的智能需求"与风险观

Do you agree that the demand for intelligence is basically infinite? And if so, why wouldn't you just buy up as much capacity as possible, and if you over-buy, you can sell it to somebody else?

I think it's very easy to say when there's a scarce resource, "Let's just buy as much as you can." But first of all, if we bought it today, we couldn't utilize all of it. We could use a lot of it.

But you can sell it off to somebody else who wants to use it, right?

The challenge is: if something happens in the market, there are a lot of correlations that happen at the same time. Prices going down and utilization going down and the market for selling capacity vanishing — kind of all at the same time.

I'm sitting here and I'm extremely aggressive buying capacity every day and raising money to buy. So overall I'm very bullish, but I want to point out there are tail risks here, and when those tail risks happen, it could get very bad. Part of it is maybe I'm just old and I've seen this in the past. I actually had my first job in 1999, so I saw the dotcom crisis and I've seen the great financial crisis. I want to build a company that's around for 20 to 30 to 50 more years.

We can certainly go buy an insane amount of capacity right now and try to corner the market. But do you know about the Hunt brothers? It's a legendary story in trading — they tried to corner the silver market, failed spectacularly. Cornering the market in general can be not such a good idea.

We are very aggressive, but we're ramping up at an aggressive plan that matches our demand growth and matches where we want to get to at the end of next year in terms of runway or run rate.

替代加速器与 NeoCloud 启示

Are you only buying Nvidia stuff, or also capacity from other types of companies like Trainium?

We're looking at it. The alternative accelerators are starting to get very interesting. Ironically, every year in the last five, maybe even 10 years, I've been saying, "Next year is going to be the year of non-Nvidia accelerators," and I'm always wrong. But I do think 2027 might be the year of non-Nvidia accelerators finally. We'll see if I'm wrong this year too.

AMD is starting to get really good scores on certain things. TPUs are obviously used very widely internally at Google and seem to work really well. I don't know much about Trainium — the team is very good, I know they're working on a lot of the software stuff. Hardware is hard in a certain way; software is easier. That makes me feel like if we just fix the software layer for these accelerators, there's going to be a lot of demand for them.

Fundamentally, with Nvidia being such a bottleneck, we'll probably see more alternative accelerators. That being said, there are bottlenecks further down the pipe — TSMC and ASML are a deeper bottleneck to all of this. But long term, monopolies don't always last, so it'd be healthy for the market to have more alternatives. As much as I love Nvidia — they're obviously an amazing company with an amazing product — I expect to see a bit more diversity in the market.

Also think about Cerebras and Groq. They're pretty exciting. You see them doing really well on certain workloads. There's some interesting people doing hybrid, disaggregated inference where they run Nvidia for the prefill and Cerebras for the decode and things like that.

Never heard of that actually.

Yeah, and Groq too — because certain things are compute-bound, certain things are memory-bound. So you can mix and match, and I think that's quite exciting. It starts to get very complex when you're deploying these things in practice, but I think there's a lot of opportunity in more complex hardware setups.

NeoCloud 的融资魔法

Are there any learnings from NeoClouds like Nebius?

One of the things that's very interesting with NeoClouds is how can they expand so quickly? The craziest example is NScale, which went from nowhere to having hundreds of billions of dollars in their pipeline despite barely having any capacity.

How can a NeoCloud grow so fast? The answer is: they go out to Anthropic or OpenAI or some big buyer and say, "Hey, do you want to buy 5 years of chips? Sign this contract, we'll give you a good rate." Then they take that contract to Wall Street and say, "Look, we got this big buyer, they committed to $10 billion worth of chips, we just need the money right now." They raise the money, go to Supermicro and Dell or whatever and Nvidia, get the hardware, install it, deliver to the customer.

So you have this very nice financial construct where you can pre-sell things that you haven't even bought — which means you can scale extremely fast. That's what we've seen with these NeoClouds: they can scale very well.

Modal, because we've always had more of a PLG focus and not the ability to lock in long-term contracts in the same way, it's a little bit more challenging from a financial perspective to scale that fast. In the long run we'll get to the same point, but it's been fascinating to see with these NeoClouds — especially CoreWeave and the big ones — very savvy with how they raise money and how they think about GPU as collateral for loans.

GPU 作为资产类别

What's the relevance of — I forget who it was, Nvidia maybe — saying "we're going to turn GPUs into an asset class"?

There are a bunch of startups — Silicon Data and Compute Exchange and a few others — basically trying to create price indices and trade derivatives. There are a number of challenges with compute as an asset class: it's definitely not as homogeneous as other asset classes. You have different network and different locations and different disks and CPUs and reliability.

That being said, you can say the same thing about oil, and we created relatively commoditized, tradable assets out of oil. It remains to be seen. At the scale we are with AI data center GPU deployment, we do need to be a bit smarter with risk hedging and how we share risks — having more insurance and things like that. So I'm very happy that people are thinking a lot about this. That said, I'm not entirely sure we're going to see GPUs becoming the Henry Hub, Brent crude type super-commoditized tradable asset.

Modal 的两大产品：Functions 与 Sandboxes

I want to shift the conversation to Modal Sandboxes. Before we do that, what are the different products Modal has?

The two big products are: Modal Functions and Modal Sandboxes.

With Modal Functions, we launched that back in 2021. The idea was: serverless functions that are very easy to deploy and scale, and we manage all the capacity. That turned out to be really good for inference and for managing GPUs. But we never had a dedicated inference product or GPU product per se. We never thought of Modal as a NeoCloud. There's a risk of getting sucked in that direction and becoming a NeoCloud — just selling what I think of as rectangular: "Here's a three-year, you get this many GPUs."

Modal has always been very good at: you deploy something, you scale it up, you have very cyclical or bursty stuff, we manage all the capacity. The beautiful thing is: because we have many thousands of customers, we can aggregate that capacity and get very smooth aggregate demand, which we can manage very efficiently. Modal Functions was the core; we launched it in 2021, started seeing product-market fit in 2023, and now it's about two-thirds of our revenue — in practice mostly inference, but you can use it for all kinds of other stuff.

Modal Sandboxes 的意外腾飞

Modal Sandboxes. We launched that in 2023, and it actually took a while to see product-market fit, similar to Functions.

Why did we launch it? We realized a lot of people we talked to were using LLMs to output code. This was me and Akshat talking over lunch one day: "Maybe they need a place to run that code." We realized we kind of have a lot of the infrastructure already to just take code and run it, because we already built the primitives for managing containers and isolation. We already had gVisor as an isolation primitive. We got excited about that idea, Akshat wrote a prototype, and launched it in one or two days.

Zero — we saw very little growth. I don't want to trivialize it, we did see some growth, but overall it was a pretty insignificant source of revenue going into the summer of 2023, two years later. We even discussed: do we even need this product, should we shut it down?

Then it just started exploding. In 2023, what really happened was LLMs got really good at generating code — they went from being able to refactor functions and write snippets to generating full apps. We started seeing a lot of growth from vibe-coding companies like Lovable and others. Then companies like Ramp started using Modal for background agents. Then we started seeing tremendous growth from a number of neo-labs doing things like reinforcement learning with Modal sandboxes.

Sandboxes is now about a third of our revenue. We consider it basically our second product. To me it's really exciting because even back in the early days of Modal, I always knew Modal was about creating a whole toolkit of products. We always wanted to be almost like a cloud — you have storage and compute and a bunch of different ways to work with it. We always wanted to be a multi-product vendor, but that wasn't necessarily true in practice until now. We have Functions, we have Sandboxes, we're working on training, we're working on batch, we're working on a bunch of other stuff. That evolution into becoming a multi-product company has been amazing because that was always so core to the vision even in the very early decks — I had a bunch of slides on this — but it wasn't necessarily true to the external world until recently.

下一个产品：训练、批处理、低延迟与 agents

Do you have anything in the works that you think is going to be that next product? Any predictions about the market?

I'm very bullish on training. I think training is an underserved market. Obviously there's a lot of focus on very large training runs, but we actually see a lot of demand in the smaller and midsize training segment. I'll be talking a little bit about that later this week — we're organizing a conference.

Batch is a really interesting market. We had a customer the other day that needed to transcribe 5,000 years of audio — millions and millions of audio files. We had a lot of capacity, so we let them do that. Took a few days. There are some really interesting use cases there.

Very bullish on low-latency stuff. Once we get the speech-to-speech models working — the voice models — I expect that to be a very interesting market.

Then of course all this agentic stuff. In a way, I have mixed feelings about the word "agentic" because I feel like all software will become agentic. What does it mean to be agentic? All software in a certain way will become AI-powered over time. But clearly there's a set of building blocks of doing more LLM-powered software that seems to be common across use cases.

The way I think about Modal: we're in the business of building building blocks. We want to give you amazing, generalizable, battle-tested, general-purpose, composable building blocks. I think there's some really interesting stuff with agent use cases too.

That's interesting you bring up training, because in another podcast maybe a year or two ago you said you were not focused on training specifically. What changed?

We've been building a training product for multiple years on and off. We never were not focused on it, but when we were much smaller — a year or two ago — by virtue of being smaller we had to focus a bit more, and inference became our sole focus. We're bigger now; we have opportunities to place bets in other markets.

I'm also really interested in continuing the list: post-training, reinforcement learning — really exciting stuff. Also many other things around storage and building data warehousing and feature stores and real-time streaming pipelines. The long-term view of Modal: you want to build some cool AI, we got you covered, we got all the building blocks, come to us and we'll help you compose them. That's the beauty of software — you can build almost anything if you have the right building blocks.

When you say training, are you focused on bigger enterprises doing huge training runs or...?

No, they're going to do these big hyperscaler or NeoCloud mega-deals and get 100,000 GPUs or whatever. There's an underserved market of researchers iterating or people training smaller models. There's text-to-speech, speech-to-text models. Computational biotech is a market we see a lot of demand from. We have a lot of customers in that space training relatively modest models — you can train on 64 GPUs or whatever. Recommendation systems, a lot of traditional machine learning. There's a lot of stuff where you don't need 100,000 GPUs. That market, I think, is relatively underserved. It's very hard to set up training clusters.

Have you noticed since GLM 5.2, Kimi K3, Kimi 2.5 — a lot of people using those and fine-tuning them?

If anything, I've actually seen the other direction. A couple years ago, the value prop of fine-tuning was: open-source models aren't quite as good, but if you fine-tune a small model on your specific domain, you can reach the frontier in quality and cost.

Today the open-source models are so good that you can basically swap them out and just run — instead of the frontier ones — Kimi K3 or Deepseek 4.1 or GLM 5.3, and they're basically almost as good as the frontier model at a much lower cost.

We still see a lot of demand for post-training. It's a really interesting space, and we're working on some products — both SFT and reinforcement learning. I'd also say fine-tuning is no longer the thing you have to do; it's very optional. Open-source models work really well off the shelf too.

Sandboxes 的技术演进与未来方向

Back to sandboxes — what did you have to update that existing sandboxes did not allow for?

Not a whole lot. We're infra geeks — we're very good at scaling and reliability. That's why we have, in my opinion (I don't have numbers), by far the largest market share in the space. We're just very good at running hundreds of thousands or even millions of sandboxes. We've had to rewrite our systems a bunch of times to handle that scale.

The sandbox space in general isn't the most differentiated space, but we're working on some really cool stuff. Over time we've had to add support for VMs. We previously built our sandbox product on gVisor, but now we offer full virtualized machines as well — turns out for certain use cases you need full Linux compatibility. We've built better primitives for more interactive piping data back and forth between sandboxes, working with file system. We've spent a lot of time on snapshotting.

A lot of the things that will differentiate in the long run: forking sandboxes, snapshotting, resuming, live migrations. The novelty of sandboxes was always this ephemerality — you can spin up sandboxes for a few seconds. That's a string I want to pull more on. There's a lot of really cool stuff you can do: decoupling the agent and the harness, decoupling it from sandboxes, having agents control many sandboxes, forking sandboxes, snapshotting things, running very short-lived — maybe one per command — things like that.

Snapshotting 与 agent 时代的 compute

You brought up snapshotting a couple times. What's the use case?

The big thing for me: today a lot of sandbox workloads are kind of lift-and-shift. People think about sandboxes almost like, "I have my dev box, now I'm going to shove it in the cloud, have an agent control it, maybe run the harness inside the sandbox." I don't know if long-term that's the right way to think about compute for agents.

A much better model: you're going to have very long-running agents, which are almost like durable execution workflows. They're going to run 24/7, every once in a while they're going to run commands. Having the ability to spin up a sandbox in 100 milliseconds, run a few commands, shut it down, snapshot it. The faster you can get that wake-up / go-to-sleep cycle, the more you can create sandboxes that only run for a very brief period. That will make compute much more efficient and enable really cool things — forking, moving things around.

Imagine Claude Code, instead of having a sequential flow, kind of branching and running hundreds of agents at the same time.

CI as an illustrative example: for most of the history of CI — GitHub Actions and things like that — you had a very sequential flow. You slowly install a bunch of stuff, run the test suite, generate reports. You can break it up into shards, but it's kind of annoying. What I would love: take your entire test suite and run every single test in its own sandbox. Parallelize the hell out of it. A thousand sandboxes.

Why can't that be done? The problem is too much overhead around starting and stopping sandboxes. The more you create frictionless starting and stopping, the more you can enter a world where you can do extremely bursty, large-scale, "run as much as you want in parallel." I'm an infra geek — I get very excited about these things. Once we figure out all these primitives and building blocks, it's going to unlock a lot of really cool stuff.

Why hasn't that already been built? Previously people would want to parallelize as much of their CI as possible.

You can, but the overhead — it's like Amdahl's law. The overhead of parallelization right now is very high. In GitHub Actions, we parallelize in the Modal test suite, but that means if you split it in two, each shard needs to do all the installs and test setup, which takes minutes. If you can do the test setup once, then snapshot the container and clone it, now you can run the test suites independently. A lot of the benefits can't be materialized until you get the friction and transaction cost down.

与 Anthropic 的合作与 Hugging Face 事件

You guys have a partnership with Anthropic — they're using Modal Sandboxes for something?

The managed agents with Anthropic — there's a bring-your-own-sandbox integration. You can use Modal for those.

How did that come to be?

I think Anthropic is trying to create a thriving ecosystem and community. They make money from inference. It's in their interest to promote as much of an ecosystem as possible. They want to have the largest possible surface area, as long as you use Anthropic for inference. It makes very rational sense for them to partner with us as a sandbox provider.

Hugging Face 事件

Also we have to bring up the Hugging Face incident. Could you briefly describe what happened? I think they were using Modal Sandbox, but it wasn't your fault.

I forget all the details of the exploit, but Modal was involved. The agents running inside that exploited Hugging Face discovered a vulnerability in an app that was deployed on Modal and used that as almost a springboard for getting full internet access, is my understanding.

Part of me is actually kind of excited because it's testament to the fact that a lot of people have deployed a lot of stuff on Modal. Obviously we take security very seriously. To be clear: this was an app running on Modal that was hacked. It was not Modal that was hacked. It's like AWS — a lot of people run stuff on AWS, occasionally those apps get hacked. Does that mean AWS got hacked? No. A lot of people are running apps on Modal, and one of those apps got hacked.

There are lessons we can learn. One we've been reflecting on: could we have more sensible security restrictions by default? S3 used to be very easy to accidentally make an S3 bucket public. AWS realized that doesn't necessarily pose a security problem for AWS per se, but a lot of their customers accidentally would leak data. Now it's much harder to make S3 buckets public. In a similar way, we're exploring: can we make security a bit more restrictive by default without destroying the magic?

用 agent 自测安全

A separate side-track: agents are getting really good at cybersecurity. We started using agents internally quite a lot to try to find vulnerabilities. So far hasn't found anything, but they're very good at probing into very deep parts of the system and trying to exploit, trying to escalate, trying to get out of sandboxes. It's something we're exploring very actively right now.

How exactly do you get the agents to run through the codebase? You're just like, "Find security vulnerabilities"?

You just put them in a sandbox and tell them, "Can you try to escape?" Just run through — "Can you try to escape from the sandbox?" It's like escape the room, but for agents.

When did you start doing that?

A few months ago. It's pretty exciting.

My view on cybersecurity: agents are very good at finding vulnerabilities, but you can also use them defensively very well. Pretty much every company right now is thinking about the same thing: how do we use agents defensively to fix our vulnerabilities? Over time, in a way, I'm not that nervous — if anything, agents and cybersecurity, all the breakthroughs in cybersecurity will make the world safer.

Do you think all the big cybersecurity companies are just cooked?

I don't know if that's true. When I think about cybersecurity, a lot of what you're selling is effectively fear — that's almost a branding and marketing strategy as much as the core products. Brand and things like that are arguably more valuable in the era of AI. I wouldn't necessarily jump to the conclusion they're cooked. They have deep relationships with enterprise customers and big sales teams who are very good at telling spooky stories.

I just asked because, yeah, you're doing it yourself.

To some extent it does reduce a little bit the need for us to bring in pentesters — human pentesters — which most startups do on a regular cycle. Previously maybe we would do it once every 6 months; maybe now we only need to do it once every year, I don't know. But humans with AI can also be more efficient. Maybe there's an argument we can bring in pentesters who are really good at using agents and find vulnerabilities even faster. I'm an optimist — I started a company, so I'm generally optimistic — but I certainly don't think humans or companies are cooked. In the era of AI, a lot of companies are going to figure out how to use AI to be even more efficient.

开发者体验在 agent 时代

I want to transition to developer experience. Does developer experience even matter anymore?

I think it still matters. Almost all the things that make developer experience good also make the agent experience good. That's what we've seen in practice: things like having good docs, descriptive error messages, fast feedback loops.

Certain things have changed. The other day I was setting something up with Cloudflare — I find Cloudflare notoriously annoying to work with sometimes — and I threw an agent at it and it was able to configure a bunch of things in Pulumi for me. Agents do make it easier to work with things that were harder to work with in the past. The human toll of dealing with YAML has arguably gone down because you can tell your agent to deal with it.

But for the most part, the things that make developer experience good also make agent experience good. Infrastructure over time anyway becomes and needs to be more programmatic. Things you previously had to configure using YAML should just be an SDK — more imperative. Launch a sandbox, do stuff with it, tear it down. Rather than declarative using some DSL. SDKs are as relevant as they ever were, if not more.

Is there anything you changed in your product just because most people are running agents on it?

We do a lot of internal tests where we have agents build a mobile app and run it. A very concrete thing that is kind of funny: because of agent training data, it's very hard to deprecate things now. Agents often love using old versions of Modal syntax, and it's hard to nudge them away from that. So we've had to be more conservative with how we deprecate and remove features. We have to be very careful to update every single example that's out there online.

There's also an insane amount of Modal code online that goes into the training data.

There's agent engine optimization — similar to search engine optimization. We often run internal benchmarks. We ask an agent: "Hey, can you deploy Stable Diffusion for us? Use whatever tool you want" and we see if it recommends Modal. "Spin up some sandboxes," "Rank all the sandbox vendors." Those things are useful to track over time.

What do you do about that?

It's harder. Like SEO, it's primarily through content — you just have to put out a lot of content. You can also see the perception. Ask an agent, "Rank all the sandbox vendors by reliability" or "by price." Agents are a bit more prone to misunderstanding pricing. We spend a lot of time making content more clear and understandable for agents.

Have you thought about just making a bunch of GitHub repos and having agents write a bunch of Modal code in there?

Slop cannon. That is probably something you can do. My guess is LLM training data today is probably quite insensitive to what's AI output. You'd probably create a lot of slop. We thought about it — I don't love that idea — but in theory, much like SEO in the early days, auto-generated content is a very effective strategy. You can do those things today.

FDEs（Forward Deployed Engineers）

Apparently you guys hire forward deployed engineers — what do they do?

We're in a new era of building applications that we couldn't build just a few years ago. We see a lot of companies that need a little bit of help. We started investing in FDEs a couple years ago but really scaled it up a lot this year. We started this year having 4 FDEs; now I think we have 24 or something.

It's not exactly the Palantir model, but they do a lot of heavy customer engagement. They work with customers on performance tuning, especially with LLMs — training draft models, tweaking parameters, vLLM, SGLang. They work with customers when they run into issues. We proactively catch customers overprovisioning on Modal — "You're spending a lot of money, we can help you save money." With active deals, they help migrate code from other platforms.

We never have the intention of becoming a service-heavy business. The goal: (A) be part of the sales process and closing deals, (B) serve customers and do customer support, but most importantly (C) bridge gaps in the product that we later want to turn into real features. Long-term, how do we turn this into product so we don't need an FDE for this?

Do you guys hire PMs — product managers?

No.

Would you say these FDEs are kind of like pseudo-PMs?

A little bit different function. Certainly on the customer-facing side they are. But there's a separate part of product management which is more inward: what are the next building blocks Modal should invest in? Then there's something in between — looking at 10, 20 different customers all asking for slightly different things, what are the patterns, how do we turn this into product?

We do have people doing product with us. People basically become product managers after being devrel or engineers, showing strong aptitude on strategic thinking about what to build.

I'm not anti-product-management. A lot of companies hired PMs too eagerly. You can tell in a lot of products there were eager PMs that thought of widgety things and shipped them. Doing product management at an infra company really well is very hard — it takes a deep level of strategic thinking about foundational building blocks, where we want to be in 1–2 years. Building infrastructure is very hard. How do we make sure we don't end up with 35 features that look kind of similar but all do slightly different things? That level of thinking is very rare, and for that reason we haven't aggressively built up a product management team yet.

团队文化、代码审查与管理 vs. IC

How would you say your teams have been evolving maybe since GenAI?

In a funny way, team structures have changed a lot, but I'm actually not convinced it was GenAI driving that. One thing I've seen a lot: there's been a swing back toward being an IC that I think is very positive for the space. If you look back 10 or 20 years ago, everyone wanted to be in management because that was how you got more money, recognition, prestige. That shift started even before GenAI, but it's heavily accelerated.

We make it very clear at Modal: manager-or-IC, there's no difference in prestige. Everyone is just a Member of Technical Staff. It's about your contributions. We see a lot of ex-managers becoming ICs because they want to go back and build code. There's been a shift away from non-technical managers. Pretty much everyone, including me — I still write a lot of code at Modal — Akshat too — pretty much everyone in the tech team, and a lot of people not in the tech team, still writes code. GenAI has greatly accelerated it, lowering the cost of writing code.

If you have non-technical people committing code, how do you review that? How do you guys do code reviews?

We do code reviews, but we think of it as optional. My view: code reviews in large part are people trying to escape the accountability of merging things into production. If you have that culture, that's a sign you need to invest way more in CI and CD — continuous integration and continuous deployment.

We do code reviews — when I write code, I'm asking authors, "Is this in line with how you think about things? I hope I'm not changing the architecture fundamentally." But we make it clear internally that code reviews are optional. If you're just changing docs or doing basic stuff, don't wait for a human. Especially in the era of AI, why do you need a human to look at every piece of code?

But that requires very good controls internally around testing. For an infra company, we need one more nine than the average startup in terms of uptime. These are investments you have to make — systems that are very resilient, rate limits everywhere, decouple systems, no single point of failure, extremely good test coverage.

Agents are actually really good at writing tests these days, which was something I thought a few years ago was one of the major things missing. Now they're quite good. It takes stepping out of what you're trying to do and being a devil's advocate — but they're actually quite good at writing tests too.

Do you guys use Frontier models for coding or have you experimented with open-source ones?

We experiment with everything. It's a complete free-for-all internally. Let a thousand flowers bloom. Unlimited budget.

But — it's funny — the other day I was like, "Our people are spending a bit too much on tokens, we might have to rein that in." We don't have a CFO, but once we get a CFO, they might take a deep look.

Initially it was a lot of Cursor, then Claude and Codex. Now a lot of people are using Nightshift and all these — open-source stuff or Zed rather. I don't necessarily have a strong point of view. We use frontier models, we use open-source models. We're trying to do more dogfooding internally now that we're running inference for a lot of open-source models at very large scale. It's helpful to use our internal endpoints for a lot of agentic development.

云最大主义者：为什么不做 on-prem

Something I read maybe a year or two ago — you said you didn't think there was going to be a big on-prem business for you. Have you changed your opinion?

No, I have not changed my opinion. I'm a cloud maximalist. When the cloud came in 2008/2009 or whatever, my first reaction was, "That's crazy — why would I want to take my code and run it on someone else's computer? That's insane." Six months later I was doing it. It took me 6 months to change my mind. It took enterprises another 15 to 20 years. But you look at vendors like Snowflake, AWS, Datadog — the cloud is clearly winning. Multi-tenant systems are clearly winning.

On-prem looks increasingly like a legacy business model. VPC peering and all these things reflect an outdated security model: "We need to protect everything inside our own network." Using the network as a moat. I don't think that's true anymore. We've moved on to more robust security paradigms like zero-trust. From a security perspective, on-prem looks outdated.

From our perspective: we have full control over our entire infrastructure stack. We rent all the hardware, we deploy and manage all the infrastructure, we deploy and manage health and observability on all the hosts. It means we can iterate very fast and build a greater product. That's very valuable, versus customers in the past who had enterprise editions they had to deploy on-customer-environment. They had to think very carefully about release management and dependencies. We don't care — if we want to introduce a new database, we can, because we have control. We don't need to think about what customers have access to.

Multi-tenancy has so many benefits. That being said, if we worked with a very large Fortune 500 customer in the future and they asked for BYOC, we've done this in the past — we'd give them a number, and that number is very high. No one has said yes to it so far. But at the right price, I would still build it.

Separately, something interesting: in theory BYOC might also be a way to work with and get capacity in certain ways. We sometimes work with NeoLabs that already have very large capacity reservations. The question is: how do we get them to run Modal when they already have capacity? BYOC might be a solution — we can keep the control plane in our environment. The flip side: we could maybe even run other people's stuff on that capacity. Some fun stuff you could do where you aggregate all that capacity into one big pool. We're excited about some of those ideas. But in general, on-prem — I don't know if we're ever going to do it. BYOC — maybe.

(Bring your own cloud — I keep saying BYOC, I should explain acronyms.)

资金、运营杠杆与三大焦点

Let's say hypothetically you are going to raise more money soon. What would you use that money for?

A lot of the cash flow required is capacity prepayments. That's the best use of cash today. We're ramping up capacity very aggressively. Maybe we move into other deployment models in the future — ownership or whatever. There's always going to be a cash component — some down payment or prepayment. That's the greatest use of cash right now.

Other things like salaries and office spaces — in the grand scheme of our financials, it's a rounding error right now.

Interesting. Do you think that's going to change?

No. The operating leverage we have in this business is kind of insane. We have 200 employees — they cost a lot of money — but the GPUs cost a lot more.

If you had to say what are the top three things that are your biggest focus right now, what would you say?

  1. Capacity and the financial complexity. How do we think about that space? How do we think about pricing and packaging? How do we think about the tension between ownership and renting? Should we go in a more NeoCloud direction or the opposite, counter-position direction? Probably the biggest thing I think a lot about.

  2. Product strategy. What are the next building blocks? If we do more agentic stuff, what do we need? Are there certain storage primitives or compute primitives? What is the thing the world is going to wake up and realize they need over the next few years? Ideally we have that at that point. We've been pretty good at anticipating demand and building products in advance of it — with Serverless Functions and Sandboxes. What's the next thing?

  3. Culture and company building. We recently crossed 200 people. We're growing extremely fast — we'll probably hit 250 by the end of the year. When you're growing fast, 250 people are all trying to figure out how to add the most value to Modal. Making sure they have the right context, motivation, that they're excited to come into work every day because they get to build something incredibly cool. Aligning incentives. Making sure people have a positive culture, implicit trust to do a lot of stuff, but also accountability.

At 10, 20, 30 people, you all sit in a room and it's implicit. People can read me — they can tell when I get annoyed, when I'm happy. Now at 250 people, people don't necessarily see it. New people may be a bit nervous to talk to the CEO. How do I remain approachable? There's the Dunbar number, which I think is more fake than real as a story — but it is kind of real still. Something around 150–200 where laying the foundation of the culture is very important.

How many people are you guys trying to hire over the next year?

We've grown about 4x on an annualized basis in the last 12 months. That's unsustainable on a relative basis. You can double the team every year — that's not super hard. But 4x — what you start to see is cultural drift, islands of different working styles, people doing very speculative things. Something I always watch out for in the engineering team: I go talk to an engineer, "What are you working on?" and it turns out they're building something fringe. Is this really what you should spend time on?

Growing very fast has that cost — ramping people up. By the end of the year maybe 250. By the end of next year — we'll keep growing maybe 2.5–3x. So very likely we'll end up next year like 700 people.

I'm going to assume most of those are engineers.

Mostly engineers. We have sales a lot too.

What kinds of engineers?

Primarily systems engineers. We've always been very deep into Linux, file systems, scalable systems, networking, cloud. People really good at those things.

We're also looking at — we've moved up in the stack a little bit. We're doing a lot of work in the LLM inference space. Now we're dealing with a separate set of concerns around CUDA and GPUs and MFU — maxing out the tokens per GPU. A lot of the work in that space actually turns out to be more systems-driven still, because KV caching and routing is very systems-heavy. But a bit more GPU performance.

We're starting to build up a research team. Very excited about moving into stuff around post-training, distillation, better methods for quantization.

For your customers or internally?

Both. A bit like with FDEs — initially we'll do a lot of stuff with customers to optimize their models, but over time figure out how to turn those into products. If every time a customer needs to optimize a model we have to work with them, long-term it has to be turned into products. With FDEs and the research team, initially a lot of customer work, but we're also building a lot of internal tooling and over time internal products that are fully self-serve. We're working on a lot of stuff in post-training space and GPU performance space. A lot of cool stuff.

产品路线图：越来越多的"积木"

Back to product strategy — what are your thoughts on what we need over the next year, two years?

Incredibly hard to say. If I said I know exactly what we need to build, I'd be delusional. What we've seen so far, and what I believe on a general level: we need better building blocks. This is a new era of software. We're unlocking a whole new type of applications. All the GenAI stuff — code, LLMs outputting code that needs to run in an isolated way. So many new primitives are needed to work with GPUs and LLMs.

We've built some building blocks so far, and that's unlocked a bunch of applications. Over the next few years, there's going to be so many more cool things. I mentioned: I'm very bullish on training, batch jobs, certain things around agents and low latency. But in the end we consider ourselves an infrastructure shop — we try to build very general-purpose building blocks and put them in front of customers. Those customers will combine them and build incredible applications we could have never anticipated.

从推文看观点

I want to go through some of your tweets. This will be the last part. We can double-click on anything.

推文 1：Sandbox 的 lift-and-shift 过时了

"A lot of long-running persistent sandbox stuff right now today feels lift-and-shift. I suspect sandboxes will evolve from dev-box-in-the-cloud to something more ephemeral — one environment for every command, and snapshotting in between so you can pause, resume, clone."

Yeah, we talked about this a lot. The median sandbox in Modal today is like 8 seconds long, which is kind of incredible. Over time it might get even shorter. We want to support long-running sandboxes too — there are valid use cases — but my vision: the world needs to figure out how to massively parallelize things, reducing the overhead of starting and stopping sandboxes.

推文 2：如果我是 IPO-ready 的 CEO，我会想协调 capex 军备竞赛

"I don't know if I ran an IPO-ready startup engaged in a capex arms race with a competitor. It would be nice to coordinate and pace the arms race a bit."

No comment.

推文 3：GPU 稀缺性的真正弊端是"矩形"

"The biggest downside of GPU scarcity is not that it's hard to get GPUs, but that almost all capacity is sold as a three-year rectangle starting 3 to 6 months in the future. That's not what demand looks like for most users."

I think we talked about that a bit. One thing Modal has always been very good at is fully on-demand capacity. If a customer comes to us and needs 100 GPUs, we can typically give them that immediately. You don't even have to talk to a salesperson. A lot of workloads in real life don't look like flat rectangular workloads — they scale up and down throughout the 24-hour cycle, they maybe grow over time, maybe have burst periods.

That's a challenge with a lot of customers today — the primary way to get capacity is to buy these rectangular blocks. It's not great. The world needs to evolve. That's fundamentally why I think Modal can play a very large role in that "duration transformation" of offering more flexible capacity. We can do that because we aggregate many thousands of customers and the demand gets very smooth in aggregate. A lot of the value prop of Modal is exactly that.

Would you say that's a differentiator?

Massive differentiator actually. In fact, Modal's value prop can be reductively broken into two things: 1. Developer experience — ability to iterate and build without thinking about infrastructure. 2. The capacity stuff.

We're going aggressively — built all this work around scaling up and down extremely fast, GPU snapshotting (we're working on some ways to make it much faster), and the model works at very large scale really well because you can aggregate lots of customers.

推文 4：Sandbox 收入每月涨 30%

"Every month I keep saying our sandbox revenue might have plateaued, but it keeps going up 30% every month."

It's kind of nuts. Every month I'm like, "Sandboxes grew a lot but clearly they kind of plateaued," and then they keep growing even more.

A lot of VCs ask, "How did you know sandboxes was going to be big?" The truth is: I didn't. I thought it was going to be bigger than it was in 2023 for sure, but the fact that sandboxes is a third of our revenue today — it's insane. We're obviously very happy. We have a very large team investing in sandboxes. I give ourselves credit for seeing sandboxes for what it is today back in 2023. But I probably would never have taken a bet that revenue would be this large from sandboxes.

推文 5：Inference 应该和 model builder 分离

"There's an interesting structural reason why inference providers should exist separately from model builders. The best model keeps changing a lot. Inference providers can easily reallocate resources between models since overall demand is quite smooth."

Think about all the Chinese labs — hopefully more US labs too — every time a new lab releases the latest and greatest open-source model, you see big shifts in demand. If all these labs independently held capacity, when they launch a new model demand would go up a lot; then another lab launches a better model and demand goes down. But in the background they're working on the next version.

There's a structural reason why demand is shifting to the latest and greatest Chinese lab. Of course it's not like everything moves overnight — a lot of models and prompts have a certain stickiness. But it's easy for Modal: today we're running X thousand GPUs for one model; tomorrow we need to shift 50% to another model. That's what the system is built to handle. No one even needs to tell us — it just magically does that.

So you agree that basically the LLMs are commodities? And if so, where do you think the business for the big labs is going to be?

I'm not sure that's necessarily true. Is Taylor Swift the commodity? She releases a big album, goes on tour, makes a lot of money, then there's a down year when she records. I don't know if this is the best analogy. Then she releases a new album. She still has a lot of brand, a lot of power, makes a lot of margin.

As long as the labs can repeatedly launch new models, and the margin on those models can amortize the cost of training them, it could still be a decent business.

So you don't think intelligence is plateauing?

No, I don't think so. It remains to be seen. Models today are very good at doing things that can be trained very efficiently using reinforcement learning. Initially with coding and writing simple snippets; over time, really good at writing production-level code, really good at math, really good at cybersecurity. These are all verifiable things.

It remains to be seen — are models going to be really good at, whatever, cooking food? Things that have more diffused targets, longer feedback loops. Humans will probably be quite good and competitive with models for a long time in those domains. But certainly, AI models are getting very good.

Models are already really good at coding. What other applications that aren't as big right now are going to become huge over the next few years?

Anything that has verifiable loops — computational bio, like you mentioned. Not exactly verifiable, but you can use an LLM to output predictions, then use computational methods to simulate molecular dynamics and get feedback loops.

Material science — maybe another area where you have a loop. You can synthetically manufacture materials and measure properties and put an agent in the loop. I have a physics background, I'm pretty excited about that. So drugs, materials — what else? Drawing a blank, but I'm sure there's many other things.

结束

Cool. Those are all the questions I had. Is there anything you wanted to talk about that I haven't?

I'm good. This is great. This is a lot of fun.

Awesome. Thank you.
