item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：Character.ai 花 16 美元换 1 美元收入——这不是"烧钱换增长"，这是**代币庞氏**
Chris 顺带一提的那个数字其实是整段讨论里最锋利的一刀，但三位主持人都没有真正剖开它。传统意义上"烧钱换规模"的逻辑是：现在亏钱，未来凭借网络效应/数据飞轮/切换成本获利。但 AI 应用公司的 16:1 支出结构背后没有这三样东西中的任何一样。
那它换的到底是什么？——**是"token 消耗量"这个指标本身的叙事价值**。风投轮次定价时看的是"每月被烧掉多少 token"，而前沿实验室定价时看的是"有多少应用在消耗我的 token"。于是出现了一个闭环：A 公司烧钱向 B 公司买 token，B 公司拿着"收入增长"去融下一轮，A 公司再拿着"token 消耗量"去融下一轮，两边同时在给对方的 PPT 作背书。
**这在金融史上有个名字：相互交易膨胀（round-tripping），90 年代末 Enron 和能源交易所做的事。**只不过这一轮用的不是电力合约，是浮点运算。
## 二、"productive bubble" 这个比喻可能是错的—

item.title: [Latent Space] AI in NYC: How Tenex Builds an AI-Native Engineering Team — Alex Lieberman & CJ Hess
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

几个让我意外的隐秘模式

1. "泰勒主义的意外回归"——AI 偷偷完成了 100 年前管理学失败的任务

整段对话里埋着一句最反直觉的话："You can't automate a process that does not exist."（你无法自动化一个尚不存在的流程）

表面上这是关于 agent 部署的工程教训，但往深里看——AI 时代正在悄悄完成弗雷德里克·泰勒（Frederick Taylor）在 1911 年没能彻底完成的事业。整个 20 世纪，知识工作抗拒标准化：律师、分析师、顾问以"每个案子都不同"为由保护自己的黑箱手艺。而现在，当 40 个人用 40 种方法做同一件事，agent 就无法接管。于是企业被迫做它们一百年来都抵抗的事：先 Taylorize 自己，再让 AI 接手。

跨领域连接：这跟军队的"doctrine（作战条令）"是同构的——Tenex 的 meta harness（元框架）本质上是在为 AI 工程建立作战条令，让新兵一上场就能打出老兵的水准。换句话说，CJ 做的不是工具，是"参谋总部制度"的数字化翻版。

2. "10x" 公司的真实差距只有 4x——这不是失败，而是 AI 作为"方差压缩器"的证据

Alex 自己承认：Tenex 最高薪与最低薪工程师的差距只有 4 倍，不是公司名所暗示的 10 倍。他把这当作一个有待解决的问题带过了，但我想反过来读它：

AI 本质上是一个"方差压缩器"，而不是"方差放大器"。叙事上大家都说 AI 让顶尖的人跑得更快、让菜鸟被淘汰；但真实数据显示——当底层模型能力足够强，中位数被拉起的速度远远快于顶尖被拉开的速度。Opus 5.5 让一个二线工程师可以 2x 产出，但同样让一线工程师也只有 2x——因为 token-per-task 的回报正在逼近 Pareto 前沿（这正是他们后面讨论为什么不再担心 token 成本的原因）。

启示：Tenex 的"10x 工程师经济学"叙事与 4x 的实际数据之间的裂缝，恰恰是未来几年知识型劳动市场最被低估的现象——AI 不是在制造超级精英，而是在压扁才华曲线。

3. Token/工资 = 2:1 的公司，其实已经是"反向麦肯锡"

Alex 轻描淡写地给出一个数字：Tenex 的 token 支出和员工支出比例在 1:1 到 2:1 之间。swyx 的反应是"That's pretty high"（挺高的）——但他低估了这件事的历史意味。

典型 SaaS 公司这个比值是 10%。Tenex 是 200%。这意味着这家咨询公司已经不是在"卖人头"了——它的首要投入要素是算力，不是劳动力。换句话说，Tenex 的损益表长得更像一家数据中心、而不是一家埃森哲。

跨领域连接：这是一个历史级的组织形态转折。工业革命时期，制造业的 COGS（销货成本）主体从"原材料"切换到"机器折旧"，催生了福特制。21 世纪的服务业现在正在把 COGS 主体从"工资"切换到"推理成本"——而我们还没有一个管理学理论来处理这种公司。Tenex 实际上是在无意中跑在一场组织架构的 regime change 前面。

4. 一个没人注意到的"内部货币政策危机"

当被问到"一年前的 1 个 story point 值多少钱、现在还一样吗？"CJ 答："we're always trying to calibrate"（我们一直在尝试重新校准）。

这句话被当作操作细节一笔带过，但它其实是人类历史上第一家公司在尝试管理一种"内生通胀/通缩"的内部货币。story points 是 Tenex 的内部法币——它为员工发工资、为客户定价、为增长做衡量。当底层模型每 6 个月让生产力翻倍，这枚货币会相对于"美元/工时"剧烈通胀——除非每季度人为贬值它。

没有央行、没有货币政策工具、没有 CPI 篮子。他们在摸着石头造一个 Tenex 元；而且他们也许不知道，罗伯特·欧文（Robert Owen）在 1832 年用过"劳动时间券"（labour notes），结果因为无法应对生产率变化而崩盘。

最反直觉的洞见：Tenex 面临的最大长期风险不是模型变贵、不是客户流失、不是人才争夺——而是他们的内部货币可能会被底层技术通胀吃掉信用。

一个贯穿全场的隐藏结构

把以上四条串起来：Tenex 看起来是一家 AI 咨询公司，但它实际上在同时运行四个历史级实验—— - 泰勒主义 2.0（流程标准化作为自动化前置） - 方差压缩的劳动力市场（AI 作为均衡器而非放大器） - 以推理成本为主体的损益表（反向咨询业） - 无央行的内生货币制度（story points 作为企业法币）

这四件事里任何一件独立出现都值得写一本书。而他们在同一家 75 人的公司里同时跑着——还没完全意识到。

这才是这段访谈真正值得记住的东西。

📝 转录文本

AI in NYC: How Tenex Builds an AI-Native Engineering Team

Alex Lieberman & CJ Hess · Latent Space

Intro & Reintroducing Tenex

Okay, we're here at AI Engineer checking in with Tenex. Welcome back, Alex.

Thanks. Thanks for having us.

You brought your Director of Engineering, CJ. Welcome to the pod.

Special projects lead at Tenex.

Okay, special projects lead. All right, you're the SWAT team.

Yes, yes.

So you've been on the pod before, and people are vaguely familiar with the Tenex story, but can you sort of reintroduce from the top — what is the 2026, how you introduce yourself?

Yeah, very simply, Tenex is an applied AI partner for some of the biggest companies in the world to help them go from AI absent to AI native. Our belief is that AI is incredible, but it is raw intelligence. And the hardest problem to solve is the final mile to actually diffuse it through the economy. And so our view is to act as the player to help enterprises to figure all of this.

Can I curse on? To figure all this shit out.

Yeah, yeah. Yeah, we have the explicit tag on Apple Podcasts. Although I did recently discover that YouTube doesn't like it.

Oh really?

They're so, like, yeah, you can't say the F word.

So did I just mess up your video? What are you going to do?

I don't care. Okay. We're for adults.

CJ's Path to Tenex: Betting on Output over Hours

CJ, what drew you to Tenex?

So I was actually the first hire. I don't even know if Alex and Armand had the name Tenex quite yet, but I have, like, a graveyard of startups I tried to start before Tenex, ultimately culminating in like my own kind of engineering consulting company. And I spent some time there doing traditional engineering, eventually moved over to doing some of this like AI consulting and just like building more and more with it. I'm a software engineer by trade. And I just felt my output getting better and faster and ultimately getting paid less. Like I was charging hourly to my clients.

And I really liked kind of the ethos of Tenex that Alex had first posted when I saw it on Twitter about kind of looking to reward engineers for their output as opposed to rewarding them for their time. I think, you know, fast forwarding two years, you can see how engineers can now parallelize a ton of work and just have a ton more output. At the time with, you know, Sonnet 3.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, it might not have been that obvious, but I basically took the bet that I think with my skill set and leaning more into AI, I could have much higher output and ultimately have like a higher earning capacity to do that. And since then I've just like fell in love with that model. I think that's what the future of engineering really looks like. And ultimately when AI is solving all these tech problems, companies are gonna pay based on outcome and they're not going to want to pay based on the time that's required to build something.

Yeah. So for more detail on that, people can refer back to our previous pod where you literally pay people by story points.

Yep. And you just have to agree what the story points are. But that also means that some 10x engineers can literally make millions of dollars a year and some others may not make as much just because they're not as productive.

Yeah, exactly. The thesis is that AI is really just a leveraged bet on a human's intellect and work ethic. And so you're just going to have more variance than ever before in earning capacity. Our model isn't for everyone, but for the person who basically wants to go long themselves, who has this incredible foundation in software engineering, but also is constantly pushing themselves to leverage the frontier, to stretch their time as much as possible while having quality output, there's no better way to earn.

The State of Tenex: 75 People, 4x Variance, and the Compensation Puzzle

What's the state of — last time I talked to you, I think you had maybe two or three people making a million a year or over a million a year. Is there an update on that?

Yeah, yeah, yeah. So just to paint a picture, we started Tenex 18 months ago. Really, we started as like an AI-powered dev shop. The original idea was engineering is kind of like the canary in the coal mine for AI. And part of the impetus was my co-founder, Armand, who's technical by trade, was starting to use coding agents a lot. And then he had some people he knew that were still typing into their IDE, like not adopting the technology at all. And so we're like, why don't we just supercharge a company's engineering org who isn't adopting this?

So we started there. Then as we started moving up market from startups and mid-market companies to now, you know, 50% of our customers are Fortune 2000, and 50% are mid-market doing $100 to $500 million in revenue. They weren't just asking for staff aug and AI engineering. They were asking for AI transformation as a service.

Today, the business is at 75 people. 90% of those employees are either engineers or AI strategists, which are basically think of as technical consultants. And I think the thesis has proved out true, which is there's a very wide dispersion in earning capacity between the highest paid engineer at Tenex and the lowest paid engineer at Tenex. It's probably something around 4X difference.

Oh, not 10X?

Not 10X difference, yeah.

That's the dream.

Yeah, exactly. But everything is proved right about the thesis. I do think there's been interesting learnings around our model of paying based on story points — there are limits to the model that we knew would be limits and how we think about that moving forward.

But overall, I think the concerns that people had around this model of paying people based on output, like the classic concerns are: well, story points are subjective. People are going to either sandbag story points or they're just going to ship a bunch of bad code.

Like barely check the box.

Exactly. Right. But not actually do the job.

Yeah, exactly. And I would say those two concerns have not been concerns at all because of our AI strategists. We incentivize, I think, perfectly at odds with engineers — where AI strategists are incentivized for customer retention and growth. Actually, the biggest challenge has been: how do you compensate engineers for all the time that's not spent coding, whether it's architecting, meeting with clients. And so that's where we've had to find nuance in the comp model, but it's still largely driven based on output.

Anything to add?

Yeah, on that, I spend a lot of time thinking about this because if I think about my tenure at Tenex, I was coding a lot, coding a lot, coding a little less, and now we're kind of getting to the point where the models are more or less — given the right context — can get you to 90% of the solution. And I do think there is some opportunity here to think about: really the value is sitting down with a customer, hearing everything that they can brain dump, and then just providing that to the model to actually get closer to the solution. So I imagine, you know, in the future, we're going to start to look more at like true what this output is, how it works, how it looks, as opposed to that traditional story point model — but still anchoring to those as the unit.

The Meta Harness: Agents, Plans, and the Repo as Memory

I think one thing — I don't know if we've talked about this before — but the idea of the meta harness, which is the engineering workflows at Tenex that we use that has allowed us to do, I think, really meaningful work on long-running tasks. Do you want to just talk through what our process is? Cause I feel like people would find that interesting.

Yeah. So we basically started trying to kind of standardize a set of skills. Most engineering orgs have done something similar by this point. And for us that grew into what is actually a very structured set of documentation within a repo and then a CLI around it that the models are using to actually drive the work that's being done — whether it's creating a plan, a visualization, creating some readout for a client — effectively building all the pieces of the process around actually writing the code to just happen more automatically and standard across our team.

So we have a couple of things. One is this big canonical plan document that has some similar structure, but I'd say as the models have gotten better, we've actually reduced the enforcements there in the structure. Kind of similarly across all of these. But once you have your plan, you actually build it out. And we have a very opinionated way on how agents will go and log their decisions and log what they're doing and just keep track of what they're up to.

Everything checked into Git.

Yeah. All of this is checked in. All of this is really kind of markdown — for me now, more HTML. I like to see these picture books that the agents fit out. But all of that gets checked in and then it serves as this surface where not only do you have the code as the source — you know, I think there's a debate on like, do you even need docs? Like the code can actually be the memory of a code base. And I do think you do. You need to know why you made a decision. You need to know the context around the conversation that was had. But ultimately, that plus the code base, if there's a question, if there's something we need to answer, if we need to look back on why we did something, we just always have that in some durable record.

And it's never in someone's head. It's always in the repo. So that just gives our agents and our tools these superpowers to have all the context that I think a lot of engineering teams still just have in conversations or have in their heads. And our goal is to kind of continue to push that forward so that all the context is in one place and more and more of that work is just driven by the agent as opposed to us having to provide everything up front.

Yeah, amazing. And one way we even measure if any of these kind of processes are working is: are we seeing an increase in trend in average story points per month of every engineer in the company?

Right. And what do you think it is, let's say compared to the start of this year?

I don't know. What do you think? Plus 50?

I think, so it really depends, because we have some people that — there's some picture that I saw on Twitter of a guy over a wizard orb, and he's got these things in the sky. And that's how I think of some of our engineers when they're whipping agents around. I'd really say, overall, it's been a 2x increase this year in particular.

Basically, if you think of December as the Opus 4.5 moment where the models really started to take on these long-running tasks — to today we're back to Opus, but Opus 5.5. I mean, that's just a magnificent model that can really do a ton of work. Over that period, I've seen the actual output of engineers roughly double in terms of what they were able to do, to what they're able to cover in the same time span now.

Is a single story point worth the same now as it was a year ago?

We're always trying to calibrate. It's a tricky equation.

Is there inflation or deflation? I mean, in theory, there should be deflation, right?

Yeah. Yeah. I don't know. And that's roughly how we think about it. I would say at least once a quarter, we kind of sit down and evaluate — what is our criteria for these story points? How are we actually estimating these projects? There's a fine balance to be made between still rewarding this output, but also as the models get better, we do need to be able to calibrate the value that we're creating. So overall I would say roughly that 2x has played a similar role in how we do these estimations. But if I just look at some of the features and things people are building and pushing out now versus this time last year, it's insane what the difference has been.

Model Preferences: The Opus 5.5 Era, AMP, and Orbing Out

So there's a couple ways I can take this, but I'm just going to check in on the model preference stuff since it's always a topic of conversation. I think you just let people choose whatever tools they like but then maybe you have some statistics on what is preferred in the office. It seems like Opus is leading. Can you care to estimate market share?

The vibe right now is Opus 5.5, I think.

No Fable?

I don't particularly use Fable, and I think a lot of people right now are just defaulting away from it. Opus is so good. It's fast, it's cheap. It kind of hits all my checkboxes. I would say I previously have had two to three models depending on whether they're cheap and fast, whether they're really smart, whether they can solve specific problems. And now Opus is kind of covering my full range.

I think a lot of the team still reaches for tools like Codex when we need to do something maybe more in the computer use world. And really workflow-wise, I think using both is still the best option — whichever your driver is, which I think for most of our team is Opus 5.5. Using a Codex to review and having them actually work back and forth on your machine, I think still produces the best results. But right now we're pretty aligned on those two.

And are you still AMP maxing or no?

Oh, I am AMP maxing.

So you're using Opus through AMP? Or that's the default model for AMP?

Yeah, they recently launched the ability to hook in your Claude Code subscription. So that's been a pretty big game changer for me.

Because that'll really cut your cost by like 80%.

Totally. I mean, I love AMP because it takes everything off my computer. They have this cloud setup, the orbs. We actually co-hosted a happy hour with them last week, so it was cool to meet the team and orb out.

That's never going to be a thing.

Oh yeah. I want to make it a thing.

This may be the first time in history that any human has said it. "We're orbing out."

We were orbing out. No, they do say it's orbing time.

Yeah. But that's my interface of choice. And models are really between that — if I'm leaning on Codex, it's Sol6.1.

Did you give Claude Tag a shot? Isn't it weird that Anthropic never captured the remote environment thing in the way that Orbs did?

Yeah, I think there's a piece of that — on the AMP side of them being very opinionated and not trying to build this general solution. Tools like Claude Code in the cloud and Claude Tag, I think, provide value for teams that are really trying to collaborate maybe on non-technical tasks. But part of the reason I love AMP is that it has all these cross-model functionalities and I can do that. Opus writes it. I can even hop to another orb and say, look at that orb and review it. And all of those things still come together to basically replicate what I'm doing on my machine. And I just couldn't quite get there with Claude Code in the cloud, Claude Tag.

Yeah, yeah. Fair enough.

Token Spend vs Employee Spend: The 2:1 Reality

Another thing I always track — I'm starting to track this year — is percent of, let's say, token spend to employee spend. I don't know if you have that number. So roughly, most companies are at maybe, let's call it $10 to $200 in spend per employee. The more sort of AI native ones would sort of convert that to a percentage, so roughly 10%. The average AI startup employee is about 1x in terms of employee spend and token spend, and then it goes up to maybe 5 to 10x in terms of token spend. Where are you guys in that range?

I actually don't have a number off the top of my head. I'd say we're somewhere between, if we're talking raw tokens, somewhere between 1 to 1 and maybe like 2 to 1.

Really? That's pretty high.

And what we think about a lot is when to reach for the biggest model. I think every company is starting to think about that. But I will say recently our costs have been driven just way down from Opus 5.5. We kind of had an era of like everyone was using Astra and Fable and they just gave the best results. But ultimately those models are expensive.

And like a lot of like, you know, since the last time we talked, a lot of people had this sort of token-maxing error, token leaderboards, everything. And then they were like, oh, no, no, no, no. Now we have too much cost.

Well, it's the most predictable thing in the world. Did you ever fear about it, or you were just getting good ROI regardless?

Yeah, I mean, there's a few ways that I think about it. We were for sure worried about it just as our headcount was growing. And I think also, even though our team — I don't feel like anyone on our team ever really ascribed to the token-maxing zeitgeist, because...

I had a few moments.

Yeah, me too. But it's like, well, if the boss is going to pay for it, I'm just going to go nuts, right? Because then you do the weird stuff so that you can scale back, but you have to do the weird stuff first to discover the lessons that you can take with you.

Data Companies, Fine-tuning, and the Pareto Point

Yeah totally. I mean, this may sound crazy, and I'd be curious of your thoughts, but I was talking to someone earlier about the debate that continues around... I promise this is related. Like I was talking to someone earlier around the data companies — Micro1, Mercor, Handshake. What does the long-term for these businesses look like, right? Because 90-plus percent of their revenue is from the labs. And a number of these founders would argue that they think it's going to flip-flop where in the next few years, it's going to be enterprise-driven.

And then the thing that comes to mind, the next thing I assume you have to believe if enterprises are going to be the core buyer of that data, is that enterprises are going to be doing a lot of fine-tuning on their own models. And then the question becomes, where is that going to make sense? It's either you think there's going to be better quality — which, again, the bar is just going to keep moving on the frontier, so that's a hard bet to make. Then it has to be price. The price one feels hard to me because we're just seeing token costs continue to go down on these models.

And so I guess part of the reason we're not concerned internally is because it almost feels like we've kind of hit this like Pareto point of costs are coming down at a per-task basis. Then it is way harder today for someone to token-max and really F the company in terms of cost than it was six to eight months ago. I almost think six to eight months ago was the point at which you'd be really concerned.

Yeah. Do you agree with that?

Yeah. I think there's a couple ways the future might play out there. If there's a world where there's an Astra 6.5, a Fable 5.5, and they're super expensive but they get the best results, I could see us trending back that direction. But generally I agree that you look at something like Muse Wonder that they launched yesterday — and it's on the frontier, it's dirt cheap, the competition is heating up, both in open source and closed source. And I think that just will continue to drive costs down. And when you really look at it, a lot of tasks that are economically valuable can be done with Opus 5.5. So it's that cliff of: would a 10 times smarter model really justify the cost of moving some cells in a spreadsheet? Probably not.

The Enterprise AI Adoption Funnel: 90 → 60 → 50 → 5

Right. So coming back to your customers and what you're seeing from the market, what is the most common ask that you guys get? And then what is something that people come to you with and you're like, no, we don't actually want that job yet?

Yeah. So one way I think about this is I think about enterprises adopting AI as almost like these different milestones in a race. And I think, especially at AIE, when I tell people about what percentage of companies have reached these milestones, they're kind of mind-blown by it.

Milestone 1: Rolling out a general purpose LLM. Of the, let's call it 100 enterprises we're talking to today, 90% have rolled out either Claude or Codex to their employees.

Milestone 2: Training and enablement. Actually teaching people how to use it — which never gets the love that it should get, but is arguably more important or as important as the technology itself. I would say that's at like 60%.

Oh, that's pretty good.

Yeah. There's some group there of companies that are like, "our people will just figure it out." But then there's a good chunk that is like, okay, we need to teach our people what skills are. We need to teach our people the features and functionality of these surfaces.

Milestone 3: Coding agents. The crazy thing is, I was asking a few people here, what percentage of enterprises do you think have rolled out coding agents to the engineering/product org in their company? And most people are like, it has to be 70 or 80%. The number is closer to 50%. Every other enterprise that we speak to either hasn't rolled out a coding agent or what they are using is closer to not having a coding agent than having a coding agent.

Milestone 4: Agents in production for non-engineering work. And this is where the biggest diffusion gap is — from raw intelligence to enterprise usage — drops to like 5%. I mean, most enterprises that we talk to that have, let's just say more than a thousand employees, do not have an agent in production that is doing work that is not building software.

FOMO, Back-Office Agents, and the Permissioning Nightmare

And so I think there's a few things. One is, this whole wave is driven by a combination of some small group of people understanding what is possible from this technology — and a way larger group of people driven by FOMO. And by the way, FOMO isn't bad. It creates some forward momentum, but it also means that people will latch onto the things that are most in the zeitgeist. I guess now for the last year and a half, people have been saying it's "the year of the agent" — or however long it is. Every year is the year of the agent.

Enterprises are like: can you help build us an agent for some back office task within the organization? That is one of the most common things. And it's why now a lot of the work we're doing at Tenex is deploying agents into production outside of the engineering org for companies — for repeatable work that they're doing.

The second is permissioning and RBAC. Basically, as every employee in a company has Claude or they have Codex and they need access to certain data, it has turned into an absolute nightmare for CIOs and CISOs. And they don't have basically a good gateway for easily doing — almost like a control panel for data permissioning.

Literally just what can you read, what can you not read.

Exactly. And that is a huge issue. So that's something we spend a lot of time on.

So you make them for people or do you buy something off the shelf?

So basically we started by building bespoke for companies, and now we actually productize that where we have our own gateway solution.

"You Can't Automate a Process That Does Not Exist"

Yeah, exactly. Is there anything else that comes to mind that's like, "we're hearing a lot from customers"?

I think that covered what we're hearing when it comes to the agent deployments. I think one of the pains that just always gets discovered — I phrase it to the team as: you can't automate a process that does not exist.

So when you have 40 people that are all roughly doing the same function, but they're all doing it a little bit of a different way, it's way harder to build an agent that's proactively doing that in the background. You can totally sit down with them, give them the tools, walk them through how they could augment their own workflow. But when you really start to get the leverage is when you have these agents that are surfacing work to you, you're reviewing it, you're throwing it back, and you become more of this — you know, everyone's been talking about becoming an agent manager, and I think we're on the cusp of that. But when you zoom out, oftentimes our recommendation to companies is: hey, first, we need to build a process around this organization within your company. And then here are the steps for us to actually hand off that work to an agent in the background. But if we don't have some form of standardization, it's going to be impossible for the agent to know whether it's doing it right, for us to build evals around this system and actually deliver the value that an agent that is doing this function would have.

The Bear Case on Vertical-Specific AI Solutions

And one thing I'd be curious your thoughts on — we were literally talking about this right before — CJ will be okay with me sharing this: we were talking about vertical-specific AI solutions and what does the future look like for these solutions. And we were generally expressing an overall bearishness with vertical-specific AI solutions in different functions or industries.

And part of it is just, from our vantage point of spending all day in the guts of enterprises, there is so much nuance and so much inertia and so many systems you have to wrangle and people you have to wrangle. And also when a buyer of a vertical solution is expecting truly a one-of-one experience — we're in an age where people are expecting one-of-one software solutions. And so if you're expecting that, it's no wonder that every software company is basically building up a team of FDEs, because there's just this convergence happening of services and software when every company wants all this nuance that was not traditionally expected from software.

And so I think it's really interesting to think about: how will vertical-specific solutions be able to do this at software margins if everyone expects a one-of-one solution? And also, why should we not expect frontier models to just gobble them up?

Yeah. So to give some concrete examples — you're talking Harvey for lawyers.

Yep.

Open Evidence for doctors. These are the classic examples of people that are winning their domains. And you're bearish on them?

I would say generally bearish on them. Correct.

Wow. Well, so far you've been wrong.

Yep.

And I think the answer very simply is access to data that ChatGPT is not going to have, which is very common. That is a moat. Obviously, Anthropic and OpenAI are also acquiring those same data sources, but they're just not as dedicated as these guys are going to be. They do have innovations. If you've tried it, Harvey — they have the Tabular Review. Legora also have them. We've had the CTO on the podcast where they have affordances and UIs and all that is just customized because they only serve them. The pitch is focus, basically. Focus, affordances maybe.

What do you mean by affordances?

In a way that you care about the last mile for your customers, they care about their last mile in terms of the software. And as long as people train in that software, like it never goes away. Like as a banker, or in my finance career, I could always access the same exact information from the NASDAQ, from the New York Stock Exchange. But why do I pay the $50,000 a year for Bloomberg? Well, it's just that's what everyone, all my peers do. And it's all consolidated for me and it's all specialized for me, so I don't make mistakes or whatever. Or it's tied into my trading system or my chat or whatever, my news system.

No, I think people play for Bloomberg is the social network. I think people love the DMs in Bloomberg.

There's that, there's that. But as a trader, I know I actually use that for...

Yeah, yeah, yeah. So, I mean, I think there's a bunch of integrations and tools — and I think ultimately it's hard to be bearish on any of them, mostly because the demand for software, the demand for tooling to do your job is just huge. And some of it, yes, it's going to be fulfilled by horizontal generalized tools like the Claudes and ChatGPTs, and some of it, you're just going to want something better.

And, you know, I always think about maybe the success of Superhuman as an email client. Everyone has Gmail, but here's just premium Gmail with more stuff for people who live in email all day long. And that's a market. It maybe wasn't the largest startup in the world, but I think reasonable people can disagree how large each thing is.

Yeah totally. I think what's not to be disagreed with is the total market's going to grow — a rising tide where there's tall boats. And then you're just talking percentage pressure market share at that point.

Yeah, yeah, I agree with that. Totally agree.

I think there's even a differentiation between some new app built from the ground up with AI involved. That's what comes to mind when I think about Superhuman. I love Superhuman. I don't even spend a ton of time in email, but anything that has...

No, you pay 30 bucks a month just to not worry about it. Anything that has cool hotkeys, I'm into.

Yeah. But when I think about products where they are really pushing some agent as the product that is doing work in some specific vertical — unless there is some very strategic compliance, data, whatever it might be, moat, I think those are going to struggle going forward as we start to see quite literally the ability to either spin up your own really quickly continue to compound as the models get better, or just those tasks start to fall into the world of the models generally. But anything that has this app and tool built around it, kind of to my previous point, changes the process and has an agent on top of it — and I think that can still be super helpful, and those will be successful.

The "Agent Owns the Interface" Thesis

Yeah. Oh, okay, okay. So there is a related view about this that maybe isn't quite as spicy as yours, which is basically: it's not like nobody wants to use... People probably don't want to use the agent that you built. They want to use the agent that they already have, and they want to plug in your data into their agent. So everyone is sitting on some part of your data, and they're like, "use my agent, please. Please pay me that $20 a month." But you can't just stack up all these $20 a month subscriptions.

Ultimately, probably a small set of companies are going to own the interface, and then everyone just plugs into that overall agent, which I agree with. Then it's interesting that Salesforce, being one of the system of record companies, is the biggest probably or the most well-known, is embracing that path as like "you will not use our agents. Like we will just provide APIs and MCPs for you to plug into your stuff."

Yeah, which is kind of cool.

Kill My SaaS: Replacing Mid-Tier Software

Okay, so I actually wanted to also walk through one example. So I just released my results for my "Kill My SaaS" competition where we replace a mid-tier SaaS. I call it mid-tier basically in the sense that it's probably not that trivial, but it's not Salesforce. It's somewhere in the middle. And I think there's a lot of mid-tier SaaS out there that people are always talking about, like the death of software. We were quoted $40,000 a year. We spent $1,000 to replace it. It's going to go into production for the next conference. So we are that customer that says, I want the one-on-one tool, and I'm expecting all these things. And we're building a domain-specific or vertical-specific thing for our business. And so far it's going okay. Tell me where it's going wrong. Also, I'm wondering how many story points that is.

Yeah, well, CJ can size up the story points on it. I mean, my general view is: the more you move upmarket in business, the harder the proposition of ripping out and building from scratch gets. I agree with you. Part of the reason — as people have said, like a very small group have said, like Salesforce is really at risk, SAP is really at risk — don't agree with that at all. Those businesses in my mind just accrue value in this moment in time. And part of the reason they accrue value is there's so much money at stake where if a company gets it wrong ripping them out, you're talking about potentially hundreds of millions or billions of dollars. You're going to be risk averse.

Yeah exactly.

I think for mid-tier, it actually comes down to: what is the size of the opportunity, and is that ever going to be the worthiest opportunity to rebuild inside of a company? I'm trying to even think. In an enterprise, let's just say there's some mid-tier SaaS that is a few million bucks a year. I think the first question is, from a percentage of revenue or cost perspective, is that going to ever move the needle enough to allocate engineer or resource to? I think it's going to be case by case. For some enterprises, the answer may be yes. For other enterprises, the answer may be no.

I think more of it is going to be the thing that gets companies outside of capability. You know, we talk about how — I forgot who created the repo — that is basically the reverse engineer repo. RIA.

Yeah exactly. Everyone's talking about that right now. And even at Tenex, we built our own CRM from scratch. What did we build? Our OS we built from scratch. And one thing I think we realized, and every company realizes this, is: one of the beauties of software is not just the utility that you get from it. It is all of the headaches you don't have to think about in maintaining it and improving it when it's not in your core.

So I think it basically comes down to: is the size of the prize big enough to justify the cognitive load that is going to take from some amount of resource in your company to nurture something that is not core to your business? Evidently, I think for your business, the difference of basically $39,000 a year, you're implicitly saying that it is worth it.

It is not just about costs. That's defense. I also think about the offense of: no, actually our experience could be a lot better for literally every party concerned.

Totally totally. And so, yeah, I think part of the thought there is: there's two pieces to it. One is like, not just we're being overcharged for a product, but the product has been mediocre for a long period of time.

Yes. What would the 10x better version of this product look like?

Yes, because we are the customers and we can iterate with minutes and not months.

Totally. I actually think what's interesting is startups and even high-growth, mid-sized companies can be nimble in that way. For enterprises where they're so entrenched in a certain capability, rarely is that going to be the thing that — rarely are they going to say, "oh, we can create a 10x better version of this SaaS we use and we're going to spin it out potentially as its own thing or whatever it is." I just don't think enterprises function that way.

Automating Humans: Displacement, Reallocation, and Agency

For sure. Yeah, it's been discussed. Actually, I would say that you talk about automation — the more spicy thing is: are they automating humans, right? And once everything is automated and smooth sailing, do we replace those jobs? I don't know how much you can speak to that.

Yeah, I mean, I think there's two pieces here. I really deeply believe that AI will produce good for humanity. It's going to augment people's jobs. It will absolutely change and displace. But I think it's more of a movement as opposed to just cutting off work.

I think A16Z posted something about how call centers are truly now on the decline and AI is starting to handle more and more of that work. And ultimately, if that is a skill you've built up your whole career, that is devastating to have something come in and take that function over.

That being said, part of what we do when we're talking to customers about "hey, an agent is now going to do this work" is actually around reallocation. I don't think any business would claim like once we have this solved, there's nothing for this group of people to work on and try to solve. So our approach really is about: what can we replace, and then what are the next biggest problems to look at? I'd make an argument in most large companies that cycle kind of continues forever. There's always the next problem.

If I think about how we've grown — infinite demands. There's always been another problem. And actually taking those people that may have this super deep subject matter expertise and bringing them above water to start to maybe work more across teams, or think about parts of the business less so on the level of a cell in a spreadsheet, and more about how these teams are working together.

Ultimately, in the long run, I think that keeps most people there and allows those businesses to become more nimble and actually tackle the big meaty problems and not the drudge of most people's day-to-day. When you're thinking about someone that's in a finance division, they're mostly in spreadsheets — but how can we elevate them to think strategically about the business and where money is allocated and things like that.

Yeah, and I also feel like when we have these conversations around job displacement or job reallocation, we talk about it as this thing happening to people. And one of the reasons I don't like that is I feel like it doesn't give enough credit to people to have agency in their own lives, meaning...

You can adjust.

Yeah, people really should be thinking. When I think about enablement or people re-skilling, I think it is the job of an employer because they want to drive growth in their business, but it is also the job of an employee. And I think when people say that AI is going to replace all of the work that people don't enjoy doing, I think that's a little bit of a cope for the reality of: just, people are going to be put out of jobs because a lot of people don't have the luxury of liking or not liking a job. They do a job to make money.

And also I think people, to the extent that it's possible, should have agency in saying to themselves: okay, what is the stability or replaceability of my job over the next few years, and if I am to try to skill up in a way that I'm better protected, what does that look like? People have agency to say that to themselves and actually take action.

New York vs San Francisco: Bubbles, Billboards, and Arbitrage

Yeah, yeah, yeah. I think that's a good message for people to reflect on. The last piece I wanted to touch on before I let you guys go is just New York. You know, greatest city in the world according to some people. What's the mood generally among the people they talk to, whether it's at work, personally, what's the feeling? I live in San Francisco all day long. Everyone's just in agents all day long. The discussion is Instinks or Grok or Muse. It's not "do you like AI or not," right? And I feel like I want to step out of that bubble for a bit, but it's still New York. It's still progressive. It's still forward-looking.

Yeah. I mean, what I'd say is I feel like, basically, there's a bubble in New York that is a smaller bubble than exists in SF. If SF is like a big bubble, I think we at Tenex feel like we are in a — what I would say is like a microcosm of San Francisco — because of the people that self-select to work at the company. And then also the companies that we're partnered with and the people that we engage with in New York.

But I would for sure say also, it is true that it is a smaller universe than in SF. When you go to SF, it feels all-encompassing where it's like everyone, everywhere you look — there was someone who, similar to AIE, how I was saying earlier when I went on stage: if people go on Twitter or X because they feel like they're on Edge City, they're living in the future, AIE is that on steroids. I feel like SF is similar to AIE. I mean, it's probably the overlap of AIE generally and people who have lived at some point in their life in SF is probably a very large overlap.

We're roughly 1% of the city now.

Actually? For World's Fair, yeah. That's crazy.

Yeah. But to that point, I just think it is in the culture and the DNA of SF where a very big population of people live in the future. I think you can find that group in New York. And I think we at Tenex have found those people. And part of our goal is to drive AI as a hub or New York as a hub for AI in the US, because there is so much commerce here that it is going to be a place where diffusion of the technology actually has such a meaningful impact on the GDP of this country.

I think the bubble is smaller now and we take it almost as a charge of ours to increase our bubble. Maybe I don't know that it's possible to get to SF size, but I do think we can have a meaningful impact on getting more people to live in the future here. There's a physical — you see it on the billboards. It's slowly creeping in.

Oh totally. People used to — remember the Friend campaign where people would spray all sorts of graffiti on that? I think that was a little bit of an intentional rage bait. But now you have the unironic AI billboards and people are like, I guess that's part of life now.

A hundred percent. Yeah, so I think there's an opportunity to bring the edge and the living-in-the-future nature that SF has created because of the economic climate that exists there — because of venture, because of tech companies, and because of the people that are attracted there. But I also think of us as: we're in a smaller pond for AI, but I would argue we're in as big of a pond, if not a bigger pond, for commercial value.

And so I actually — the way I put it is: the reason I do AI in New York is I bring all the people from San Francisco to come here and meet their customers and also get a reality check.

Totally. And I actually think there's a really interesting arbitrage there.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, totally.

Hiring Call

Okay, awesome. Call for hiring. I know you guys are always hiring.

Yep. What are you hiring for? What's changed?

Yep. We're hiring forward deployed engineers at Tenex. Just go to tenex.co. We're also always hiring AI strategists, which are basically technical consultants who are leading client engagements. And the team is 75 strong in New York City. We're continuing to make New York City our home. And then if you are an enterprise who is looking to actually get AI native and you've tried it and it's not working, hit us up. I promise we'll do better work than — not going to name them — but a lot of other traditional consultancies.

Ooh spicy. CJ?

Yeah, I mean, I echo all of that. I'm particularly looking for engineers.

What's a special project? What is that?

A special project involves anything outside of our client work. So I think about my brain right now. It is building that meta harness and system internally — basically, find the bleeding edge of what the models can do and give them tools to augment how well they can do it. And then also internally working on the platform that Alex mentioned. Big goal there: diffuse these background agents and actually get them out to enterprises in a way that's truly, truly helpful to them.

Yeah. And solve a lot of those messy IT problems that we hit on earlier.

Dude, when you have some solutions, we take guest posts on the Latent Space blog. I'd love to welcome some sharing of knowledge. But otherwise, thank you so much for your time. And good to see you again in New York.

Yeah likewise. Appreciate it.

Once a year, once a year.

Hell yeah. Thank you.

item.description:
# 几个让我意外的隐秘模式
## 1. "泰勒主义的意外回归"——AI 偷偷完成了 100 年前管理学失败的任务
整段对话里埋着一句最反直觉的话："You can't automate a process that does not exist."（你无法自动化一个尚不存在的流程）
表面上这是关于 agent 部署的工程教训，但往深里看——**AI 时代正在悄悄完成弗雷德里克·泰勒（Frederick Taylor）在 1911 年没能彻底完成的事业**。整个 20 世纪，知识工作抗拒标准化：律师、分析师、顾问以"每个案子都不同"为由保护自己的黑箱手艺。而现在，当 40 个人用 40 种方法做同一件事，agent 就无法接管。于是企业被迫做它们一百年来都抵抗的事：先 Taylorize 自己，再让 AI 接手。
**跨领域连接**：这跟军队的"doctrine（作战条令）"是同构的——Tenex 的 meta harness（元框架）本质上是在为 AI 工程建立作战条令，让新兵一上场就能打出老兵的水准。换句话说，CJ 做的不是工具，是"参谋总部制度"的数字化翻版。
---

item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的观察：这期视频其实暴露了"马斯克帝国"在市场心智里的坍缩

你注意到了吗——整期视频反复说"Spacex 财报"，但聊的全是 Grok 模型、算力租赁、训练推理、Cursor 营收。这不是转录错误那么简单。这揭示了一个被忽略的结构性事实：xAI 在市场心智中已经和 SpaceX 发生了语义性融合，因为它们共享同一个核心变量——马斯克的"叙事发动机"。当一家公司（无论叫 xAI 还是 Colossus）的估值的 80% 来自 CEO 口头下的 ARR 指引，它事实上就已经从一家"算力公司"变成了"叙事期权"。更深的洞察是：马斯克的"非零概率"是一种贝叶斯锚定武器——视频主自己也捕捉到了，"非零概率 = 接近零的概率"。但市场并不交易概率，市场交易锚点。他把 10GW 抬到 13GW 再隐性抛出 20GW，是在以极低认知成本把整条分布曲线向右推——这是一种语言套利，和期权做市商放一张远虚值报价把 IV 拉高是同一套机制。

二、跨领域连接：算力短租市场 ≈ 2007 年的 VLCC 油轮市场

马斯克 all-in 短租、拒绝长约锁定、相信"智能/瓦"永远上升——这几乎是 2007 年希腊和挪威船东们的翻版剧本：John Fredriksen、George Economou 当年也坚信"BDI 永不下跌"，于是在波罗的海干散货指数 11000 点时疯狂下单 VLCC，用现金流最大化逻辑拒绝长约。结果是 2009 年 BDI 跌到 663 点，十年破产潮。结构性相似点有三：(1) 订货到交付的半年-两年前置期，使"看到价格下跌再停"物理上不可能；(2) 单一赛道极度资本密集，退出成本接近总投资；(3) 收入模型是短期现货敞口。视频主用了"芝士店全部卖光"的比喻来形容算力紧缺——这和 2007 年航运圈说"船坞三年内一只新 Suezmax 都排不进来"是一模一样的句式。真正的问题不是短租价格会不会跌，而是：当马斯克自己一个人就带着 13GW 入场，他本人就是在建造那条压垮自己价格的供给曲线。 他的"全押"策略，在博弈论上恰好会触发它所依赖的那个前提的瓦解。

三、被所有人忽略的一个数据裂缝：55/50 的自相矛盾

视频主一笔带过了一个细节——马斯克说未来 13GW 算力中内部/外部"55/50"分配，又说"也可能 40/60，也可能 60/40"。这不是口误，这是认知状态的直接外泄：他没有做过内部测算，他在直播中实时估算。但更惊人的是现状——目前 7B AI 营收里，Cursor（内部产品）只贡献 0.6B，也就是说当下的真实比例是 9:91 外部占优。他宣称未来会把一半算力留给内部，这意味着他相信 Grok+Cursor 在 15 个月内要翻 50 倍。这不是"ARR 翻 10 倍"那么简单——这是说内部需求必须翻近百倍才能撑起他自己给的分配比例。这个数据缝隙比估值泡沫更危险，因为它暗示马斯克要么在用虚高的内部需求为未来的供给过剩找借口（为短租价格崩盘铺叙事退路），要么他真的打算让 Grok 以 Anthropic 级的烈度训练——而后者意味着烧钱速度要再上一个数量级。

四、一个几乎没人提的 Netflix 盲点：注意力的"认知卡路里"重分配

视频主自己非常敏锐地提到了"中国 AI 视频"威胁，但管理层只字不提。这不是傲慢，是 Kodak 1998 年看数码相机时的那种"数据还没出现在报表里"的典型盲点。但真正的洞察不在"短视频/中视频/长视频"的分类上——分类是误导的。真正的变量是"每分钟认知卡路里"：Netflix 一小时剧集给用户的"情绪卡路里"是 X，TikTok 是 2X，AI 生成的个性化视频流可能是 5X。人类每天的"注意力代谢率"是恒定的（约 4-6 小时娱乐窗口），谁的"卡路里密度"高谁就胜出。跨领域连接：这和 1980 年代"精制碳水 vs 全谷物"的食品工业演化完全同构——高密度、低饱腹感的东西短期不可战胜，但长期会反噬整个消费心智。Netflix 当前 18 倍 PE 看似便宜，但如果"注意力卡路里竞赛"进入 AI 加速阶段，它的护城河——昂贵的工业化叙事——恰恰是最先被降维打击的部分。它不是输给对手，是输给了用户的多巴胺曲线。

五、GE 的隐藏身份：被所有人错标的"反石油对冲工具"

视频主提到了，但没点透：GE 的航空服务模式让它在油价上涨（航空公司减班）时仍然增长，在油价下跌时会超额增长。换言之，GE 已经被 silently rewired 成了一个负 beta 石油衍生品。这不是宏观意外，是业务模型的几何属性：引擎卖出的那一刻，GE 锁定了未来 20-30 年的服务现金流，而油价决定的只是"折现时间线的拉伸或压缩"——不是现金流本身。这给了我们一个被低估的组合构造启示：传统 60/40 组合里的"能源对冲"位置，可以用 GE 这类"订单积压型工业服务公司"替代，获得负相关性 + 复合增长的双重收益。这和 Danaher 用服务合约把自己变成"反周期 SaaS"是同一个 playbook，而市场仍在用传统工业股的 PEG 框架给它定价——这就是 33.7 倍前瞻市盈率看起来"略贵"但其实不贵的真正原因。

一、周二市场回顾

我先快速地回顾一下周二资产价格的走势。周一我没有录视频，整个市场出现了小幅的反弹，那周二是继续出现了小幅的反弹。纳指相对会弱一些，但随着美债收入率，特别是长债收入率这一块的一些下跌，TLT 的反弹，我们可以看到标普的等权指数相当的强，大多数的一些价值股的标的，在这一周，在过去的一周，都出现了比较好的这个反弹。

那么在周二的市场里边，银行板块也上涨了 1.4，公共事业 1.3，REITs 1.8，基本上所有和利率相关的一些价值股板块都出现了反弹。所以标普的等权指数上涨了 1.2%，其他科技股是下跌 0.4，那伴随着同时半导体板块也下跌了 0.4%。但整个市场如果从参与度这个角度去看的话，我相信纳指可能仍然是在减弱的，但是同时标普 500 应该是在扩张的。然后罗素 2000 在周二也出现了 1.7% 的这个反弹，所以罗素 2000 这个参与度和周一去做对比的话，应该也出现了比较好的反弹。

所以现在从三大指数去看的话，纳指仍然是相当的弱，然后排名倒数第二弱的或者排名正数第二，就是罗素 2000，相对最强的其实是标普。

二、GE 财报解读

2.1 整体业绩

那我们先来看一下 GE 的财报。GE 是在周二盘前所发布的财报。那财报本身从数据这个季度的数据或者对于明年的这个指引，GE 都非常的强。这一个季度超出了市场预期，EPS 超出市场预期 12% 至 13%，明年的这个营收指引要往上抬，整个 26 年的全年指引也往上抬。所以这一份财报本身从数据去看是非常好的一份财报。

2.2 油价逆风下的强劲基本面

那 GE 业务本身其实不会有太大的一些波动。主要是因为什么？我们从他们财报会里边来看一下。公司管理层有聊到：虽然各个航空公司的一个航班计划有可能会有所缩减——为什么？这段时间 GE 的格鲁什其实就是因为全球油价的这个上涨，油价的这个上涨使得航空公司的一个航班计划可能会有所缩减。但是我们确实看到了起飞架次的这个增长，其中第三季度还增长了 1%。

你知道 GE 在什么样的宏观环境下仍然实现了 EPS 的增速超市场的预期，然后明年也给了这个指引。也就是说，如果接下去油价出现任何放缓的话，GE 的这个财报本身，最后的结果只会比现在市场的预期给出的这个预期更加的好。

我记得在第一季度财报的时候，就是今年的 4 月份，当时正好是美伊战争开打的那时候，当时第一季度的财报超出了市场预期，但是没有上调全年的这个指引，就是因为油价所带来这个全球地缘政治所带来这个不确定性。而现在我们已经三个季度过去了，可以看到最后的结果，其实这个基本面仍然非常的强劲，就是在这样一个宏观逆风的这个情况下仍然做到了非常好，且明年的这个指引也给下来了。所以接下去只要有油价出现任何的一个反弹，对于 GE 在这一块，在 commercial 这一块的业务其实都是一个利好。

2.3 订单积压与服务模式

管理层有说到，从服务这个角度看，才是他们推动业务的一个核心。从 commercial 这一块主要是卖引擎和卖服务。引擎卖出去之后，卖出去一笔的这个引擎，伴随着是未来几乎是这一个引擎本身终身的一个服务。那么所以 GE 未来的这个增速全部是来自以前所卖出引擎的这个订单。那订单增长了 23%，那订单本身和未来这个营收是有非常强的这个正相关。

我们看右边部分：未来我们可能会受到这些压力——宏观的这些压力——但是从 GE 利航天业务这个角度去看，我们认为 2027 年的这个增长主要将会来自于现有的这些积压订单和航空公司已飞行的循环架次。

2.4 增速与估值

那在这样的一个背景下，我们来看一些数据。市场预期 26 年的营收增速 19%，公司管理层这次给了一个预期了，差不多在 20% 左右。27 年市场预期营收增速 11%，管理层也给了 low double digit，差不多是在 13、14 左右。那最终的结果高于 15% 我也不会感到意外，而且如果油价下跌情况下，可能这个营收的增速会更高。市场的预期，27、28 年就是平均下来差不多每年就在 10%，但实际上最后的一个结果，营收的这个增速可能就在 15% 左右。

所以我在，我记得上次我在聊 GE 的时候，我就认为我说市场对于 GE 未来这个营收增速是低估了，那所以对于他们 EPS 这块的增速也是低估了。

如果一家公司营收的增速每年 10%，那你基本上可以预计它的 operating income 的一个增速、运营利润的增速可能就在 14%、15%。那么假设这家公司有一个 operating、有一个运营效率在那边的话，在这个基础上，然后再做一些回购，那最终的 EPS 每年的这个增速可能就是停留在 16% 至 17% 左右。一家公司如果它的一个 bottom line 平均每年可以增加 15% 的话，五年翻一倍，其实也可以是一家算作是一家合格的增长公司。

而从 GE 这个角度，如果营收增速最终如果每年能够平衡在 15%，那最终的 EPS 这个增速应该是要 north of twenty，就应该是在 20% 以上了。那对于这类的公司，你去看一下它现在如果静态市盈率在 38 倍、39 倍左右，除以 20% 这个增速，那 PEG 在 2 倍。2 倍的 PEG 是相对来说是属于高的，但是 GE 本身所在的这个行业，我认为他们是应该有一个溢价在那边。

对，我们来看一下估值。这是 forward PE，向前看前瞻的这个市盈率。前瞻的市盈率在今天周二的这个收盘之后是在 33.7 倍。你可以看到在 24 年之前，它的 PE 相对会低一些，但是在 24 年的时候，他们进行拆分了，拆分完之后 GE 的这个 PE 最低的时候是 2025 年的 3 月份，当时跌到了 30 倍。那我个人认为一个合理的区间可能就是在 30 倍至 40 倍之间，如果去到 45 倍的话，可能相对会比较高一些。所以我认为现在 GE 的这个估值就是在一个非常合理的一个阶段。如果继续往下跌，接近于 30 倍，在 31 倍到 30 倍左右的话，那就是一个低估的一个区间。

三、Netflix 财报解读

3.1 盘后下跌与营收减速

然后我们来看一下奈飞。那奈飞盘后发布完财报之后，盘后出现了下跌。我看了一下它的财报，其实没有到那么的糟糕。那市场的一个担心很简单——那你从结果去出发的话，市场的一个担心就是他们第四季度这个营收增速将会持续放缓。

那这张图所显示的是奈飞在过去 6 个季度它的一个营收增速。基本上在 25 年底和 26 年初的时候都是在 16% 以上，然后今年的第二季度、第三季度连续下降，从 16% 连续下降到 12% 以上，和第四季度给的这个指引是在 11.5%。所以市场交易的一个逻辑性就是奈飞的这个营收增速持续放缓。

所以在财报会议里边，分析师问的是：你们在明年能不能保证你们的营收增速在 10% 以上，或者在两位数？

3.2 市场预期与估值分析

那我们来看一下市场的预期。2026 年现在马上还有一个季度就要结束了，现在市场预期是 13%，未来的两年市场预期是 11% 和 10%。所以市场的一个担心也不是说不是非常的合理，是合理的。24 年 16%，25 年也 16%，你 26 年一旦放缓到 13%，市场马上做一个线性外推，假设你 27 年是 11%，28 年变成 10%。

那我们假设，未来营收增速 10%，EPS 增速 15%，结合它静态市盈率 19.5 倍，差不多它 PEG 是在 1.3 倍左右。那 1.3 倍的 PEG 相对来说是比较低的。然后我们来看一下它的 forward PE 前瞻市盈率，周二的收盘是 18.35 倍。18.35 倍从历史长河去看其实是相对比较低的，即使在 22 年全部算进去的话，当时 22 年最低的时候是在 15 倍，稍微低于 15 倍一点点。那现在 18 倍其实离 15 倍并没有太远。

那么所以，现在奈飞的这个估值这个角度去看，无论是 PEG 也好，还是前瞻市盈率也好，都是相对比较低的。

3.3 定性风险：中国 AI 视频的长期威胁

市场对于他们美国这一块的业务稍微有一点点担心，管理层也有聊到了美国这一块的业务，他们能够做到更好。所以奈飞这次财报我并没有看到太多令人比较担心的，管理层也看到了美国业务可以做到更好。

唯一从长期、从定性这个角度去看的话，我比较担心的是最近这段时间中国 AI 所做的一些视频的一些兴起会抢了人们很多的一些眼球。而这些视频它也不是——它又不算是短视频，又不算是长视频。而且我们知道从短视频到现在的中视频，到未来 AI 所制作这些长视频，整个行业所发展的速度其实相当的快。

当然这些东西到他们最后能够影响到奈飞可能需要一段时间，在这一次财报会里面也从来没有人去聊这个点。那未来有可能，如果真的要会影响到奈飞的话，可能会从他们某一个季度的财报的数据里面所显现出来。

但是从短中期这个角度去看，市场的一个担心是他们在美国这一块的落地可能没有那么的好，Engagement 可能没有那么的好。那公司管理层也看到了，可能在今年第四季度、包括明年的话，试图去解决这个问题。所以我前面聊的这个定性角度上的一个风险，短时间之内应该还不会完全蔓延开来，或者体现到它那个财报里面。

四、SpaceX 财报深度解读

4.1 整体财报与市场反应

OK，最后我们来聊一下 Spacex 的一个财报。那这一次财报无论从任何一个角度去解读的话，都是非常好的一份财报。三个业务你可以看到营收分别是超出市场预期 24%、8%，和 AI 这一块超出市场预期 20%。总体三个业务全部加在一起，从 adjusted operating income 调整之后的一个运营利润一个角度去看，市场预期是 2.2 个 billion，最后的结果是 2.79 个 billion，超出市场预期 25%。

然后我们来看一下财报会，财报会才是这一次一个重点。老马在里面聊了很多一些令市场惊掉下巴的一些预测。当然了，市场盘后出现了一个上涨，我认为完全离不开的是整个市场的一个 setup——必须市场有一个悲观的 setup，然后这一次 Spacex 的财报出来之后，对于短期数据算力这一块的一个需求非常的强大，所给出这些展望才使得市场出现这个反弹。我认为 setup 在那边和这个财报本身是分不开的。你即使有这个财报，你没有这个 setup 的话，也不见得盘后一定会出现反弹，那因为当下市场对于半导体板块、对硬件板块确实非常的悲观。

4.2 13GW 算力与 20GW 数据中心的指引

好，所以我们一条一条来看。首先第一个，在上一个季度财报的时候，老马说到在 27 年的话，他会有 10 个 GW 算力的这个上限。那这一次老马又说到 13 个 GW，就算上接下去的一个季度加一起的话，到 27 年底会有 13 个 GW 的算力上限。

算力上限和数据中心是两个概念。他说有可能在 27 年底之前，我们会有 20 个 GW 的数据中心。所谓的 20 GW 的数据中心是不包括芯片的，包括芯片的话就是 13 个 GW 的算力的一个落地。所以 13 GW 的算力和 20 GW 的一个数据中心，两者是不冲突的。他所聊的 20 GW 的数据中心是：你把其他数据中心里面所有需要的一些东西全部上线，芯片先放在一边。为什么呢？因为既然整个行业都认为现在的电力本身非常地去难获得的话，那我先把数据中心建完，然后我先把电力弄完，弄完之后芯片本身可能不是那么的紧缺。

然后第三点，他说一个非零概率，我们明年将上线二十几万的算力——原本说 10 个 GW，现在变成 20 个 GW。当然他说一个非零概率，在我对于老马的一个理解里面，所谓的非零概率就是接近于零的这个概率。他只是给了一个非常 aspirational 的一个 goal，那非常令人就几乎难以做到，但是是一个目标，就你如果真的能够做到的话，那非常非常的夸张了。

所以这是第一部分：明年对于整个 27 年，包括最后一个季度，加上 27 年的一个指引在那边。

4.3 ARR 一万亿的夸张预测

然后照这样下去的话，他说到这个数据非常的夸张。他说 Spacex 的 ARR——就是年化的一个收入——在 27 年底能够达到 0.5 个 T 至 1 个 T，就 500 个 billion 至 1 个 T。

我今天在 X 上我做了一个算术：如果老马 ARR 能够做到一个 T 的话，一个 T 的 ARR 它基本上全是卖算力获得的。能够卖掉一个 T 的 ARR 全部卖算力，谁是他的客户？只能是两家模型公司是他的客户。两家模型公司如果是他们的客户，购买了一个 T 的算力的话，那即使我假设这两家模型公司的毛利润只有 50%——且不说他们现在的毛利润是在 80% 以上的，我不去做这个假设——假设他们的毛利润只有 50%，也就是一个 T 的营收对于 Spacex 来说，一个 T 的营收就接近于或者约等于，这两家模型公司全部加在一起会有两个 T 的营收，两个 T 的 ARR。

而现在他们的 ARR 是多少？50 个 B 加上 80 个 B，130 个 B，或者 0.13 个 T。0.13 个 T 到明年年底两个 T 的 ARR，它翻的一个营收不只要翻 10 倍以上了，这是非常非常夸张的一个预测。如果真的能够做到的话，那现在市场根本不存在任何的一个泡沫，因为这就告诉市场说 Anthropic 它的一个营收今年和上年比翻了 10 倍，然后明年和今年这个基础上再翻 10 倍，已经在那么大体量的情况下还能够翻十倍，这已经是非常非常夸张了。

4.4 内部营收结构与"NeoCloud 化"

然后 Spacex 的内部，刚刚过去这个季度 7 个 B、70 亿美金的 AI 营收，只有 0.6 个 B 是来自于 Cursor，也就是大部分的一些营收呢——超过 90% 的这个营收在 AI 这块的营收——全部是来自于卖算力。也就是现在 Spacex 基本上完全变成了一家建数据中心、买芯片、然后去卖芯片，它变成了一家 NeoCloud，超级巨大的一个 NeoCloud，你也可以说它是一个执行力非常非常强的一个 NeoCloud。

然后他们的 CFO 有说到，他期待未来会有更多的一些其他客户。那以现在这个价格，回报周期是小于一的，上一个季度也聊到了小于一年，现在仍然是小于一年。现在价格差不多是 30 至 50 美金 per watt。

4.5 55/50 内外部算力分配之谜

然后接下去一个问题：未来如何去分配这个算力？因为既然如果你未来到 27 年底你要建 13 个 GW 的算力的话，那 13 个 GW 你怎么去分配？你内部需要那么多的算力吗？

那老马说这个问题问得很好，但是老马说差不多 55/50 吧，内部和外部。我不相信这个背后的一个数据，这个 breakdown 是真实的。因为你想，现在它就不是 55/50——现在是多少？现在你想 0.6 营收啊，营收这一块 0.6 个 billion 来自于 Cursor，剩下的 6.4 个 billion 全部是来自于算力上的一个出租或者卖算力。那你怎么可能未来自己这个这个算力，你预期——除非你预期未来的 Cursor 这一块的落地会非常的好。不然的话，这 55/50 的外部和内部算力这个分配其实是不合理的。

从 Anthropic 这个角度去看是合理的，因为他们现在已经有了非常好的这个落地。当然有个前提是老马可以通过卖短期的这个算力来弥补或者来回补自己在 Cursor 这一块的训练、自己在 AI 模型、在 Grok 这一块的训练。这是可以实现的，因为确实短期这个算力现在非常的值钱。所以他有可能通过卖短期的算力来回补自己在训练这一块。模型公司差不多是这样，你只要砸算力下去，你只要在训练这一块砸钱下去，基本上都是会出结果的。

所以针对这个问题，老马的一个回答是 55 是外部和内部，但是从他这个回答的一个语气，我估计他现在是没有这方面的一个思考的，就是它是一个浮动的嘛。他之后也聊了，他说有可能 46/60，有可能 60/40，我现在还不知道。但他说为什么他这么去做——他说"智能/电力"（intelligence/power）是在增加的，就是每一个 power、每一个电力你所能够产生的智能是在增加的，而且未来只会越来越增加，因为模型随着模型越来越聪明之后，你的 Intelligence/Power 只会增加。所以我们决定只做短租市场。

4.6 All-in 短租市场的风险

那这一点和其他的所有的云厂商、星云也好、Hyperscaler 也好，完全是不一样的。同样，我今天也发了一条 X，我说这样去做，你的确短期之内可以最大化你的回报，你也可以最快时间去缩短你的回报周期，但是也必须要承担一个非常大的风险——你假设这一个短租市场的一个价格会持续上升，这其实是一个非常危险的做法。而且你投入这个数据中心的这个体量又那么的大。

那有些人可能会认为：哎，你可以停啊，一旦看到短租市场价格下跌，你可以停嘛。你停不下来的。你怎么停下来？你和英伟达这边的下单，你起码是提早半年就去英伟达那边下单了。然后比如说你在今天你看到了短租这一块的价格出现了下降，然后你把你半年之后的一个单可以停掉吗？停不了的。你必须要提前去下单的。整个现在整个数据中心这个建造里边，很多的这些 component，你早在半年前、一年之前就必须要去下这个订单，包括 HBM。

那所以只做短租市场这个决定本身，我认为风险是相当高的。你可以把 Spacex 理解为是整个市场里面的个超级贝塔，算力这一块的一个超级贝塔，就是压住短期这个算力只会往上，就只会单向上涨，而不会出现任何的一个调整。如果从这个角度去出发的话，你做短租市场、或者选做只做短租市场是最明智的这个决定。

那为什么呢？NeoCloud、为什么星云和大科技——大科技总有钱了吧，你可以说 NeoCloud 他们口袋没有那么的深，那么所以他们只能够用这些中长期订单来锁定未来这个订单、锁定未来这个现金流，然后可以去融资。但是大科技钱袋子够深了吧，大科技为什么不去做？或者大多数业务为什么还是做长租和短租？是因为整个行业会有周期的。

所以我个人认为在算力这一块，老马是出现了一个丰富的情况。而且如果他真的明年上线了 13 个 GW 的算力，而且这 13 个 GW 完全全部用来做短租市场的话，我相信也会把短租市场这个价格给往下压的，除非背后的这个需求真的非常的大，大过了你额外的这 13 个 GW 算力的落地。

4.7 算力紧缺的生动描述："芝士店全空"

好，那然后是一些行业里面所看到的一些现状，我认为这也挺好，这也形容了当下整个算力到底有多么的紧缺。

那老马说到：他说我们甚至和某些云厂商商量，牺牲自己一部分的推理去换训练。因为我们训练所需要的芯片和推理所需要的芯片是不一样的，我们拿一部分的推理芯片和你去换一些算力，算力用来干嘛？用来训练。所以这就说明当下那个市场——而云厂商告诉他们：我们没有，我们没有任何的一个多余的算力给你去做训练。这就说明当下那个市场对于算力有多么的紧缺。

而且他也把当下那个市场形容为是一个芝士商店，就是你去一家芝士商店卖芝士的——卖 cheese——然后你进去你说我要 Mozzarella，然后他说 Mozzarella 没有，你要不要其他的 goat cheese？然后 goat cheese 也没有，然后你要不要其他的？就基本上整个芝士商店里面所有种类的芝士全部被卖掉了。即使你可以妥协，Mozzarella 没有，我买一些其他的芝士——没有，全部卖完。

那老马说的，他说明年有可能 6 个月的回报周期也不是不可能。现在是小于一年，他说 6 个月就能够把现在这一波投资全部赚回来。

我不知道老马选择这么去做能不能够维持多久。但是如果明年他真的能够——我们假设从结果去出发——如果明年他真的能够去落地 13 个 GW 的算力的话，那一定代表从今年到明年年底，那一定代表整个市场从今年现在到明年年底这段时间里边，整个算力仍然是持续紧缺，就需求仍然是大大多于供给，这才会出现这个结果。不然的话，中间有任何需求出现一定程度的放缓，他绝对不可能去落地 13 个 GW，中间他一定会选择进行放缓。当然我说了，某种程度不是他愿意放缓就放缓的，因为背后你的订单必须是提前半年去定的。

4.8 与特斯拉合并问题

最后可能是从特斯拉的投资者也非常关心的一个问题，就是有人问到了，他说和特斯拉之间的这个合并你怎么看的？

老马说道，两家公司都成立了工作小组，他自己是不参与其中的，所以两个工作小组彼此之间会进行一个沟通。他说有人认为一定会合并，那我觉得可能过于自信了。为什么他认为可能过于自信了？他说因为特斯拉是必须要 50% 以上的投资者股权都同意，而不是投票的人里面 50%——是所有特斯拉 50% 以上的投资者都同意，最后特斯拉才有可能会和 SpaceX 之间进行合并。当然他说，如果你问我的话，我觉得是一个好主意。

4.9 总结

最后我们做一个总结：这一次 SpaceX 的财报，如果要去挑一个重点出来的话，老马对于当下短租市场的算力的一个需求进行了非常强的这个倍数，因为他选择拿 Spacex 去 all in 短租市场。

五、活动与直播预告

OK，今天的活动来自于 Seeking Alpha。第一个 Alpha Picks 量化选股策略 YTD 标普 14%，他们的这个策略本身 22.6%。那最近三个所挑选的个股回报还是不错的，都跑赢了市场。

差不多在 4 个月之前，他们推出了另外一个量化选股策略。那这个新的量化选股策略的所选的这些标的全部是集中在价值股身上，所以都会有一个收益率、都会有一个 yield 在那边。你可以看到这个投资组合平均收益率是 2.8%，那即使股价不上涨的话，每年也可以有 2.8% 的一个平均的利息和回报在那边。那在过去的四个月里面，他们所对标的这个指数上涨了 0.12%，而他们这个策略本身上涨了将近 10%，还是不错的。

前面我们第一个看到 AlphaPicks 的量化选股策略，现在正在有一个免费的试用期。如果首年订阅的话，可以立即节省 50 美金。如果对于这两个量化策略都感兴趣的话，现在有个 combo 的价格，原价是 998 美金一年，现在是 719 美金一年。

那最后要提醒一下大家，是在周三的晚上，在我的 APP 里边会有一个会员的直播，大家别忘了。

好，那今天这期内容就到这边。下期见。

item.description:
## 一、最意外的观察：这期视频其实暴露了"马斯克帝国"在市场心智里的坍缩
你注意到了吗——整期视频反复说"Spacex 财报"，但聊的全是 Grok 模型、算力租赁、训练推理、Cursor 营收。这不是转录错误那么简单。这揭示了一个被忽略的结构性事实：**xAI 在市场心智中已经和 SpaceX 发生了语义性融合**，因为它们共享同一个核心变量——马斯克的"叙事发动机"。当一家公司（无论叫 xAI 还是 Colossus）的估值的 80% 来自 CEO 口头下的 ARR 指引，它事实上就已经从一家"算力公司"变成了"叙事期权"。更深的洞察是：马斯克的"非零概率"是一种**贝叶斯锚定武器**——视频主自己也捕捉到了，"非零概率 = 接近零的概率"。但市场并不交易概率，市场交易锚点。他把 10GW 抬到 13GW 再隐性抛出 20GW，是在以极低认知成本把整条分布曲线向右推——这是一种**语言套利**，和期权做市商放一张远虚值报价把 IV 拉高是同一套机制。
## 二、跨领域连接：算力短租市场 ≈ 2007 年的 VLCC 油轮市场
马斯克 all-in 短租、拒绝长约锁定、相信"

item.title: [Mercatus Center] The Hayekian Triangle: James Buchanan and the Challenge of Self-Government
item.dc:creator: Mercatus Center
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

布坎南两篇文章背后的隐藏结构：一个意外的发现

一、这不是矛盾，是"创业者悖论"的政治学版本

表面上看，《自然人与人造人》（1979）和《害怕自由》（2005）像是乐观与悲观的分裂人格。但如果你把布坎南的另一篇文章《经济学家应该做什么》放在中间作为桥梁，你会突然看到一个被所有评论者都忽略的结构——

布坎南其实在描绘一个"创业者悖论"：越是具备"自我建构能力"的人，越会在面对不确定性时渴望"被托管"。

这不是分裂，这是同一枚硬币。能力越强，意识到的可能性空间越大；可能性空间越大，选择的焦虑就越深；焦虑越深，就越想把方向盘交出去。这就像硅谷创业者在IPO前夜疯狂寻找导师、冥想大师、"父亲型"投资人——不是因为他们不够强，恰恰因为他们"artifactual"（自我塑造）的能力让他们看到了太多可能的自己。

跨领域连接：这与心理学家Barry Schwartz的"选择悖论"（Paradox of Choice）结构完全同构，但走到了更深的政治层面。Schwartz告诉你：选择太多会让消费者瘫痪；布坎南则预言：选择太多会让公民投靠利维坦。超市里的果酱实验，放大到国家尺度，就是福利国家的扩张史。

二、一个让人意外的观察："害怕自由"其实是一种成功综合症

对话中Pete提到"19世纪末，自由主义西方达到了前所未有的自治、财富与和平——而恰恰在那一刻它最脆弱"。这句话值得停下来品味。

真正反直觉的洞察是：古典自由主义的失败不是因为它做得不够好，而是因为它做得太好。

当自由把绝大多数外部敌人——饥饿、瘟疫、暴政、短命——都击退之后，人类面对的最后一个敌人就剩下自己选择的后果。而这是最难承受的敌人。中世纪农民不需要"害怕自由"，因为他从未拥有过；他害怕的是领主、瘟疫和冬天。只有在那些敌人退场之后，"自由本身"才会变成需要害怕的东西。

这就解释了一个被所有政治学家都未能很好解释的现象：为什么福利国家不是在最贫困的时代诞生，而是在最富裕的时代扩张？ 为什么北欧——人类历史上最富、最健康、最平等的社会——同时也是家长制国家最强大的地方？

跨领域连接：这与神学家克尔凯郭尔《焦虑的概念》里的论断惊人一致——他说焦虑不是奴隶的情绪，而是自由人的情绪。亚当没有焦虑，是因为他还没有选择；只有当他被赋予"不吃那个苹果"的自由时，焦虑才诞生。布坎南在不自觉地重演克尔凯郭尔，只是把神学语言换成了公共财政语言。

三、被忽略的致命细节：教育是唯一能同时"扩大"和"驯服"artifactual nature的技术

对话里关于教育的那一段，看似离题，其实是整场讨论的秘密钥匙。

Buchanan说教育不是人力资本投资，也不是消费，而是"spending on becoming"（变成的开销）。Pete和Chris都在正面讨论这件事。但他们几乎错过了一个结构性的洞察：

教育是人类发明的唯一一种制度，它既让人更有能力自我塑造（因此扩大了"natural artifactual man"的可能性），又让人学会与这种能力共处的焦虑（因此可能免疫"afraid to be free"的诱惑）。

换句话说，教育是对冲布坎南两篇文章之间张力的那张唯一有效的保单。

这解释了为什么现代国家对教育有一种近乎病态的控制欲——不是因为它想生产工人（那是经济学的解释），而是因为国家与教育在争夺同一个灵魂的塑造权。国家希望你成为"afraid to be free"的那种人；真正的liberal arts education希望你成为"natural artifactual"的那种人。两者无法并存。

跨领域连接：这就是为什么极权主义政权——从斯巴达到苏联到朝鲜——总是优先改造教育而不是优先改造经济。改造经济能让你听话一个季度，改造教育能让你的孙子都听话。乔治·奥威尔在《1984》里让温斯顿最终"爱老大哥"，走的不是经济路径，是教育路径——改造他对2+2等于几的信念。

四、一个大胆预测

如果布坎南的框架是对的，那么AI时代会是"害怕自由"的终极加速器——因为AI第一次让"把方向盘交出去"从政治决定变成了日常微决策。你每天都在用ChatGPT选餐厅、写邮件、决定周末做什么。每一次微托管都在训练你的神经通路：选择是痛苦的，外包是舒服的。

二十年后，当有人提议把更大的决定——职业、伴侣、公民身份、投票——也外包给算法时，你不会抵抗。你的"artifactual"能力不会消失，但它会萎缩，像不用的肌肉。

布坎南在2005年担心的"害怕自由"，可能在2026年已经不是政治问题，而是UX（用户体验）问题。 利维坦这次不穿制服，它穿的是光滑的黑色玻璃。

📝 转录文本

The Hayekian Triangle: James Buchanan and the Challenge of Self-Government

开场：Hayek Program Podcast 介绍

You're listening to the Hayek program podcast. This podcast includes audio from lectures, interviews, and discussions from scholars and visitors of the FA Hayek program for advanced study in philosophy, politics, and economics at the Mercatus Center at George Mason University. To learn more about the Hayek program, visit hayek.mercatus.org. To learn about graduate student fellowship opportunities with the Mercatus Center at George Mason University for students at Mason as well as at universities across the globe, please visit students.mercatus.org.

一、主持引入与今日主题

Virgil Storr: Welcome. My name is Virgil Storr. I'm thrilled to be here again with my great friends, colleagues, co-authors Chris Coyne and Pete Boettke. This is a part of a series of conversations that we're going to be having about political economy and social philosophy.

Today, what I want to talk about is I want to talk about James Buchanan. And specifically, I want to talk about his arguments about human nature and the uses that we as humans might make of freedom. And in particular, I want to talk about these two essays of Buchanan that seem to maybe be arguing different things, maybe be arguing different sides of the same coin, maybe be completely and wholly contradictory — his article "Natural and Artifactual Man" from 1979 and his later article, "Afraid to be Free."

But before we jump into that, Pete, I wonder if you could tell us a little bit about Jim Buchanan's biography. Who was he? What is he known for? Maybe importantly for this conversation, why should we even care what he thinks about liberty?

二、布坎南小传：从田纳西到诺贝尔奖

Pete Boettke: Yeah, great. Thank you. And thanks again for putting this on and being here with you, Virgil. I look forward to these conversations all the time.

So the first thing is just the basic facts. Jim Buchanan was born in 1919 in Tennessee. He's educated at Middle Tennessee State and then the University of Tennessee. He then goes to war in World War II where he's in the Navy in the Pacific, and when he comes back he goes to University of Chicago where he studies with Frank Knight — and I should point out a very young assistant professor Milton Friedman who teaches him one of his price theory courses as well.

He later goes on and wins a Nobel Prize in economics in 1986 for his development of the field of public choice and constitutional political economy.

布坎南的核心主张：政治经济学的再统一

And if I can, I'd just like to maybe drill a little bit into that and try to be as quick as I can. His core claim was that you cannot do public finance without postulating a theory of the state. In other words, you can't do economics without also doing political theory, because you actually have to decide on the right and wrong of compulsion by the state in order to then understand what it is that you're financing in the first place.

The flip side of that is also true: you cannot do political theory without a theory of public finance, because you have to figure out how are you going to produce these goods, for whom are you going to produce those goods, and who's going to pay for them.

So Buchanan is reuniting economics and political philosophy at a time when they had been pushed apart. And so that's why the importance of the constitutional political economy agenda that he does.

I would argue that Buchanan, both analytically and methodologically, he might be the person most responsible for the resurrection in the second half of the 20th century for a return to political economy as understood by the great practitioners from Adam Smith to John Stuart Mill. So related to our earlier conversation about Adam Smith, it's legitimate to maybe argue Hayek is the modern Adam Smith of our day, but within the professional discourse, I think Buchanan had the greatest impact in terms of getting economists — technical economists — to recognize again this link between political economy and social philosophy.

三、Virgil 的追问：自由关切能否与技术经济学分离？

Virgil Storr: You know what I find interesting and maybe controversial about the way that you framed his work is that concerns about liberty are throughout — including in his sort of more technical economics — that you sort of have to be mindful of liberty concerns. And so I think that's interesting.

And it maybe raises the question: can we economists divorce these concerns about liberty from what we do in our sort of day-to-day economic analysis? And so that's an interesting hopefully we get to that later as well.

But what I want to do is — Buchanan, as I mentioned, had these two pieces on human nature essentially that I want to put in conversation today: the "Natural and Artifactual Man" piece and the "Afraid to be Free" piece. And Chris, I want to ask you for your interpretations later, because much of this is going to be about our reactions to those pieces. But to just start us off, could you just summarize those two pieces really quickly? Just a few sentences on each.

四、Chris 的两篇摘要：可能性 vs. 脆弱性

Chris Coyne: Sure. So cliffnotes version, as you said, we'll dive into the nuances of this.

"Natural and Artifactual Man"（1979）

In "Natural and Artifactual Man," the core argument I would say is that what Buchanan says is: look, people are, at least in part, self-creating beings. That is, we don't only act on what he calls the natural aspects of ourselves — those are given preferences or dispositions that we already possess. But there's an artifactual aspect, and that artifactual aspect is that we have some scope for agency to shape our preferences, our character, our identity through time.

And so Buchanan in that article, which we'll delve into, is pointing out — among other things, by making this distinction — that his fellow economists, to his way of thinking, have overemphasized the natural aspects of human beings while underemphasizing, or completely neglecting perhaps, the artifactual aspects.

"Afraid to be Free"（2005）

So then we shift to "Afraid to be Free." Perhaps the way to think about "Afraid to be Free" at a high level is: an exploration of the other side, or another aspect of that self-creating capacity — which is that because we have agency and the ability to be self-directing to some degree, there's also responsibility tied to that. There is also uncertainty tied to that.

And in that essay, Buchanan points out that because of those things — because of the uncertainty, because of the responsibility tied to the artifactual aspects of our being — people might decide to surrender some of that freedom to the state for promises of protection, care, and so on.

一句话总结

So one line to sum these up: one way to think about the first essay, the "Natural and Artifactual Man" essay, is on human possibility. The way we might think about the second essay, "Afraid to be Free," is human vulnerability and the implications of what that means.

五、Pete 的补充：可能性 vs. 脆弱性 vs. 人类弱点

Pete Boettke: I assume that we're going to get into some of the nuances of the implications for the way we do things in economics that's related to that. But I thought that was a really nice summary and I really like this last point that he just made about the difference between possibilities and vulnerabilities.

To tell you where I'm coming from: when I first heard Chris say that line, my anticipation was he was going to talk about human frailties — rather than human possibilities versus human frailties. And I think that might reflect that I'm a less caring person than Chris, because I'm talking about the fact that dependence as desideratum is an implication of our failure rather than our vulnerability. But that's okay.

六、乐观与悲观：同一个布坎南如何写出两篇？

Virgil Storr: So, this is — I do, even in the way that Chris framed it, and I think he did a really good job of bringing them together — there's a couple of things even in what he said that feel like they're pushing us in different directions.

There seems to be possibility talk and capacity talk that's all a part of the natural motif of the natural man essay. There seems to be limiting talk and sort of inability talk that's a part of the "Afraid to be Free" essay. One seems optimistic and one seems pessimistic about who we are and how we feel about the world.

And so I guess I'm curious about: how did the same person write both of these essays? And I guess I'm going to offer a couple of possibilities and ask you to react to them.

假设：理想主义的布坎南 vs. 现实主义的布坎南？

One possibility is that "Natural and Artifactual Man" is Buchanan in his idealistic moment, and he's sort of imagining who human beings can be — a really hopeful thing, because it's his Shakespearean-man-in-his-infinite-nature type speak. And "Afraid to be Free" is just realistic — it's who we are in the muck when faced with "oh my goodness, I have to be responsible for my actions, I'm just going to turn it over to the state."

Is that the right way to think about it? One's Buchanan optimistic/idealistic, one's Buchanan realistic?

七、Pete：时代背景、Katrina 项目与"父母式社会主义"

Pete Boettke: I think it's important to remember the timing of the essays and the context.

时代背景

One of them — the second one, "Afraid to be Free" — is published in 2005. It comes on the heels of 9/11, it comes on the heels of the failure of the post-communist period to generate the kind of outcome that we all were optimistic about in 1989 and 1992. Whereas in the first one, that's published in 1979, the context is important here because his original ruminations begin with a referee report to the American Economic Review of the De Gustibus paper by Becker and Stigler.

So a large part of what Buchanan is doing technically there is he's trying to argue that our economics has to deal with real choice, not with this mechanical notion of choice — if we're going to recognize that, then it has all these other implications which open us up to the field of entrepreneurship, to the field of discovery, the field of what you call possibilities and opportunities.

两种解读的联结

One is an optimistic reading of what could happen if we opened our space up to the idea that we are the ones who create the rules under which we operate. So not only are we the entrepreneurs over our material life, but we're the entrepreneurs over the rules of the game. So that's the constitutional moment. So I have to be this artifactual man — man wants liberty to become the man he wants to become. As Chris said, it's this self-architecture issue.

But then in the second one, we've had an opportunity for self-architecture. And it's obvious that we're not going to turn back to managerial socialism — that's dead. And we all get annoyed by paternalistic socialism — socialism telling me I can't smoke, socialism telling me I can't drink. We don't like that. But it turns out we really, really like parental socialism. We want to be protected. We want to be — as Chris put it nicely — we want to be guarded against our vulnerable selves. And it turns out that that's the thing that's going to prevent us from achieving the promise that was laid out in the first one.

Katrina 项目的智识动因

If I could say one other thing, Virgil — this actually might be very relevant — it's actually an aspect of these papers [that] became one of the motivators for the Katrina project, and why it is that we originally set it up the way that we did (which failed because you couldn't do the experiment). We were going to look at Biloxi, Mississippi, and New Orleans and then try to look at the way in which they both responded to the storm. But the storm of course hit Biloxi different than it hit New Orleans. And so that changes the whole dynamics of that.

But a large part of this was the idea of the civil society that we wanted to see as vibrant and responsive to our most desperate situations and the act of recreating themselves in the wake of that — that was really motivated by the first essay. And then the fear that the argument in the second essay would block the ability to achieve that. And that's really the intellectual motivating force behind that original — I mean, it got lost, not in a bad way, but we moved beyond it in so many different ways — but that was the original thing going on in my head back in 2005.

八、Virgil：日常生活的英雄与两篇文章的张力

Virgil Storr: Yeah, I think that seems right. One of the fantastic things about that project and the people we ended up interviewing as a part of that project — it clued me in in a way that I hadn't before to the heroes of everyday life, right? The amazing capacities of people — faced with something that difficult — to reshape who they are, reshape what's going on, and even reshape their communities.

But I want to return to this, and Chris, I want to ask you to react to something that Pete said.

布坎南是否"改变了主意"？

One way to take what he's saying about "Buchanan recognized that we really liked having the state as parent — we really liked being protected" is to say Buchanan recognized that what he said in "Natural and Artifactual Man" was just wrong: that we don't want liberty to become the people we want to become; we want protection so that we don't have to face the vagaries and challenges of life.

So is that the right way to understand the relationship between the two essays — that Buchanan just changed his mind, or recognized that he was incorrect?

九、Chris：条件、"保险者"的来源与依赖的张力

Chris Coyne: Yeah, I don't know what Buchanan would say to that. You've certainly identified a tension.

One way to read it is that the line at the end of "Natural and Artifactual Man" about liberty is — it's an attempt to be punchy and maybe too cute in a way (I don't mean that in a derogatory way; I like it — it's in italics of course to emphasize it as well, that last line about man wanting liberty). But maybe it's "sometimes they want liberty," or maybe not very often. Or maybe we need to unpack under what conditions people want liberty versus when they don't.

作为互补的两篇文章

So one way to view the two essays — if we want to view them as complements — is to view the latter as perhaps identifying, or pushing us at least to identify, the conditions under which maybe people do or don't want liberty.

Of course, Pete pointed us to the constitutional aspects. The other really — and this gets at the Katrina point — one of the other fascinating aspects to link the two together is: given people's desire or concern or desire for some kind of insulation from vulnerabilities, what's the source of that insulation? The state can be one, of course; that's not the only one. As you pointed out in your own work, and others in our network have pointed out, civil society can be a very rich insulator from the vagaries of life — a family, community. All of these alternatives are rich ways of thinking about it.

恐怖主义与依赖性：一个耐人寻味的张力

But there's all these tensions that run throughout this. Real quick, I'll highlight one and then we can move on and return to it if we want. At the end of "Afraid to be Free," as Pete said, he's talking about post-9/11. So terrorism he brings up repeatedly throughout this essay.

Well, I don't know if you caught it — at the end when I was rereading it last night, in the postscript for "Afraid to be Free," he says: "look, terrorism automatically puts citizens in a relationship of dependency to the state." That's kind of fascinating. Let's replace the word dependency with the protective state, which includes security. So then the protective state, which Buchanan viewed elsewhere as kind of protecting people's fundamental rights — if I'm reading this correctly — at least threatens, if not automatically puts people in a state of dependency as it pertains to the state. So then how do you deal with that?

So there's these fascinating tensions to unpack, which to my way of thinking is the research program — or the forward-looking research program — in constitutional political economy.

十、Virgil 的坦白：两篇文章交替吸引的心境

Virgil Storr: I want to confess — we've talked quite a bit about what maybe Buchanan meant, and I want to push us for the rest of this conversation to maybe speak to what we think is right about human nature and its relationship to liberty. And maybe one way to do that is to react to some of what Buchanan said and then get our own perspectives on it.

I'll confess, cards on the table, that I find both these essays appealing — but never at the same time. When I'm in a certain sort of mood with a certain kind of optimism about the world — when I'm talking to disaster survivors and hearing the amazing heroic things that they're doing, when I'm looking out at the world and seeing possibility — the "Natural and Artifactual Man" essay becomes appealing to me and interesting to me.

And when I'm annoyed at the growth of government, or I turn on the news and bombs are flying left, right, and center, or we're trying to tariff our way to prosperity in some strange or peculiar way — I start thinking, yeah, maybe the "Afraid to be Free" thing is right, and that's the key.

So maybe that's something about me, maybe it's something about the essays, maybe it's something about their compatibility — but I want to get us to unpack some of this in detail.

关键引文一

As I said, one way to maybe do that: I'm going to read a series of his passages and try to get our reactions. We can just take them in turn. I'll start with Pete and then Chris, and we can go back and forth.

In "Natural and Artifactual Man," he says the following:

"We are and will be at least in part that which we make ourselves to be."

So this is his self-architecture point that Chris was getting at earlier — that we construct our own beings within limits.

"We are artifactual as much like the pottery shards that archaeologists dig up as like animals whose fossils they also find."

I want to just react to that: is that really an important aspect of our human nature in your view? And is maybe what he's getting at in "Afraid to be Free" that we don't quite trust ourselves with that — in particular, that we recognize that we can make ourselves, but we're not confident that we'll make ourselves correctly?

十一、Pete：真正的选择、经济学的"精神分裂"与奈特的"假装直到做到"

Pete Boettke: So, this is perfect, because I actually wanted us to talk about maybe the implications of some of this stuff for the way we think about economics. Because I think that that's always in the background here.

经济学的"精神分裂"

Buchanan of course had this little bit of schizophrenia in the way he thought about economics, because he would say that if men were like rats, then all of the sort of modern neoclassical apparatus just falls right out of it. But if instead men were these creative creatures, then it's going to be modified — neoclassical economics will have to be modified. That's a major point about what's going on there.

He tries to find these roots in Knight, because in the "Natural and Artifactual Man" the Knightian position is that we fake it until we make it. So we're these aspiring people who want to be different in time t1 than we are in time t0. And so therefore we have to go about trying to do something which we in fact may not yet be able to do. We're trying to acquire those senses, tastes, sensibilities — whatever — to be something different. And he wants to give that aspect a critical part.
