市场作为开放式选择的过程

The reason why I think that's the case is because he wants to see the market as this ongoing process of exchange. And so this is another essay that you could link in here is "What Should Economists Do?" How do "What Should Economists Do?"'s arguments feed into these two arguments?

What he argues in "What Should Economists Do?" is: no fixed utility functions. Decision science is not economics. It doesn't say decision science isn't a science — says it's just not economics. Economics is about open-ended genuine choice. Open-ended genuine choice leads to exchange relationships. And then the contrast is the way in which we model or think about exchange relationships in markets versus in politics.

艺匠人 vs. 政治中的"流氓"

And what's fascinating is that Buchanan takes the Humean dictum in politics — which is really saying men are like rats, which is the idea that men are knaves. So in economics, he sees men as artifactual men, these self-architects, these individuals who recognize and deal with the agony of choice and are trying to fake-it-until-they-make-it. Whereas in the other one, the political actors are going to be very predictable — they're knaves; all men are knaves.

And I think it's because of the different purposes that he has in those two different realms of what he's trying to explore. Yeah. And I think that's fascinating.

十二、Virgil：规则与策略——"流氓"假设的用武之地

Virgil Storr: Well, it's fascinating. But can you hold both positions? Can you both say: in our private lives, we're not merely in the business of maximizing utility — we have these greater purposes and goals, we're trying to move towards them, so you can't really neatly use revealed preference to indicate something about what our intentions are, because we're in this process of growth that may or may not be successful, and that's sort of who we are at our core.

And then we go into the voter's booth, or we become somebody in public policy, or we join an administration at some local, state, or federal level, and all of a sudden we become narrow profit-maximizing people with no aspiration, no higher purpose, no goal, just like — can you hold both those? Does that even make sense to have both?

十三、Pete：规则 vs. 规则内的策略；尤利西斯与自缚于桅杆

Pete Boettke: So I think the way there's a reconciliation possibility — and I think it's in the issue of the difference between rules and strategies within rules.

规则层面：抱负与善；策略层面：机会主义与傲慢

When we're talking about what are the good rules, we are talking about issues about what we aspire, what we think is good or whatever. But then the question is: what are the strategies that are pursued once those rules are set up?

And I think this is where Chris's actual term — vulnerability — matters. Because if we are opportunistic (with guile — that would be the knavery aspect), and that can come in terms of opportunism or arrogance if you take Smith and Hume and put them together — so if a rule system that we set up is subject to vulnerability to those human frailties, opportunism or arrogance...

《奥德赛》的教训

Right now we're in the context of the summer of 2026 — on everyone's mind is the Odyssey. What's going on in the Odyssey? What is the human frailty that's being exposed in that tale of Odysseus? I was taught way back when that what it is is the gods are punishing Odysseus for his hubris.

We recognized from the beginning that Odysseus is the most cunning of all warriors. He's able to out-trick everyone. But then what happens is his arrogance — from being the most cunning warrior — runs into the gods, and he hits the gods, and so then the gods toy around with him for a decade, putting him through this challenge or that challenge.

Sometimes his cunningness is amazing — which is the symbol of constitutional political economy: Ulysses tied to the mast. Other times, when he defeats the Cyclops and he tells the Cyclops his name — Poseidon is going to then condemn him. And so it's this kind of interesting thing about our vulnerabilities.

布坎南的综合尝试

And I think Buchanan is trying to wrestle with that analytically: how is it that we solve these classic questions in political philosophy — from Hobbes to Rousseau to whoever you're talking about? How do I use that with the tools that I've been given by modern economics?

And it's this wrestling, I think, that allows him to maybe at least suggest to you there's a way to square a circle. At least that's what I would say.

十四、Chris：公共选择与两种解读

Virgil Storr: Chris, are you convinced by the circle?

Chris Coyne: In part, I certainly am. I think it opens up an array of interesting possibilities — and this is where perhaps more traditional public choice comes into play.

自然人造人的最后一句话："man wanting liberty"

Look, I said before about the last line of "Natural and Artifactual Man" perhaps being too cute, but maybe it's not. If we just take it in isolation — that article — and we take what Pete was saying earlier about kind of engaging his fellow economists, then it's a good line. Because what Buchanan there is saying perhaps is something like: look, people don't want liberty just for free exchange and free trade (even though that's great in order to allocate resources to their highest-valued uses, if it's some kind of optimization problem). There is the allocation and reallocation of resources, but there's something deeper as well. So it's a richer conception of the benefits of freedom in terms of people reaching — or engaging in the process of — self-actualization and discovery, and so on.

"Afraid to be Free"的多种理解

But then coming to this point on "Afraid to be Free": one could perhaps argue, look, people turn to the state (as he's arguing there) because of fear of responsibility and uncertainty — but that presumes that the state's going to give you those things. So that's one possibility. Another possibility is: the state is the source of those things. Another possibility is that even if it gives you the security and certainty on certain margins, on other margins it undermines your individual agency, and perhaps people misrepresent the costs.

Now we might come back and say — well look, if people in private settings are able to engage in this process of self-experimentation, why doesn't political office make people noble and good? Because don't they engage in the same process there? And they might; we can't rule that out. If anything, it might check our thinking. But then we have to have an argument for why that setting does that versus leads people to engage in the kind of opportunism that Pete pointed out. And there, that's where I think then we need to focus on comparative institutional analysis.

十五、关键引文二：教育作为"becoming"

Virgil Storr: I like this conversation, but I want to move to something else that he says in "Natural and Artifactual Man" that is quite relevant for us who are engaged in the education business. Because there he makes a case for education that I take to be quite a novel one — or at least one that may have not been novel to Buchanan but we make less and less now.

He says in that article:

"A good part of education can be modeled appropriately neither as capital investment nor as consumption of final services... Instead, it must somehow be modeled as spending on becoming. We do not educate children primarily to produce income streams or even utility streams. We educate them to make them over into 'better' persons, better and different from those that they would be without the educational process."

问题：教育的目的是什么？

There's a lot of talk today about the return on investment to education — much of the pushback on, say, higher ed is: does it have the returns that it ought to have to justify the outlays? There are even pushes in certain places to say we're not going to support educational programs that don't produce people who can earn a salary above a certain amount. So it's entirely about the point of getting this thing so that you can earn more money.

So Buchanan seems to be saying something different — seems to be saying the purpose of education is transformation, that it's not human capital, it's to make our kids better kids. Is it? So is that what Buchanan's saying? Seems to be what he's saying — but is that what he's saying? And if so, is he right?

十六、Pete：Smith 作为道德教育家与品味的培育

Pete Boettke: So if I can take a stab at this — this is a really great question. First of all, I agree with him 100%, because I myself am a product of a transformative educational experience. Totally changed my trajectory — I became something totally different. And I always was hoping that for my own kids as well. I wanted them to be exposed to teachers that were truly transformative and could move them, or coaches that could be truly transformative in this idea. So my view of education is broader than just necessarily classroom kind of things.

Bree Wolfe 与"自由主义品味"

Recently I had a conversation with a colleague of ours — former fellow and now works with us on our various different programs, Bree Wolfe — and talking to her about Adam Smith and liberalism, and her use of the term "taste" is quite interesting. She doesn't use the term "sensibilities" or anything like that — she talks about liberal tastes.

I think this is important for going back to the original issue — that relates to the review of the De Gustibus article. Because what Buchanan is arguing is that in that argument there's no disputing tastes, and Buchanan's argument is that we actually have to talk about the cultivation of taste — in some sense he doesn't use that term, but that's what he means by the artifactual man becoming something other than what they are. They're developing new and interesting tastes, and education is about that.

Adam Smith 作为道德教育家

Adam Smith, in many ways, if you think about the Moral Sentiments, he's a moral educator — he's just not a moral scholar. He's a moral educator. He's trying to communicate to people about how to live a better life. And you have to cultivate certain things to live that better life — paying attention to the man inside the breast and all these other things that he invokes.

自由技艺教育的被低估价值

So I would say that we miss those aspects of education when we think of it in terms of skill training, signaling, or even the networking aspects — those are the three that we normally look at. But what we miss in this whole idea is: how it is that maybe education is what is preparing us to be able to be something other than what we are.

Which might mean why classic liberal arts education is actually higher valued than anyone's giving it credit for at the moment, precisely because it helps develop enough of the tastes and sensibilities that you're able to adapt and adjust to whatever changing circumstances may exist in the world. Today you need to learn how to think in order to be able to learn what to know. These tools of teaching us that are truly transformative. So I'm a big believer in education.

十七、Virgil 的个人见证：从马克思主义者到自由市场支持者

Virgil Storr: So, Chris, I want to ask you a question in a little bit, but I wonder — there's something interesting about how you talked about it and how Buchanan talks about it: it puts parents in a pretty challenging position. Because it means if the thing is truly transformative, it means me, as a parent, I don't know how my children are going to turn out. I'm investing in a process that's going to change them without really being able to say "oh, my kid might come back and they may have views or values or beliefs that are contradictory to what I believe because they've been through a transformative process."

一个教师改变了我

Both of you know this, but when I went to Beloit College, I was a Marxist. I believed at the time that markets were wholly and totally exploitative, and that working in a market system was going to be alienating, and that if we wanted to move beyond exploitation and alienation we needed to essentially get rid of the market system.

I left my undergraduate — because of a teacher, Emily Chamblee-Wright — I left with the entirely opposite view: that in fact, as I say in one of my recent books, markets are in fact not only spaces where we can improve our lives, but that they're spaces where we can become better people. And so they're not exploitative or alienating; in fact, it's the reverse.

I couldn't have predicted that when I went to college. And potentially, if you told me that would happen before I went to college, I might have said "I'm not going to college — this is wholly problematic." But ex post, in my own eyes, I think I'm better off.

学生与家长的处境

So Chris, this is the question I want to ask you: if in fact education does what Pete says it does, what Buchanan seems to be saying it does — what kind of position does that put the student in before they engage in an educational process? And what kind of position does that put, say, the parent in before they engage in that educational process? And does that have anything to do with why maybe people are uncomfortable with education?

十八、Chris：共同生产、"更好"的定义权与国家的进入

Chris Coyne: Testing my parenting skills here. I don't know what I'm talking about or what I'm doing on a daily basis as a parent.

"更好"为什么要加引号

You know, I think it's important to put — the word "better" has been used a lot here, and it's in the quote too — you held up your hands to indicate the quotes, but people may be listening to this — in the Buchanan quote when he says "we educate them to make them over into 'better' persons, better and different from those they would be without the educational process," "better" is in quotes. And I think that's intentional. And it's a very Buchanan point, which is that it makes them better, but there's no "better" out there that we know. It's not something that we know. Or perhaps another very Buchanan insight that I know — I know for you what you should do.

对家长和学生意味着什么

So this leads to your question: what does it require? Well, as I jokingly said — but I actually believe, I'm not quite sure as on the parental side — but I imagine it might mean something like a broader sense of education for your kids beyond what is viewed as traditional, textbook, or institutionalized education.

For the student, it might mean something like a commitment to co-production, broadly understood. In plain English, they have to want to learn stuff and be open to it, or it's going to be miserable for them. They won't have either passion, willingness, or desire to be a participant in that process of discovery.

多样性与一刀切

And so then what does that mean? Then that might mean we start to think about education — I know you mentioned higher ed, which is one important manifestation of it, but it's something broader than that — but also we think about it in terms of being a diverse and context-specific portfolio of activities and settings that are dependent at least in part on the person, rather than a one-size-fits-all.

当国家进入时

So then this gets us back to the state and "Afraid to be Free" — which is when you turn to the experts. Because then there's different views on this, like: who gets to define "better"? That's another interesting thing. Do parents get to define it? Does the child get to define it? Does society get to define it? And then when society gets to define it, is that some equivalent of the Department of Education, because they're the experts after all?

But when you turn over that decision-making to the state — whether you are confident or not that they know it better — that comes with certain costs. One of them is that it's going to crowd out other forms of education that we may not even realize. Another is that it's going to tend to lead to all the standard predictions of public choice when it comes to bureaucracy. So rather than focusing on "well, we don't know what that should look like at the end" — well, we're going to know what it's going to look like because we need to measure it somehow. We need to be able to gauge success or failure, and to do that we need observable outcomes and we need to homogenize people into clean categories.

And then we get into some fascinating questions about what imposing those top-down bureaucratic processes and structures onto education looks like and what that means in terms of crowding out the kind of stuff Buchanan's getting us to think about.

十九、Pete：教育被承认具有转化性，只是转化方向之争

Pete Boettke: If I can just follow up on that as well — I think that you're exactly right, Virgil. Another part of this discourse and disappointment is not just the ROI, but actually an admission that education is transformative. They just don't like what people are being transformed into.

单一文化的危险

And so at one level it makes it kind of complicated for us because we also are advocates for transformative education, but we don't want to impose that through the aid of the state. We simply want to win arguments in our science and in our persuasive techniques, because we're trying to avoid having a monoculture.

So part of the issue — and I know we disagree a little bit about this — is whether or not modern academics reflects a monoculture, and whether or not that monoculture was generated by in fact the massive involvement of the state in higher ed and therefore the homogenization — and all the things that Chris is talking about — and it just happens that a certain set of ideas captured the definition of those things and then imposes it, makes others look silly; or if this was a bottom-up natural evolution, the more persuasive argument won out over the other ones.

凯恩斯主义的霸权

If we think in economics — I tend to be myopic in some sense, so I think in economics — I tend to think about how the hell did the Keynesian revolution get orchestrated and take off such that it totally transformed education and economics from 1950 all the way up until the 1980s? It dominated one particular approach, and there wasn't the kind of diversity of ideas, the bouncing off, the challenging of those ideas.

How did that all come about? Was it because Keynesianism was just a superior way of thinking about it, or was it actually just simply it became the monoculture because after the war we ended up having more and more people go to school in the 1960s, and everyone wanted to see economics as a tool of social control, not a tool of social criticism or social understanding?

So the Smithian way had to go out, the Samuelsonian way had to come in. And it's all these kinds of things that go on. And so yes, it was still transformative — but what it transformed us into was thinking economics as a tool of social control.

So therefore, it's important for us to battle what it is that's being taught as a transformative notion. Which is why it is we care so much about ideas and curricula and programs and all that stuff — because we're trying to — why is it that we're in the business of creating the next generation's professors? We want them to be change agents — but not just change agents to change them into the current things, because we disagree with the status quo. We want them to challenge the status quo and be change agents of that. Methodologically, analytically, and social-philosophically.

二十、Virgil：转化 vs. 编程——谁来做判断？

Virgil Storr: Yeah. So there's a — both of y'all said a couple things that I want to react to, and maybe I'm in this space of why I'm wanting to dwell on this a little bit longer.

Chris's answer was way less rent-seeking than an answer from a college professor ought to have been, in the sense that it sort of opened the door for varieties of educational alternative strategies, all these sorts of things. And so I kind of do want to push you a little bit on that — in particular this notion about linking it to this notion about transformation.

徒弟式学习 vs. 课堂讨论

Yes, surely being an apprentice to a master plumber or master builder of some sort is going to gain you a certain set of skills, and you might yourself one day, through practice, become a master builder or master plumber. But is that the kind of process that's going to truly transform who you are as a person, and your thinking around life, liberty, and those kinds of deep fundamental questions?

Or do you need — is there a way to have that happen absent your reading, your writing, your discussing, your being challenged, your being pushed, your having to push and push back — the kinds of things that actually happen in the classroom?

转化还是编程？

So that's a question for you, Pete — to your question about people maybe don't like what folks are being transformed into, and your talk about the monoculture, which suggests that what's happening is less transformation and maybe more programming in some spaces.

I guess I'm curious about how we can know whether programming is happening or whether transformation is happening — and who's the best judge of that, given the epistemic humility that Buchanan pushes for.

You'd think our answer would be something like: well, only the student at the end of the process can decide if they were programmed or if they became a different person. And so the judge would be their satisfaction with what happened to them in college or in school. Is that the right criterion, or is there some other external criterion that we can bring to bear that lets us know transformation happened versus programming happened?

So Chris, I'll ask you to go first and then Pete.

二十一、Chris：没有外部标准，只有过滤机制的属性

Chris Coyne: Your point's well taken. Certainly an apprenticeship, whether it's plumbing or whatever else, is going to give someone a different set of experiences, a different framing, a different education if you will, than sitting in a classroom reading the great books in a Socratic dialogue.

布坎南不提供评价标准

But here's the thing: I don't think Buchanan — certainly not in these papers, I don't think in his body of work — offers us any kind of criteria for evaluating one of those being better or worse. And in fact, I think it's just the opposite — he says that "I don't know and I can't know."

And so this goes back to — some, perhaps many, people hold the argument that there's certain standard subjects, certain topics, certain classes that everyone should take in order to provide that common foundation. You can see why people make that argument. I think that assumes a lot of things about the nature of those requirements — number one the selection process for them, and number two the delivery of them.

自治社会的前提

But it's an interesting question to think about: could you have freedom that led to certain types of activities for some, perhaps many, people where they weren't exposed to certain things, and then what does that mean? I don't know. My priors are that we shouldn't force things on people in Buchanan's framework.

And so then we run into fascinating things like: what set of beliefs and what knowledge — and is it formal or informal knowledge — leads to a self-governing society?

从未真正摆脱责任

The state stuff — the turning to the state — poses a major issue, because people might say, "all right, people turn to the state in order to insulate them." You can never escape responsibility in Buchanan's framing. Even if you don't want to take responsibility for my spending habits, so I turn to government to protect me — well, it still presumes I can pick the people for government that are going to insulate me effectively from those things. And so at some point, you have to take responsibility. Where? I don't know. But at some point you do.

二十二、Pete：过滤机制与"看不见的学院"

Pete Boettke: I think that that's a very problematic issue to sort between transformative and programming. And I think that your point about who it is that makes that judgment in the end is probably accurate — the judge of that has to be the person that has experienced this process.

作为分析者，我们能研究什么

But as analysts stepping outside the system, what we can study is the properties of the filter mechanisms that are involved in education. And we can study those filter mechanisms for the incentives that they set up, for the information that they provide, and the learning that results in those systems. And not all systems, not all educational filters provide the same kind of experience.

And so we can't improve outcomes in terms of knowing in advance "I want the person to believe X, Y, and Z." But I can improve the way in which we talk about ABC and XYZ and therefore give more — back to the earlier points — more of that inputs into that individual becoming something other than what they are. And I think that's all we can ever do.

Mercatus 项目的证据

To be a little self-interested — not rent-seeking, but self-interested here — one of the things that I like to point out to people that talk about the failure of higher ed and the inability of kids to want to read anymore, or to want to discuss ideas: I always try to tell them about our own programs. Because we get these kids that come from the best schools in the world, all over the world. And what they come — they're hungry as hell to talk about Adam Smith or Hayek or Buchanan, or any of these other people, Tocqueville, whoever we're having these deep conversations with in these Socratic dialogues.

These kids, they're not self-selecting because they are part of the libertarian club and they want to come and learn more about libertarianism. They're simply political philosophers, political theorists, economists (not as many economists as I would like), political scientists, historians. And some of them come here even somewhat suspicious — like "I got to learn what these yahoos that call themselves classical liberals believe." And then they come and they have a conversation with us about these texts and these ideas, and they're hungry for deep conversation.

And it's like a demonstration effect: you claim people don't want to talk anymore because of the monoculture — we actually can get them talking. But I think the difference is that the filter mechanism that we have is different than the filter mechanism that many of them experience in their day-to-day college.

"看不见的学院"的模式

And so I think what we do in our quote-unquote invisible college is actually force people that want to become social scientists and policy kind of people. Our model is the model of education — it's a tried-and-true model that goes all the way back to Athens, and even to Bologna and to the origins of Oxford — which is a lot different from viewing the social sciences as social engineering subjects in which it's like plug-and-play. Instead, we're all about questions and answers.

Don Lavoie 的教诲

Don Lavoie, who was both Virgil's and my teacher — I don't know how you remember this, but in moving to Gadamer, he kept trying to get us to think about this difference in philosophy when we move from the problem-solution mindset to the question-and-answering mindset. Because the problem-solution mindset is an engineering mindset — it's very valuable, no doubt — but it's different than the questioning-and-answering mindset in terms of an open-endedness. Because if you have a problem, you have a solution, you have an exit — it's called the solution. You solve the problem. But in a questioning and answering, it's ongoing, it's constantly in the process of going.

And when Lavoie got me to think in those terms and then tie it to Michael Polanyi and to Gadamer and the nature of science, and then linking that back to Hayek, it was like I was on the greatest high in the history of mankind — because it was like, oh my God, the more we know, the more we don't know. This is an unending project. And so to me, I think that mindset is what's needed for the transformation — not the idea that there is a monoculture that gives us "this is a problem, here's the solution."

二十三、Virgil：自治公民的教育——从建国者到今天

Virgil Storr: No, but to the epistemic point that you and I agreed on — what is also true, and a thing that's heartening about our fellowship programs, is that when you ask the fellows at the end of the process how they feel about what they experienced, almost to a person they say that (1) they were transformed, and (2) they're happy with the transformation. They feel like they have a better framing for making sense of the world, and they have a toolkit that they can apply going forward, and they're satisfied with that.

自治公民如何教育出来？

I want — you and Chris mentioned something that it's maybe useful to say at least a couple more sentences about: how do we educate for a self-governing citizenry? Buchanan certainly seemed to have wanted that, we the three of us know we want that — but the question is how do we get it?

One of the things that's always so striking to me is that when you look at the founding fathers — right, we're in the 250th anniversary — we're in this moment that there's a deeply literate group of people. They spent a lot of time reflecting on Montesquieu and Adam Smith. And not in some surface way, and not in a meme way, and not in a blog way, and not in a "AI gave them a summary of it" sort of way, but in a deep substantive kind of way.

So I guess I'm wondering: is that what it in fact takes to get this push towards a self-governing citizenry? Is that what's required for it to work, or is there some way to have that without doing that kind of up-front personal investment in becoming the kind of person who's ready for that?

二十四、Pete：从思考"像我"到思考"与我"；美国革命的激进主义

Pete Boettke: So I'll go very quickly, because the first thing I think, as an educator, the biggest transformation for me was to realize that I was not in the business of trying to get them to think like me, but get them to be willing to think with me. And that's a big difference.

苏格兰启蒙与美国革命

Related to the founding this summer, of course, it's been on our minds. I read Gordon Wood's book, The Radicalism of the American Revolution, as well as Gary Wills's book, Inventing America. And what's fascinating in both of those books is they tie it to the Scottish Enlightenment — and not necessarily just Hume and Smith, but also Adam Ferguson. And a big part of that — Gary Wills does this language analysis of the Declaration and then relates it to the words in the Scottish Enlightenment.

不只是精英的革命

Now, your point about that is that those were the elite of the elite of society — they were deeply thinking about those things. What I think Gordon Wood's book is so vital is to show how the American Revolution, based on those ideas, totally transformed society — not just the elite. Now, it never did it perfectly, but compared to everywhere else in the world, it opened up space for ordinary individuals to live their lives as they wanted to live and do extraordinary things in a way that had never been achieved before.

So a lot of social hierarchy gets torn down. You think about it — primogeniture gets eliminated state by state. And so now all of a sudden, what's the implications of that? You're no longer dependent on the first son to be able to tell you how it is that you can live your life. And so step by step, it eradicates what used to be the privileged system of the previous idea. So the ideas erode what had been the structure that had prevented ordinary people from being able to live in freedom.

And so that's the spirit of the revolution — pursuing that and perfecting that, I think, is the American project, and all that's entailed. Thinking through those things and understanding what are the preconditions for a self-governing democratic society — yeah, that's crucial to all of this.

二十五、关键引文三：责任与功劳的孪生

Virgil Storr: Yeah. There's an interesting quote from "Natural and Artifactual Man" that I'm going to ask Chris to talk a little bit about — and this is where he's talking about responsibility, because you mentioned it earlier, but he's also talking about credit too.

He says:

"Man must bear the responsibility for his own choices because he is artifact. Because of his artifactual nature... Because man makes his own history, if individual man is to be free, he is to be held accountable, he is to be deemed responsible for his actions. But at the same time, he's allowed to take credit for his actions."

自由与责任的双重链接

One of the things I want you to talk about is this twin link between freedom and responsibility — not just in the "well, maybe we're afraid to be responsible, and so that's why we're willing to give up some of our freedom," but in: is it critical, our ability to make choices or to be free to make choices — how dependent is that on us having to either be willing to be held responsible for those choices, or willing to be open to being able to take credit for those choices?

二十六、Chris：外包的悖论与和平共处的能力

Chris Coyne: Well, I think this ties to what we were just talking about with the self-governing nature of individuals. There's two ways to think about it.

狭义与广义

In a narrow sense, I think they need to be linked, because if I have the freedom to do stuff but don't have to take responsibility, it's very easy for me (1) to cost-shift onto other people, but (2) not take into account the full cost of my actions.

In the broader sense, it matters precisely because of the self-governance point. If I just want to shift things off onto other people and then just say "well, I'm alleviating myself of the decision-making, I'm alleviating myself of the consequences, when things don't go right that's because someone else made the wrong choice" — I think that's going to lead to some perverse consequences, which is: it's going to atrophy our ability to engage in certain kinds of decision-making where I do have to take responsibility for the choices I made.

As I mentioned earlier, I still don't think you ever alleviate fully from this — even if you want to shift it onto others, because at some point you have to make the decision-making or engage in the decision-making process to outsource it.

Elise Boulding 与孩子们的和平建设能力

On the self-governance point, oftentimes — this is to your point, Virgil, about the pessimism and optimism — I oftentimes think this is a strong critique of not just Buchanan but free society in general: that the burden it places on people is too much. But then I think oftentimes we overblow the magnitude of it too.

Elise Boulding, who is a sociologist — didn't consider herself a classical liberal by any means — but I like her point about peacemaking capabilities. Because she says: if you want to see the peacemaking capabilities of human beings, just look at children play. Children can be bullies, but they also figure stuff out in ways we don't give them enough credit for. And adults oftentimes try to teach them certain general principles: "You don't hit people," "You don't take their stuff," "If other people jumped off a bridge, would you jump off a bridge?" — these sayings that are often attributed to parents or guardians.

But that actually gets you a long way. Like, imagine we took the principle "don't hit people, don't take their stuff" and just started applying it to stuff in general. We tend to forget that when we leave the sandbox and we go out into the world — like, "no actually, I want to hit people and take their stuff; I just want government to do it for me, and then I'll call it redistribution." But what if we actually took those principles — recognizing they don't answer certain questions and we need to operationalize them — but we thought in those terms? That would actually get you pretty far.

承担责任是自由社会的前提

And so when we think in those terms, people have self-governing capabilities. They exercise them all the time from a young age, and it's really then cultivating those things and figuring them out. So that's how I think about responsibility: it is giving people responsibility but also learning how to wield it correctly, and also understanding the consequences of what that means.

All of us try to outsource some responsibility for things. Every single person does that. "Oh, that wasn't my fault, there's factors outside of my control" — and I think that's true to some degree. But if the project of a free society is going to function and sustain, then it requires people to take responsibility at some point. Now, what that means, I don't know exactly — I can't give you a list of what that means, and I don't think anyone can — but unpacking what that means I think is one of the key things that Buchanan is pushing us to think about, and that in itself is quite valuable.

二十七、Virgil 的追问：功劳的可能性

Virgil Storr: Pete, I want to ask you about this other side — because I've heard you talk about merit in other spaces, and the importance of essentially the potential of merit. This might also be linked to how we think about profits and the potential to retain the profits that one makes.

I'm curious about whether, in your view, people recognize that: you can't actually take credit for anything if you're not free. Or you can't credibly, meaningfully take credit for stuff if you're not free. And the total legitimacy of profits is only maybe possible in a world where you can in fact suffer losses — where you can actually have consequences for making the wrong decision.

A world where we try to take out all the vulnerabilities is maybe also a world where we can't be a champion of anything. We can't be a winner. We can't have succeeded. Can't say "I did good work," even — because you've done it in a context where you're not really responsible. So did you really do it? Can you really claim it?

二十八、Pete：经济学家的"肉与土豆"回答与 Forest Gump 时刻

Pete Boettke: This is obviously, as you know, a major philosophical issue.

经济学家能回答什么

The meat-and-potatoes economist, I think, can respond to some of this stuff by saying: I can not tell you whether or not profits are deserved or not, but I can tell you the consequences of your answer to that question. If you say profits are not deserved, then what do you think economic actors are going to do following? If you say profits are deserved — but let's, we're in the business of doing economics and social philosophy, or political economy and social philosophy — so we should in fact be engaged in this other debate, but not necessarily as technical economists, but as social philosophers that are then going to feed that back in.

And I think you're right: if we do not view that individuals have agency, then they are not going to also have responsibility for their losses or rewards for their insight. So what happens to a society in which rewards to insights and responsibilities get lost? We have examples we can point to — look at what the consequences of having soft budgets are. What happens when people have soft budgets, when people find that the returns from trading are going to be less than the rewards from raiding — what are the consequences of that? We've had all these different experiments.

Forest Gump 式的生平

But again, I'm not sure that we know precisely, because the world's complex. You know, it's funny — I've realized, and I know you guys have had to put up with this because I'm doing all this self-reflection in a weird way — rather than self-reflect, I share-reflect (which is probably too much) — but it's like my life is completely like a kind of Forest Gump moment. There's all these moments where I just bumped into things and they changed me in ways that if that moment hadn't happened, I never would have experienced any of it.

Maybe this comes from getting to be in my mid-60s now. But I'm kind of always shocked about how little I had to do with it, and how circumstances hit me and sent me this way rather than that way. And that never could have been anticipated and were not a construction of my own effort to be a better person than who I was. I just wanted to be who the hell I was. I was just a kid who wanted to be exactly who I was. And then all of a sudden I got hit and I was like, "oh jeez, okay."

我们是在被塑造之后才成为自塑者

So, am I responsible for that? Because I wasn't being a self-architect — I became a self-architect after I had already been shocked out of my complacency. And I think those are different things. So it's a complicated question to me, but I think as an economist I can stick with the meat-and-potatoes line, which is that I cannot tell you this is deserved or not, but what I can do is I can tell you what the consequences are of your answer.

二十九、Virgil：偶然性的两种解读与 Hayek 的"最大化意外"

Virgil Storr: There's a book — The Unbearable Lightness of Being. It's a novel, and in that novel it points out that, you know, but for showing up a few minutes later or early, your life could be radically transformed. That gets to your thing about bumping — you bumped into the stuff and then it changed you.

两种可能的回应

But I guess there are two responses to what you said that are possible.

One — one could look at that and say that's a beautiful thing: that what we want to do is create even more opportunities for Pete Boettkes and others to bump into the things that can change them. And part of that means that we want to be comfortable with Pete Boettke both getting the benefits of that — happening to meet the love of your life at 16 or whatever — and we also want you to have the consequences of that.

The other — some might look at that and go: well, that's a shame; that seems very artificial and random, and nothing you did is really deserved as a result of that — because you bumped into it, not somebody else, and you did nothing to be the person. And but also you shouldn't bear any of the cost for the bad stuff either. And so we should really try to sort of insulate that.

教育与自治公民

So is that this — this may get back to "what does it take to educate for a self-governing citizen?" Is holding one view or the other simply that we have different orientations — people just have certain perspectives on the world and we have one or the other? Or is it that we can be educated to think through the full consequences of one of those views or the other, and to see maybe the advantages of one or the other?

Do we need to read something like the first few chapters of The Constitution of Liberty to really understand the value of the accidents? And so I'm curious, I don't know if either of you have a reaction to that.

Hayek 关于意外的最大化

Pete Boettke: I do think that one of the things that's fascinating is when you first encounter those passages from Hayek where he says that it's about the accidents — maximizing the opportunity for the accidents to happen. It's puzzling. It makes you sort of, you know, "like what the hell's going on here? What's the argument?"

And I think it just invites so much learning when you dig into it, as opposed to dismissing it. It might be easy to dismiss it to some, but if you start thinking about it, it's hard to ever stop thinking about it: what are those conditions that make that possible for the number of accidents to be maximized so that individuals can discover things that no one would have ever discovered had they not had that opportunity?

三十、关键引文四："害怕自由"的核心段落

Virgil Storr: Chris, I want to ask you — there's two passages in "Afraid to be Free" that I want to put on the table and maybe get your reaction to. Because in part he offers — he talks about socialism, but he talks about it in a kind of strange way.

对社会主义的宽泛定义

Early in "Afraid to be Free" he says:

"If we loosely describe socialism in terms of a range and scope of collectivist controls over individual liberty of actions, then socialism will survive and be extended."

He's talking in the context of — he doesn't think central planning is going to survive, but maybe this version of socialism will survive. And he says:

"This result will emerge not because collectivization is judged to be more efficient in some meaningful economic sense, or even because collectivization more adequately meets agreed-upon criteria for distributive justice, but rather because only under the aegis of collective control, under the state, can individuals escape, evade, and even deny personal responsibility. In short, persons are afraid to be free."

And then later on in that thing he says:

"The state has replaced God as the father and mother of last resort, and persons will demand that this protective role be satisfied and amplified."

对古典自由主义者的挑战

I think this creates a real challenge for classical liberals — anybody who would want to expand the range of freedom, anybody who would say "let's limit the state." I want you to talk some about what that challenge is, and then talk some about —

Let me back up. I'm curious if you think this is true. Like, this is really a part of human beings — this is what we are, this is where we are: that collectivization will always be popular because we will always demand that the state be a parent at some level.

If it is true, what does that mean for those of us who might say "well, but we want the state to be less of a parent, we want people to have the freedom to make choices and either be held responsible or be valorized or celebrated because of those choices"? What does it say for that? And is this maybe a — "kiss your Thor" point — is this Buchanan giving up on the liberty project when he puts this on the table and says "well no, people just want it"? Basically one way to read it is: people just don't want the thing that we'll sell them.

三十一、Chris：对社会主义独特定义的解读与政府的"门面"

Chris Coyne: Well, there's a lot there. So I'll say a couple about each and then we can hear what you and Pete think.

对社会主义独特定义的解读

The socialism question about the definition — it's certainly, I'll call it, a unique use of the term. And it's not usually the way we as economists think about it as an economic system. There's no discussion here about nationalization of the means of production, no discussion here about controlling economic production (whether it's in capital markets, labor markets, or other markets). It's a broader conception.

The way I understand he's using it — very evident in the passage you read — is: it's a political relationship. It's a relationship between the individual citizen and the political authority or collective authority — to the point of collectivism, as you were pointing us to.

So then the question becomes: well, what does that mean? Given his definition, that's a very big question. The way I think about it is: how do we respond as liberals? It might be something like this.

政府作为门面

Look, the state is a façade. The grand promise that somehow government can take care of you — that you can alleviate yourself of responsibility — is simply not true. And it's not true for a couple of reasons.

Practically, for the reason I said earlier, you're still responsible even for outsourcing. But practically, you can't alleviate yourself of responsibility because government's not often going to do what you want it to do. You think you're somehow getting insulated from all of the vagaries of life, but you're not. Government — no matter what political party, what ideology is running government — promises people that it can take care of them: that if you just give them more control, more resources, more of your freedom, it can make you more secure. Whether that's against terrorism (as in this paper that he's talking about), whether it's against various inequalities — it can't. Because even if it gives you certain stuff on some margins, it takes away on other margins. It sticks its hand out with some goodies while sticking its other hand in your pocket, or the pocket of other people, to pay for them.

复杂系统与"计划的混乱"

So pointing those dynamics out, I think, is extremely important. And that requires nuance — that's not just a talking point of "government being inefficient." It is a nuanced point, because people need to be able to see that the promise of government insulating you from certain things is a façade — because you can't insulate yourself from certain things in a complex system.

As thinkers like Mises, Hayek — on the left, thinkers like James Scott — have pointed out, efforts to impose control on a complex order is not order; it's planned chaos. And it's planned chaos because it replaces the general tendencies and organizational patterns of complex systems with limited human reason, and that more often than not is a recipe for disaster.

布坎南对自发秩序论证的批评

So that's why I think the kind of points that we typically make about complex systems, spontaneous orders, and so on are so important.

Now, one final point: Buchanan kind of chides what I just said about focusing on spontaneous orders and self-ordering properties — he chides that way of thinking in "Afraid to be Free." This is the section on the lacuna in classical liberalism — because he says that's not going to convince many people, saying "just let things play out, orders and patterns will emerge." He says we need something deeper. He uses the language of the psychology of self-responsibility, I think, in that paper, and says that classical liberals have neglected the psychological component.

That might be interesting, even though outside of my area of expertise. But in other essays, like "The Soul of Classical Liberalism," Buchanan says we need to kind of ignite the fire in the belly of ordinary people. And one way to do that is by turning to things like the morality of the system, the ethics of the system — and how claims about the morality of, for instance, income equality perhaps is not what you think it is. Because in order to get that outcome, as Hayek pointed out, you have to treat people unequally on other margins. And so you never can have full equality across all margins. It's again one of trade-offs.

While we can debate those issues, as economists perhaps the best we can point out — which is quite valuable in itself — is that there's going to be real-world consequences for how you answer those questions. And so once we start to think of things in those terms, perhaps it doesn't get us all the way to answering the question, but it does provide some entry points for having that conversation.

三十二、Pete：自由与经济学再统一；布坎南对正义理论的追求

Pete Boettke: I'd like to tackle something that you just said, which is about the liberty project.

把自由带回经济学

If you go all the way back to one of your first comments, you argued that Buchanan makes us think about liberty seriously, analytically, as part of what's required to do our everyday economics. And this of course is an idea which now is getting a little bit more traction in contemporary literature. This is something Bill Easterly has recently stressed in his most recent book on violent saviors. It's also something Barry Weingast has tried to do: that the concept of liberty needs to be brought back into economics, because it was such a big part of economics in Adam Smith, and we lose something when we lose it as an analytical device.

布坎南对自由的严肃态度

The liberal project in liberty is hard — beginning all the way from soup to nuts with Buchanan. And too many people, I think, miss this in him, including many of his students, who tend to then think of him just as doing public finance, or public choice in the hardcore sense of public choice.

《社会组织人类的潜力与限度》

I want to — Buchanan was great with titles: The Limits of Liberty, The Calculus of Consent, Democracy in Deficit — most of his titles are pretty amazing. This is one of the essays that's his least pithy title. It's called "The Potential and Limits of Socially Organized Humankind."

In that essay, what he argues is that in the late 19th century, humankind had experienced more autonomy — individual autonomy — than we had ever seen before. We had more wealth than we had ever seen before. We actually had more peace than we had experienced before. But it was precisely at that moment that the liberal West was proved to be its most vulnerable. And his argument is: it was most vulnerable because it didn't have a theory of justice that could stand.

布坎南的真正遗产：问题而非答案

And so what modern political economy needed to do was develop a theory of justice. And of course, this is in Buchanan — it sets him off on his link with Rawls and all kinds of other people where he's trying to actually do that theory of justice. And I think that's such a key part of what he's trying to do in his economics: to bring to bear the tools of neoclassical economics as he understood it — let's say Knightian tools of neoclassical economics — to bring to bear on the discourse having to do with justice in society, and not limited to merely redistributive justice.

Your question, I think, is a fundamental one about what it is that we mean by a theory of justice. And he opens up that space for us intellectually. And that's — not any one of his answers (go back to questions and answers, not any of his solutions to problems) but the fact that he's putting these questions foremost to us — is, I think, his greatest bequest as a scholar.

三十三、Pete 的回忆：92 岁的布坎南与终身学习

Pete Boettke: I want to tell a story. I know this — but I want to tell this story because I think it captures the essence of Jim Buchanan and his project that we can all learn from.

Remember, I was his student in the 1980s, and then became his colleague in the late 1990s. And when I returned to GMU and then I ended up taking over his classes, I had to talk to him quite a bit about those things, so we talked frequently.

In August of 2012 — so he's 92 at the time — I attended a talk of his on money, which was inspired by the global financial crisis. After the talk, I went up to him and I just sort of asked him a simple question, which is, "How are you doing, Jim?" He's 92, I hadn't seen him for a couple months.

But he was never one for small talk. So he just looked at me and he said: "Well, that paper has some problems. I got to go home and do some revising." And then he just walked away.

And I kept on thinking to myself afterwards — my god, when I'm 92, I want to be able to say the same thing: "I'm going to go home and do some more revising."

I think the issue with Buchanan: he was a lifelong learner. He had these problems that he had recognized all the way back in 1949 about the nature of public finance and political theory, and he wanted to constantly be taking different bites of the apple at those. And so when you talk about the relationship of these two essays, it's quite fascinating because on the one essay he thought he had an answer, and the other essay he's like, "oh, but that answer didn't work." And so he's constantly stressing. And then as Chris pointed out, that answer doesn't work — but then he writes "The Soul of Classical Liberalism": "well, let me take another bite at this."

And so I think what we learn from Buchanan is this embracing of lifelong learning — trying to constantly question ourselves and question the literature that's out there to keep trying to explore these issues.

三十四、关键引文五：古典自由主义的空缺

Virgil Storr: Oh no, thank you. This has been fantastic. I have one more question, and it actually picks up on where Chris took us in his answer to the last question, and it's about how Buchanan ends that essay.

He's got this quote where he says:

"The lacuna in classical liberalism lies in its failure to offer satisfactory alternative to the socialist collectivist thrust that reflects the pervasive desire for the parental rule of the state."

So he puts that as: that is the gap that we classical liberals need to fill.

用什么来填补？

One way to maybe — I want to ask this both: what in fact would we fill it with? What would we offer as maybe a persuasive argument against the desire for parental rule? But even maybe a positive account?

One way I read — and this may be unfair, so Chris, push back — one way I heard what you were saying was more like a negative sort of pushback, which is to say: "yeah, you want the parent, but some parents are abusive, and so do you really want the parent?" Is that the best answer that we have to this question? What's your answer to this question?

三十五、Chris：自由主义已交付的巨大收获；"你可以离开家"

Chris Coyne: Yeah. So that's part of it, but I don't think that would be my answer. The abusive certainly — I think that's true in oftentimes with government. But I think here's what I would say.

自由主义其实有答案

First of all, I think in some sense "the liberals don't have answers" — I think is too strong is what I'm going to say. I think liberals have great answers. I think we underestimate how far the liberal project has become, how much freedom there is in the world compared to history.

布坎南留给我们的乐观理由

But here's where I think Buchanan perhaps leaves us a reason for optimism. We can point out the economic benefits of liberalism, but those are limited. Let's say those are limited. What else can we do? Visions. Visions of what the world could look like. And then you say, well, that's just utopian thinking — which might be valuable in itself.

But here's the thing. Let's stick with the parentalism thing. One of the things, to my way of thinking, a good parent does is to educate their kids — whether formally or informally — that eventually you can leave the house, you can leave the nest, you can live your own life.

"你可以离开"的力量

So maybe it's as simple as this: people of the world, you can leave. You don't need Uncle Sam, or whomever you take as your parent, to make you breakfast, wash your clothes, and so on. You can do it. You don't need that. And that's quite powerful in and of itself.

自由不等于原子主义

Now, what does that mean? That doesn't mean atomism. I think that's the other mistake people make about liberalism — "oh, it's just a narrow atomistic view of people." No, there's community, there's social networks, there's all different forms of organizations, whether they're in markets (as you've highlighted in your own work, Virgil), outside of markets (as you've highlighted in your work also). Those types of arrangements allow people to both leave parentalism behind, but also live flourishing lives — both as individuals, but also members of society as well.

Highlighting those things, I think, is the important aspect of the project.

政府的滥用

The abusive part comes in because, of course, what government highlights is: "you need us; without us you cannot survive." And that's not true. Making people realize that possibility, I think, is quite powerful in and of itself.

三十六、Pete：家长制使人幼稚化；机会社会解放人

Pete Boettke: I don't have much to add to that — that isn't just what I believe. I guess I had down here in notes: parentalism infantilizes, and that the opportunity society empowers and liberates.

Ordinary people can do extraordinary things if they're just given the freedom — rather than the idea that they need to have a boss.

老板的另一面

And I think it's what you were mentioning before — there's kind of a linkage. If I need to have a boss, then I'm not going to be able to have the scope to become who it is that I want to become. I'm going to become what the boss wants me to become.

And I think people don't recognize that downside of it. They only recognize the one side of it: "oh, I have someone that's going to take care of me." But on the other hand, if I have a boss, the boss is going to tell me what I can do in time A and what I can do in time B, and that will affect me as well. Chris said it better than I ever could say it, so I should be quiet.

三十七、Virgil 的收尾：母亲、宵禁与自由的礼物

Virgil Storr: So one of the things that's interesting — I've been blessed to have an amazing mother. I had a fantastic childhood, had an amazing mother. Lived with her until I went off to college. I'm also lucky enough that she lives with me now — she's in our home and gets to be with her granddaughter and all of that.

宵禁的消失

There's a dramatic difference that happens between me living with her then and me living with her now. Me living with her then, I had a curfew. She was quite liberal even, but she had an expectation that she knew where I was and that I was home at a certain time. And so there were real constraints on how and what I could do and how I could live my life.

Her living with me now — I have no constraint. That constraint doesn't happen. I don't have a curfew with my mother in the house.

不再做孩子的美

Part of that is to Chris's point: the beauty of no longer being a child is that being a child comes with all sorts of protections and securities and all those kinds of things, but it also comes with all sorts of constraints. They get to say, "Are you dressed like that?" — and because they control, they pay the bills, you then have to decide how you're going to respond to that.

In a world where government is consistently taking care of us, we're forced to be a certain kind of person.

丧失的美好

The other thing that's true of that, though, is that with that sort of someone else maybe controlling your life, you also don't get some of the beautiful things that happen as well. You don't get to make the sorts of decisions that Buchanan is talking about about who you actually become. Someone else gets to weigh in on that. Someone else gets to decide "I don't want a kid with red hair," "I don't want" — like, somebody else gets to decide "I'm a vegan." Somebody else gets to say "no, that's not what your diet's going to be."

父母也会成为老板

And so in a world where the bargain that we may be tempted to make — that says "let's let the state be parent" — is a bargain that comes with a lot of stuff on the back end too. It means, as Pete says, "oh, let's also let the state be boss." We can't have it both ways. There's no way to walk that line where you get just the parent who's taking care of you, but not the boss weighing in on where you go and who you go with and how you do that. That's a thing that I think it's important to share.

自由已经交付了什么

But to the positive point — again, I think Chris pointed out something really beautiful that we don't say enough of, which is that freedom has delivered for human beings — not just tremendous material wealth, but some of the things that are connected to that. We live way longer than we used to. My mother gets to live in my house as an 82-year-old person because we've had a world that's free that allows for the medication and all the kinds of things that allow for people to live that long to exist.

Freedom has delivered the possibility for — not forced community, but genuine and true community. Community that we opt into, community that we choose, community that reflects who we really are, community that we desire to be a part of.

And then this: freedom does at least give us the opportunity to be a better person. If all we're doing is responding to what the boss tells us to do, there is no good or bad in that. There's just: are you listening or not? If you actually have space to decide what to do or not, there's the space to become better or worse. And that's another thing that I think we ought to be saying more of.

But it's also something that I actually think — contrary to what Buchanan is saying — I actually think that's a thing that comes out of classical liberalism and classical liberal thought. The really persuasive arguments on all those fronts.

Thank you both for what I thought was a great conversation.

Pete / Chris: Thank you, Virgil. Appreciate it.

结尾

Narrator: Thank you for listening to the Hayek program podcast. To learn more about the research, scholars, and work of the Hayek program, visit hayek.mercatus.org. For more information about graduate student fellowship opportunities for students at Mason as well as at universities across the globe, please visit students.mercatus.org. We hope you recommend students to our programs or consider applying yourself.

item.description:
# 布坎南两篇文章背后的隐藏结构：一个意外的发现
## 一、这不是矛盾，是**"创业者悖论"的政治学版本**
表面上看，《自然人与人造人》（1979）和《害怕自由》（2005）像是乐观与悲观的分裂人格。但如果你把布坎南的另一篇文章《经济学家应该做什么》放在中间作为桥梁，你会突然看到一个被所有评论者都忽略的结构——
**布坎南其实在描绘一个"创业者悖论"：越是具备"自我建构能力"的人，越会在面对不确定性时渴望"被托管"。**
这不是分裂，这是同一枚硬币。能力越强，意识到的可能性空间越大；可能性空间越大，选择的焦虑就越深；焦虑越深，就越想把方向盘交出去。这就像硅谷创业者在IPO前夜疯狂寻找导师、冥想大师、"父亲型"投资人——不是因为他们不够强，恰恰因为他们"artifactual"（自我塑造）的能力让他们看到了太多可能的自己。
**跨领域连接**：这与心理学家Barry Schwartz的"选择悖论"（Paradox of Choice）结构完全同构，但走到了更深的政治层面。Schwartz告诉你：选择太多会让消费者瘫痪；布坎南则预言：选择太多会让公民投靠利维坦。超市里的果酱实验

item.title: [Zhang Xiaojun Podcast] 155. 和科沃斯钱程聊，父与子、企二代接班的样本与肌理、机器人，和我内心的追寻
item.dc:creator: Zhang Xiaojun Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的发现：他把"不想输"活成了一种节律

钱程亲口说，他30岁前的底层驱动力不是"获取"，而是"不想失去"——"守住底线，而不是追求上限"。这句话放在一个CEO身上几乎是反直觉的，但它解释了科沃斯一切看似矛盾的选择：

  • 为什么他父亲做了二十年"农耕式"企业而不是深圳式的"狩猎式"扩张？
  • 为什么他把自己微信头像里的狗眼睛P成红色？——这是一个极其耐人寻味的细节：一个本能上防御型的人，必须用视觉符号人工制造狼性，因为狼性不是他的天性，是他的KPI。
  • 为什么他反复说"自信和自大就一线之隔"？因为对他而言，欲望本身是外接设备，不是内置系统。

真正的洞察在于：中国第一代企业家靠生存焦虑驱动，二代接班人最大的难题不是能力，而是如何在没有饥饿感的身体里，重新装一个饥饿感系统。钱程的"红眼睛狗头像"，可能是中国企二代接班史上最诚实的一个心理学标本——它不是炫耀，是自我PUA的仪式器具。

二、"三个11年"：地理拓扑学意外对应了科沃斯的产品哲学

深圳11年 → 加拿大11年 → 苏州11年。他自己把这当作一个有趣的巧合，但这个结构里藏着一个无人指出的同构：

地理 气质 对应企业阶段
深圳 热带丛林、搏杀 父辈的OEM/贸易起家
加拿大 冰原、慢速、规则 产品定义与品牌思维
苏州 "历史上没有自然灾害" 多品类、慢节奏复利

他说苏州人"富久了，没有逃离感和扩张感"，又说这和加拿大很像。但他没意识到的是：科沃斯的产品哲学——农耕式、不与巨头抢肉、种一颗种子等它长——恰恰是"没有自然灾害的地理"才会孕育出的商业模式。

如果让一个深圳土生土长的90后接班，科沃斯今天大概率是另一家公司——更凶、更快、更脆。地理不是背景板，是决策无意识的操作系统。钱程的三段地理史，让他意外成为了科沃斯最合适的继承人：他身上有深圳的血（出生）、加拿大的脑（教育）、苏州的胃（现在）。而企业的DNA需要的，恰恰是这三样东西的化合物，不是任何一个单一的极端。

三、跨领域连接：接班问题的本质，是生物学里的"遗传vs变异"困境

他讲了一个极深但没有展开的观点："企业的短板，其实是创始人长板造成的。"

这句话翻译到演化生物学语境，就是基因的多效性（pleiotropy）：让一个物种在特定环境中极度成功的基因，在环境变化后会变成最大的脆弱点。镰状红细胞让非洲人抗疟疾，也让他们得贫血。

父辈的"长板"（亲力亲为、决策果断、全军听令）锻造了20年的企业，但这个长板在AI时代、全球化时代、组织规模化时代，是科沃斯的最大短板。

而钱程作为接班人，面对的是一个生物学意义上的两难： - 完全继承父亲的"长板"→ 企业会在新时代灭绝（像柯达的工程师思维） - 完全替换为自己的"长板"→ 企业会失去过去20年的结构性优势（像诺基亚换CEO后的塌陷）

他的解法——他自己可能都没完全意识到——是用"农耕civilization"这个比喻给自己上锁。农耕的本质是跨代际的时间复利，意味着他必须既保留父亲的根系，又允许自己长出新的枝条。这不是管理策略，是演化策略。

最意外的推论：科沃斯最大的护城河，可能不是扫地机技术，不是品牌，不是渠道——而是钱程这个人本身的"杂合性"。他是深圳的躯体 + 加拿大的大脑 + 苏州的消化系统 + 父亲的骨架 + 自己的红眼睛。这种程度的"文化杂合优势"，在中国A股所有二代里都极为罕见。

反过来说，他真正的风险也在这里：杂合体通常不稳定，需要持续的能量输入来维持——这就是为什么他要把狗P红眼睛，为什么他说"人是环境的动物"，为什么他把采访本身当作一次外部激发。他的"欲望系统"是外挂的，不是内生的。这个外挂一旦掉线，科沃斯的大脑和毛细血管的连接会立刻松弛。

一个尖锐的预言：如果科沃斯未来十年真能跨越，不会是因为具身智能，不会是因为出海，而会是因为钱程找到了一种让"外挂欲望"内化为"自源欲望"的方法。而这件事，没有任何商学院、任何咨询公司、任何同龄企业家能教他——这是他必须一个人完成的、属于他父亲一辈走过但没留下地图的那段路。

📝 转录文本

和科沃斯钱程聊：父与子、企二代接班的样本与肌理

开场：小军的介绍

Hello everyone, I am Xiaojun. Today our guest is Kowals' CEO Qian Cheng. He was born in 1990, and was once the youngest CEO of an A-currency listed company in China. He is also a second generation start-up.

I am very curious about when a generation of Chinese companies started to hand over to the second generation, what was the motivation for the complex relationship between the rich and the poor, the upper and the lower classes, and the handover? Qian Cheng has a kind of age-related phobia. He cares about business. His favorite food is oatmeal. His circle of friends is his dog. He specially changed the color of the dog's eyes to a red color that will shine. It is to remind himself to be more wolf-like.

Next is my interview with Qian Cheng. Looking forward to the year 2026. We will make progress together with AI.

节选金句（预告）

I found that CEO is really difficult. I was actually not interested at first. I found out that I was the CEO. Right? It's the peak of life. Then I found out that this was definitely a historical mistake.

I've been describing our internal situation. I said that we are actually more like a agricultural civilization, not like a oil and wood civilization. We like to buy a seed to grow and let the food grow. It's another way of doing it, right? This industry is huge. I'm going to bite the meat.

How do you see those many entrepreneurs like Wang Xinxin, JK, Liu Jingkang after 90s? Do you think you have something different? It's definitely different. They are entrepreneurs. It's inevitable that their entrepreneur spirit is more intense.

更浓厚。就是自己的孩子。这可能只是我的兄弟。

你刚才说到你父亲的欲望, 还变成了科沃斯这家公司的欲望。你觉得你自己的欲望是什么呀? 这是个好问题。

你享受战斗吗? 我觉得以前我不是一个特别有血性的人。还是那句话,就是说你可能拥有的比较多, 所以没有需要去拼搏厮杀和获取。但我觉得我是有的。你是被环境激发了。是的,人是环境的动物。

一、三个11年：从深圳到加拿大到苏州

Hello, David.

Hello everyone, I am Qian Cheng from Kowalsk Robot. People usually call me David, so I will be called David this year.

David is the current CEO of Kowalsk Robot. There are many different identities of people who follow you. For example, you are the CEO of the youngest A-Bit listed company after 1990. Of course, you are also the second generation. So I really want to explore your entire growth experience.

I am also very curious. We just talked about you not growing up in Suzhou, right? You actually grew up in Shenzhen.

Yes, I was born in Shenzhen in 1990. Of course, I'm a little older now. I was talking about it a few years ago. I said that my life is about three levels on average. Because I was born in Shenzhen and lived there until I was 11 years old. And I rarely was born in Shenzhen. Including now I meet a lot of Shenzhen entrepreneurs, right? I said everyone is in Shenzhen. I said I was born in Shenzhen. Then I went to Canada when I was 11. I graduated from college when I was 22. When I came back at the age of 22, I was 33. So I went to three places on average. I spent 11 years in each place.

父亲的轨迹

Your father started his business in Shenzhen before he founded the former Tidekai Electronics Company in Kowalsk.

Yes, my father graduated from Nan Da and went to Shantou University to be a teacher. He went to Hainan and Shenzhen. During his time in Shenzhen, he worked in the state-owned enterprise. Later, I went to a business in the sea to do trade. Then, based on my choice in the trade process, I chose to start a business in Suzhou. I was still young at that time, so I stayed in Shenzhen. Then I went abroad.

忙碌的父亲、听话的孩子

Was your father a busy father since you were a child?

I think so. I don't think I've seen him much in my memory. I remember there was a photo of me wearing his leather shoes and wearing his... What's it called? I was a postman. So obviously I had more work and more business.

What kind of kid were you? Were you a good boy?

I was a good boy. I wasn't a troublemaker.

What did your father think of what you were doing? Because he was working and working in the industry.

I think it was only when I was 17 or 18 that I thought about it. I think it was after I went to college that I thought about it deeply. I didn't have a strong feeling about it when I was young.

11岁去加拿大

How did they persuade you to go to Canada at the age of 11? Why did they send you to Canada?

I didn't persuade them. I just told them. What choice can a 11-year-old child make? I think I started my own dream not so early. They told me a few months ago that they were going to Canada. I didn't know where Canada was. One night, my father took me to school to find a class director. He told me that he wouldn't come next. So I packed my bags and flew to Canada.

Was he a strict father?

I think my father's education was more about growing up on his own. I think he didn't have much time. So he didn't have much education to teach. I felt that he was a person who wanted me to grow up on his own.

What was your first impression of Canada?

My father accompanied me when I first arrived there. I had to memorize 10 words every day. I chose 10 words from the dictionary and memorized them. I stayed there for a few months and he came back.

二、大学时期：开始理解父亲在做什么

You said you realized some things your father was doing since college. How did you get to know this?

When you're in college, you start to have a deeper understanding of the world. What are your parents doing? What is your father doing? What are you going to do in the future? And at that time, mobile Internet really opened up a bigger world for you. Your amount of information will be more. And then at that time, I actually thought I was thinking about what I wanted to do in the future. I started to get confused about doing business. I read some books and I thought about what my father was doing. That's how I started to realize my father.

Before you decided to come to Kowloon, did you have any personal dreams?

I think back then, I'm sure there's no such thing as a clear direction. Who can plan their life perfectly when they're 20? I think it's hard. You always take one step at a time. Of course, I think I'm definitely lucky. Because I had summer vacation before, I could come back to China. I could come to the company and see what the company was like. I thought it was interesting. I remember thinking about it overseas. I thought it was popular to make apps.

— You were in 2008 to 2012. — Yes.

It was the beginning of mobile Internet. I started to have a sense of it at that time. I wondered if I should do something about it. But I never thought about it. I think it's not a deep understanding of this matter. Just take a step back.

三、2012年回国：进入科沃斯做电商

When did you decide to return and take over the company?

I think it's hard to say that I will take over when I come back. I think it's rather like in Canada, China should have a better future. After returning home, if I have a business, it's a smooth path. Like anyone else, you can only choose a good job after graduating from college. Of course, my first job choice was to work until now.

You didn't think about that at the time?

I didn't think about it at all. I think it's the same as many people. Most people may not work in the same field for the rest of their life. I've been in this industry for 14 years. I chose a starting point.
