I think to a certain extent I do understand my own shortcomings, right? Confidence and arrogance may be just a fine line apart. So I think I still overestimated myself. But I don't think I need to feel inferior either. Once you figure it out, it's actually all fine.

How will you deal with competition going forward?

First of all, competition is always there. Competition won't, because of you — especially in this industry — competition won't cease to exist because of anything you do. Right? Competition is always there.

In this process, you need to — actually, I think for a company it ultimately comes down to three things: First, whether you can see far. Second, whether you run fast. And I think the third is that you don't make mistakes. A company generally won't run into huge problems if you do these three things relatively well. Most situations arise from these three things, right?

For example, whether you see changes clearly enough, see your own capabilities clearly. What we call running fast is your company's ultimate execution, right? Whether your management can make this body run strongly enough. The third thing, I think, is what we call the inner issue: that is, your pursuit of reasonable desires and the restraint of unreasonable desires — the relationship between them. Many companies make mistakes. Making mistakes is actually the biggest fatal wound.

So you think this competition ultimately all comes back to the company itself? You think it has nothing to do with these external competitors? Do you analyze them?

I think I do look, and after looking, in the end you find it's just about what you need to improve and adjust. You can't envy... When you work out, you can't envy someone's great body while you don't exercise and still eat junk food — what's the use? Right? If you believe you can do it, just put it into action. It's not that hard. And then, step by step — discipline, step by step, based on your goals, take real action and achieve your goals.

Mm, has competition ever really troubled you?

Being troubled means not being able to figure it out. It's just not figuring it out. It's just — in the end you find it's just that you hadn't figured it out. If you figure it out and actually know how to change, I think it's all fine.

I think a company had best follow: 70 to 80 percent is replicating your capabilities and 20 to 30 percent is improving capabilities. I think many times people might hope for 70-80% improvement and 20-30% replication. Actually, replication itself is the process of you expanding and getting stronger. Like we said, exercise itself is actually doing enough repetition. Right? Then you master that skill and capability.

I think today Ecovacs, in our strategy execution, does exactly this — we don't overthink having some powerful, earth-shaking change in capability in the short term. I think we should do the replication that should be done, while following, say, the reasonable boundaries of your industry. So actually today, I think in our choice of industry and choice of market, we are following this path.

I think in the end it comes back to this: you'll actually find that the process of a company's development isn't just one straight road and one destination. It actually involves certain choices and certain twists and turns. So it's hard to say that, you know, I have a rival and this rival is my goal. I don't think a rival is your goal. Right? I mean — and in most cases, this life-or-death struggle — I can't see what it ultimately becomes. Look at the so-called, in China, what we've seen: so many well-known companies going head-to-head and nothing much came of it. They're each still around. Tempering each other, steel against steel, I'd say, making themselves better. I think it's that kind of process. It's not a company's development goal. A rival is not a company's development goal. It exists, and you have to respond, and in this process, you have to make yourself better. It's a touchstone. The goal is still your company's own vision for the future, including the things you hold on to. I think that is the goal.

For example, what do you think of Yu Hao?

I don't have any particular view. He just exists.

十三、消费电子没有护城河

Creating user value — that's what I think is most core. Consumers actually never like anything mentally taxing. I'll say it again: the best way to do right by consumers is to truly deliver what they expect — the results. Because I think the products we make — actually, many times newly created categories haven't been standardized or defined — you have to define them. It's not like in the past, when this thing was already defined — you have to define it. I think this is of course a very exciting thing. You can constantly, based on the elements of industry innovation, constantly define better products.

But within this, it's a constantly cycling process. Consumers give you feedback. Actually, the globalization we just talked about is the same — global consumers are actually very different. I think the future competition of Chinese companies must be global competition. It's about who can do global competition better, earlier, and better. In a reasonable state, Chinese companies should only — I mean, revenue from the China market might be just 30%. So there's actually a huge market space overseas. But then, how do we understand overseas markets? You actually find that global consumers differ greatly. So I think this is actually one of the most critical things for a company's development.

What do you think is the core moat of consumer electronics?

There's no core moat.

No core moat?

What core moat is there? I think... Brand might be... Brand, I think, is just the consumer's perception from their last purchase of your product, helping them quickly decide on the next purchase. But if your next delivery isn't good, then it's not a moat anymore. Right? I think it's just a memory.

Of course, it depends on what it is — for example, Coca-Cola never changes its taste. OK, but in consumer electronics nothing stays the same forever. Right? Water never changes; many things can stay unchanged. They can create permanent memories, or very long-lasting memories. But consumer electronics is changing. I think it can only be said: today a consumer bought this product, and it created a memory of your brand, which might help him make a choice next time. But by the next choice, the consumer electronics industry will have changed. So next time, if you've changed for the worse, then... this memory, I think, just comes to an abrupt end. So it's definitely not brand.

Then what could it be?

I think it depends. I think you — you could say Apple definitely has one, right? But there are also many — I think even the vast majority of consumer electronics doesn't. Apple's — its existence is based on its network effect, to a certain extent, right? But actually, if consumer electronics is pure hardware, there's no network effect — it's just a scale effect. So this doesn't really exist.

So you don't try to build a moat? Investors all hope you have a moat, right? So you can keep making money endlessly.

But the only real moat is monopoly. Honestly, to a certain extent, in today's world of rapid change and explosion, monopoly is very hard to form — theoretically it can't exist. So I actually think companies can only relatively find your scale effect. But — not many companies can necessarily build a moat.

Mm, so in this process, you have to quickly find your own scale effect.

Iterate — the speed of iteration, right? I think that's all there is. I think I'm a fairly realistic person. I find it hard to rashly say, OK, hey, I'm building a moat — this moat comes from Ecovacs' brand and our so-called understanding of global consumer households. Yeah, you could say it that way, but — it's not necessarily true. Many companies might choose to say these things, but I don't think it's true.

How do you win in competition?

See far, see clearly, run fast, restrain desires, make fewer mistakes.

What's your biggest mistake? In the past few years?

I think it was having desires that didn't match our capabilities.

But you just said your directions were right.

Right. The so-called mismatch is where capabilities didn't match. It's not necessarily the desires — it can be the capabilities that didn't match. Then you need to improve your capabilities. Not necessarily change the desires. I think the direction wasn't wrong — it's the capabilities. Just change the capabilities.

Have the capabilities changed now? Have they improved?

I think there's definitely been change. But nothing is absolute.

十四、关于AI与具身智能:大锤子找小钉子

At the end of 2022, ChatGPT came out. AI large models actually began to change the entire industry. How do you view this new technological change? Since a company is also a company of its era, in the next era, what do you think Ecovacs will do?

I think there are two aspects. One is how your company, with such a technological change — I think for a company, first let's split it in two: there are two kinds of impact. One impact is today's model-based AI Agent, right? The way your company operates and manages, the changes it can produce. And then there's your product, right? One is your way of operating, the other is the direction in which you can generate revenue.

I think today let's talk about the second one first, right? First, we can see that in the past few years, the ones actually generating positive revenue are the ones making industry infrastructure companies. Suzhou has many of them too. Actually making things like optical modules, right? All these various things — I mean, what we call the whole token infrastructure business. That's definitely not our industry. So what we can still choose is today's what we call Physical AI, the embodied AI thing.

Of course, I think looking at it from this angle, I think we look at it the same way: if we look at a 10-year horizon, first, I think today, using the whole large model and including the embodied AI thing, I estimate that within 3 to 5 years there can be some commercial and factory applications. I estimate. But we do to C — we serve consumer household needs. I think that should be a 5-to-10-year process. Of course, if we look at a typical startup — it's really hot right now, right? Unitree also took 10 years to go public. So actually I think this might be a 10-year process.

So within 3 to 5 years, if it's to B, to-factory, to-industry demand, I think that one has the conditions to land. Because I think robots, in daily life or rather in applications, what they can best replace are the jobs where today you train people more to become like robots. They're highly standardized and don't demand such strong generalization ability, I'd say.

But if we come back to the home, we actually believe that, whether hardware or software, the conditions for maturity are still some time away. So I think for me, if we put this on a 10-year cycle, I would more think — I'm not exactly saying — that Ecovacs needs to be overly urgent today about making some embodied robot to bring into the home, because it's not realistic. But we will, in this industry process — and we've always thought of ourselves this way: we are a company transforming from making tools to making a kind of butler robot in the future. So I think this is what we call what this whole era brings — if we're talking about Ecovacs' entire products and the change in the direction of your revenue generation.

The other one is the organization. I think everyone has talked a lot about this too, right? The changes AI brings to organizations today. As a company, we certainly think about it this way too, and we're also practicing it. So I think... today internally, our consensus on this matter is roughly this.

Do you think in the future Ecovacs will be a manufacturing company or an AI company?

I think the products and industry we're in today aren't built entirely on manufacturing genes either. You inherently have to use innovation to define consumer needs or to explore consumer needs, and use innovation to satisfy them — that itself is technical work. It's not that you're just relying on large-scale manufacturing's cost reduction or efficiency to do better. I don't tend to think a company needs such an absolute definition in this regard. No need, I think.

Many car companies are already spinning off their embodied AI — that's one path to choose.

Right? I mean, the industry has hype today, right? What we call heat — there's heat, there's a bubble. Yeah, you could say that, right? Actually everyone is working in one direction. Honestly, there's no essential difference. I just don't think there's an essential difference. Anyway, everyone rushes in. In the end you'll find there's not much difference.

I think today, in China's supply chain, putting together a robot isn't too hard. Right? Putting together a robot in Shenzhen isn't too hard. I even think a leading embodied-AI company could sell you one, and you could package it as Ecovacs — that probably wouldn't be hard either.

Right now this industry is actually still a case of taking, I think, a very big hammer to hit a very small nail. Of course, I think there's nothing wrong with using a hammer to hit a nail. That is to say, many companies started out like this too, I remember. I remember back then, actually, when drones first came out, nobody was sure what exactly this thing could do. There was a French company called Parrot. Back then they were probably on par with DJI, maybe even earlier. At that time, that company later chose — I think they once partnered with Walmart to turn it into a toy. Of course, that nail may have been the wrong one to find, right? DJI, in the end, chose to position itself as what we call prosumers — the so-called semi-professional consumer scenario. And it eventually became a productivity tool. That nail was probably a better find.

So today, actually, the whole embodied AI field, I think it's all a process of holding a hammer and looking for nails. Searching here and there — I don't think there's much difference. Everyone's doing it. They say they're going for the home, but in the end they all end up in factories.

You feel this isn't the most important thing for you at this stage.

I don't think this is absolutely the most critical thing for us at this stage. If it were, I think we'd definitely have to think about how to carve out a path of our own. Because being the same as everyone else — there's no essential difference. That's meaningless. Everyone doing the same thing, right? And others may have more of a comparative advantage in this competition, right? Say you're a startup — you don't have to worry about delivery, revenue, or profit. You just need to put out papers and demos. Another case is, you'll find listed companies doing it or big companies — unless they're of absolute scale, with truly, so-called spare cash to do this kind of thing.

But I saw XPeng just spun it off too, right? XPeng doesn't have spare cash to do this either, you know, or he has to think about how his investors face this matter. He also hopes to raise more outside capital. He can't possibly drive this with his own capital. He must have made a choice and a decision on this. And startups are also better at allocating interests to the core team. Right, so there are really only a few paths to choose from here. If you do the same as everyone else today, ah — but I don't think this is something that we need, today, to make a judgment on.

Yeah, we can wait a bit. Although we ourselves make robots, and we also hope that in the future, in 10 years, Ecovacs can develop in robotics. That's for sure — I don't think that goal has changed. I think it's just that we ourselves need to explore a path of our own, right? Following the hype, I mean, I don't think that's where our comparative advantage lies.

But you also just said you think Ecovacs should do things like a farmer tilling the land. Then it needs to start early. So today, is everyone nomadic or farming?

Today it's nomadic. Right? Everyone thinks this is a piece of meat, everyone thinks it's easy to raise money in the primary market, thinks this is a good direction for startups — that's nomadic, right? I think so.

So if it's farming, I think we're definitely doing some things. For example, we're working on things like "Bajie." We definitely have R&D investment in this. We also, definitely — including investing in the supply chain, making some key investments and laying out positions. But I don't think it's something we need to scramble for meat over today. There's nothing — what meat is this meat? So far I haven't seen where the meat is. This meat is illusory. Everyone is describing a — I mean, you know — With cars, you have something comparable and referenceable. Back then, the annual car ownership in China was right there. Electrification replacing gasoline and gas power. That's completely comparable data, right? And cars didn't become more numerous because of it. There was just substitution happening within it.

But how do you quantify the meat of embodied AI? People can now imagine it's a new market. Right, yes, it is a new market. It is a new market, but how big is it? It could be infinitely big in the future, right? Because we're talking about replacing humans, right? It could be infinitely big in the future. But if — but I think at that stage, you'll actually find that this market, for a company's valuation — roughly how big can it get?

Today Unitree is at 200 billion. China's most valuable company is at 4 trillion. Suppose this is the most important industry of the future. Investing in Unitree today, say. Let's assume any random individual, hmm, right? Then it grows 20x. Of course, maybe it exceeds 4 trillion. Right? But as I keep saying, I think people are very enthusiastic about the changes technology brings. But how big a thing it ultimately becomes actually has to go through quite a long process before it lands.

Take autonomous driving. Yeah, I often observe on the road how many consumers today are using autonomous driving in all scenarios? I mean, every car sold has it — everyone talks about this feature. But using it in all scenarios — I don't think it's more than half of Chinese consumers. I have a Tesla Model S. When I bought it, Musk said this thing had FSD. It's an old car from over ten years ago. And looking at it today, autonomous driving globally is actually worse than in China. China is already a leader in this accelerating space. Actually, not that many. So I think I'd rather think about this question more rationally.

What do you think the path that belongs to Ecovacs might look like? Do you have some ideas now? You don't want to do the same as them, homogenized?

First, I think if we look at it, I mean, first, China's future supply — the hardware supply capacity will be very abundant. So actually, maybe — I think in terms of hardware, the whole industry chain should be very rich in the future. So the thing you master — what's the key thing you really need to master? Maybe it's — you know — maybe software. But with software, as we also know, if you want to build a world model today, the investment is huge. It's just huge, right? And actually everyone's doing data collection today, right? And the standardization of data collection is iterating fast, right? A data collection method from maybe a year ago might not even be useful by now, right? Yesterday — a couple of days ago I just saw Figure released an app, saying everyone come do data collection. So I think the whole industry is still in a genuinely early stage.

I think for us, it's about choosing a reasonable pace. If and when we see hardware and software able to land in commercial scenarios to a certain degree, and moreover, I think it's with high robustness, replicable and scalable, then by that time it won't be far from home use. And at that time, I think for us it would be a very reasonable thing.

In your imagination, do you think this wave of AI or intelligence-driven home appliances will undergo huge changes?

Home appliances have been intelligence-driven for years. They've all been said to be intelligence-driven, right? TVs have AI, air conditioners and fridges have AI. But I think consumers are very rational. One is, in the process of competition, everyone talks about this thing. But when consumers finally pay with real money, I think they're still quite rational. In the end it still comes down to whether the value for money you deliver is good.

Our products all have AI in them, all empowered by it. Of course — robot vacuums need to avoid obstacles. Our robotic lawn mowers need obstacle avoidance, object recognition — things that help improve efficiency — it's always been there.

But I think — many people also ask me, once embodied AI comes out, will Ecovacs as a company cease to exist? Right? Because it feels like a straight replacement. But I actually think, by the time it develops to that stage, robot vacuum penetration should be quite high. People shouldn't be at the point of having your robot where you'd need to buy a vacuum cleaner for your robot. It shouldn't come to that. Including today, for example, us doing robotic lawn mowers overseas. Consumers have effectively already replaced the push mowers. So when embodied AI comes in, it shouldn't be that for this robot they'd buy another push lawn mower.

So I think actually I personally lean toward thinking about robots as a bit like Darwin's theory of evolution. In the future there will surely be all kinds of robot species. And they'll evolve deeply based on their scenarios to reach the optimal experience or fit for that scenario — the capabilities they grow. Of course, maybe there will be ones with two hands and two legs, humanoid beings. But there will also be, I think, very many other kinds of robots. That would probably be a relatively reasonable state. Relatively diverse. Because we too — we humans are just one species in the natural world. Never the strongest, either. So I think that's a relatively reasonable state.

So you will, at what you consider the right pace, do future product definition. Do you think Ecovacs will cease to exist in that era? Do you feel pressure?

I think ceasing to exist has many other reasons and factors. It's not that in this era it's solely because of this change.

You don't think it's brought about by technological change?

Technological change is very important. But companies replaced by technological change, companies that went under — are there really that many?

It marginalizes many companies.

Right, but that's just — that's just some companies failing to keep up with the times. and some other key factors. I think it's just that — it's not absolute. It's not like once it appears, you're gone.

Robots are also divided into the brain camp and the body camp. You definitely belong to the body camp, right? If you do it, would you go into the model layer?

I think not at present — we haven't entered models.

Have you tried investing in any models?

No. I think we're probably better at product definition, thinking about consumers based on — us understanding consumers' needs at home, what exactly they do.

Is your attitude toward AI relatively on the conservative side?

I think the impact it brings definitely exists. That's beyond doubt. Whether for individuals or industries, it exists. But whether within a very short time it produces earth-shaking change — I lean toward looking at it more rationally. So far, what I've perceived, or what ordinary consumers have perceived — I don't think it's brought decisive change.

You know, before Sam Altman talked about AGI. Now he doesn't talk about it anymore. Right? He's off doing coding too, right? Back then when he talked about it, it felt like, wow, it's over — like superintelligence was coming any moment — now that doesn't exist either. Of course, in some places you can indeed feel it. If AI today could do this kind of AGI capability — actually making videos and content is already strong, right? We're still talking face to face, right? Yes, your content product is still a key, necessary existence in the content ecosystem. It's not like it completely replaces today's creators and they're gone. It just gets generated and they're gone. People will use this capability to make improvements, I think. People still like to watch human content. I think so too. Of course people, you know, used to say maybe AI-generated content wasn't good enough, right? too AI-ish, and then they keep making it better, better and better. But you have your own judgment too. People still like watching people, still like human content.

If a consumer sees an embodied robot dancing outside, what does the consumer see? There are lots of these on the street, right? I think what they see is just a spectacle. They find it interesting that it can wave at you. Ordinary consumers are really like this. Of course — I think practitioners have a kind of sentiment, right? Our drive for technology, our drive for industry change. That sentiment is important. I think desire is important — I'm not saying desire is bad. Desire is important; it's a powerful driving force. It makes the world change in some way. But I think today, you say the Spring Festival Gala has a bunch of robots dancing — what change do consumers feel? What change to their lives? Hmm, as for doing real work, it's still a desert. Ha, right.

I hope one day — of course it will absolutely be like that — I hope one day, and I also hope Ecovacs is a key player in that, able to bring a robot into consumers' homes. At our core, we make these products hoping to help consumers solve problems — no doubt, we hope to save their time. I've always believed one key thing we actually do is not just helping everyone sweep the floor clean or mow the lawn well. At the core, it's even about saving them time. With embodied AI like this, such robots appearing in the future — I think that's of course great. We can free up more of consumers' time. But whether it's something that will appear tomorrow — I don't — I absolutely don't think it will appear tomorrow.

I mean, is this restraint, pessimism, or conservatism, or is it just rationality? Do you think this wave of technology could possibly take Ecovacs to the next level, the next rung of the era? The possibility? From that angle, shouldn't you embrace it more actively?

I think all companies probably think this way. So actively embrace it — but I think when running a company, when doing corporate governance and management today, there must be a right pace — it's not, I think, just emotional wishful thinking. As I just said, maybe it's just personal imagination — I have a — facing a huge incoming wave, we can change dramatically, earth-shaking. That's of course a matter of desire, I think — not a mistake either. It's a correct direction. But when doing it, I think you still have to think about the steps. Which steps are reasonable? Can they be what we can do today, what we can bear? I think this is a balance.

十五、苏州这座城:安心做事的土壤

You've also lived in Suzhou for exactly 14 years now. Do you like this city? I always thought you were from Suzhou. Only today did I find out you're not.

This city is interesting — historically it hasn't had natural disasters. So I think it nurtured some local culture. I personally feel you rarely meet Suzhou people around the world or even across China. Suzhou people don't go out much; they mostly live in Suzhou. It was a land of fish and rice, relatively wealthy. They never felt the need to flee or expand outward. It really is, I think, a culture at Suzhou's foundation. It's also — to some degree I sometimes feel it's quite like Canada — pretty laid-back. It's not like Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Shenzhen, a particularly, particularly excitable city.

But Suzhou is also important. Suzhou is still one of China's top industrial cities. And actually, looking at today — today's Suzhou, whether it's robotics, there are very many companies. Including what we just talked about, AI infrastructure — there are also many companies here in infrastructure. It's a place where you can work with peace of mind. Less hustle and bustle, but very solid. Working with peace of mind.

You think Suzhou is quite like your personality?

Maybe, ha. But I'm not sure if it's from living here so long that I became like this, or I was always like this. That I'm not sure of.

十六、再谈父子、交接与自我

As the CEO's brain, do you feel you've now connected with the company's capillaries — connected?

Already connected.

As you go deeper into this company, the longer it gets, do you feel you understand your father better?

Of course I think getting to know — He's an entrepreneur, right? This was built by him. A company. For a long stretch of his life, his dedication to this was extremely strong. And I don't think that will change much. Something you've been used to for decades is very hard to change. So I can understand his love for his own enterprise.

So what do you think your responsibility is? As a second-generation successor?

I'm also one with this company now. I've invested such a long time and dedication into it, right? I'm not something separate from it. I'm definitely merged into one with it. Just like the many long-serving employees in the company. It's actually part of everyone's life. It occupies my life, my own personal — I think my spiritual investment is also in it.

Hmm, you've grown together with it.

Right, there's no way to separate — you definitely. So your mission, as one of the company's key managers today, is to make this company develop better and better.

Just now you didn't seem to tell me what your desire is, a desire from the heart, right now.

Actually, running a company or being a CEO, on this road there's no retreat, right? You can only do better and better. Getting better and better is a kind of desire. Of course. You could also stay in place. Staying in place means getting worse and worse — you're all racing. You can only get better and better.

But how do I quantify it? Me saying I become number one in the world, or whatever rank. Honestly, I think that kind of thing is pretty hollow. Right? Is it important? Many companies are already number one globally. Their entrepreneurs are still working, still striving. Right? So your desire, in some sense, ultimately is self-actualization, self-fulfillment, right? Whether you can keep setting goals, setting difficulties for yourself, or face difficulties based on goals that you must overcome. Your desire or sense of achievement comes from that.

I think maybe I've seen a lot of it in my father. You know, I remember maybe at 40 he told me he'd retire. At 50 he told me he'd retire; at 60 he told me he'd retire. And you find he just can't seem to stop. So even if you set a limit for yourself or a goal of your own, once reached you're still thinking what's next. Sometimes, actually, when you've reached a peak you feel, ah, I've got it all. When you're the CEO, often you actually quickly lose. I think, ah — most of it, actually, you see. I mean, if everyone feels they've gotten what they deserve, and then I've hit my goal, then actually you'll slack off, you'll lose the sense of the next goal. What often greets you next isn't more gain, I think it's more loss. But I think this is also part of understanding him. You realize that someone who's always been fighting just keeps fighting.

Do you enjoy the fight?

I don't think I used to be a particularly fierce person. It's the same point: you may have a lot already, so there's no need to struggle and fight and grab. But I think I do have it.

You were sparked by the environment.

Yes. People are creatures of their environment.

You were sparked these past few years.

I think it's gradually solidifying, or becoming an increasingly core part of me. You can't say it wasn't there before. If it really wasn't, I could have just not come to work, just lie flat. You must have had some desire, to some degree, wanting to gain something. But it grows more and more with the process. I think all entrepreneurs are like this. Who says on day one, "I want to—" They just have a small goal, achieve a small stage, then define the next stage of growth and goals, then achieve that. I think it's all like this. Everyone — I believe everyone you've interviewed is like this. Most people, if they come out saying they want to define a goal as far as the sky, that's probably not realistic either.

When you first joined the company, or when you first became CEO, you were probably facing many of your father's old subordinates. How did you win people over?

Do you need to do that? I think the deeper thing is actually understanding. I mean, people need to build trust with each other. But what you never know is what this person went through with my father, and when. Right? How did they build trust? How did they communicate? How did they communicate behind closed doors? How did they communicate on WeChat? There's no way you can know these things. So in this, there really does arise a difficulty you have to overcome. Honestly, in the end, this thing — sometimes personally, I honestly think it comes down to fate. There's no absolute method. Because how two people get along depends on themselves. Sometimes I still think that I can't force myself to be exactly like my father. Maybe that's everyone's expectation. You know, they'd best think I'm like my father. But that's impossible. So it takes mutual adjustment from both people, not just my own adjustment. If it's only me adjusting, I actually don't think that's realistic. So this really does happen — things you need to solve, right? Of course. Some can be solved, some can't, haha.

What do you do when they can't be solved?

When they can't be solved, then we think — I think, my personal view, I think a company is still goal-oriented, right? Based on what goal it's oriented toward, whether your personal ability matches that goal. If you can adjust, adjust. If you can't, then you have to think about how to supplement the capability. Look at it fairly objectively.

Do you think that in these 7 years under your leadership, Ecovacs' organization and culture have changed?

What I hope to see is that we've gotten younger. Right, I mean — And yes, like I just said, our China region head manages a business of several billion yuan. He joined the company the same year as me, right? Which means, actually, we have key young people in key positions. I think this is a very good direction. If all these years — going back to your question — if the key positions were only held by my father's old subordinates, then maybe not much would have changed. So I think this is actually what I hope to see: we have more — more young people growing, in key positions. That's a good thing.

十七、"二代"身份与接班的真正难题

Mm, I believe many people want to ask you — including many around you whose status may be similar to yours — whether it's "factory second-gen" or "rich second-gen," or "founder second-gen," however you put it. None of these labels are ones you gave yourself, haha.

But it's a fact. I can accept it.

What do you think is the hardest part of succession?

I think the hardest thing is: the company you enter today, or the company you're going to take over — you, well, there's an intersection point here, I think. The company was built — maybe the father's generation, in a certain era, based on the elements of that era, became successful. So those elements include the era's background, they include, say, organization and talent, right? They include, say, customer relationships. And I think with succession, everyone's expectations — whether it's the father's generation or personal expectations — they always say, can you take it into the next era, right? Crossing over — the so-called crossing the cycle, crossing the cycle into the next era.

And I think this — the intersection point is: do all the elements of the last era necessarily exist in the next era? I think it's not 100% yes and not 100% no. You have to find some of the most critical things. But on the other hand, you need to keep adjusting and building inside a house whose framework already exists. I think the core difficulty is actually this.

And of course it comes back to whether you personally have the ability to master the new era itself, to master the elements of this era. If I'm just the person expected to represent the new era, but I step into the old era and I don't change either, and I can't bring it — bring the company into the new era, then the succession isn't a success either, right? So this is how I think about it abstractly, how I understand this thing.

Mm, more concretely, for Ecovacs, what do you think the old era's elements are? What elements does the new era need to add? What elements need to change?

Actually, I think in the end it's a lot about culture. Because the way of doing business will definitely change somewhat. A Chinese company becomes an international company — that's a very natural change. Actually, I think it's about cultural things, right? We say, for example, when the father's generation was founding the company, some of the keys to the company's underlying governance culture, right? Our company is, for example, very pragmatic — a very pragmatic company. Like just now, you thought I'm pragmatic. Our company is very pragmatic, ha. We're just a very pragmatic company. We don't do overly flashy things. We also think — but that doesn't mean we don't — we say, my father calls it "look up at the starry sky, keep your feet on the ground." My father says: look up at the starry sky, keep your feet on the ground. Without looking at the stars, Ecovacs couldn't have changed over so many years, adjusting to each era. But I think keeping feet on the ground means we pursue running a company that's steady and long-term. I think at the bottom it's about understanding these cultural things.

I'm thinking, we talked many times just now, over and over, about that question of desire. Is that also a very critical element of succession? Because you need, in these second-gens, to find that such a desire sprouts from within them, and this desire isn't from zero to one — it continues from the foundation the fathers built.

I think desire — some people have it, some don't, right? Some don't take over.

Are there more who take over or more who don't?

I think those who can take over are lucky first of all. Like I just said, I think in many cases there's nothing to take over. The company is gone, or companies will perish. Right? Of course, I think China, actually, from reform and opening up to this era — frankly, this is a topic. Because here's how I see it, right? After all these years, actually the first-gen founders have basically all reached a certain age. Right? So this is actually facing a problem that America or Japan have faced before. It's impossible for all companies to succeed here, otherwise society wouldn't change, there'd be no iteration, right? So inevitably some companies will make it. And I think this thing is actually, first of all, sifted out by the waves washing away the sand.

There are also — if you look at past European, American, Japanese companies, many no longer exist, and many are doing very well. So I think ultimately, if you look at those key elements, it still comes down to whether, when you take over, your personal desire for this thing, you know, exists. But actually I think 90% of it is, in the end, overcoming difficulties. The desire part is relatively simple. Having the desire is actually a simple thing. Overcoming difficulties is hard. Right, in the end you have to overcome difficulties.

On your path of succession, what were the biggest few difficulties?

It seems all difficulties can be crossed. Sometimes I think it's probably that my father and I have the same thinking on company development, the same result we want. That is, the desire is the same, right? We both want the company to get better and better. But the paths to get there are different. And in this process, how do we communicate and divide the work, reconcile.

Do you think a first-gen founder like him and a second-gen like you — do you think there's any difference?

Today I don't think so. Not necessarily a big difference. I still think of myself as creating. I don't feel I haven't created for Ecovacs. I think it's just that maybe I embrace more how to truly fulfill this responsibility. I think it's not just being in this position, feeling the responsibility you have to bear, but how to truly do this responsibility well.

十八、关于名字:"钱程"背后的期待

Why did your father name you Qian Cheng? "A bright future ahead."

This name — I wasn't, as a kid, I didn't particularly like it. It felt like a lot of pressure.

Oh, and then?

Then you just have to accept it. Didn't really like it, lots of pressure. As a kid, whenever I met people they'd say, "Oh, what a great name! A bright future, a boundless future." Right? It just felt like a name carrying huge expectations. Of course it's a good name, right? And I think, you know, a lot of the time, what kid gets to choose their own name? No kid gets to choose their own name. It's all an expectation, right? It's all the parents' expectation.

Do you like it now?

It's good, it's good. Accepted.

Are you under a lot of pressure now?

Of course the pressure is huge. Being CEO, can you say there's no pressure? Impossible. There's definitely pressure.

Do you like pressure? Now?

I think I'm enjoying a process of constantly transforming and growing. If it hasn't crushed you, then you're definitely getting stronger.

So you hold yourself to very high standards, right?

Inevitably. The demands can't only come from the people around you, third parties. Third-party demands are useless anyway. In the end it has to be self-demands on yourself.

十九、同代人:王兴兴们与自己的差别

How do you view those post-90s entrepreneurs, like Wang Xingxing and such, JK, Liu Jingkang?

Right, I know JK.

Mm, they're all around your age. Do you think there's any difference between you and them?

Definitely different. They founded their own companies, right? I think, inevitably, the entrepreneurial spirit in them is stronger. You can feel it — stronger. That's — this is their own child. This one is maybe just my brother. That's my child. I think there's a blood relation here too. It's still different. A brother. Right, the company is only 8 years younger than me.

Oh, that angle — it's your brother. Oh oh, it's your dad's other child. Doesn't every entrepreneur feel their company is their own child?

Yes yes. Right.

As a kid, were you jealous of this child? Because your father poured too much time into it?

No no. I — No, I never had that feeling. It was fine.

Then do you envy someone like JK? More fierce, more driven?

I don't think so. It's not envy. This thing — I can have it too. Like me — you just asked me — I think I have it too. It's not that I don't. I think today's me is not without it. So I think it's an element you need to succeed. You can't envy it into being anyway. You just accept that there's a difference. I just see the difference. I've seen a certain difference. But I think that doesn't mean I don't have it. There's just some difference. Doesn't mean I don't have it. It's not a have-or-have-not relationship, I think. We're all growing, learning, working hard. I still feel there's a lot I can do well, and also a lot worth reflecting on. Not necessarily such a big difference, I think.

Do many friends around you take over family businesses?

There are some. There are some. After reaching a certain point, succession actually isn't the core topic. It's not a goal. It's just a process. The goal is always how to make the company better. You could say, so-called "completed the succession" — so what if the company's not doing well? Right? I mean, then what have you gained? Right? There are many, I believe, who've completed succession, but the company may not, in today's era, find a path better suited to its development. Right? Then — it's just like every other CEO: everyone's thinking about how to fight for better development. So I've never felt this is a knot, a — like a sticking point. It's a transition. It's just a trans— a transition and a process. With enough wisdom, I think you can face it.

二十、十年后的科沃斯 & 快问快答

In 10 years, what do you hope Ecovacs will look like?

Good question. First, I'd think about what the key elements of this era are. First, I think without a doubt, we just talked about these changes in technology. We talked about two kinds of impact, right? One is the impact on your choice of products and industry. The other is the change to your organizational management. This is something that will definitely happen in this era — it's inevitable. Third, I think Chinese companies going global is also a very interesting topic, right? We've seen a lot of success. Ecovacs is also practicing it, and — I believe, given the macro environment, there will be many different challenges. So I actually think this should be a main theme for the next 10 years.

If Ecovacs doesn't achieve something, would you feel you weren't successful?

I'd certainly hope that, in the future, based on what we say — what we believe ourselves — how we go from a single category to multiple categories, how we go from tools to a future home butler — I definitely hope this can succeed. Today, at this company, what I pursue is living up to the responsibility I should bear, setting a good development goal for the company, leading the company to reach that goal. I hope to accomplish some things that are valuable, that create something.

Do you personally have an entrepreneur you really admire, or other business leaders?

I don't think there's a fixed one. Actually, as a CEO, you find that even going out to a noodle shop, having a bowl of noodles, you're thinking about how they run the shop. It's — it's like we say — anywhere, anytime, it seems you can learn, learn from it. Really, I have this feeling. Going out and seeing a coffee shop, I'd also think about how they run this coffee shop. Right? Of course, whether you're in consumer electronics or tech, you also look — this is how you get your energy. It seems to be everywhere, or it should be everywhere. And the times keep changing too, right? It's hard to pin down and quantify that it's some one person you must imitate and learn from. I think this is — From what I know, most entrepreneurs are eager to learn, willing to actively learn different things.

Who's a CEO teacher you've met recently? Maybe it could be a noodle shop owner.

A while back I took a trip to Pang Dong Lai. I think for him to be in a fourth-tier city and actually build a company like that — it's pretty interesting.

We ask every guest to recommend a book of their life. Do you have one?

I think the one that left an impression on me was back when I was in college: my father gave me Kazuo Inamori's "A Life" (The Philosophy of Living). That's pretty good. Mm, that probably, in my early days, about how a company or an entrepreneur should run things, formed some ideas in me.

Mm, I also have some rapid-fire questions, ha. A favorite food, anywhere in the world?

Oatmeal bowl.

Why?

It's quick. It's healthy.

Oh — a favorite place, anywhere in the world?

Shenzhen.

Why?

I think it's the place I was born. It's quite interesting — that place is full of warmth, full of passion. Even the people I meet — I took a cab and the driver asked, "Young man, where are you from?" I said I'm from Suzhou. I didn't mention I was born in Shenzhen. He said, "Ah, look at me — at my age I still came to Shenzhen to make it. You should come to Shenzhen." I thought that was just great — Shenzhen's calling card. And maybe it has something to do with where you were born.

Based on your current understanding, what's one key, important bet?

I think it's global competition.

Our studio is called the Language Is the World Studio. When you first heard this name, what did you think of?

Two thoughts came to me. First: language is a great invention — a great invention of humanity. Language can — I think it accomplishes two things. One is what we call the transmission of information — preservation and transmission, memory and transmission. The other thing: it can create, right? That is, we say, you can write — you can record an event, you can write a story. It's all language. So I think our understanding of the world is like this too. Part of it comes from what we call this preservation and transmission — our understanding of the world. And part of it comes from using language to describe a world you want, or the world you imagine.

item.description:
## 一、被精心设计的"狼眼":一个关于缺失天性的系统性补偿
最耐人寻味的细节不在他的策略里,而在他的微信头像——那只被PS成血红色眼睛的狗。这是一个极少被谈论的现代企业管理学题目:**当一个人"天生拥有"时,如何为自己人工合成"饥饿"?**
传统创业者的狼性来自环境的匮乏——它是生理反应。而钱程面对的是一个相反的任务:他必须用认知层去模拟一种本应来自肠胃的欲望。他的处理方式不是道德说教,而是**环境设计学**——给自己每天要看一百次的头像植入一个视觉触发器。这其实和行为设计学里 BJ Fogg 教授的"微型习惯触发器"是同一套机制。换句话说,他在用产品经理的思路对自己做"用户体验改造"。
意外之处在于:**这揭示了他看待自己的根本方式——他把"钱程"当成一个需要被运营的产品,而不是一个有机生长的生命**。这解释了他为什么在企业里反复用"保底"与"冲顶"、"硬件/软件"、"打钉子的锤子"这类工程语言描述人生——因为他的自我管理本身,就是一场精密的组织变革。
## 二、"农耕文明 vs 游牧文明"的隐藏对称:一个比战略更深的身份谜题
他用"农耕 vs 游牧"来定义公司的扩张风格

item.title: [Bits + Bips] Chips Crack, Bitcoin Holds. Is Crypto Finally Trading on Its Own Drivers?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：Bitcoin 的"平盘"恰恰暴露了它的脆弱，而不是韧性

市场叙事都在欢呼"芯片崩了、比特币扛住了"，仿佛这是去相关性的胜利。但 John 的说法藏着一个被忽略的真相：Bitcoin 之所以看起来"独立"，不是因为它找到了自己的驱动因素，而是因为它的市场深度不够承接 AI 泡沫的溢出资金。 这是一个让人意外的反转——流动性稀薄既是上涨时的加速器，也是下跌时的放大器，而"平盘"只是两种力量恰好对冲的瞬间结果。

真正值得追问的是：如果 AI 真的进入系统性去杠杆（数千亿美元 CapEx 收缩），那笔资金不会流向比特币。它会流向美国国债和黄金——因为撤资的是机构、是债券市场的"math people"，不是零售 degen。所以"crypto trades on its own drivers"这句话在今天可能是对的，但一旦 AI 真的崩了，相关性会在最糟的时刻跳回 1，正如 John 悄悄埋下的那句话："correlation tends to hop to one at the worst possible time."

二、跨领域连接：AI 泡沫、代际庞氏骗局与 Luigi Mangione 现象是同一个系统的三个症状

这期播客表面谈了三件事——AI 估值、通胀、年轻人虚无主义——但它们其实是同一个代际资本错配问题的三副面孔：

  • AI 泡沫：老一代掌控资本的机构把钱堆向尚未证明单位经济学的 frontier labs，因为他们没有别的地方可以放资金来追上退休负债缺口。
  • 代际 pump and dump（Nick 的妙语）：婴儿潮世代把美国债务从零推到 40 万亿，同时享受了 40 年的利率下行红利——两头通吃。
  • Luigi 现象（John 的洞察）：年轻人在镜头前为凶手欢呼不是"愤怒表达"，而是退出系统的公开声明——financial nihilism 的政治化版本。

这三者的隐藏连接是：它们都是同一个 duration mismatch 的爆发点。老一代用长久期承诺（社保、医保、养老金）绑定了未来几十年的国家现金流，然后用短久期政治周期不断延后清算。当年轻人意识到自己是这个久期不匹配的最终接盘方，他们的理性反应有两种：要么线性退出（Luigi 式、meme 币式、不生育式），要么非线性暴力（巴黎街头、米兰骚乱）。AI 泡沫其实是老一代的最后一次 duration gamble——"我能不能在清算到来前，用 AGI 把生产率撬动起来，让我的养老金承诺不违约？"

这是一场和时间的赛跑，而不是和技术的赛跑。

三、被所有人忽视的"稳定币真实曲线"：Tether 的市值占比才是最诚实的宏观指标

Nick 不经意间给出了一个所有宏观分析师都应该追踪的信号，但没人在用——Tether 相对 USDC 的市占率。他说："once you see USDC pass Tether, that's when crypto trading will be a minority of the market."

反过来理解：只要 Tether 还在赢，说明稳定币的真实用户仍然以投机和灰色跨境结算为主，而不是企业支付。 这意味着当下所有关于"稳定币颠覆 B2B 1.6 千万亿市场"的论述都还只是叙事，不是现实。更有意思的跨领域连接是：Tether 市占率的斜率，可能是一个比 CPI 更早的全球南方通胀/资本管制指标。因为 Tether 的真实用户是阿根廷、尼日利亚、土耳其、东南亚——那些本币崩溃的地方。当 Tether 份额上升，不是加密牛市在来，而是全球货币秩序在裂开新的缝。

四、关于"productive bubble"的隐藏陷阱

Chris 说 AI 是 productive bubble 不是 Dutch tulip，这是对的——但有一个被忽略的细节：productive bubble 的受益者和买单者往往不是同一群人。铁路泡沫让美国有了铁路，但买铁路债券的人破产了；互联网泡沫让世界有了光纤，但 Lucent 和 WorldCom 的股东归零了。

那么谁会在 AI 泡沫中捡起光纤？按历史模式，不是 OpenAI、不是 Anthropic——它们会像 Netscape 一样被遗忘——而是五年后那些在便宜的二手 H100 和被银行强制拍卖的 data center 容量上做应用的小公司。所以如果你真的相信"productive bubble"叙事，你应该在不良资产清算时期去追踪二手 GPU 市场和破产 data center 的 REIT 拍卖，而不是去抄底 CoreWeave 的债。

这是加密 degen 该学的教训：speculation 推动基础设施，但 speculator 不是基础设施的受益者。

📝 转录文本

开场金句

"I call it the generational pump and dump, right? Both sides of the aisle were complicit in growing the debt burden of the U.S. from effectively zero when they were born to $40 trillion. And interest rates went down for 40 years. And so they really like got it on both sides."

节目开场

Hey, everyone. Welcome to Bits and Bips, where we explore how crypto and macro collide one basis point at a time. We're here with two special guests today to discuss the latest stories in the worlds of crypto and macro.

But before we begin, a quick break. This episode is brought to you by Nexo, the premier digital assets wealth platform. Earn daily interest on your crypto or borrow funds all through one platform trusted by more than 10 million clients. Find out more at nexo.com. Geo restrictions, eligibility and terms apply.

Before we get started, I want to ask you for something. We're making a bunch of decisions right now about Unchained — what we make next, when we go live, what we should be doing more of — and I'd rather hear from you before we make them than after. So we put together a survey. It takes just a few minutes, it's anonymous, and there's a box where you can tell me what we could be doing better. I read all the responses. The link is in the show notes, or you can snap the QR code on screen, or go to unchainedcrypto.com/survey. Thanks.

All right. As always, I'm your host, Austin Campbell, high scholar of Zero Knowledge Group. I'm here with one of my usual co-hosts, Chris Perkins, the golden hand of Franklin Crypto. And today we have two guests: John D'Agostino, head of strategy at Coinbase Institutional, and Nick Van Eck, CEO and co-founder of Agora.

第一部分：芯片崩了，比特币扛住了——加密终于走出自己的行情？

Guys, let's start with a topic that slams together a bunch of things we've been talking about here for a while, which is: chips are cracking, but crypto is doing okay.

To set this up: NASDAQ had its worst week since June. The chip index lost 11.4%. South Korea's KOSPI had its worst week since 2008. Bitcoin finished the week roughly flat.

So the question that I have for everybody here is, as we're looking at this: did crypto trade on its own drivers, or did it just take losses earlier? Because equities — NASDAQ down 4.5%, chips down over 10%, KOSPI down almost 15%, it rebounded 1.7% today, so not totally dead. Bitcoin was essentially flat. ETH was essentially flat. But the equity component — strategy and Coinbase — traded down in line with the market, down almost 10%, about 5% respectively.

So Citrini was out saying crypto now has fundamentals. He has a 15-token basket. They skipped Bitcoin and ETH with the statement: "we can't assume that the majors, primarily Bitcoin and ETH, will make new all-time highs on this. Even if they do, there are better expressions."

Milk Road shot back: "Thankfully, Bitcoin and ETH don't derive value from Citrini's assumptions."

And in the Kobayashi letter: "we believe the S&P 500 is a bear market within a bull market," noting 84% of S&P stocks are 10% off their highs.

John D'Agostino 的回答：流动性才是答案

John, I want to flip it to you as somebody who thinks a lot about macro themes and strategy. What do you make of the AI trade cooling off, the performance of the S&P, but crypto actually holding up decently well here?

John: Well, first of all, thanks for having me. It's always great to be on with you and Chris, and it's a pleasure to be here with Nick — big fan of all you guys.

Look, we've seen this story before. I'm always very hesitant and concerned about describing any asset — whether it's my old days in commodities or Bitcoin or crypto — as non-correlated over the long term. Because as we all know, that correlation tends to hop to one at the worst possible time.

So here's the good news — and the bad news in some situations — the answer to why Bitcoin is trading the way it's trading is just a function of its liquidity level. While Bitcoin has good liquidity, it goes through periods of tighter liquidity, and you have these liquidity gaps. We've been the beneficiary of those gaps on the upside many, many times, and it's harmed us on the downside. We talk more about the downside than the upside.

I think this is one of those times. There are people who postulate that we're going to have this massive correction in AI, and all those hundreds of billions or trillions of dollars of forward investment is going to shift back into other assets like Bitcoin. If that is what we had seen over the last few weeks, then we would have seen Bitcoin do more than just tread water.

So I think it's getting some of the runoff. I think some of this is the post-high of clarity not passing, and people kind of just pricing in that. And it's also just a beneficiary of thinner liquidity than AI markets. Strategy making big buys. The overall thesis continues to hold. The market's not as large as the AI equities market, and so it takes less to hold it up.

I wouldn't read too much into it, because then people get extremely disappointed when it trades risk-on in other environments. But it's nice when we see these handles being held through choppy periods.

Chris Perkins 的宏观焦虑

Austin: Can I just jump in and say that John has the authority to speak on AI today because, for people who are listening, he's dressed like Jensen Huang.

John: Yeah, you caught it, right? That's why I'm cosplaying as Jensen, so I get credibility.

Chris: John, I'll chime in. Look, it feels like the world is blowing up right now. Look what's going on in France. I was driving up 95 this weekend, and diesel was at like $6.55. That's pretty crazy. And I think it's really impacting people at home.

I threw the radio on as I was driving up 95. The first thing I hear is a Governor Hochul ad commercial saying how she's going to focus on destroying data centers. So it feels like so many things are coming to a head — with inflation, with AI, with social unrest across the globe.

Against that backdrop, for crypto, that kind of feeds into the long-term thesis around crypto, right? Trustless, permissionless, Bitcoin, independent of government — it's a store of value that you don't need to depend on. That original Bitcoin thesis is still real and live.

There's some risk as we're starting to see more and more threats to cryptography — we should talk about that. But that underlying thesis still lives. And on top of that, we have regulatory de-risking that continues to occur, extending beyond Bitcoin into the other asset classes. If you happen to be a security, if you happen to have fundamentals, it's not a death sentence anymore. You can actually accrue value because you have those fundamentals.

So it does feel like the crypto market, at least, is starting to change a little bit. It feels like the setup is good when you see relative resiliency during a period of weakness. I'm oftentimes bullish on this show, but it doesn't seem like a terrible setup.

John 的"ETF 分销"视角

John: Pick your poison, right? Do we think it's a risk asset? Do we think it's a hedge against geopolitical risk? Do we think that it's a long-term monetary debasement trade? In theory, all of those parties, regardless of what your thesis is, should be spending a lot more time and a little more risk capital thinking about crypto and thinking about Bitcoin as its leader. So it doesn't surprise me that it would have some level of resiliency.

Also keep in mind this huge wave of ETFs opening up for everyday RIAs to sell continues to expand as more and more of these banks get comfortable. That ETF product is sold, not bought. Now that you have more and more of those RIAs being able to sell it, we can see more distribution.

We're seeing good pickup on our tokenized equities offering out in the UAE. So there's a lot of reasons to be optimistic. Chris, I'm sorry you think the world is blowing up. I'll remind everyone we're not even close to highest levels of inflation-adjusted crude oil. I hope we don't get there, but I get why people are scared right now.

Nick Van Eck：稳定币三到五年的"拉快"效应

Austin: So I want to go the other way on this and ask Nick. You're an operator actually in crypto markets right now, the CEO of a company in this space. What are you seeing?

Nick: We obviously operate a stablecoin business. What we've seen over the last year — and you've seen this with Bitcoin as well — is the asset class is really maturing. But I'd say stablecoins and the growth of that sector is completely separate from what is happening in the risk-assets crypto.

My full thesis on Bitcoin from 2016 has always been the monetary debasement trade. That continues to look good and has moved at a faster clip over the last decade than I would have expected.

But with the stablecoin market, GENIUS really pulled forward enterprise demand by three to five years when that passed. That was a big surprise. I certainly didn't think we were going to get the most important piece of banking legislation in my lifetime six months into a new president's term, given what had been happening in the prior administration.

We are seeing enterprises across the spectrum race to adopt stables — telecom companies, mobility businesses, hotels — because it's a better form of value movement across the world. That market is accelerating and heating up at a probably much higher rate than what is happening with regards to Bitcoin and other risk assets.

比特币的"冷漠期"（apathy stage）

My view on where Bitcoin is, having been in the space almost a decade personally, is that we are in the apathy stage. We're past the max bearishness — people think Bitcoin is going to zero. My view is that it's been mostly unchanged because people have forgotten about it outside of the people that treat it as the monetary debasement trade.

I think things will start to look more positive for risk assets in the crypto markets over the next year. The AI trade falling off is going to bring liquidity to a ton of other markets, crypto being one of them. AI has completely sucked the liquidity out of the room of every other market.

I was listening to Josh Brown's podcast yesterday, and they were talking about how some of the memory names are off 54% from their all-time highs year-to-date and are still up 100%-plus. The markets have been really sucked into everything that is around AI. So that trade starting to unwind is positive for a lot of other markets.

稳定币市值的下滑：真实用户仍是加密交易者

Chris: Hey, Nick, so we've seen stablecoin market cap actually come down a bit, which was not on a lot of people's bingo card. Do you attribute that to the AI trade as well?

Nick: I think the stablecoin market today is still mostly correlated to risk assets and crypto trading. The enterprise adoption of stablecoins is still minuscule as part of the overall pie of stables. There's about $300 billion in stablecoins outstanding, give or take.

There are companies that we're working with that are planning to adopt stablecoins — that do that in revenue on an annual basis. They're not going to move to stablecoins overnight, but it goes to show that it's a drop in the bucket.

I put out a chart a month ago where B2B payments with stablecoins was about a quarter trillion last year. And on an annual basis, B2B payments in general is $1.6 quadrillion. So it's a fraction of the market, and I think it's still mostly crypto trading today.

That's why Tether is still the largest stablecoin. Once you see USDC or some of these more institutional-grade stables pass Tether, that's when crypto trading will be a minority of the market.

第二部分：代币化股票与"一小时上手"理论

Austin: On that note, I want to pile in and go back to something, John, you were saying earlier. As I'm interpreting crypto price action, you were talking about this earlier — there's not one mindset about why these things have value, especially Bitcoin. The fragmentation of thesis there might be larger than most assets and commodities that we've seen over the last two decades.

One of the things you said that was interesting to me is you guys have seen really good results in the UAE on tokenized stocks — which is not selling Bitcoin, not selling ETH. That's something totally different. So what are you seeing on the Coinbase side there?

John 的"一小时上手"门槛

John: I do think there's something to be said for training people outside of our ecosystem to get comfortable transacting on chain. Tokenized stock is not the same as Bitcoin — they're completely different creatures. But I do think overall, if people get more and more comfortable holding value on chain and doing it in a simple, easy-to-do way...

I have a one-hour thesis. If the average person — the average technically literate individual, they can work their home PC, they can work their phone, they can engage in online transactions — if they can't learn to use a new system in under an hour with some degree of confidence, I think the probability of getting widespread adoption goes down measurably.

Chris: That's right. I've got to jump, guys. Good to see you this week. Good to see you, Chris.

Austin：汽车红旗手的类比

Austin: Let's end on a positive note there as well. One of the discussions I was having with a friend about quantum cryptography — we were talking about the news thing. He still works in the mathematics space. He said, "if you have a working quantum computer that can decode essentially all encrypted communications, we're going to be traveling into space at extreme rates of speed in the very near future and probably doing things like curing cancer." The upsides will be much larger than the downsides. By the way, we'll discover new ways to communicate securely.

There is this natural tendency — like when the automobile showed up, they had people having to walk in front of them, waving a red flag at first, and everybody's focused on the downside. But I don't hear much "hey, back to horses" today. So I think it is important to focus on the positive side of things.

The quick analogy I'll give — and it's been useful to me in explaining this to my parents — is: imagine that we all believe teleportation would exist in like 100 years or 50 years, and something happened which made us think that teleportation would be viable and economic for the average person within five years. That would be scary to some degree — your locked door would be irrelevant at that point. So we could focus on the scary parts of it, or we could focus on the fact that we can now teleport goods and services and food anywhere in the world cheaply, instantly, and without delay.

So I think of this impending Q-day, I think of recursive AGI, as in those lines.

节目收尾

All right. So on that note, we can pause here for today.

I want to let everybody know Unchained is running a listener survey, and it decides real things — things like recap shows, what time things stream, what goes into premium. It's anonymous, takes a few minutes. Everybody who finishes it gets a free month of premium. Go to unchainedcrypto.com/survey. It is open through November 8th.

On that note, I want to thank you two guys for joining us. This was definitely fun. You are welcome back anytime, regardless of what my cranky two co-hosts say. So we'll see you guys again. Take care and thank you.

Thank you for watching, and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips. Just remember, nothing we say here is investment advice. And please check unchainedcrypto.com/bitsandbips for more disclosures. We'll be right back.
