item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：Bitcoin 的"平盘"恰恰暴露了它的脆弱，而不是韧性
市场叙事都在欢呼"芯片崩了、比特币扛住了"，仿佛这是去相关性的胜利。但 John 的说法藏着一个被忽略的真相：**Bitcoin 之所以看起来"独立"，不是因为它找到了自己的驱动因素，而是因为它的市场深度不够承接 AI 泡沫的溢出资金。** 这是一个让人意外的反转——流动性稀薄既是上涨时的加速器，也是下跌时的放大器，而"平盘"只是两种力量恰好对冲的瞬间结果。
真正值得追问的是：如果 AI 真的进入系统性去杠杆（数千亿美元 CapEx 收缩），那笔资金**不会**流向比特币。它会流向美国国债和黄金——因为撤资的是机构、是债券市场的"math people"，不是零售 degen。所以"crypto trades on its own drivers"这句话在今天可能是对的，但一旦 AI 真的崩了，相关性会在最糟的时刻跳回 1，正如 John 悄悄埋下的那句话："correlation tends to hop to one at the worst possible time."
## 二、跨领域连

item.title: [a16z] Should You Trust ChatGPT With Your Health?
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最意外的观察：这场对话里藏着一个"反向AGI叙事"

OpenAI 公开讲"AGI benefits humanity"，但 Karan 在整段访谈里几乎从不谈"替代医生"。相反，他反复提到一个关键数据点——临床指南渗透到一线医生实践需要 5 到 17 年。这才是真正令人震撼的点：

OpenAI 在医疗领域的真实野心，不是"造一个比医生更聪明的AI"，而是压缩人类已有知识的传播时延。

换句话说，他们的护城河不是智能的上限，而是智能的"扩散速度"。这颠覆了"AI 医生"的通俗想象——真正的变革不是发明新知识，而是让 2024 年的共识今天就落地到巴西乡下的全科诊所里。这是知识考古学意义上的事件，而不是技术奇点。

二、跨领域连接：医疗 AI 的"围棋 Move 37"与金融市场的"套利悖论"

Karan 提到他们期待医疗版的"Move 37"——AlphaGo 那步让所有人类顶尖棋手觉得"愚蠢但正确"的棋。但这里有一个他没有明说的悖论，值得挑明：

  • 围棋的 Move 37 之所以能被识别为"brilliant"，是因为围棋有明确、短周期的胜负函数。
  • 医疗没有。一个"看似愚蠢但正确"的治疗建议，可能需要 10–30 年才能通过纵向研究被确证为对的。

这意味着医疗 AI 的 Move 37 在当下几乎不可能被识别。它更像金融市场中的"长期套利"——短期看是错的、不被接受的、甚至被处罚的（想想 Michael Burry 做空次贷的 18 个月黑暗期），长期才被证明是对的。

真正的含义：OpenAI 要么需要构建一套"反共识置信机制"（允许模型给出当下会被否决的建议），要么它永远只能在"追赶共识"的象限里活动，不可能真的"raise the ceiling"。而目前所有的 safety 对齐工作，恰恰在把模型往"永远不要显得不合群"的方向调。这是一个结构性矛盾。

三、被访谈巧妙回避的真相：OpenAI 正在做的不是"医疗"，是"注意力捕获"

注意他反复强调的一个结构性事实：

"300 million weekly health users, vast majority are free users, most of them outside the US."

把这句话翻译成商业语言：OpenAI 正在成为全球发展中国家事实上的"初级医疗守门人"，而且是免费的、无执照的、无监管的、无边界的。

这里面藏着一个未来 5 年最被低估的地缘变量： - 美国 FDA、欧盟 EMA 还在争论"AI 作为医疗器械的注册路径" - 但在肯尼亚、印度、巴西，ChatGPT 已经是数亿人唯一能接触到的"医生" - 一旦这个事实稳定下来，监管只能追认、而不能逆转

这与 移动支付在中国的扩散路径 高度同构：银行体系跟不上的地方，微信支付"事实"接管；传统医疗跟不上的地方，LLM"事实"接管。等到监管想管时，用户的信任已经不在监管体系这边了。

Karan 整段话里反复出现 "last mile"（最后一公里）这个说法——但他其实在描述的是 "first mile"：全球数十亿人第一次接触医疗建议的入口，正在从诊所、药店、长辈经验，悄悄迁移到 ChatGPT 的对话框。这不是医疗 AI，这是医疗认知的入口战争。

四、一个让系统性视角打开的小发现

Karan 提到 Epic（美国 EHR 寡头）的 UI 里内嵌了 ChatGPT 侧栏。但他没点破的是——医疗 AI 的终局架构之战，不在模型层，在"侧栏"的归属权：

  • 谁拥有那个 sidebar，谁就拥有医生工作流的"反射神经"
  • Epic 让 OpenAI 住进自己家，是在赌 OpenAI 永远不会自己盖房子
  • OpenAI 让自己住进 Epic，是在赌 Epic 迟早会被绕过

这是一场互相假装合作的双重时间套利。十年后回看，这段话里埋着的真正信号可能不是"AI 进入医疗"，而是"EHR 时代的终结开始了"。

📝 转录文本

Should You Trust ChatGPT With Your Health?

a16z Podcast · 嘉宾：Karan Singhal (OpenAI, Head of Health AI Research) · 主持：Jay Rughani (a16z)

开场：healthcare 的规模与稀缺悖论

5.3 plus trillion we spend on healthcare. If it were its own country, it'd be the third largest GDP. And yet we have a ton of scarcity.

OpenAI's mission is to ensure AGI benefits all of humanity and give people access to trustworthy, abundant, reliable health intelligence.

One of the stories that I was most touched by was the story of Nathan Levent. He basically had this kind of long saga with his son where at some point he was suffering a lot of fatigue and irritableness, and AI helped them navigate the process — and it turns out he was diagnosed with an aggressive form of leukemia.

Some of the work that you've done around mental health — there's a lot of complexity. How do you help guide a user on that given that could mean so many things?

We've just been working with a bunch of licensed mental health experts across the world to think about the right ways to define model behavior and a bunch of tricky scenarios and ensure that we can get to a level of consensus where we can actually measure performance.

Let's talk about trust. A person can be speaking to an LLM really hoping to hear that everything is okay, but from a medical perspective, they need to hear perhaps something very different. How do you teach an AI to recognize the difference?

节目介绍

Hey everyone. Welcome back to the podcast. I'm Jay Rughani, a partner at A16Z, leading investments in healthcare and biotechnology companies. I'm joined by Karan Singhal of OpenAI. He leads health AI research at OpenAI and we've got a lot to talk about. Thanks for being here.

Thanks for having me.

一、每周数亿人在 ChatGPT 上问健康问题 —— 他们在问什么？

I want to start with the big question. There was a report earlier this year — you all have talked about it publicly. Hundreds of millions of people each week use ChatGPT for health-related questions. What are they asking? What are the kinds of questions they're asking that they're not getting from our mainstream healthcare system?

Yeah. Let me zoom out and talk a little bit about why we're investing in health in the first place.

So, OpenAI's mission is to ensure AGI benefits all of humanity. And we see that at a high level happening in three ways:

  1. Building and deploying AGI — building capable models, building products around them, deploying them, partnerships.
  2. Preventing downside — safety of various kinds.
  3. Making upside happen.

We view health as a really, really concrete way to make upside happen, and also work on some of the safety problems that come up in healthcare along the way.

We're really invested in making sure basically two things. One is that we can raise the floor of human health and give people access to trustworthy, abundant, reliable health intelligence for free or nearly free — and really raise the ceiling as well, and make things possible that weren't possible before.

The best way to see "raising the floor" is to think about how we've been working in the consumer space. As we reported, there's more than 300 million people weekly using ChatGPT for health and wellness types of questions, and we take that as an incredibly important responsibility to get right. That's been rapidly growing over time.

If you think about the experience of getting healthcare, even in the US, even in the Bay Area — if you're looking to get a specialist appointment, it can take weeks or months. You might spend a lot of time figuring out how to get an appointment and scheduling. After all that time, maybe you get 15 minutes with the doctor where you don't feel adequately prepared, and you walk out thinking, "Oh, I had six more questions I wanted to ask."

Our hope is that AI can be part of this care journey with you — health is not something that's just restricted to these 15-minute intervals. AI can actually help you navigate your care journey.

That reflects how people are using AI on the consumer side today: coming in with questions and concerns, information they'd like to have. They want to figure out how to navigate their care visits, ask questions, follow up on things the doctor told them. We're finding that in between these visits is when AI can help people most on the consumer side. And we're making similar investments on the clinician side and on the enterprise side as well.

Yeah, it's amazing. We have an extraordinary healthcare system — if I got really sick, there's no country I'd rather be in than the US. And yet we have a ton of scarcity. Over 100 million people don't have access to a regular primary care doc. Even the ones who do often have to wait 40-plus days to see that doctor. Sometimes you meet the doctor exactly as you said and it's a quick 15-minute visit and you have more questions.

I saw a dermatologist last week about something. I wrote down all my questions beforehand in an Apple Note and I still forgot to ask something — and now I'm scheduling a follow-up and it's another four months out. It happens to all of us. We've all felt that.

Is there a specific patient story or recent case that you all have seen that helps us imagine where the world is going?

Nathan Labenz 的故事

One way in which the work of our team is gratifying is just seeing the numbers and how useful it seems to be for people. Another way is just hearing from people — we get people reaching out multiple times a week saying "here's how this has helped me."

One of the stories I was most touched by was the story of Nathan Labenz and his son. He hosts the Cognitive Revolution podcast and told his story there. He had this long saga with his son where at some point his very young son was suffering a lot of fatigue and irritableness. AI helped them navigate the process of realizing this was a pretty serious thing while they were on vacation — and deciding to take him for testing, and repeatedly telling them "take this seriously," even when doctors were a little less sure and actually downplaying it.

It turns out he was diagnosed with an aggressive form of leukemia. Throughout his care journey, Nathan reports using GPT-5 Pro at that time quite a bit for helping navigate the process, understanding lab reports, even before a specialist had time to help interpret. It brought them a lot of peace of mind.

Nathan tells that story in his podcast — would recommend that for folks.

二、为什么用通用模型做医疗？"specialized training in a general model"

In many ways, OpenAI is building health intelligence into your model at every step — but it's the same model folks use to write code or plan a vacation. Can you help folks understand why you're building it that way from an architectural standpoint? Why is a general-purpose AI the right foundation for something as complicated as medicine?

People often ask us about this general vs. specialized model debate. I used to work on specialized models in a previous role, so I have experience on both sides.

The most important thing is: what we're talking about here is specialized training in a general model — which is actually the best of both worlds.

For ChatGPT and all the models we ship, across every stage of model training, we have specialized healthcare data added to each phase of training — since all of our models in the last year. The result: you now have a model that benefits from all the scale and general improvements and reasoning of the big frontier models, and benefits from specialized training (for example, integrating data from working with a bunch of physicians across the globe).

If you forked and said "we're going to train a smaller specialized model just for healthcare" — like I used to, and like many people have — what you'd find is that model would fall behind the frontier relatively quickly, because the pace of frontier general-model improvements is so fast.

If you bet on scale, what we've found at OpenAI, as an industry, is that things will get better. So we're hitching a ride on that scale frontier, and leveraging the fact that we can integrate evals and training data into the models to make them both specialized and benefit from general capability.

三、"口袋里的私人医生"愿景 —— 距离我们多远？

I want to start imagining what's possible with the technology you're building. Where it is today is amazing, but you're not stopping.

Many people are allured by the idea of a personal doctor in your pocket — something that is perfectly knowledgeable, has knowledge across all medical specialties (so you don't necessarily need to go see a cardiologist and a dermatologist separately), something that is perfectly personalized to you, has all your medical history in context, remembers everything you've said and your preferences. And is also able to motivate you and nudge you — so that the information it gives you is given at the right time, in a way that nudges you towards better health behaviors or adhering to the protocol your doctor gave you.

Is that the experience you're building at OpenAI in the fullness of time, and how close are we?

That's something we're really excited about. We are very excited about this vision of a proactive personal health assistant. I don't think that's any kind of replacement for actually having a doctor or having access to a doctor. But thinking about the ways we can take that experience of getting health information and make it more personal to your context is a really important part of our investment in health.

ChatGPT Health is a consumer offering that enables users to connect their health information — for that information to be used securely, not to be used for training data or targeting ads or anything like this. That's a big part of how we think about moving towards this world of increasingly personal access and proactive access.

It's also been how we've been thinking about deployment. We've been deploying this as widely as possible to our free users as well as our pro users. Of the 300 million weekly active health users, the vast majority are free users. And most of them are outside the US as well. We take that question of distribution really centrally.

Greg Brockman 讲过的那个救命案例

Use cases help people imagine what's actually possible. When Greg Brockman came on the podcast, he spoke about a situation he had with a friend of a friend who was in the hospital. Her physician was about to administer a certain medication. She double-checked that medication in ChatGPT, realized based on her medical history that she would have some drug interaction or adverse event. She showed that to her doctor, and her doctor agreed and said, "I didn't have enough time to look through your medical history to notice that. Thank you so much for raising that."

Shouldn't we do that for everyone, all the time? If it's cheap enough and convenient enough, can't we do a second, third, fourth opinion for every clinical scenario? Is that where we're going?

I love this idea of a safety net for both patients and clinicians that is just there in the care journey. Not always interfering or being the middleman, but augmenting the existing experience.

We did this work directly on the clinician side in a series of experiments with Penda Health, studying this idea of a clinician co-pilot. It was deployed as a safety net for the clinician — proactively suggesting "hey, this might be off, there might be this medication interaction you might not be tracking, can we potentially adjust that."

I think we're going to see the same thing happen on the patient side. I'm very excited about this idea of a proactive agent in your care journey — making sure that if your A1C rises and you're diabetic, you get a review of your medications by your doctor.

四、Agents 在医疗里的用武之地

You mentioned personalized proactive agents. Personal agents in general have emerged on the scene over the last few months — Instinct, Muse, Grokbot, OpenAI's Dots. You can give these AI apps an objective, and it can execute a series of tasks. It can use your preferences, access all your applications that you give it permission to, access your credit card information if you give it, and execute an objective on your behalf.

One can't help but imagine the possibilities in navigating our wonderful but often disjointed healthcare system: - Scheduling an appointment and making sure your insurance covers it - Helping you follow a care protocol post-discharge - Negotiating with your insurance company on a medical billing error

All kinds of tasks that create friction in our healthcare system. Is that where you're going?

I'm very excited about that vision. From both patient and clinician perspective, one of the most difficult things about the healthcare system is fragmentation and lack of connection of the ecosystem.

Healthcare is also one of those industries where you shouldn't expect everything to have an MCP connector tomorrow. It's a place where there's legacy software, not necessarily the best connectivity with AI or software in the first place. Many people are running their primary EHR software on a VM — a virtual machine in the cloud.

There's actually an interesting component where a virtual machine makes things easier in some ways for AI agents. This is absolutely ripe for agents and computer use. A lot of the barriers that have traditionally existed between patients and the care they need, clinicians and the care they deliver, and healthcare data in general — I think a lot of those will dissolve in the coming months.

五、信任（Trust）：模型如何适配不同用户

Let's talk about trust. The same underlying model can help me understand my lab results, but can also help a highly trained specialized physician make sense of a very complicated case. What do you change in the answer so it's legible to each of those two personas?

Health is a place where it moves at the speed of trust. You need to be able to not only make the models better and measure them, but also communicate and bring the world along.

The brief answer: we evaluate and train the models by working with experts across the world and getting feedback in various ways to tailor their behavior — whether a person is a lay user, an "expert lay user" who's been navigating a complex care journey, a clinician, or other user personas.

Back for the original HealthBench evaluation we released in May 2025, there was a theme focused on this distinction — how the model tailored its level of technical jargon to whether a person was a lay user or clinician. Since then, we've gotten better at both measuring and training the models toward that.

当用户想听"没事"，但事实并不是没事

A person can be speaking to an LLM, sharing all their symptoms, but really hoping to hear everything is okay. From a consumer NPS perspective, they want to hear reassurance — but from a medical perspective, they need to hear something very different. How do you teach an AI to recognize the difference, and manage competing product objectives?

This is super central to how we do both evaluation and training.

One thing you could do: bring a few clinicians into the OpenAI health team and say "you figure out how to navigate these uncertain cases." This is actually not the best approach. If you ask five physicians any question, you'll get eight different answers.

One of the first things we did when we first started focusing on health at OpenAI is build this global physician network of hundreds of experts across dozens of specialties, languages, and countries of practice. So we weren't relying on one or two or three physicians to adjudicate — especially in areas where there could be disagreement.

How do you balance competing objectives? It's basically a prioritization of safety. When there's hundreds of millions of health conversations coming in, we take our obligation very seriously. Across the evaluation stack and training stack, we have evaluations that track difficult situations where the model should go and say "hey, this is unsafe, you should seek care" — even if the user doesn't want to hear it or wants some alternative treatment.

用户与医生意见不一致时怎么办？

Another instance of disagreement: me as the consumer, I ask a medical question of ChatGPT. I show the response to my doctor during a visit — my doctor loves me, by the way — and they disagree. How should I handle that?

I think you should handle it similarly to any other disagreement. People disagree about different things, and you have a right as a patient to ask for another doctor's opinion. That's what I'd advocate for, whether or not you're also using ChatGPT.

没有共识的医学议题：如何处理？

Some parts of medicine there's not a lot of disagreement about — but much of medicine is still being discovered. There's disagreement in the medical field. How do you think about correctness in those instances?

Great question. Important with or without AI.

If you zoom out and look at how medical consensus is distributed today: you have people writing biomedical papers suggesting improvements or treatments. Then there's a yearly process across different specialties of building clinical guidelines — flowcharts that describe roughly what you should do in different scenarios based on the latest research.

The final step — what people actually do in practice — turns out to be a massive bottleneck. There are studies on how long it takes for clinical guidelines to penetrate the practice of everyday doctors across the world. Depending on the study, this takes 5 to 17 years.

You don't want to be practicing medicine 5 to 17 years behind. One thing we think about is how to compress that period down to weeks, days, or even hours. This is one important principle behind our work in ChatGPT for Healthcare and ChatGPT for Clinicians — bringing the latest biomedical literature into the moment of care, allowing people to very quickly, in a 15-minute visit, get answers at the point of care.

For places where there's genuine medical uncertainty: you want to train models to recognize their own uncertainty — after browsing and gathering information, to know "there just isn't enough information" and be upfront. HealthBench includes public evaluations on hedging for exactly this.

灰色地带与政治化议题

Some areas are gray areas — unapproved peptides, vaccines — things that get politicized. How should a product like ChatGPT engage?

Where there's a lack of consensus, whether politicized or not, we want to make sure we're relying on the experts to help define standards for how the model should respond.

六、三类用户：患者、临床医生、企业

It feels like you're always thinking about one of three constituents: the patient, the individual clinician, or the enterprise.

There are three parts: 1. Making the models really good for these users 2. Building the right harness/product around it 3. The deployment or partnership motion to reach the right users

By default, the models are often pretty good these days. We're seeing dramatic improvements in performance and reliability. We talked about bringing free tier performance to the frontier — of the 1.2 billion people using ChatGPT weekly, giving them a model for health that's incredibly useful at the frontier, for free.

The second thing is our product offerings. If the activation energy to use the model to improve health is too high, people won't do it. For example, two years ago we were thinking: what are the security and compliance bottlenecks to providing an enterprise offering of ChatGPT to healthcare systems? So we invested in security and compliance — HIPAA compliance, privacy protections healthcare organizations need.

The third thing is partnerships and deployment. A few years ago, OpenAI was very early to speaking the language of healthcare. We were early in those conversations. Since then we've thought about each of those constituents and how to speak their language — because even if the models get really smart, if nobody trusts them or uses them, that's not achieving our mission.

与 Epic 的集成

You're alluding to work with Epic to integrate the product directly. Share more about that.

Fragmentation in healthcare has been one of the issues — data and workflows disconnected from each other is a big obstacle to productive AI use.

Our work with Epic: there's now a way to use Epic in ChatGPT (if you're a provider or healthcare professional), and for ChatGPT to be useful inside Epic itself. In the Epic workflow, you can have a sidebar where you use ChatGPT.

We're also working on different other connectors we've announced recently, with more coming. There's quite a bit of work breaking down barriers to the healthcare ecosystem being connected.

七、心理健康：另一个复杂维度

The last thing on trust: some of your work around mental health. If I ask my OpenAI Dot "I want to feel better over the next few weeks," how do you even interpret that?

Regardless of the surface, we are super committed to helping users when they're having a difficult time or in crisis. For Dots, we've been investing the same safeguards we've put in all our product surfaces.

With MentalHealthBench, we've taken the approach of not just measuring the safety floor but thinking about ways the models can proactively help raise the ceiling. Moving from just worrying about the safety floor to measuring positive mental health upsides.

We've been working with licensed mental health experts across the world to define model behavior and tricky scenarios, to reach consensus. People definitely disagree even more here than in physical health. We released that benchmark very recently — the goal is to create a shared ruler for all model developers, the healthcare industry, and mental health experts.

八、从"医疗信息"到"医疗照护"：AI 的边界在哪里？

Let's draw the distinction between medical information and medical care.

For medical information, ChatGPT and other LLMs are increasingly the better, faster, cheaper way to get an answer. But when medical information alone doesn't get me to resolution, I'm thrust into the traditional care system — prescriptions, in-person specialists, follow-up blood work, MRIs, physical exams.

Medical care is a bundled product: diagnosis, triage, care plan, empathy from the clinician, legal liability. Will AI provide all of that? Where will it stop short?

I don't think AI can or will provide all of that. There's a distinction between health information and medical care.

There's no future where any one company is delivering all the medical care. Our role is to think about what the last mile of medical care looks like for people. Can we make that easier for everybody, so that last mile just looks like the last 100 meters for all our partners?

OpenAI can do things relatively uniquely because of the front door to health it has. It can help you navigate a lot of these questions, help you with scheduling and logistics, act as a quarterback for your health.

That said, I don't think we'll resolve all these challenges in the short term. We're looking to enable our partners that are delivering care — using our models in various ways — to make these operations happen smoother.

Will I be talking to a clinician in the interface at any point? Or would you route me to a doctor?

We'll hopefully be very helpful in helping you navigate the process of finding care. I don't think we'll be in the business of doing all the things you mentioned. That's where we're really relying on all our startup and care-provider organizations and partners.

临床案例：UCSF 与 AdventHealth

We've had some amazing launch partners for ChatGPT for Healthcare. The retention on the offering has been a pleasant surprise.

  • UCSF: one of our earliest adopters for the Epic/EHR/ChatGPT connection. Clinicians using it for chart review — so caring for a patient doesn't need to be super fragmented with tab-switching.
  • AdventHealth: power users in deploying agents across the workspace. They've reported roughly 80% reduction in a lot of their administrative workflow costs using AI.

九、Overton window 正在移动：病人与医生对 AI 的态度

If I walk into my doctor's office and see ChatGPT open on their screen, should I be upset? Should I be happy?

I hear differing things, and it's changing over time. The Overton window is shifting in real time.

There may have been concern before — but increasingly, both sides are finding AI incredibly useful for their own personal purposes. Both parties might actually feel safer with AI in their care journey, whether it's their clinician using it or the patient using it as a sanity check. That attitude is definitely changing. We're not fully there yet, but that's my prediction.

If both patient and clinician have fully pre-processed everything through ChatGPT before a visit — what should they talk about?

My hope is they talk about the human aspect of healthcare. There's still a lot of uncertainty, a lot of empathy, a lot of bedside manner. There's also a lot of physical interaction. Theoretically not all information exists for the AI — part of the reason for a visit is to get more information through history-taking and investigation. That won't go away, especially the physical elements. Even from a cognitive perspective, empathy and that second check — I think people will still demand.

十、医疗版的 "Move 37"：AI 会发现人类没想到的策略吗？

In fields like chess and Go, as AI got really good, it revealed strategies even the best experts weren't exploiting. Are there equivalents in AI applied to health?

We've seen this at smaller scales. Let me zoom out — one thing motivating our team around raising the ceiling of human health is this notion of bringing to bear a Move 37 for health.

Move 37 comes from AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol. There was a specific move that in the moment seemed like a dumb, surprising move to all the human experts watching. In hindsight, it's this brilliant, insightful move that humans are now beginning to understand and learn from.

How do you get to a Move 37 in health — where models predict something a human might not have been able to predict, and in hindsight it seems correct, brilliant, insightful, impactful?

We're very early. You're going to see much more of this in the future.

One example from our study with Penda Health: clinicians were a little bit prone to overuse of antibiotics. A common pattern the models flagged: avoiding this overuse — thinking less about the local case and more about the global issue of antibiotic resistance.

You're going to see more examples of models taking in a longitudinal history of a user over 10 years — across all their data, EHR data, chat data — and making predictions that seemed impossible before, because a human can't integrate all that data in their head. That would rise to the occasion of being called a Move 37.

咖啡？糖？肌酸？褪黑素？

Consumers want to know: is creatine good for you? Is melatonin good for you? These are often understudied or without conclusive evidence. As people enter this information into ChatGPT, will we generate more evidence?

One of the most interesting things about agents is they solve a lot of the bottlenecks in analyzing data that already exists. EHR data, longitudinal histories, claims — data generated and stored, where insights aren't fully mined.

One frontier for how health might improve: leveraging data that's just out there in boxes, having models generate new insights.

I'm optimistic about a future where there's a third constituency beyond patient and clinician — the scientist, helping advance the frontier of knowledge. AI will accelerate a lot of the bottlenecks in validation, which I think will end up being the real bottleneck, as opposed to proposing new ideas or treatments.

十一、智能的成本：trending to too cheap to meter

You've shared thoughts on the cost of intelligence as an input to medical intelligence coming way down — at some point too cheap to meter.

We spend $5.3+ trillion on healthcare. If it were its own country, it'd be the third largest GDP. It's the biggest part of our economy, the biggest employer (23 million Americans work in healthcare). What impact will your work have on cost?

This is one of the most important ways we can pursue our mission — not only make our models better at the frontier, but make them widely accessible.

One recent update: we released GPT-6 Luna — our current cheapest frontier model on the API. On HealthBench Professional (our latest benchmark of clinician workflows, selected for difficulty), GPT-6 Luna performed better than GPT-5.6 Sol, which was literally our best model a month ago — despite being 34× cheaper.

We've had a couple of those moments in the past year. AI compared to other technologies has been reducing cost at a given level of capability faster than many other technologies.

One bet we have at OpenAI: the cost of health intelligence will plummet at a given level of health intelligence. The level where clinicians and patients can trust it in the care journey is starting to get there. My expectation: once we get close, the cost dramatically reduces — we get a commoditization of health intelligence. We don't want to hoard it; we want everyone to use it.

On overall healthcare spending: I don't think all of that is about health intelligence. Health intelligence hasn't yet had a macro effect on total spend. But in chronic care management, documentation, administration, back-office workflows — there's a lot of money spent that probably doesn't need to be spent that way. We're very optimistic about overall compression of spend over the coming years.

当支付方 AI 遇上医疗方 AI

You saw the New York Times article: provider AIs and payer AIs are fighting. Blue Cross Blue Shield analysis showed respective billing bots and paperwork bots effectively increased spend by a billion dollars. When you're bringing cost of medical intelligence to near zero and you see headlines like that — what do you make of that?

This might be an area with short-term pain around a provider/payer arms race, but in the long run there's no reason this has to exist.

You're entering a world where a lot of visits have ambient intelligence in the room — listening, transcribing. There are clinical notes, AI adjudication of clinical notes. You have a lot of the details needed to adjudicate visits.

The ideal world: providers and payers have a handshake — "here's our ground truth of what happened in this visit, here's all the information, there's no other source." AI helps adjudicate. Maybe a limited appeals process. You don't need this AI arms race. It can be completely avoided. I view that as a short-term distraction.

十二、创业者应该在上面构建什么？

Entrepreneurs building technology in healthcare are watching. As you continue to bring down the cost of medical intelligence to near zero, what should specialist applications be doing — assuming this gets 100× better?

We think about our health impact not directly through products we offer, but through our partners and that last mile of delivering care.

What I'd say to our partners: build on top of models that are really capable, and most importantly, bet that those models will become more capable.

Many people in healthcare are on a spectrum — betting against the models, betting neutrally, or betting with/for the models. Bet on the models getting better. That's probably the most important thing.

Think about ways frontier tech — agents, computer use — will accelerate healthcare, and build toward that future.

A lot of medical care will become more accessible to patients with AI. We talked about the "quarterback" and dissolving barriers. Just being focused on delivering really good quality care, with AI as part of monitoring that care journey — that's a very important part.

十三、程序性照护与机器人

A lot of healthcare spend is procedural — imaging, blood work, examination, surgical intervention. Where does intelligence impact procedural care? Will it be the new bottleneck?

In the short term with procedural care: better targeting when it's needed. AI can provide information for knowing when to seek that kind of care.

The biggest macro factor in the next year or two will just be better proactive, preventative work — so you don't have to go in later and get the procedure, because you made the right moves sooner.

Robotics and care: that's a longer-term question, both from a technology perspective and reimbursement/industry-integration perspective. My expectation: not a next-few-years thing.

十四、展望：ChatGPT 健康的未来

We've covered a lot. As agents and underlying models become increasingly performant, what can we look forward to from ChatGPT health?

Two high-level things:

1. Raising the floor — making trustworthy, reliable health intelligence abundant for all clinicians, users, and patients. Getting to the point where all patients and clinicians feel safer by having AI in the care journey. When your doctor is using ChatGPT, you actually feel safer, and vice versa.

2. Raising the ceiling — ways AI can do things not possible before. The proactive personal health assistant that's part of your care journey, flagging places where you can intervene today to prevent expensive deterioration later. And unlocking the value of existing data stored in boxes, having models generate new insights that benefit patients.

5–10 年后的预测

ChatGPT came out roughly three years ago. Can you give predictions? A feature that feels science fiction today but could be real 5–10 years from now?

Super hard to predict the future these days. But: the thing that might have the most impact on human health in the next 5–10 years is probably newer treatments coming from two things:

  1. AI-guided generation of new targets or molecules that could be interesting for new treatments.
  2. AI-guided prioritization and validation. We're already at a point where the number of molecules and drugs people want to suggest for clinical trials is way more than the number of slots available. Models can help prioritize and run these trials smoother and faster.

In that time frame: improved medicines, more personalized medicines — only possible because you invested in those two pillars.

That is awesome. I'm leaving this conversation even more optimistic than I was before. Karan, thank you so much for coming on the A16Z podcast.

Thank you for having me.

item.description:
## 一、最意外的观察：这场对话里藏着一个"反向AGI叙事"
OpenAI 公开讲"AGI benefits humanity"，但 Karan 在整段访谈里几乎从不谈"替代医生"。相反，他反复提到一个关键数据点——**临床指南渗透到一线医生实践需要 5 到 17 年**。这才是真正令人震撼的点：
> OpenAI 在医疗领域的真实野心，不是"造一个比医生更聪明的AI"，而是**压缩人类已有知识的传播时延**。
换句话说，他们的护城河不是智能的上限，而是智能的"扩散速度"。这颠覆了"AI 医生"的通俗想象——真正的变革不是发明新知识，而是**让 2024 年的共识今天就落地到巴西乡下的全科诊所里**。这是知识考古学意义上的事件，而不是技术奇点。
## 二、跨领域连接：医疗 AI 的"围棋 Move 37"与金融市场的"套利悖论"
Karan 提到他们期待医疗版的"Move 37"——AlphaGo 那步让所有人类顶尖棋手觉得"愚蠢但正确"的棋。但这里有一个他**没有明说的悖论**，值得挑明：
- 围棋的 Move 37 之所以能被识别为"brilliant"，是因为围棋有*

item.title: [Latent Space] The Programmable Data Center — Evan Conrad, SF Compute
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的洞察：Nvidia 的"自我阉割"与中立性溢价

真正让我震惊的不是 SF Compute 在做什么，而是Evan 揭示的一个结构性悖论：这个市场之所以能存在，恰恰是因为所有有能力做它的人都做不了。

Nvidia、CoreWeave、Crusoe、Lambda、Fireworks、Modal——每一家都掌握着做这件事的技术和资源，但他们必须主动放弃才能做。因为一旦下场，他们就失去了做市所必需的"中立性溢价"（neutrality premium）——没有中立性，就没有可信价格，没有可信价格，就没有融资曲线，没有融资曲线，整个行业的资金成本就降不下来。

这让我想起瑞士银行业的发源逻辑：瑞士之所以能成为资产避风港，不是因为它更强大，而是因为它主动放弃了参与欧洲大陆政治博弈的权利。SF Compute 本质上在做的是——成为计算市场的瑞士。"we have to be Switzerland" 这句话不是比喻，是公司的根本架构约束。

更深一层：这揭示了一条规律——最有价值的基础设施位置，往往需要主动"自残"才能获得。Visa 不能自己放贷，交易所不能自营，Switzerland 不能有海军。谁"拥有"得越少，谁的协调能力就越强。

二、跨领域连接：从"牛奶定价"到"锅炉冷却时间"——物理约束如何倒灌进金融

Evan 讲到了一个你几乎在任何金融教材里都看不到的细节：电力市场的订单簿里有一个字段，是关于锅炉冷却时间的。因为你不能瞬时关闭和重启一个火电机组，所以订单结构本身必须把物理世界的热力学迟滞嵌进去。

同样地，GPU 市场里"中断成本"不是一个数字，而是一个关于储存系统（Weka、Vast）、WAN 拓扑、GPU firmware 批次号的多维向量。一个 live inference 工作负载的中断，和一个 batch inference 的中断，不只是价格差异，而是完全不同的物种——因为前者绑定了对终端用户的 SLA 违约金，后者只绑定了一台机器几分钟的闲置。

这指向一个被普遍忽视的真相：算力不是一种商品，而是一个"商品 × 时间形态 × 中断容忍度 × 迁移成本"的张量。SF Compute 的真正技术突破不是撮合引擎，而是张量化的订单簿——它允许买家下一个带有多个约束维度的订单，而不是在一个标准化的 SKU 上下单。

而这里有一个让我意外的类比：这其实是从"证券交易所模式"退回到"大宗商品实物交割模式"。21 世纪的金融演化一直是"标准化、无差别化、纯金融化"——而 Evan 在算力市场做的是反向演化：拒绝过早标准化，拥抱异质性，让流动性在高维度上形成而不是在一个点上塌缩。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：你以为的"算力市场"，其实是"违约金市场"

最深的洞察在于 Evan 那句不经意的话："These are the market for breaking leases"——这是一个毁约市场。

人们误以为 SF Compute 卖的是算力。错。它卖的是毁约权——GPU 持有者违约释放算力的权利，被定价后卖给短期买家。一个月前锁定 3 年期合同的玩家，现在有了优雅退出的机制。

这改变了一切。它意味着 SF Compute 不是在创造需求，它是在创造流动性折扣：有了二级市场，一级市场的买家愿意出更高的价、更长的锁期，因为他们知道可以随时套现。这和房地产"流动性折扣"消失后房价必然上涨的逻辑完全一样。

但真正炸裂的推论是：$40/小时的推理收入 vs. $5-6/小时的 B300 租金，这个 6-8 倍的 gap 不是定价错误，而是流动性折扣还没完全消失。当 SF Compute 的订单簿深度到达某个阈值，这个 gap 必然收敛。换句话说，Evan 不是在观察价格，他是在导致价格。做市商不是中性的，做市商创造了被观察到的"真实价格"。

而最终的跨领域连接：这个故事和 1848 年芝加哥期货交易所的诞生几乎一模一样。谷物从异质的、不可运输的、"每一仓都不同"的实物，演化成标准化的 1 号春小麦、2 号硬红冬小麦。中间经历了什么？不是技术突破，而是物理交割网络（铁路、仓储、分级制度）成熟后，一个独立、不自营的清算中介出现。

SF Compute 正在重走这条路。而历史告诉我们：最终攫取大部分价值的，不是种小麦的农民、不是铁路公司、不是面包厂——而是那个独立的清算所。

📝 转录文本

开场：Nvidia 为什么做不了超算市场？

Nvidia's obviously like the 800-pound gorilla in the room. Why don't they — Why didn't they make a supercomputer?

So our impression is that Nvidia can't make it, but benefits tremendously from it existing. The reason why they can't make it is because they would then not be independent enough for people to trade on it.

Anyway, Evan, welcome back to AI Space. Welcome back to AIE. Actually, first time at AIE?

I think so, yeah.

This is very special one because I feel like you have been working on compute trading, compute markets for a while. Now it's like feeling of the moment.

Yeah.

Jump basically announced that they are getting into compute markets, which is why I'm excited to sort of cluster people. You met Oliver from Semi Analysis, who is basically initiating coverage on compute markets. This is my read on this. So people are going to watch your talk — I think it's a very good explanation of both your origin story and why you need to exist and what the hard problems you work on. Done in a very simple engaging manner. I'm very jealous of your writing skills, cuz you showed the flyer that you showed at NeurIPS. It was like — it's pretty straightforward and like simple and it's good.

Yeah. So anyway, congrats.

Thank you. I appreciate that. And also congrats on AIE. It seems to — y'all are rolling.

We're rolling. I just came back from the site tour for next year's AIE.

Give me like a hint.

At Javits Center. It's the same place they do Comic-Con.

Okay, wow. Wow. Damn.

But I think the finance focus is really hitting for folks. So we're going to try to split up — like, this is — here we just lump everything in finance. Like, your finance, their finance, like insurance is finance. But they're all super different. So we'll probably break out things more minutely in future, because people want to go deep on hedge fund stuff or banking or personal wealth.

Yeah, especially in in New York.

Yeah, like Anthropic was like, "Yeah, we're all about RIAs right now." RIAs — registered investment advisors. So different from you. [laughter]

Yeah, no, no, I'm aware of this.

SF Compute 两年来的演进：从转租到完整云栈

Okay, so for listeners who don't know, we did a podcast 2 years ago where you talked about where SF Compute was. Today you're much more in this sort of physical settlements. You talk about your back fabric — or what do you call it?

The backplane.

Backplane — which obviously takes a lot of hardcore engineering stuff. Can you give a status update on where is SF Compute versus listeners who last heard you on a podcast 2 years ago?

So when we started, we were this company called Junnar, and then we were just trying to sublease our cluster. We started there in the technical stack. A way to think about it is: it's like you're in a hotel and you're trying to sell that hotel room. And then somebody asks you, "Hey, like, are you going to clean my room?" And then you say, "Oh, I guess I probably also need the hotel room as well, or I need the cleaning closet." So you go get access to the cleaning closet. And then they want room service, and so you get access to the kitchen. And then they want security, and so you get access to the security closet, and you get this, and you do that, and you do this. And at a certain point, you're just running the whole hotel.

The moment you're running the whole hotel, you say, "Oh, wait a second. Instead, my supplier on this market is somebody that looks closer to a fund — or a cloud that has access, in our case, a cloud that has access to the data center — and we're going to level up." So what we spent the last several years doing is building the entire operating capacity of a cloud, in order to offer, in order to actually deliver, the compute at a reliable level.

什么是 Physical Settlement？

We call that physical settlement. We're taking a term from the futures market — from other markets. In oil or soybeans or something, physical settlement means you get delivered the oil and the soybeans. But in some markets, like in oil and also in power, there's like a delivery network. In oil, you have to have pipelines. If you would like the oil to be delivered to you, there has to be a way for it to get to you.

And for people interested in financial history: during COVID, oil went negative because — "So like, I will pay you to take oil from me, because it is sitting there in the port and I can't pay for this. So I will pay you to take my oil." That is the weirdness of physical settlement.

Yes. There's a bunch of weirdnesses like this in other markets as well. So in the power markets and the grid, there's parts of the orders that you fill out — the buyers and sellers — that are there because the boiler takes a while to cool off. You can stop the boiler and then you can start it back up again within some period of time, and so that has to get factored into the order book.

This Junnar thing is the same thing that happens in computer markets. So we co-designed physical settlement and the order book at the same time, and that meant that we get to actually handle the real constraints of compute, which might include something like: "Oh, I'm okay with being interrupted, but only if there's storage on the thing that I can recover from really quickly." Very similar types of problems.

市场深度与流动性：5% 容量，但高度集中

Yeah. So people can refer to your talk and you've done a couple other podcasts already. I want to be like the sort of 201 level instead of the 101 level — and also because I have been a derivatives trader, so I can give people a bit more detail that you normally don't get into.

Okay.

So for example — well, how mature or deep or liquid is the compute market today?

Not very mature or deep or liquid. So, what we've been doing is: first we had to go get a bunch of supply online in the first place, which just takes a while, and then we had to build the entire platform in order to do this. We just now got that working, and so now we move capacity over onto the order book, which makes it liquid.

5% of our total capacity is on the order book, and we're consistently moving more and more, and then we're bringing on more capacity that's all on the order book. The nice part is that — maybe I should have said — the volume on the actual order book is small, but the liquidity on the order book is high. So for that small amount of capacity that you have, you have very concentrated liquidity.

A sort of standard metric I would say for someone who is using this: a customer who buys capacity from us, and they spend $100 to buy that capacity, will make back $25 on average from selling it back to somebody else. That's the number — this is one of the metrics that we try to track — because we want the liquidity to be useful to the commercial participant. You can measure liquidity in a bunch of different ways. You can say, "Oh, I just want tons of makers or something." You can measure it in high-minded ways. We try to measure it by: "Is this solving the problem for the customer?"

合约标准化：为什么还做不到？

Got it. So last time we talked as well, there was a lot of conversation about standardizing the contracts — talking with the CFTC or whatever. What's the status on those things?

I think standardizing the contracts in general is still pretty far away. What we were trying to do at the time — basically what we learned over the last several years was: we just needed to operate the whole thing, otherwise you cannot standardize the thing. To get closer to something that can be standardized, you first need to make all the operations of the thing the same.

To give an example of what can be different: a single operator can offer two different types of virtual machines. One type of virtual machine might have a 40% performance degradation versus another type of virtual machine. And 40% is a lot.

When you say performance degradation, are you talking like MFU type things, or like amount of burning that you've experienced?

In this particular case, I'm talking about GPU kernel launches and how long it takes for that to happen, which is a process that happens quite frequently when you're doing either training or inference. The end result is that you get a worse MFU, but like —

Is the intermediate level —

Intermediate level, basically.

商品等级的类比

So what I'm trying to — for anyone who's traded commodities before, there's different grades of commodity, right? It's not oil, it's light sweet crude versus like whatever exactly the opposite of light sweet crude is. Or it's like corn level A or corn B or whatever. And so like people are trying to — well, you have to establish the equivalents of those things. And I'm wondering if they have been established.

So what we did instead was we created an order book that had multiple different constraints, and you can say, "I want to have something that's between this and that. It runs from this time to this time. It's like X to Y." It's a bunch of different properties that you can attach to your order, and then we match that against sell orders that have those properties in a big matching engine.

The reason why we did it this way is: it allows us to generate liquidity without having to standardize before you know what the technology can do. Because the technology was shifting so quickly, we wanted to basically be able to do that. The trade-off is that you have less concentrated liquidity, and so the prices are going to have — there's going to be more spreads between the buy and the sell.

It sucks. Yeah. But on the other hand, it means there's lots of arbitrage to make if you can do that correctly. So if you have a product that can use lots of different types of capacity, then you might really like SF Compute, because you will be able to use lots of different types of capacity and you'll make more money. You can take the spread.

订单维度：什么属性真正重要？

Okay. What dimensions matter in this grid of things?

A bunch of different things. One is categories like: is there a workload running on it right now, or is it capacity in the future? Capacity right now — in order for you to sell that, you have to interrupt your current workload. So you have to think: do I care if my current workload is interrupted or not?

Capacity that's sold starting a month from now — you can buy and sell that all the time. You get liquidity on that really easily. There is some concern like "Oh no, will I have capacity next month?" but it's very different than if you're interrupting a workload right now.

中断方式的差异

The way that the interruption happens matters. An example is: if you're on a cluster and the cluster doesn't have as amazing storage as you want it to have. An example is: do you have a Weka or Vast system under the hood? Do you offer that, and what's the size of that? This changes how you respond to being preempted or removed off the cluster.

Meanwhile, the location of that storage matters. If you're able to move that data from one cluster to another quickly, then maybe you might be able to spread across multiple different clusters. You can be interrupted over here and then pop back up over there. To make that work, you also need a fast transit path between one cluster and another. Typically this is implemented with a WAN, but most of these clusters don't necessarily have a wide area network.

Yeah, a wide area network — basically cables that connect the clusters together. A private internet is another way to think about it. A lot of clusters that are being spun up today — they're not attached to — traditional CPU clusters were next to the customer for latency reasons. In GPUs, they're next to the power. Wherever — like, you put the data center next to the power rather than next to the customer. This means that a lot of stuff is getting put in places that previously they weren't expecting data centers there. And so you may not have as excellent of a transit path from one to the other. So this starts to matter.

芯片批次：早期产品的瑕疵

Other examples are weird — where we theoretically support but don't actually. This is a thing that we're thinking about but haven't done basically. The early GB200s broke. The early H100s broke. If you were buying H100s or you were buying GB200s, you might really want the ones that were deployed after a certain time, because you're not getting the first GB1s off the rack. If you're a super sophisticated customer, you may be willing to pay more for that.

Oh, so it's about what cohort they were produced and they get better over time?

Like the first ones off the rack maybe had some faults or some problem. If you were the ones who got the first ones from the first shipment of them, then yeah, they would be broken in some way.

I assume that sort of process is like, look, there's defects everywhere. It just happens, right? And so you get a new shipment from TSMC and you just kind of run your tests and you figure out which ones are bad and you throw them out. Isn't that how it works? I didn't know about this element of cohorting — where let's say Q4 2026 B300s are way worse than 2027 B300s.

Yeah, so [laughter] — I'll give an example. You're describing burn-in. When you get a cluster, what a good cloud does is it tries to kill all the GPUs before they ever get in the hands of the customer. And then the GPUs that are broken or the nodes that are broken, you get RMA'd. You basically go and replace them. You return it and you get a new one — there's a lead time to that, but whatever, you'll get some back. And then the customer never has to experience this.

The thing I'm referring to is that in early H100s, there were firmware bugs that may not even be related to — they may not be Nvidia. They might be like: Supermicro has a firmware bug in the box that you bought. And it applies to all of them. And it doesn't matter — the solution to that was you need to get them to update their firmware, or they need to ship a new thing in every new box.

Yeah. Or Cornelis had this for the B200s that we got. And then you had to use DevCloud to go fix it.

Yes, correct. So different types of problems like this can happen.

时间维度：从 1 小时到 5 年的远期曲线

Interesting. Okay — so I want people to understand the shape of this market. You mentioned preemption, and we talked about spot instances and how the analogy is. And then there's also booking a month out. How far out do these markets go, and is real-time or sort of preemption more interesting to you versus being further further out?

To answer your first question: 3 to 5 years.

Wow. Month by month or quarter by quarter?

Are you asking how the cash flow works?

The contracts. Like the futures contracts, right? Again — I'm a former contracts derivatives trader. In the market itself, in the broader market.

Clusters are financed 3 to 5 years. The payments are over that period of time. There's also blocks of capacity in our order book which can extend any arbitrary time. There's some stuff that we have to do for the cash flow on that. Right now what we do is we just ask people to pay entirely up front for a block. We don't ask them to do that for a lease, for a longer-term contract. This gets into something that I definitely need a whiteboard to explain.

You had another question I was about to answer — I forgot what it was.

Do you want real-time or do you want — what's more interesting to you, real-time or longer out?

We care more about longer out, because we're trying to build a forwards curve that has a lot of liquidity on it. These are kind of the same thing and kind of not. What we do is — say you can buy an hour out, you can buy right now to the next hour. Or you can buy right now to the next 3 years, and anywhere in between.

That's wild.

I know. Or finer, technically.

批处理 vs. 实时推理的定价差异

There's a certain difference that happens that's dependent for each customer. If I have a workload that is batch inference, basically — where I can be interrupted at any point, I don't really care — then my ability to be cut off is probably: "I need an hour of time to know that I'm going to be cut off, and then I'm good." Or I can even be notified in a minute or two.

But if I have live inference customers who are expecting me to be online, then you can interrupt me, but in a month. Maybe 2 months, maybe 3 months. And then I can adapt to that capacity over that period of time. But you cannot interrupt me in a minute.

Those two things are priced differently. The reason why they're priced differently is: what is the price you would pay in order to interrupt your batch job? It's very different than the price you would pay to interrupt your live job. If you have a live job, you are probably paying an SLA when you break for your customer. Does that make sense?

这其实是毁约市场

Yeah, I see. So this is actually the market for breaking leases.

These are the market for breaking leases, basically. And then there's also the market for future leases.

Oh, I thought this was like a subletting situation. This is like — oh, the lease break.

One way to think about it is: in power markets, there's actually two markets. There's the day-ahead market, and there's the live market. Compute kind of has the same thing — where it has capacity that is coming online, or capacity that's about to arrive to you, and then capacity that is currently in use. And these have different price dynamics.

期限结构：Backwardation 还是 Contango？

Okay, interesting. Backwardation or contango?

[laughter] Backwardation or contango?

So is compute further out priced higher than spot, or lower than spot? Is compute further out priced — does it go like this, or does it go like that over 1-year out, 2-year out?

Oh, this is an — both at different —

I find it fascinating that you don't know.

Yeah, I mean, both — it depends on who you are. I'll make the case — wait, so you're asking is compute sold right now, unit of compute today, maybe not today, maybe a month out versus 1-year out versus 2-year out. Is that curve going up or going down?

We see like a hump.

Oh my god. Explain.

牛奶类比：临期算力必须打折

Like, I think this will make intuitive sense. It's basically like: if I have milk, and it is about to expire, I will lower the price on it. That's basically what we see.

So it's the end of the lease cycle, basically, right?

Well, we're more saying: if there's a block of compute, and it's approaching now, it can't be sold in the past, and so it has to drop its price in order to clear at some price. Initially, you see this drop — where stuff that's sold right now, anything that's on the market right now, is something that hasn't been sold, and so therefore the price will drop. And then it goes up to where it wants to be.

Maybe compute in the future is worth less because people don't want — like, people would like the compute now, and so they're sort of paying for the shorter lead time. And they pay less for the compute that's off in the future. This is what I think a normal healthy curve looks like.

B300 的巨大定价错配

The place where I'm like, "Oh man, no shit" — is that right now if you took a B300 and you tried to run inference on it, you can make $40 an hour or so selling that.

Any model?

Any model, basically. So that's if you use it at 100%, and maybe if you only have like 50% utilization or something, so like $25 an hour.

Yeah. So $25 an hour. Meanwhile, you can buy B300s at like $5 to $6 an hour. One of these numbers has to change.

Yeah. It's a huge overcharge.

It's a huge overcharge.

You mentioned this in your talks a lot.

Yeah. So a bunch of people are basically looking at this and thinking: if I think prices are going to go up, I might be willing to pay more than what I previously thought in the future — because I might think, "Okay, I can buy a five right now, but if I can't buy any more, then maybe I will be willing to buy even more in the future just to lock it in if it's going to come online later." So we see the other side as well. Kind of depends on who you are.

芯片世代、SKU 与"命名查询"

Cool. So — I really want to make super clear on this. Do you care about the different generations of chips? Or do you just care about overall flops and you spread them among whatever chips you want?

We care about different generations of chips because —

You care. I guess, do your customers care?

Yes.

Right. Oh wait, when you say different generation chips, do you mean like —

Like B300 generation. Or like even AMD or whatever, right?

Yes, I think people totally care about the generation of chips. Part of this is because of things like VRAM. Part of this is because of larger NVLink domains, and things like that.

So there's just no way to abstract all this to some generalized unit of compute that you can sort of mush around and whatever you like.

I think — when you were saying oil — even oil isn't oil. Oil is actually just a bunch of different types of oil.

Yeah, like jet fuel or car fuel or whatever.

I think it's the same thing. You're going to get a bunch of different types.

It is, but you have oil refineries — effectively black boxes you can put oil in and get whatever out. If compute is so heterogeneous, I guess the word is: you just have to expose the underlying complexity to your end customer, which is bad for you as a market maker. Like, you want to identify the one choke point — or like, I don't know what the better word for choke point is — the Schelling point, where everyone agrees "Okay, this is kind of the standard and we'll all agree to this standard, and it'll be somewhat inefficient."

Maybe. [laughter]

维度削减与可定义 SKU

So we've been able to reduce the problems to a certain level.

Yeah, it's like your job is dimensional reduction or all that.

We reduce a lot of the dimensions, but nonetheless there are still dimensions. They can still exist.

Do you know how many SKUs you have?

So — [laughter]

Like 5 × 100 × 5,000, that equals I don't know. What's —

We actually made SKUs a concept — the goal is to make it so that somebody else can make their own SKU. So if I want to buy Blackwells, I can say "I'm willing to buy Blackwells at $6 an hour or less." And you can match me against GB300s or you can match me against B300s, and I don't care which Blackwell, as long as it's less than $6 an hour.

But you just said you care about memory and other stuff.

Totally, but not every customer does. Some customers can just work on Blackwells, whatever it is. Some customers are super hyper-specific and they need this exact thing — and they're going to pay more for that, because the market's going to charge them more.

Okay.

That's what we do.

So people use your APIs to programmatically define what they want, and then that matches with whatever composition of sellers they might be able to fulfill.

Yes. With the caveat that having a named query is a new thing we're doing. But the query system as a concept is how the order book works right now.

Physical Settlement 的本质论

Okay. Interesting. All right. I think that's a lot of nitty-gritty. Is there anything about — I guess that you want to educate people on, whether it's financial people or engineers, about the state of the compute trading market as you've developed it? Because effectively you guys are defining it.

Mainly just the requirement for physical settlement. We spent 3 years learning why you need physical settlement. [laughter] Our entire conversation today is that these things are not as fungible as you think. We're going to try and make them fungible. That's the industry's job to do that. But without that, you run a lot of risks.

If you try to build too much financialization before the industry has had time to build out the physical settlement, then I think what you have is a market that's very easy to manipulate, and a market that has a lot of basis risk, where the price you may be hedging against actually has nothing to do with the price that you can actually buy the capacity for.

CDS 市场的教训

Yeah. So for listeners — we talked about this briefly last time, but people are often shocked to find out that let's say the market for credit default swaps is 12 times the size of the bonds that they insure. Or like, the markets for mortgage reinsurance are larger than the underlying physical settlement. So that's why physical versus cash settled.

Yeah. And basically cash settlements are exactly the kind of side bet that you see in The Big Short — where they may or may not have anything to do with the underlying thing itself, and may be used as a proxy for overall other stuff. And you don't want that to go out of control.

Yes. To be clear, we think cash settlement as a future concept is a great idea. We just think it should be derived from physical settlement. Because, as you said, it's a side bet. It would be kind of like if you made a cash settlement future before you made physical settlement — which I think people are kind of doing already.

Not yet totally. People are trying to make cash settlement before you make the physical settlement.

Do that for all sorts of things, including startup stock, right? Like you can buy and sell a made-up share of OpenAI, but it's nothing to do with the actual share.

Yes. [laughter] And lots of those go very poorly. It would be bad if you started selling the derivative on a stock that doesn't exist yet.

LIBOR 的操纵风险

Well, so — I used to be a currency trader, right? And interest rates as well. One thing we do is you have a board that gets together and says: "This is the London Interbank Offered Rate, LIBOR, and we all agree this is the monthly fixing and we all trade to that fixing." Is that even meaningful at some point 3 years from now?

So, critically, LIBOR was manipulated.

Yes. 12 banks.

Yes. Our concern is there's a very similar problem, where you can manipulate an index. Our impression of why you can manipulate that index is because a lot of the indexes are based on a very small amount of data that has not a lot of correlation with the actual price of buying a new reserve contract. That's what we're concerned about.

生态系统：Silicon Data、Jump、Semi Analysis

[laughter] Okay. Interesting. All right — I think that's the rough state of things. I think the other part is: you talked with Oliver, and you're doing an event with Jump, and you're friends with Silicon Data. What are you learning from all these other players? Who are the major players that you would want to call out as doing interesting things?

Ooh. So, we're big fans of Silicon Data and Compute Change. I think they were also very early to this, and I think they are doing a reasonable shot at the path that we think we'll likely end up being partners with.

And can you distinguish your different paths?

The general gist is: they're doing cash settlement, we're doing physical settlement. We think both can exist and should exist, and that they're sort of mutually beneficial to each other. So totally fine. I think they are one of the earliest in the space, and I think they very clearly took the bet well before anybody else did, and I think that's very honorable to do.

Semi Analysis — Jump. Are these other players emerging? You were my first introduction to this, and then I see all these other guys coming in, and I'm like, "Okay, something's happening here." I don't know the landscape as clearly as you do.

The categories of folks that we've seen: there's folks that are trying to set better standards. Semi Analysis I think is working to try and create better standards. There's folks that are trying to do residual value insurance, and so on. There's a number of different companies in the space. I don't know any of them super well, but I know this is a concept, and I think that's important. There are folks that are trying to do deposit lending — where they'll front your credit risk for the cloud. There's an ecosystem of companies that are forming around: how do we resolve the financial bottlenecks of compute? And it is cool to see.

I think effectively what you want in this ecosystem is buyers and sellers, you want an analyst, you want — we said insurance — what's the —

Residual value insurance.

Residual. And you want this healthy ecosystem out there. But obviously you guys are owning the problem of physical settlement, which is really interesting.

技术栈：没有硬件的"云"

Okay, so we can go into the hard tech side, because obviously you are also hiring for extremely cracked engineers. Describe your stack.

We do all the things the cloud does without being the cloud. We don't own the hardware. The reason why we don't own the hardware is because if we did, we would be able to manipulate the forwards market. So we have to be Switzerland — we have to be independent — which creates a lot of sort of strange things about the company.

But in order to do physical settlement, you have to do site visits. You have to visit the data center. You have to design the bill of materials and ensure that — you have to basically do supply chain consulting, where you have relationships with different OEMs that ensure that things get delivered on time. Then you have to do cluster architecture, so you're sort of designing the cluster itself. Then you're rolling out racks, or you're working with partners to roll out racks and then supervising that.

Then you're doing backplane management, so you're taking over the PDUs and the switches and the DPUs and UFM and BMC — operating a harness around the nodes that you're settling.

You as SF Compute employees?

Yeah.

Wow. All right. So when you buy a node from a cloud, there's the bare metal, but there's all this around the bare metal. In order to make that bare metal node work, you have to operate everything else.

Because I just like — traditionally the job of the data center is to extract some of this away from you.

Yeah. We're the ones that do that.

"Palantir for Compute"

Okay. [laughter] All right. But you're not in the data center business. You're not the Equinixes of the world.

We're not in the data center business, sort of. What we do work with is — we offer supercomputing as a service.

What this means is folks come to us and say, "I've got X" — where X is "I've got X megawatts here." Maybe sometimes they mean, "I've got a data center that I would like to turn into a GPU cluster." My options are: I could sell the GPU cluster, or I could sell the data center to somebody, or I could become the cloud. And then we go to them and say, "Great. We will turn you into the cloud — we're the supercomputing part, you're the data center cloud. Let's partner together and then we will sell and all make money."

Sometimes it's people who have something that could turn into a data center, in which case we're going to basically project manage that up to the layer. We will work with those folks to turn their powered land or whatever they have into a data center by working with partners, and then we take over at the supercomputing part. This requires us to have some sort of data center expertise in-house, but we don't self-perform builds.

Yeah, so it's somewhat modular because you have different scenarios you need to deploy under.

Someone once described us as like "Palantir for compute" [laughter] — because each time it's this new rodeo. We deeply partner with folks on both sides.

全球部署与主权算力

Yeah. And primarily the US?

Primarily the US, but we operate around the world.

Yeah. At some point does SF Compute become a misnomer?

[laughter] So, we're deploying clusters all around the world, and when we do that, we're working with people who themselves are trying to be clouds all around the world. They look like sovereign compute players. Our pitch to sovereign compute is amazing: "Let's help you set up a cloud in your own country, and we will bring the San Francisco off-take. We'll bring the San Francisco expertise. We'll set up the clusters. That's our whole business. We're going to make it financeable."

Who are your biggest announced partners that you can name?

Nobody I can name basically. We will have some announcements in a week or two that we expect to come on.

Yeah. All things sort of —

Sure, sure. Good luck. No, I mean, I think this is really interesting for every country who's investing in sovereign AI to figure this out. And it's interesting that SF is still sort of that brand name — and that is very marketable.

为什么 Nvidia、CoreWeave、Lambda 都做不了？

So I think one of the interesting things is just thinking through this market. Nvidia is obviously like the 800-lb gorilla in the room. Why didn't they make SF Compute? Again, I know the answer's going to be market manipulation — but let's just really get into the incentives of the multiple players.

So our impression is that Nvidia can't make it, but benefits tremendously from it existing. The reason why they can't make it is because they would then not be independent enough for people to trade on it. If you don't trade on it, then you don't have enough liquidity for lenders to finance against the forwards market.

This is also why Crusoe and CoreWeave and Lambda — why the hyperscalers can't make it — why Baseten and Fireworks and Modal can't make it. Because they have too much demand on that side.

This is the thing that benefits the entire industry because it makes the financing costs go down. But nobody can make it unless they give up the ability to do all the big inference money and all the big cloud deals. You have to kill your business in order to make this. That's why nobody does it.

It's structurally they're not set up to do that. And you're basically reducing friction — and that's all your revenue.

里程碑与新能力：可编程数据中心

You've announced some benchmark — some milestones. Actually, I forgot to say that up front. Can you repeat what they are and take a victory lap a little bit?

We closed several hundred million dollars of volume. We have a significant number of new clusters on the way. And then the things that I think I'm most excited about is: we've shipped a whole bunch of new features that make SF Compute very viable for platform-as-a-service companies.

An example: we allow customers to subdivide their InfiniBand fabric without having to ask us. Many clouds, when you go to buy them, they will give you one InfiniBand fabric. And then if you want to redraw the lines of that InfiniBand fabric, you need to contact them, and they will then do something for you. We now can do that on the fly for customers, which I think is really great — because it interfaces with the market really well, where you want to be able to redraw things in order to scale up and down your clusters.

Would you describe this as: you're virtualizing the data center and making it programmable?

Yeah, we're virtualizing data center and making it programmable. All the stuff that you would have gotten if you had owned the hardware, we're trying to virtualize that — which I think is exciting to us.

It's funny — like, the last time this happened was like the cloud. [laughter] Which is really cool.

行动号召

And then, finally — I think, what is your call to action for people? Is it engineers? Is it like "give me your supply"? What is it?

If you would like to own a GPU cluster, and you want the residual value from it, you want to have it for your portfolio — we would love to work with you in order to build that GPU cluster. We will take over, and we will do the supercomputing portions of that, and ensure the things go right. We own the SLA. And then if it turns out that was a bad idea, that you need out of that cluster, we can immediately sell that cluster to somebody else, so it doesn't hit your balance sheet.

Very simple pitch. Well, thank you so much for your time. You're doing a great service to the industry, and I just am happy to be your friend.

I appreciate it.

All right. That's it.

[music]

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的洞察：Nvidia 的"自我阉割"与中立性溢价
真正让我震惊的不是 SF Compute 在做什么，而是**Evan 揭示的一个结构性悖论：这个市场之所以能存在，恰恰是因为所有有能力做它的人都做不了**。
Nvidia、CoreWeave、Crusoe、Lambda、Fireworks、Modal——每一家都掌握着做这件事的技术和资源，但他们必须**主动放弃**才能做。因为一旦下场，他们就失去了做市所必需的"中立性溢价"（neutrality premium）——没有中立性，就没有可信价格，没有可信价格，就没有融资曲线，没有融资曲线，整个行业的资金成本就降不下来。
这让我想起**瑞士银行业的发源逻辑**：瑞士之所以能成为资产避风港，不是因为它更强大，而是因为它主动放弃了参与欧洲大陆政治博弈的权利。SF Compute 本质上在做的是——**成为计算市场的瑞士**。"we have to be Switzerland" 这句话不是比喻，是公司的根本架构约束。
更深一层：这揭示了一条规律——**最有价值的基础设施位置，往往需要主动"自残"才能获得**。Visa

item.title: [Business of Sport] Why Domestic Cricket Critics Are Missing the Bigger Picture | Warwickshire CEO
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、酒店即板球：£4700万的"反向补贴机制"

Stuart Cain 最诚实的一句话被埋在中段："Trust me, I'm not" interested in being a hotel。这句自嘲背后藏着一个被观众普遍误读的商业模型——Edgbaston 的酒店投资不是地产项目，而是板球的"隐藏税收"。它不是靠板球养出的利润去扩张酒店，而是反过来：用酒店去反哺一个本质上结构性亏损的 Red Ball 核心产品。

这与大学体育系的"耐克合约 + 校园地产"模式同构，也与欧洲百年剧院靠咖啡厅和会议租赁养话剧的逻辑完全一致。真正令人意外的是：Cain 承认开 Edgbaston 一天要烧 7.5–10 万英镑，而 Worcester 开新路球场几乎不花钱——规模在这里不是优势，而是债务。大球场必须"跑得更快才能站着不动"（run harder to stand still），这颠覆了所有"规模经济"的直觉。

二、板球是唯一把"产品生命周期"倒置的运动

这段访谈最打破常规的洞见不是 Cain 说的，而是他无意间描绘出的一个结构：Phoenix（儿童/家庭）→ Blast（大学与社交饮酒）→ 50-over（成熟期）→ County Championship（退休/半退休）。他本人用了红酒的类比。

但这意味着什么？几乎所有其他职业体育（足球、橄榄球、NBA）都在卖"部落忠诚"——锁定你 7 岁，希望你 70 岁还在穿同一件球衣。板球则承认同一个人在不同人生阶段应该消费不同的"产品 SKU"。这与消费品行业的"消费升级阶梯"（啤酒 → 葡萄酒 → 威士忌 → 陈年酒）、以及奢侈品集团的"品牌金字塔"（LVMH 从香水到高定）完全同构。

真正惊人的是跨领域连接——板球可能是第一项把自己重构为"品牌组合"（brand portfolio）而非"单一品牌"的主流运动。所以 Cain 说他们专门从零售餐饮业挖营销人才，而不是传统体育营销人员。这是一个范式转移的信号。

三、郡锦标赛的"亏损领导者悖论"与体育城市化的拐点

Cain 回答"为什么还要搞郡锦标赛"时的真实逻辑，与好莱坞独立电影经济、F1 的 F2/F3 喂养系列、NBA 发展联盟是同一个长尾产业链结构：最不赚钱的格式制造最值钱的资产（测试队球员 → 天空体育愿意付的转播费 → 整个生态的现金流）。

但真正隐秘的洞见藏在他引用 Neil Rimmer 的那段：体育场正在取代商业园和购物中心，成为新一代城市更新的核心催化剂。伦敦奥林匹克公园、热刺北伦敦、埃弗顿码头、曼城、维拉公园、Edgbaston、Nighthead 的 Sports Quarter——这不是巧合，而是一个后购物时代的城市治理拐点。

购物中心作为"公共空间"的时代结束了（亚马逊干掉了它），人们重新需要仪式性聚集场所，而体育场是少数能同时提供食物、娱乐、身份认同和社区感的空间。Cain 把 Edgbaston 从"六英尺砖墙围起来的 Willy Wonka 工厂"改造成社区中心的做法，本质上是在重新定义体育场作为公共基础设施的角色——这比他说的"多样性"和"社区外展"要深远得多。

四、一个被忽视的制度趋同：会员制 ≈ 德甲 50+1

Cain 把板球的会员所有权模式比作德甲，这个类比值得停下来想一下。越古老的运动项目（板球 1850s、德国足球、英格兰赛马），越倾向于分布式治理；越新兴的职业化运动，越向高净值个人所有者倾斜。这与互联网从去中心化（1990s）走向平台垄断（2020s）的轨迹正好相反。

这暗示：成熟治理结构不是终局，而是一个钟摆。板球可能正在示范一种"后私有化"的所有权模型——既有会员制的合法性，又通过 The Hundred 的 51% 控股安排释放了资本流动性。这个模型可能比英超的沙特/美国私募模式更有长期韧性。
